text:
Over the weekend, the Massachusetts Lottery shared a picture of Ariel Velasquez-Morales smiling gently as he gripped an oversized check for US$1 million in winnings. On social media, commenters congratulated him, with one person writing they hoped he would be able to “make any dreams come true.”

But Velasquez-Morales was arrested Tuesday by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in East Boston, the same neighborhood where he bought the $10 winning scratch-off ticket from a local market.

He now faces deportation as ICE says the Salvadoran national has been in the country illegally for more than a decade.

“Looks like his luck ran out,” said ICE Assistant Director of Public Affairs Micah Bock in a release announcing the arrest.

It is unclear whether the publication of his lottery winnings attracted ICE’s attention. ICE declined to answer questions from CNN about what led to the arrest or where Velasquez-Morales is being detained.

Velasquez-Morales illegally entered the United States in 2013, during the Obama administration, in the Rio Grande Valley in Texas. Border Patrol agents issued him a notice to appear before an immigration judge, and he was released into the country with a list of free legal service providers, the agency said.

“A Department of Justice immigration judge ordered Velasquez-Morales removed in 2014, but he illegally remained in the country,” the ICE release said.

He will remain in ICE custody pending his removal from the U.S.. CNN has been unable to determine whether he has legal representation.

U.S. President Donald Trump has overseen a massive immigration crackdown after promising to lead the largest deportation operation in U.S. history. In his second term, arrests have shifted away from the border and focused more on the interior of the country, where aggressive tactics have become a hallmark of ICE’s ramped-up detention efforts.

By July 2026, there were nearly 66,000 detainees in ICE custody, an increase of nearly 70 per cent from the total detained when Trump took office the year prior.

But after a Republican wipeout in the midterms, Trump has publicly questioned whether the tactics were too hard-line and unpopular. It remains to be seen, though, whether he is considering significant changes to his immigration policies.

“Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the United States and will be removed as quickly as possible,” ICE said in its release on Velasquez-Morales. “Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin’s leadership, ICE is delivering on its mission to enforce our nation’s immigration laws, restore accountability and protect American communities.”

Velasquez-Morales was playing the lottery’s “$2,000,000 50X Cashword,” in which players scratch cards resembling crossword puzzles to try to reveal complete words. It was the first puzzle he had scratched, the lottery said, and he matched 11 words.

He chose to accept his winnings in cash, which would give him a one-time lump sum of $650,000 before taxes, according to ICE. It is not clear what will happen to his winnings.

Massachusetts lottery participants do not need to be legal residents of the state to play, but they must be 21 or older and be located in the state at the time they purchase or play.

CNN has sought comment from the Massachusetts State Lottery Commission.

title: What so many people got wrong about the Kilmar Abrego Garcia case - Reason Magazine
authors: Billy Binion, Christian Britschgi, Agustina Vergara Cid, Charles Oliver, Veronique de Rugy, Meagan O'Rourke
description:
Who is Kilmar Abrego Garcia?
So why was Abrego Garcia still here until just this week?
This was in August 2025; Abrego Garcia said he was willing to go.
This is relevant here, because the African countries the Trump administration set its sights on for Abrego Garcia—Uganda, Eswatini, and Ghana—did not agree.
Put differently, Abrego Garcia could have been gone long ago.
text:
Who is Kilmar Abrego Garcia? For the last year and a half, that question has animated the fight over the Trump administration's approach to immigration. Is he most accurately a "Maryland man" whose American wife, family, and work grounded him in the community? Or is he merely an illegal immigrant whose removal from the country was long overdue?

As of today, he is technically neither. The Salvadoran national is now a tourist in Madrid, having just self-deported to Spain.

His departure from the U.S. caps off a saga that became a microcosm for the immigration debate. It was, in some ways, an apt case for that. But often not in the way people thought.

Abrego Garcia catapulted to a subject of national discussion and derision in March 2025 after the government deported him to CECOT, the notorious megaprison in El Salvador. This was complicated, most notably because a court had granted him a withholding of removal to that very country. (Abrego Garcia came to the U.S. illegally in 2012 at 16 years old because, he says, the Barrio 18 gang had threatened him and his family.)

His deportation was only the first domino. The Trump administration subsequently said it had sent him to El Salvador as the result of an "administrative error." In turn, the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland ruled that the executive branch was obligated to "facilitate" Abrego Garcia's return, which the Supreme Court affirmed unanimously.

After many protestations, the administration facilitated that return in June of the same year. So why was Abrego Garcia still here until just this week? The answer to that question does tell you something, yet it is also where this controversy has been the most confused.

When Abrego Garcia arrived back in the U.S., the Department of Justice brought a criminal indictment against him for allegedly participating in a scheme to transport undocumented immigrants. "We got him out of here," Todd Blanche, then the deputy attorney general, told Fox News' Laura Ingraham in June 2025. "And a judge in Maryland and many members of Congress…questioned that decision" to deport him. So the government "started…investigating him."

Wrapped up among those charges was an offer: The government had solicited Costa Rica to accept Abrego Garcia, and the country—which has a standing agreement with the U.S. to take deportees who cannot go to their home countries—had accepted. This was in August 2025; Abrego Garcia said he was willing to go.

But that proposition came with a catch. He would need to plead guilty in the criminal case, something he refused to do, as he maintains his innocence. When the Trump administration was not able to extract that win—a P.R. victory would have been helpful after it was forced to bring him back from El Salvador—it set out on a legal odyssey to instead deport him to Africa. (The indictment was ultimately dismissed altogether in May after a judge ruled it was tainted by vindictiveness.)

It is true that people here illegally are not permitted to point anywhere on a map and demand their deportation destination of choice. At a minimum, the receiving country has to agree to accept them. This is relevant here, because the African countries the Trump administration set its sights on for Abrego Garcia—Uganda, Eswatini, and Ghana—did not agree. (When news broke that the U.S. government would seek to send him to Eswatini, for example, the country's spokesperson said in a statement that the country had "not received any communication regarding this person.") The Trump administration's final attempt, Liberia, agreed only on a "temporary" basis.

Put differently, Abrego Garcia could have been gone long ago. It's defensible to portray his protracted stay in the U.S. as a reflection of America's immigration quagmire. But it wasn't rolls and rolls of red tape, or radical judges, or administrative paralysis, or that this individual simply had nowhere to go. These last many months, Abrego Garcia has been in the U.S. because the government made sure of it, explicitly barring him from self-deporting so it could attempt to send him somewhere it viewed as undesirable. It is part of the Trump administration's larger push to ramp up so-called third-country deportations, including to places where Americans are not supposed to travel for any reason.

text:
Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt is calling on Congress to work toward immigration reform, even after being criticized by the vice president.

Earlier this month, Oklahoma GOP Gov. Kevin Stitt called for Trump to push for a bipartisan immigration reform effort.

“It’s not that complicated,” Stitt said during an interview with Politico. “But the problem is Washington, DC, each side thinks they’re winning on it. That’s why you saw this huge swing in the midterms.”

Following the interview, Vice President JD Vance took to X to ask Stitt what "bipartisan immigration reform" means to him.

"I like Kevin, but what does "bipartisan immigration reform” mean? If you mean making it harder for megacompanies to defraud our visa system, great. If you mean we should pass legislation to make it harder for employers to violate our immigration law, I'm all ears. But to a lot of people, this sounds like an effort to give amnesty to people who have broken our laws. It is morally and electorally disastrous," Vance said in the post.

Now, Gov. Stitt is doubling down on his position.

In an opinion piece published in The Oklahoman, Stitt said leaders should use President Trump's "60 Minutes" interview as an invitation to "help build what comes next."

"Not everyone in Washington has accepted that invitation. When I called for bipartisan immigration reform, Vice President JD Vance answered with one word: amnesty. He said my proposal "sounds like an effort to give amnesty to people who have broken our laws." I have never called for amnesty. But the vice president and his allies use the word like a dog whistle for an online audience. It confuses the issue and, by design, shuts down a debate that deserves rigor.

'Amnesty' has become the weapon of choice for ending a conversation our country badly needs to have. The president has opened the door to a serious discussion. Reducing a complex issue to a single word is a dangerous game, and it slams that door shut," Stitt wrote.

Stitt says he has urged the Trump administration to consider visa reform that makes state governments partners with the federal government.

"In Oklahoma, I support our farmers, manufacturers and aerospace employers. When they succeed, they create opportunity for generations of Americans, while we retool, retrain and upskill our own workers. A legal visa system that fits local economies and a firm national security posture are not in conflict. We can have both," he wrote.

Stitt says Congress has the responsibility to deliver a safe and orderly visa system to the American people.

"If our country ever drifts toward citizenship without people paying their dues, it will be because Republicans did not finish the job of reforming the system when we held a full majority," he wrote.

Recently, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that he is open to a bipartisan immigration deal where individuals under DACA can get permanent legal residence, but is against amnesty. He said that amnesty is never going to be a solution and that the Trump administration won’t allow it to happen.

text:
Democrats taking control of Congress in just a few weeks will have a chance to rebuild their reputation after years of Republican attacks on the party's brand.

They'll be better able to shape the narrative on the nation's top issues, including those which contributed to their fall into the minority. Republicans seized on Democratic failures during the Biden administration to communicate effectively on the economy, immigration and presidential missteps, but now, after the blue tsunami that was the midterms, the GOP is on its back foot on the very same issues.

Successful Democrats in this month's elections resisted the bait dangled by Republicans to focus on cultural issues tied to the public's top concerns. They'll likely face more of the same challenges when they take power, and they'd do well to avoid the wars the GOP's long tempted them to fight.

The sensitive issue of will be an important test. Democrats must strike a balance between defending immigrants' rights and opposing the Trump administration's mass deportation policies without falling into traps set by Republicans and the conservative media that's ready to pounce.

Representative Jamie Raskin, the Maryland Democrat, showed the dangers of entertaining right-wing fights last year, when he went toe-to-toe in an argument with a conservative X user over Kilmar Ábrego García, the immigrant involved in an illegal deportation fight. The two yelled over each other on Capitol Hill, fueling Republican attacks against sympathetic Democrats.

Raskin and other Democrats appear to have learned from their mistakes as they prepare to take control of Congress. The party's largely united around the goal of lowering prices that have concerned Americans for the past several years, brushing off Republican attempts to stir up anger over sensitive topics.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and his Senate counterpart, Chuck Schumer, pledged after their party's electoral triumph to address voters' most important issues, like the that's risen under President Donald Trump.

"The American people have forcefully rejected MAGA extremism and are demanding dramatic change in their lives," the Democrats said in a statement. "House and Senate Democrats have been given a clear mandate to aggressively address the affordability crisis, stop the reckless war of choice in Iran, meaningfully expand access to affordable healthcare and hold the crooks accountable who have unleashed unprecedented corruption on the country.

“A new day is coming on January 3rd. Democrats are united and ready to lead.”

text:
OGDEN — Weber County leaders will be scrutinizing the future of the Weber County Sheriff's Office's cooperative agreement with federal immigration authorities, focus of increasingly vocal concern by immigrant advocates pressing for its end.

"Please understand that we take your concerns and your questions very seriously. This is one of our top priorities we'll be addressing over the next two to three weeks," Weber County Commissioner Gage Froerer said Tuesday evening, after more than 20 people addressed commissioners on the issue, most of them critical of the accord.

Many of those speaking during a public hearing at Tuesday's Weber County Commission meeting said that immigrants who don't pose a threat to the community are facing detention and deportation as part of the ongoing immigration crackdown. They charged that the sheriff's office accord with Immigration and Customs Enforcement is aiding the process.

"They are not going after the worst of the worst, as the sheriff has claimed," said Amy Wicks, one of the many Weber County residents who spoke out on Tuesday. "Our decent, hardworking neighbors are being targeted. This is not making our community safer. It needs to stop."

Froerer didn't state a stance one way or another on the sheriff's office's accord with ICE, known as a 287(g) accord. But in the context of the criticism from those who spoke out, lauded the diversity of Weber County and Ogden, where Latinos account for more than 30% of the population.

"We welcome diversity in this community. That's what makes us strong. That's what, in my opinion, separates Weber County from some other counties that I see across the state," he said. "So it's my intent that we embrace that diversity and look at this policy in more detail and answer your questions."

'We're following the laws'

Weber County Sheriff Ryan Arbon, for his part, offered a strong defense of the county's 287(g) agreement with ICE. Eleven Utah counties in all have 287(g) accords with ICE, along with a handful of police departments.

"The county should absolutely not get rid of it," he said Wednesday, a day after Tuesday's meeting, which he didn't attend. The Weber County Sheriff's Office is one of several sheriff's offices and other law enforcement agencies in Utah with 287(g) accords, a tool in the ongoing immigration crackdown that's designed to aid ICE officials in locating immigrants in the country illegally.

One of the chief criticisms of 287(g) accords and the immigration crackdown in general seems to be that immigrants without criminal records are being rounded up as part of the effort. President Donald Trump had stressed the importance of the crackdown as a means of removing immigrants with serious criminal records, "the worst of the worst."

Some of those who spoke out Tuesday, though, noted the case of a Chilean couple, parents of an infant, stopped last month by Weber County Sheriff's Office officials because the car they were traveling in had canceled or suspended registration. While they didn't have criminal records, ICE officials were called in after neither could produce a driver's license. They were later detained by immigration officials for overstaying their 90-day visa by more than two years.

ICE data compiled by the Deportation Data Project, moreover, shows that 45.1% of immigrant detainees in Utah last July had convictions for violent or non-violent crimes and that 54.9% did not have criminal convictions. Just 2.6% of detainees in the period had convictions for violent crimes.

Arbon, though, argued that law enforcement agencies can't pick and choose which laws to enforce, including laws pertaining to immigration.

"When do we get to decide which laws are for us and which are not? I mean, the laws have been enacted. We're following the laws. Every single one of our stops are legal and lawful," he said. "If they're here on a visa, and they're not complying with the visa, does that mean because they haven't committed a crime while they've been here that (they) all of a sudden don't have to comply with the law?"

He said two Weber County Sheriff's Office deputies take part in the cooperative efforts with ICE under the county's 287(g) task force model agreement, distinct from cooperative efforts with corrections officials. They only contact ICE when they come across suspected immigrants in the country illegally in the normal course of their duties. They don't specifically search out immigrants.

'They are everyday people'

Whatever the case, while one speaker at Tuesday's meeting defended the sheriff's office's 287(g) accord, 20-plus people criticized it, many calling for an end to it.

Kelly Quiroz noted, with chagrin, the case of the Chilean couple. "These were not violent criminals, as we were led to believe the focus of this agreement to be. They were a young family with no criminal record," she said.

Moreover, she questioned the notion of local law enforcement working with federal immigration officials.

"I recognize that immigration laws exist and must be administered, but Weber County is not required to lend its own deputies and resources to every aspect of federal immigration enforcement, especially those that separate families. This is injustice," she said.

Read more:

C.J. Hernandez, a Democrat who won election earlier this month to a post in the Utah Senate that represents part of Weber County, said the sheriff's office's cooperative agreement with ICE is causing "a lot of stress and fear" in the community.

"I request the termination of Weber County's 2879g) agreement," she said. "Once we know better, we do better, and I ask for that from you."

Cirilo Franco warned that the county's accord with ICE has prompted some to lose trust in the sheriff's office. He also spoke of the humanity of those being detained.

"They're my family. They're my friends. They are young parents with newborn children," Franco said. "They're mothers, they're fathers. They are everyday people who are simply trying to make ends meet and provide a better future for their children and for themselves."

text:
WASHINGTON — A federal judge in the District of Columbia Wednesday issued a classwide injunction to prevent the Trump administration from implementing its second attempt at redefining the constitutional right to birthright citizenship.

The order from Judge Christopher Reid Cooper will remain in effect while litigation continues. A classwide injunction blocks action affecting a defined group of individuals, as opposed to a nationwide injunction.

In a memorandum opinion, Cooper noted the Supreme Court earlier this year denied President Donald Trump’s executive order that would deny citizenship to babies born from immigrants either in the country unlawfully or on a temporary basis, in the case Barbara v. Trump.

“Yet Barbara’s ink had scarcely dried when the President issued a second executive order—Executive Order 14418, at issue here—directing federal agencies to withhold recognition of citizenship from additional categories of U.S.-born children with noncitizen parents,” he wrote. “As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the President cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws.”

The American Civil Liberties Union, which led the first challenge against the Trump administration’s birthright citizenship order and is leading the second, welcomed the ruling.

“Enough is enough,” Cody Wofsy, deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, said in a statement. “The Supreme Court has twice rejected efforts to gut birthright citizenship, in 1898 and again earlier this year. Third time is not the charm, and the President needs to accept that birthright citizenship is the law of the land.”

The Department of Justice did not respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment.

Earlier this month, Cooper seemed skeptical of the legality of the Trump administration’s second attempt to redefine the constitutional right to birthright citizenship.

The president’s recent executive orders would deny citizenship to babies born in the United States to parents deemed part of a designated terrorist organization and to parents who purposefully came to the United States to gain citizenship in what critics call “birth tourism.”

The executive order also aimed to deny citizenship to children born to foreign diplomatic staff and children born in U.S. territories where Congress has not passed a law granting citizenship.

There is already a small carve out for birthright citizenship, extended to children born to foreign diplomats.

But the Trump administration's aggressive immigration enforcement efforts, highlighted in part by the Nov. 21 detention of two people at the Seattle-Tacoma Airport, has some people reconsidering their movements.

That includes immigrants with the legal right to live and work in the U.S. but who want to avoid being stopped and questioned, said Zachary Mueller, a senior strategist with the advocacy group States at the Core.

"Some people are terrified to leave their house," said Mueller, whose organization has trained about 75,000 people to monitor and record ICE detentions. "For some people, that fear has become so palpable in day-to-day life that this holiday is nothing new on that level."

Mueller added: "For others, they're asking 'is traveling to go see family for the holidays worth the risk of never seeing my family again?' That's a real calculation."

The exact number of people facing deportation is unclear, but roughly 350,000 Haitians and about 600,000 Venezuelans lost Temporary Protected Status in the past two years.

The Department of Homeland Security reports that in fiscal year 2026, ICE carried out more than 483,000 deportations, the most ever in a single year. President Donald Trump has promised the largest mass deportation in U.S. history, and during his second term DHS reports that more than 3 million people have already left the United States either via deportation or self-removal.

Immigrants who leave the United States voluntarily can receive a $3,000 payment and a free flight to their home country.

Administration officials said they will continue to enforce immigration laws, including those that make it harder for undocumented immigrants to fly. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers routinely check Transportation Security Administration manifests for potential immigration violators.

Last May, the Department of Homeland Security began requiring flyers to show REAL ID-compliant identification to board airplanes, a move that made it easier to detect people who lacked permission to live in the United States. People without REAL ID can fly but are subject to additional security checks and may have to pay a $45 fee.

"DHS reversed the horrendous Biden-era policy that allowed aliens in our country illegally to jet around our country. Under President Trump, DHS will no longer tolerate this," an unnamed DHS spokesperson said in a statement. "This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport."

Immigrants who are considering travel should check first with their attorney and make sure to carry copies of relevant paperwork, said Krish O'Mara Vignarajah, the president and CEO of Global Refuge. She said many refugees who sought safety in the United States are now worried about being targeted by the same government that asked them to fill out paperwork and register their home addresses.

She said many refugees, including those from Haiti and Venezuela are frustrated because Trump keeps saying ICE is targeting the "worst of the worst."

"These are people who did everything right, went through vetting, did all the paperwork," she said. "And now they're asking us whether following the rules has somehow put them more at risk."

Mueller said the harsh enforcement tactics also have impacts on travelers who witness anonymous and masked federal agents grabbing screaming people at airports. He said driving may not be a safe option for some people, particularly if they are driving through communities that have signed cooperative agreements allowing local police to help enforce immigration laws.

"It's not just the people who are first affected, but that kind of fear and trauma and concern, the wanton separation, the ability of ICE to do whatever it wants and create these chaotic scenes ... millions of Americans have been seeing this," Mueller said. "They're asking themselves when they travel, 'am I going to see something that's going to ruin my holiday because this administration wants to rip apart families?' That's the absurd reality of this moment."

Marjory Wentworth, a board member of the Haitian Support Center in Springfield, Ohio, said her family is hosting a handful of Haitians for Thanksgiving. Many members of Ohio's Haitian community lost their Temporary Protected Status in July. The Trump administration has revoked their work permission and urged them to leave the United States.

Wentworth said none of the Haitians she knows will risk flying. She said at last one local church hosted a Thanksgiving dinner for Haitian congregants over the weekend, allowing them to celebrate without traveling far from home.

"People can't go work, they've got ankle monitors," she said of her own invited guests. "I feel like people are still pretty fearful. I'm hoping we can distract them for a day."

text:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran national whose mistaken deportation became a major legal and political dispute for the Trump administration, has left the United States for Spain.

Abrego Garcia departed on Tuesday, November 24, and arrived in Madrid on Wednesday, according to reports by the Associated Press and other US media outlets.

His departure follows months of legal battles after he was mistakenly deported to El Salvador in March 2025, despite an earlier immigration court ruling preventing his removal to his home country because of fears of gang persecution.

He was arrested in Baltimore and transferred to El Salvador’s notorious CECOT prison, where he remained for months.

Following public pressure and a court order, the Trump administration brought him back to the United States in June 2025.

However, authorities subsequently pursued plans to deport him to other countries, including Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana and Liberia.

Abrego Garcia challenged those efforts in court, arguing against being sent to countries where he had no established ties.

His latest departure followed months of uncertainty over his immigration status and the possibility of another removal order.

In a statement, Abrego Garcia described the departure as a moment of freedom.

“I am leaving happy. I am leaving with my freedom,” he said.

His lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, described the move as temporary, saying his client hoped to remain abroad until the end of the current administration.

The lawyer said Abrego Garcia could seek to return to Maryland under a future administration to reunite with his American wife and child.

However, the US Department of Homeland Security presented a different account of the departure, describing it as a self-deportation carried out under an existing removal order.

The department said he received no financial incentives for leaving and would not be permitted to return to the United States.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin welcomed the development and repeated the administration’s allegations that Abrego Garcia was associated with a criminal gang.

Abrego Garcia has repeatedly denied the gang allegations.

His case became a prominent test of the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement policies after the government acknowledged that his initial deportation to El Salvador was an administrative error.

His arrival in Spain marks a new chapter in a dispute that has involved immigration authorities, federal courts and the White House, although his long-term immigration status in Spain remains unclear.

text:
SEATTLE, W.A. — U.S. Representative Pramila Jayapal (WA-07), Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Immigration, Integrity, Security, and Enforcement, released the following statement regarding the SeaTac arrest last week:

“Following the appalling incident at SeaTac Airport where a father and daughter were arrested in a brutal and heartbreaking way by ICE agents at an Alaska Airlines gate counter, I have been working to get to the bottom of what happened. I immediately reached out to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin to ask questions and to express directly to him the trauma and fear that the arrests had on Ricardo and Sofia, as well as on all the passengers who watched this take place and the entire community that lives in fear that their families, loved ones, and neighbors will be separated and taken away.

“Secretary Mullin informed me that, in what he indicated is the normal course of operations, TSA at SeaTac sent DHS a pre-flagged list of passengers on the flight that had outstanding warrants of any kind against them. Ricardo’s name was flagged due to an alleged final order of deportation against him. According to Secretary Mullin, ICE then notified the airport one day prior that they would be operating at the airport to arrest Ricardo.

“Because this information differed from the Port of Seattle’s accounts that they were not given any notice of the operation, I contacted Port Commissioner Hamdi Mohamed and asked her to investigate on her end. Commissioner Mohamed acted quickly on this information and has informed us that she is calling for the Port to undertake an independent investigation into the actions of the Port employees in this incident.

“My office also contacted Alaska Airlines, which told us that the only notification they received of this arrest came on the day of at the gate. DHS is supposed to be operating under a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) that gives airlines advance notice of any such operation, and it does not appear that this SOP was followed. I will be following up with Secretary Mullin to determine whether DHS is still utilizing the SOP.

“I also asked Secretary Mullin to share the body camera footage from the ICE officers with me. While he indicated this is now part of an ongoing investigation, as the incoming Chair of the Immigration Subcommittee, I will not rest until we see that footage. Far too often, what ICE claims to have happened is contradicted by the actual evidence.

“Since Donald Trump came into office, we have seen thousands of people separated from their families in brutal ways. We have seen people, including U.S. citizens, killed in the streets. I have visited and conducted oversight on many for-profit detention facilities around the country that are incarcerating tens of thousands of people every single night, and listened to terrible stories of abuse, neglect, and violations of rights. I have worked with dozens of families to advocate for the release of their loved ones, and when Republicans refused to investigate or hold any hearings in Congress, I held eight shadow hearings of my own in Washington, DC, Minneapolis, and Chicago beginning last spring to lift up these stories and demand they get attention, even before anyone began paying attention. The truth is that for every terrible video we see, there are dozens more that we do not see that rip families and communities apart. This is the plan that Trump and Steven Miller outlined in Project 2025, and they have implemented it with cruelty and vigor, with absolutely no regard to due process or constitutional rights, much less humanity. As I have said over and over again, the immigration system is a civil system, not a criminal one and yet ICE and CBP have unleashed an armed group of federal agents into our streets to treat people like criminals. This is simply unacceptable.

“ICE should not be operating in our airports, and I intend to push to include this restriction as well as to ban masks and require judicial warrants to break the incarceration pipeline as soon as we take control of Congress. When I am Chair of the Immigration Subcommittee, we will claw back the hundreds of billions of dollars Republicans and Trump gave to ICE, prosecute the officers who have violated people’s rights and killed people in the streets, end the use of for-profit detention centers, and finally pass immigration reforms that keep families together, provide legal pathways for people to come, stay, and contribute to the United States, and treat immigrants with the humanity they deserve. We will do this in the House, pressure the Senate to do the same, and send it to Trump’s desk for his signature. If he vetoes these bills, the American people will continue to rise up in nonviolent protest at the ballot box and in the streets against him and anyone who supports these cruel policies. And we will not stop in our effort to completely dismantle DHS and ICE and instead create agencies that actually respect the civil system that immigration is.

“I understand the anger and frustration that our community has. Authoritarians and dictators consolidate power, and our work to dismantle that power and remove them from office had an enormous beginning victory in November, but not a final victory. Donald Trump remains in office, and Stephen Miller continues to push a cruel and unconstitutional anti-immigrant agenda, and we will continue to have to contend with these abuses and violations. But Americans voted for an end to the cruelty of this Administration, and when Democrats take control in January, I intend to do all I can to deliver on that.”

text:
A San Diego federal judge has temporarily blocked Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) from redetaining people who are not a flight risk.

In a ruling Tuesday, Judge Dana Subraw said ICE has to determine, on an individualized basis, if there has been a significant change in circumstances that would make the person a flight risk or a danger to justify redetention.

Critics have said it was a signature enforcement tactic by the Trump administration to redetain people previously released, who are currently having their removal cases heard, at their ICE check-ins or appointments.

“ICE was luring those people into check-ins or ICE (appointments) or other appointments and redetaining them for no reason,” said Monika Langarica, the legal director at Center for Human Rights and constitutional Law.

The organization represents one of the plaintiffs in the case, that of Chancely Fanfan, a Haitian minister.

He and his wife entered the United States legally to seek asylum. Langarica said the family did everything they were asked to do, showing up to every court hearing and immigration check-in.

“They even had a U.S. citizen baby in the United States in reliance on the government's promise that they were free in the United States and that they would not be subject to detention unless they violated the terms of their previous releases, or broke some of the rules that warranted detention,” she said.

Nevertheless, Fanfan was detained during a routine check-in last year. He was finally released in December 2025, missing his baby’s first birthday.

Arresting people at their immigration check-ins is a tactic that ICE still uses. The latest case went viral and outraged the San Diego community and the nation when an 8-year-old Haitian child was detained following his check-in earlier this month.

“We cannot confirm, based on the publicly available information, whether that little boy was a class member in this case,” Langarica said. “But it's precisely that practice, luring people, including even third graders, into these dark offices on a floor of a federal building in downtown and then subjecting them to detention again for no justifiable reasons.”

Sabraw has also certified the case as a class action, meaning anyone in circumstances similar to the original plaintiffs is protected. The order only applies to San Diego and Imperial counties, but Langarica said there is an analogous case in San Francisco with a similar ruling.

Immigration attorney Andrews Moreno II said the ruling was in response to ICE ignoring the law.

“They have to do a pre-deprivation hearing before they can re-detain you,” he said. “ICE has been ignoring that completely and detaining people.”

That has led to a flood of habeas petitions as attorneys try to free their clients. Moreno said that in 26 years of practice, prior to this administration, he’d never had to file a habeas petition.

“That's why there's a stay in effect right now to try to minimize the effect of people having to file habeas corpus petitions for reasons that they shouldn't have been detained to begin with,” he said.

The ruling does not mean that all redetainments will stop, but it will protect a significant number of people in San Diego and Imperial Counties.

text:
The Loudoun County Sheriff's Office will suspend its 287(g) agreement, which allows law enforcement to partner with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

What we know:

The change comes after Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger signed a law ending the agreements in Virginia. The move faced challenges in court, but an attempt to block the state law failed.

The law, HB 1441, lays out conditions required for any agreements between local law enforcement and federal immigration officials. It gave jurisdictions until Sept. 1 to submit new agreements that follow the guidelines.

READ MORE | Loudoun County Sherriff's Office reconsidering agreement with ICE

The Loudoun County Sheriff's Office began its 287(g) agreement in August 2024. At the time, they were the only jurisdiction in Northern Virginia with this type of agreement.

The sheriff department's agreement did not include field enforcement, meaning deputies were not allowed to help ICE agents arrest undocumented immigrants in the community. The agreement instead honored ICE detainers, allowing officials to hold inmates who were booked for unrelated criminal charges in the detention center for up to 48 hours until ICE could pick them up.

"The practical difference going forward will be the release of persons with warrants or detainers concurrent with their scheduled release date from the jail. We will not be holding them up to 48 hours for ICE to arrive as required under 287G," a spokesperson for the Loudoun County Sheriff's Office said.

Department officials said they have released 330 undocumented immigrants to ICE in 2026. In August, officials said the agreement led to more than 500 ICE arrests in the past two years. In 2025, ICE made 419 detainer requests and 253 pickups, officials said. Between June 2024, and December 2024, ICE submitted 229 requests and made 91 pickups.

Dig deeper:

Maryland moved to end all of its 287(g) agreements in February, with Gov. Wes Moore signing a bill that prevented state agencies and employees from entering into the agreements. The law also ordered that all existing 287(g) agreements in Maryland end by July 2026.

text:
Four people once held at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center say a GEO Group manager ran an off-the-books night cleaning crew enforced by threats, and that two staff members sexually abused detainees. The case tests how far federal trafficking law reaches inside immigration detention.

A GEO Group lawsuit filed in federal court in Louisiana accuses the private prison company and two former employees of forcing detained immigrants to work overnight shifts under threat of solitary confinement and deportation, and of sexually assaulting some of them. The four plaintiffs, all formerly held at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center in Basile, filed their complaint on Nov. 23 in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Louisiana, Lafayette Division (No. 6:26-cv-04906), seeking compensatory and punitive damages.

The suit arrives as ICE detention, much of it run by contractors, sits near record levels; the complaint, citing TRAC data, puts the population above 65,000 as of July 2026. GEO runs Basile under an ICE contract, and the complaint calls it the country’s largest immigration detention center for women, with 1,000 beds.

What the four plaintiffs allege

The plaintiffs are Luis Renteria-Gonzalez and Mario Garcia-Valenzuela, transgender men from Mexico; Kenia Campos-Flores, who is nonbinary and from El Salvador and is now in federal custody in South Carolina; and a woman suing as Jane Doe, who will ask the court for permission to proceed under a pseudonym. Their detentions spanned 2023 to late 2025.

The central labor allegation targets Emmanuel Reyes, a former assistant warden. According to the complaint, Reyes recruited transgender and masculine-presenting detainees into a “cleaning crew” that worked roughly 8 p.m. to 6 a.m., stripping floors with chemicals and moving furniture without protective gear. Pay, the complaint says, came “irregularly, if at all,” and the plaintiffs say they were handed an English-language “Detainee Voluntary Facility Activities Program Application” to sign only after weeks of unrecorded work. Refusal, they allege, was met with threats of solitary, deportation, denial of medical care and harm to relatives.

The complaint also accuses Reyes of sexually assaulting two plaintiffs, including forcing Jane Doe into sex acts from February to May 2024. It accuses David Courvelle, a former GEO detention officer, of sexually assaulting Garcia-Valenzuela three times in 2025 and forcing him and Renteria-Gonzalez to stand lookout while he abused a detained woman. Courvelle pleaded guilty in December 2025 to a federal sexual abuse charge involving a detainee at the facility and was sentenced in July 2026 to three years in prison, according to WAFB’s reports on the plea and sentencing. The allegations against Reyes and GEO have not been tested in court.

The plaintiffs say they reported the abuse through Prison Rape Elimination Act channels, grievances, the DHS inspector general’s hotline, ICE and the FBI. One PREA complaint was closed as unsubstantiated in August 2024, the complaint says, and a plaintiff who gave ICE a written statement about Reyes was then put in solitary for 14 days. GEO’s response had not been reported as of Tuesday night; Acadiana News First said it had asked the company for comment. No public comment from ICE on the suit could be found.

Why a trafficking statute, not a wage claim

ICE’s 2011 detention standards allow a voluntary work program paying at least $1 a day. This complaint does not argue over that rate. It rests on the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act, whose civil remedy at 18 U.S.C. 1595 lets a victim sue anyone who obtains labor through serious harm, threats or abuse of legal process, plus Louisiana claims for sexual assault, emotional distress, negligence and negligent supervision.

The open question is how the work was obtained. If threats of solitary or deportation, rather than choice, kept the plaintiffs on the night crew, the “voluntary” label would carry little weight. GEO is likely to answer that the work fell within an ICE-approved program and that any abuse by individual employees fell outside their jobs. Louisiana holds employers liable for torts within the course and scope of employment, so that question may decide how much of the sexual assault claims reaches the company.

GEO has argued elsewhere that it shares the government’s immunity as a federal contractor. In a Colorado forced-labor case, the Supreme Court held that GEO could not immediately appeal a trial judge’s refusal to dismiss on that ground, PBS NewsHour reported, so the defense generally must wait for review until after trial.

It joins other recent challenges to detention conditions, from a lawsuit over pregnant women in ICE custody to testimony on solitary confinement of ICE detainees in Alaska and scrutiny of GEO’s finances in the Tacoma detention center sale.

What comes next in Lafayette

Pseudonym motion: Jane Doe’s request to proceed anonymously is likely to be among the first filings.

GEO’s response: an answer or a motion to dismiss, likely testing whether the alleged threats meet the forced-labor standard and whether contractor immunity applies.

Courvelle and Reyes: each must respond individually, and Courvelle’s conviction may limit what he can contest.

The plaintiffs are represented by the Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights center, the National Immigration Project, the National Immigrant Justice Center, the ACLU of Louisiana and the Southern Poverty Law Center.

This article is for general information and is not legal advice.

text:
An Arizona man who was detained by immigration agents in Maine in July said in court filings that ICE apparently lost his passport and driver's license, effectively stranding him here for months after he was released from custody.

It's part of a national pattern of ICE failing to return documents and personal items to detainees after they are released from custody.

Arthur Mutegetsi, 28 and originally from Rwanda, was transferred to a Massachusetts jail after his arrest this summer, according to federal court filings.

He was released on bond a couple weeks later, but immigration officials did not return his driver's license and passport, despite a court order.

In a letter to the court earlier this month, Mutegetsi said he was left "effectively stranded" in Maine, unable to travel back to Tucson without the documents.

The court ordered immigration officials to issue a new work permit so Mutegetsi could replace his driver's license. Immigration authorities sent the new permit on Friday.

His lawyer was not immediately available for comment, and it's not clear exactly where Mutegetsi stayed while he was stuck in Maine.

Court filings show Mutegetsi first entered the U.S. in 2024 and applied for asylum. His asylum case was denied earlier this year, and he has an appeal pending with the Board of Immigration Appeals.

In a separate class-action lawsuit filed last month, the Washington, D.C. chapter of the American Civil Liberties Union said ICE has demonstrated a "de facto policy" of not returning personal property, including documents, cell phones, and cash.

text:
Over the weekend, the Massachusetts Lottery shared a picture of Ariel Velasquez-Morales smiling gently as he gripped an oversized check for $1 million in winnings. On social media, commenters congratulated him, with one person writing they hoped he would be able to “make any dreams come true.”

But Velasquez-Morales was arrested Tuesday by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in East Boston, the same neighborhood where he bought the $10 winning scratch-off ticket from a local market.

He now faces deportation as ICE says the Salvadoran national has been in the country illegally for more than a decade.

“Looks like his luck ran out,” said ICE Assistant Director of Public Affairs Micah Bock in a release announcing the arrest.

It is unclear whether the publication of his lottery winnings attracted ICE’s attention. ICE declined to answer questions from CNN about what led to the arrest or where Velasquez-Morales is being detained.

Velasquez-Morales illegally entered the United States in 2013, during the Obama administration, in the Rio Grande Valley in Texas. Border Patrol agents issued him a notice to appear before an immigration judge, and he was released into the country with a list of free legal service providers, the agency said.

“A Department of Justice immigration judge ordered Velasquez-Morales removed in 2014, but he illegally remained in the country,” the ICE release said.

He will remain in ICE custody pending his removal from the US. CNN has been unable to determine whether he has legal representation.

President Donald Trump has overseen a massive immigration crackdown after promising to lead the largest deportation operation in US history. In his second term, arrests have shifted away from the border and focused more on the interior of the country, where aggressive tactics have become a hallmark of ICE’s ramped-up detention efforts. By July 2026, there were nearly 66,000 detainees in ICE custody, an increase of nearly 70% from the total detained when Trump took office the year prior.

But after a Republican wipeout in the midterms, Trump has publicly questioned whether the tactics were too hard-line and unpopular. It remains to be seen, though, whether he is considering significant changes to his immigration policies.

“Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the United States and will be removed as quickly as possible,” ICE said in its release on Velasquez-Morales. “Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin’s leadership, ICE is delivering on its mission to enforce our nation’s immigration laws, restore accountability and protect American communities.”

Velasquez-Morales was playing the lottery’s “$2,000,000 50X Cashword,” in which players scratch cards resembling crossword puzzles to try to reveal complete words. It was the first puzzle he had scratched, the lottery said, and he matched 11 words.

He chose to accept his winnings in cash, which would give him a one-time lump sum of $650,000 before taxes, according to ICE. It is not clear what will happen to his winnings.

Massachusetts lottery participants do not need to be legal residents of the state to play, but they must be 21 or older and be located in the state at the time they purchase or play.

CNN has sought comment from the Massachusetts State Lottery Commission.

text:
Loudoun County Sheriff Mike Chapman’s office told 7News that Loudoun County will suspend its 287(g) agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement because of a state law Gov. Abigail Spanberger signed this year.

The law Spanberger signed effectively outlawed 287(g) agreements in Virginia.

The law was challenged in court, but that attempt failed in the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals this week.

READ | Appeals court allows Virginia restriction on local ICE cooperation to resume

Chapman’s 287(g) agreement with ICE did not include field enforcement, meaning sheriff’s deputies weren’t helping ICE agents arrest immigrants living in the country illegally out in the community.

Rather, Chapman’s agreement with ICE honored detainers, meaning if ICE lodged an immigration detainer on someone in the Loudoun County Adult Detention Center who was booked for criminal charges unrelated to immigration, Chapman would hold the inmate for up to 48 hours until ICE could pick them up.

As of today, the sheriff’s office has released 330 immigrants living in the country illegally to ICE this year, according to the sheriff’s office.

The Loudoun County Sheriff's Office released the following statement:

"The Loudoun County Sheriff's Office (LCSO) is aware of the U.S. Court of Appeals decision to uphold Virginia's restrictions on 287g agreements, and will abide by this decision.

The LCSO will continue to work closely with all of its federal, state and local law enforcement partners to ensure public safety and keep Loudoun the safest locality in Northern Virginia. This includes honoring criminal warrants and immigration detainers concurrent with a person's release from the ADC."

text:
A man arrested in October by immigration authorities has been linked to threats against President Donald Trump, the White House has said.

Hector Alejandro Mujica-Hernandez was arrested on October 16 in Provo, Utah, by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has released images of stickers they say Mujica-Hernandez created that threaten the president's life.

"The Department of Homeland Security will not tolerate death threats of any kind," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said. "The media and the far-left must stop vilifying U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement law enforcement officers and President Trump."

Read More on News

The images released by DHS come from an independent, student-run publication at Provo's Brigham Young University (BYU); it first revealed them back in August. The Cougar Chronicle linked the stickers to Mujica-Hernandez and a group of which he is a member, called People of Provo Against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (POPAI).

The stylized wording on U.S. Postal Service stickers says: "Shoot Trump, be a hero, become unforgetable."

BYU student and Cougar Chronicle writer Jackson Gallini said he started looking into POPAI and attended one of the group's meetings.

"I discovered the 'Shoot Trump, Be A Hero' stickers that Mujica posted and found them shocking. Days later, Mujica handed these stickers out as treats for everyone at their meeting, including to myself, and the members were encouraging him both on Discord and at their meeting to post them around Provo," Gallini said.

"We had no idea that, when we attributed the stickers to Mujica in our reporting, it would lead to an FBI investigation and to his arrest by Immigration and Customs Enforcement."

The Cougar Chronicle describes itself as a "student-run newspaper with a conservative perspective" at the private university operated by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.

Gallini said he was compelled to speak out following the September 2025 assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University (UVU) about four miles away.

"In the wake of Charlie Kirk's assassination happening just a few miles away at UVU, we felt an urgent need to report this to the public," he said.

DHS officials said Mujica-Hernandez entered the country legally from Venezuela in 2016, but overstayed his visa.

Utah court records obtained by Newsweek show Mujica-Hernandez has three traffic citations since June 2022. Most recently, he was cited on August 29 for using a wireless device while operating a vehicle and fined $100.

Members of POPAI said on their Instagram page that Mujica-Hernandez was "entrapped and abducted" from a Provo coffee shop.

Newsweek has contacted the POPAI for comment and is awaiting a response.

A person saying he is a friend of Mujica-Hernandez is raising money for his legal defense on a GoFundMe page. As of early Tuesday, $10,610 had been raised.

"He is a pillar to our community, and we just want him home and safe," Kyler Jensen said in a statement on the fundraising page. He is also listed as a POPAI leader on its Discord page.

title: Loudoun Sheriff's Office to End Jail Agreement With ICE | News | loudounnow.com
description: The Loudoun County Sheriff’s Office will abide by a state law ending 287(g) agreements between local law enforcement in Virginia and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
text:
The Loudoun County Adult Detention Center is located at 42035 Loudoun Center Place.

The Loudoun County Sheriff’s Office will abide by a state law ending 287(g) agreements between local law enforcement in Virginia and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The law, SB783, was passed in this year’s legislative session and prohibits local agencies from “maintaining, renewing, or entering into any federal immigration agreement unless such agreement contains certain provisions.” Those provisions include authority granted in other laws, the transfer of someone currently in custody, or to comply with judicial warrant obtained by ICE.

LCSO was part of ICE’s 287(g) program, “Warrant Service Officer,” which meant that LCSO deputies were sworn and trained to hold inmates up to 48 hours beyond their scheduled release from the Adult Detention Center to allow ICE agents time to pick them up for either a judicial or an administrative warrant.

Many of the inmates had only administrative warrants, called detainers, issued for them. Those do not need to be signed by a judge. LCSO has turned hundreds of people over to ICE over the past two years under the program. FOIA requests by organizations monitoring immigration enforcement also led to the discovery that LCSO had given ICE information about people they encountered in the field, a practice which led to disagreements between Sheriff Mike Chapman and the Board of Supervisors.

This week, the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals lifted a lower court’s injunction blocking implementation of the new state law. On Wednesday, LCSO Media Relations and Communications Director Tom Julia told Loudoun Now that LCSO “is aware of the U.S. Court of Appeals decision to uphold Virginia's restrictions on 287g agreements, and will abide by this decision.”

text:
The Trump administration will cut Medicare coverage for 300,000 legal immigrants who have paid more than $6 billion into the program.

A letter sent by the Social Security Administration said coverage would be terminated in less than three months, despite the recipients paying into the federal health insurance benefit for years.

It's estimated that among the 300,000 immigrants who stand to lose Medicare access will be older, disabled noncitizens and those with end-stage renal disease affecting their kidneys—a result of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, or H.R. 1.

Read More on Health Care

A redacted copy obtained by The Washington Post said: "A review of our records shows you may no longer qualify for Medicare due to a change in the law."

It added that recipients can appeal the decision by calling the Social Security Administration hotline or uploading documents showing they have changed their immigration status.

"Terribly, the new law provides no exceptions,” Tiffany Huyenh-Cho, Director of California Medicare and Medicaid Advocacy at Justice in Aging, told Newsweek in an emailed statement Wednesday.

“To keep Medicare, individuals must fall within one of the four remaining eligible categories, leaving many older immigrants with few affordable health coverage alternatives,” she said. “We are also deeply concerned that some people who remain eligible for Medicare may wrongly receive notices terminating their coverage because the Social Security Administration does not have accurate information about their citizenship or immigration status. These individuals should appeal immediately to avoid a gap in coverage."

Newsweek contacted the Social Security Administration for comment via email on Wednesday and is awaiting a response.

Medicare Reserved for Four Groups

From February 1, 2027, refugees, asylum grantees, those with temporary protected status, and certain trafficking victims will no longer meet the qualifications for the program. There will be an appeal deadline of 60 days, according to SSA guidance.

Eligibility will be limited to U.S. citizens and nationals, lawful permanent residents, some Cuban and Haitian entrants, and migrants from specific countries under treaty.

Asylum grantees and refugees vetted and approved by the federal government who have been living and working in the country for at least a decade will lose out on the benefit. This is despite federal data estimating that they have paid more than $6 billion to fund it.

The Center for Medicare Advocacy said in a statement to Newsweek: "For the first time in the history of the Medicare program, coverage is being stripped away from groups of people, in this instance, specific categories of lawfully present individuals who previously qualified for Medicare through their work history.

"Because of H.R. 1’s corresponding immigration-related changes to Medicaid and Affordable Care Act coverage, many affected individuals are likely to end up uninsured.

"To add insult to injury, these are folks who have paid into Medicare for years—and will continue to do so through taxes—but have no recourse. We urge policymakers to reverse these changes."

Concerns for Overstretched Hospitals

New York-based policy and public affairs expert Babar Khan Javed said patients who lose their health insurance in the cuts will likely delay medical care and then seek emergency care at already-stretched hospitals.

He told Newsweek: "It's inevitable that stripping Medicare eligibility from older or disabled enrollees replaces predictable, insured outpatient and preventive care with delayed, acute crises."

Legal immigrants with end-stage renal disease, for example, are currently eligible for Medicare for dialysis treatments, treatments many of them are expected to go without come February.

Javed, co-founder of consultancy firm The Aberrant, said hospitals "already operating on thin margins" will be forced to eat the unpaid care costs, straining budgets at the local level.

He said: "Without routine management of chronic conditions, patients show up later at hospital emergency rooms, where care is far more expensive and far less likely to be reimbursed.

"Then you have safety-net and community hospitals already operating on thin margins, higher uncompensated care erodes operating cash flows, strains emergency capacity, and forces cost-shifting onto insured patients and local budgets."

One Big Beautiful Bill Act

Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act into law July, marking the largest rollback of federal support for health care in American history.

The package included new 80-hour-a-month work requirements for many adults receiving Medicaid and food stamps, including older people up to age 65.

More than 71 million people rely on Medicaid, which expanded under Barack Obama’s Affordable Care Act.

Over $1 trillion will be cut from health programs—meaning an estimated 10 million people will lose their health insurance coverage by 2034.

Despite this, the act is still projected to increase national debt by at least $3.4 trillion and speed up the time it takes Medicare's trust fund to become insolvent.

text:
ALEXANDRIA, Va. — U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement filed a response on Wednesday to a habeas corpus petition from Princeton neuroscience Ph.D. student Eva Yi Xie GS. In the filing, ICE opposed Xie’s arguments that her arrest and detention were unlawful and urged the court to not issue a writ of habeas corpus to immediately release Xie.

Xie, a Chinese national, was detained on Thursday at the Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Virginia, where she intended to board a domestic flight. She is currently being held at ICE’s Caroline Detention Facility in Bowling Green, Va., ICE’s detainee locator shows.

According to Xie’s habeas corpus petition, filed on Friday, she arrived in the country on a B-2 visitor visa, commonly known as a tourist visa, in March 2016. Xie’s mother filed for asylum in July 2016, prior to the visa expiring in September. Xie was included in her mother’s asylum application because she was a minor at the time.

In September 2024, according to the habeas corpus petition, Xie’s asylum case was referred to the immigration court system, where she has a hearing scheduled for Jan. 18, 2028.

description:

And the court limited his ability to use the 1798 Alien Enemies Act to quickly remove certain migrants from the country.
White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis dismissed Wang’s assertion that the court will find Trump’s immigration policies illegal.

text:
Democrats want to sideline President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda when they take control of Congress next year, but the real fight may take place across the street where the conservative Supreme Court is poised to uphold several of his most controversial policies.

The court will soon consider blockbuster appeals on the president’s asylum ban, his vast expansion of mandatory detention of migrants and his push to send certain people in the US illegally to countries other than their homeland — including some with dubious human rights records.

Decisions in those cases are expected by late June.

Though those three cases and several others are less flashy than this past summer’s blockbuster decision upholding birthright citizenship, the outcomes in the nuts-and-bolts disputes will have profound implications for policies the administration says are “indispensable” to its overall immigration crackdown.

“In all three of these cases, the Trump administration is trying to rewrite laws enacted by Congress, in service of a radical anti-immigrant agenda that has hurt not only immigrants, but the rule of law,” said Cecillia Wang with the American Civil Liberties Union, which is opposing the administration in two of those cases. “These Trump policies are not only illegal but also unpopular.”

Trump has had a mixed record on immigration at the 6-3 conservative court since returning to power last year. His unprecedented push to upend birthright citizenship was rejected. And the court limited his ability to use the 1798 Alien Enemies Act to quickly remove certain migrants from the country.

On the other hand, six-justice majorities in June allowed Trump to end a form of humanitarian relief known as Temporary Protected Status and to limit asylum claims made at the border.

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis dismissed Wang’s assertion that the court will find Trump’s immigration policies illegal.

“If the American Civil Liberties Union cares more about criminal illegal aliens than they do about American citizens, then they should change their name,” she said.

Some Democrats have framed the recapture of Congress as a rejection by voters of the administration’s immigration policies. Minnesota Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan vowed to “rip ICE apart.” New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is all but certain to become the next House speaker, told CBSthat Democrats would “put an end to Donald Trump’s violent mass deportation machine.”

But Republicans have already frontloaded funding for ICE for years. And Trump this month named Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, as White House chief of staff — a sign that the administration has no intention of slowing its immigration agenda.

“It stands to reason that hyper-aggressive immigration enforcement will continue to be one of the hallmarks of the Trump administration even as it faces Democratic majorities in both chambers of the legislature,” said Steve Vladeck, CNN Supreme Court analyst and professor at Georgetown University Law Center. “Whether the extremism of these policies will be allowed to continue is therefore going to be up to the Supreme Court.”

Conservatives who support the policies see a court that is prepared to back the president’s program.

“Over and over, judges in the district courts and the courts of appeals have interpreted the law contrary to clear congressional intent as evidenced by the text. And as a result, those decisions keep getting overturned,” Iowa Solicitor General Eric Wessan, whose state led briefs supporting the administration in two of the biggest cases, told CNN.

Wessan predicted that the justices will view lower court decisions on immigration against the administration with similar skepticism.

“Looking at the immigration cases the Supreme Court has taken this term,” he predicted, “I think it’s doing the same kind of cleanup.”

Human rights and arrests

The showdown will begin on December 9, when the justices will hear arguments in a case challenging Trump’s push to remove certain migrants to countries other than their homeland. In many cases, those removals are carried out without giving the migrant an opportunity to raise human rights concerns.

Federal law allows such “third country” removals in cases when a migrant’s home country refuses to accept them. The administration has used that provision to remove an Iranian national to Nicaragua, for instance, and Venezuelans to El Salvador, according to immigrants’ rights groups.

In some of those cases, immigrant rights groups say, migrants were sent back to their homeland from the “third country,” even when an immigration judge ordered that the administration not return to them to their native country.

Congress has also required the administration to ensure migrants won’t be tortured or persecuted once they land in a third country. That determination was previously made on a case-by-case basis. Under the second Trump administration, the government now accepts blanket assurances from a foreign country that no torture will take place, and migrants are often removed to that country without notice.

The Supreme Court, on its emergency docket, three times allowed the administration to pursue the policy while the case remained pending. It has not explained its reasoning.

Increase in arrests of migrants

Next year, the court will turn to the Trump administration’s decision to funnel not only recent border crossers into mandatory detention but also people who have been living within the United States for years.

That shift has permitted the Department of Homeland Security to dramatically increase the number of migrants arrested. And so if the court rejects that change, it will almost certainly jeopardize the administration’s ability to carry out massive sweeps for migrants that have played out in cities like Chicago and Minneapolis.

Immigrant rights groups say no prior administration, including Trump’s first, has interpreted federal law to require mandatory detention of so many migrants. But Justice Department officials told the Supreme Court that it is simply following the law that Congress enacted.

Asylum ban

And in the spring, the court will hear a challenge to Trump’s asylum ban. The president argues people crossing the border are making false asylum claims as a way to enter the country then stall the deportation process, since it can take years to resolve them.

US Solicitor General D. John Sauer, the administration’s top appellate attorney, warned the court of a “vicious cycle” that encouraged “illegal entry by millions of aliens, who (quite justifiably) inferred that even if they lacked meritorious asylum claims, they would ‘be released to live and work in the United States during their removal proceedings.’”

But the Immigration and Nationality Act specifically allows migrants to claim asylum, even as it leaves the decision about whether to grant safe harbor up to administration officials.

In stark language, the Justice Department has described its asylum policy as one of the “most important and effective” policies for stemming illegal immigration. A lower court order against the policy, the administration said, “threatens to revive the chaos along the southwest border that the proclamation has fended off for the past year and a half.”

The ACLU, representing 13 individuals and three immigrant rights groups that challenged the policy, said that if Trump wants to change the way asylum works, he should have passed a bill in Congress during the two years the chambers were in Republican hands.

Richard Caldarone, a senior litigation attorney at the National Immigrant Justice Center, said that the policies at issue in the cases had already put tens of thousands of people in harm’s way.

“These policies have been overwhelmingly rejected by lower courts across the country, and they flatly violate US immigration law as it has been understood for decades,” said Caldarone, whose group is fighting the administration in the asylum case.

“If the court validates the policies,” he said, “it will enshrine a new generation of internment camps, all but end the US asylum system as we have known it for almost half a century, and shatter our nation’s commitment to upholding human rights and democratic norms.”

text:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Maryland resident who became the face of the Trump administration’s heavy-handed deportation efforts, reportedly self-deported Tuesday to Spain.

The move ends 20 months of legal wrangling between the administration and immigration advocates fighting on behalf of Abrego Garcia, an immigrant from El Salvador who was picked up by immigration agents in March 2025 and erroneously deported to his native country.

Neither his attorneys nor the Department of Homeland Security immediately responded to requests for comment Tuesday from States Newsroom.

But in a statement released shortly after midnight Wednesday morning, the immigration advocacy group We Are CASA said Abrego Garcia had “cleared his name of the Trump administration’s bogus charges against him and walked out of the United States a free man.”

The statement said Abrego Garcia was accompanied on a commercial flight by his wife, Jennifer Vasquez Sura, his attorney and a We Are CASA representative. It said they were met at the airport by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who removed the ankle monitoring bracelet Abrego Garcia has had to wear since courts ordered him released from detention and returned home to Beltsville.

Abrego Garcia said in the statement that “justice prevailed under this administration in a way that many people never thought was possible.”

“I am leaving happy. I am leaving with my freedom. I am leaving with the love of an entire community, with people who cared for me, believed in me, and joined my family in this fight,” his statement said. “I feel good. I feel confident. I believe everything will be okay because God is with us.”

Abrego Garcia’s deportation attracted international attention to the administration’s immigration crackdown, early in Trump’s second term, and brought attention to the notorious CECOT prison in El Salvador where U.S. deportees were housed.

Legal challenges were immediately filed to the detention and deportation. The case ultimately reached the U.S. Supreme Court, which unanimously ordered the administration to “facilitate” the return of Abrego Garcia.

It also brought a visit from Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md. who traveled to El Salvador and demanded to meet with Abrego Garcia, who had been kept largely incommunicado since he was detained. In a statement Tuesday evening, Van Hollen confirmed that Abrego Garcia was leaving the U.S. and said he was “relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free — including from this administration’s constant persecution.”

“A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego Garcia to rot in a Salvadoran gulag,” Van Hollen’s statement said. “Today, Kilmar is traveling to a country of his choice, a free man — unharmed and with dignity.”

Neither Van Hollen nor We Are CASA specified Abrego Garcia’s destination, but news reports Tuesday said he was seen getting on a plane to Spain.

The apparent self-deportation also ends a monthslong fight with the Department of Homeland Security, which had proposed deporting Abrego Garcia to Liberia, Uganda, Eswatini or other third countries where his safety and his future would have been in doubt.

A 2019 immigration court order barred the government from sending Abrego Garcia back to his native El Salvador, for fear of his safety there. But it did not prevent the government from trying to send him to a third country — an increasingly popular deportation tactic of the administration.

Abrego Garcia had offered to self-deport to Costa Rica, but the administration opposed that move.

“Mr. Abrego Garcia had been asking permission to leave the country since August 2025,” said Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, one of his attorneys, in the We Are CASA statement. “The Trump Administration held him and refused to allow him to depart, first in an ICE detention center for five months and then on electronic monitoring in Maryland for almost a year, all the while insisting on deporting him to a series of African countries. That retaliatory deportation campaign has now come to an end.”

Abrego Garcia was eventually returned from El Salvador in June 2025, but was immediately arrested and charged by ICE with human smuggling in Tennessee. Those charges stemmed from a 2022 traffic stop for speeding in Tennessee, when Abrego was driving an SUV carrying a number of Latino men.

Abrego Garcia was let go with a warning after the traffic stop and the case was closed. But federal officials reopened it two years later and charged Abrego Garcia with human smuggling as soon as he was returned from El Salvador.

Abrego Garcia’s attorneys argued the flimsy charges were mere pretext to punish their client after he beat the administration in court. A federal judge in Tennessee agreed in May and tossed the case out as a vindictive prosecution and an abuse of government power.

It is not clear when or how the European deportation plan was agreed to. But Van Hollen’s statement said that as Homeland Security had been “trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the Administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation.”

“I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this Administration’s constant persecution,” Van Hollen’s statement said.

Ama Frimpong, We Are CASA’s chief of legal services and another of Abrego Garcia’s attoenrys, called it “a victory that Kilmar gets to choose what comes next.”

“He is choosing where and how to lead his life. He is beginning this new chapter with the safety, freedom, and dignity he fought to reclaim,” Frimpong said in the statement. “That victory belongs first to Kilmar; to Jennifer, whose voice carried their family’s fight across the country; and to their family, who endured more than any family should.
