Scott. “By improving the exchange of customs information and investigative cooperation, this agreement will help both nations detect and disrupt transnational threats while protecting and enforcing legitimate commerce.”

Once entered into force, the CMAA will allow the United States and Jamaica to exchange information and provide mutual assistance on customs offenses, thus strengthening the collaboration between the two countries. This bilateral agreement reflects the United States’ commitment to its relationship and collaboration with Jamaica on a wide range of issues, including securing the countries’ borders against terrorists, combating drug traffickers, and disrupting the operations of transnational criminal organizations.

CMAAs also allow for the sharing of information that is used to assist governments in investigations and judicial proceedings involving suspected violations of customs laws. They provide the legal framework for the exchange of information and evidence to assist countries in the enforcement of customs laws, including duty evasion, trafficking, proliferation, money-laundering, and terrorism-related activities. CBP and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement are the implementing agencies for the United States.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran migrant whose mistaken deportation became a major flashpoint in President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, has left the United States for Spain after a closely watched legal battle.

According to NBC News, a federal judge ordered Garcia to leave the US by Tuesday.

The 31-year-old was seen boarding a commercial flight bound for Madrid at Washington Dulles International Airport on Tuesday night, accompanied by his wife, brother and lawyer.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin welcomed the development, describing Garcia’s departure as voluntary.

“We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported,” Mullin said in a statement. “Now, this El Salvadoran man cannot terrorize innocent Americans.”

The remarks stood in sharp contrast to those of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who had previously visited Garcia while he was detained in El Salvador.

In a statement on US social media company X, the Maryland Democrat said Garcia was “traveling to a country of his choice, a free man — unharmed and with dignity.”

Garcia’s case drew attention after he was mistakenly deported to El Salvador in March 2025, despite a 2019 immigration court ruling barring his removal there because of the danger he faced from gang members.

He was held at the country’s CECOT prison before being returned to the US. Immigration officials later acknowledged in court filings that his deportation had been an “administrative error.”

Following his return, Garcia faced federal human-smuggling charges linked to a 2022 traffic stop in Tennessee. A judge later dismissed the case, finding that the government had failed to overcome the “presumption of vindictiveness.” Prosecutors appealed the decision.

text:
BURBANK (CNS) – Burbank police denied Tuesday, Nov. 24, that officers were collaborating with federal immigration agents during a Monday night confrontation with activists at Providence St. Joseph’s Hospital, but were called twice to the facility to prevent protesters from blocking the hospital’s ambulance bay.

Activists with Union del Barrio went to the hospital Monday evening, with the organization saying it received reports from community members that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents had gone into the medical facility and “possibly assaulted medical workers at the hospital then threatened to take everyone in the [ER] waiting room.”

“When people in the ER waiting room heard the verbal threat from the ICE agents, many of them ran out of the hospital,” according to a statement from Union del Barrio. “This is highly concerning because we do not know what kind of medical treatment these people needed before they decided to leave the hospital due to their fear of possibly being kidnapped.”

Activists were seen on video loudly questioning the presence of ICE agents at the hospital. Many of the activists were seen shouting while filming the federal officers with cell phones. ICE officials said Tuesday they had gone to the hospital to seek treatment for a suspected illegal immigrant who had been detained earlier in the day.

According to Lt. Brent Fekety of the Burbank Police Department (BPD), officers were called by hospital staff around 6:30 p.m. Monday after demonstrators “followed the ICE agents to the hospital, where they gathered outside the emergency room, used noise-amplifying devices and blocked the ambulance bay. Their actions prevented emergency medical personnel from bringing patients requiring immediate medical attention into the facility.”

Fekety said officers were able to restore order and left, but they were called again an hour later “due to demonstrators blocking the ambulance bay.”

“Officers directed the demonstrators to move from the ambulance bay to the public sidewalk along Buena Vista Street, restoring access for emergency medical personnel,” Fekety said in a statement.

He said the department “respects and supports the constitutional rights of individuals to peacefully assemble and express their views. However, such activities must be conducted lawfully. Assaulting officers, blocking an ambulance bay and interfering with emergency medical personnel attempting to bring patients into a hospital can jeopardize public safety and will not be tolerated.”

Hospital officials issued a statement Tuesday acknowledging “the community’s concerns about last night’s activity on our campus. As a place of healing, our focus remains on caring for every patient who comes through our doors.”

But the hospital denied suggestions by Union del Barrio that any of its medical personnel were “assaulted” by ICE agents.

“Our employees, physicians and patients remained safe throughout the brief event,” according to the hospital. “Patient care remained uninterrupted, and the Emergency Department remained open for patients throughout the evening.”

According to ICE, the patient agents took to the hospital Monday was Razmik Arevya, a suspected illegal immigrant from Armenia who was arrested during an enforcement operation earlier in the day. ICE officials said Arevya has a criminal history that includes two counts of inflicting corporal injury on a spouse, inflicting injury upon a child, disobeying a court order, violating a protection order to prevent domestic abuse and several other related domestic violent crimes.

Federal officials said Arevyan entered the United States in October 2010 with authorization to remain temporarily but failed to leave the country after his authorized stay expired. In March 2024, an immigration judge issued a final order of removal after Arevyan failed to appear for a mandatory immigration hearing, according to ICE.

“During the arrest, Arevyan refused to comply with officers’ lawful commands and resisted his arrest. Officers relied on their training to safely control the situation without further incident, placing him under arrest,” ICE said in a statement.

He was then taken to the hospital for evaluation and was medically cleared and placed into ICE custody, where he is expected to remain pending his removal, according to the federal agency.

Fekety insisted that BPD does not collaborate with ICE in carrying out immigration enforcement, and it only responded to the hospital due to concerns about activists possibly blocking the ambulance bay.

“The department does not have the legal authority to prevent federal agents from taking lawful enforcement action or interfering with federal agents,” he said.

Union del Barrio lashed out at hospital officials for calling police “to threaten members of the Community Self-Defense Coalition who showed up to the hospital to denounce ICE for kidnapping and physically assaulting a community member, and for threatening hospital staff.”

Protesters “were not attempting to disrupt hospital operations. They were there to protect the public from the armed and dangerous ICE agents. Hospital administrators should protect their patients, not ICE agents who try to kidnap patients,” according to the group.

Video from the scene showed a large presence of Burbank police and federal agents leaving the hospital with a man, presumed to be Arevyan, in a wheelchair around 9 p.m. The man was then placed in a vehicle and driven from the scene.

“Today’s incident at Providence St. Joseph’s Hospital marks yet another dangerous escalation by ICE agents and the Trump administration,” according to the statement from Union del Barrio. “Hospitals should be a place of healing and the general public, regardless of citizenship, should never have to fear seeking medical treatment.”

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have arrested an illegal immigrant days after he was pictured claiming a $1 million lottery prize.

The Massachusetts State Lottery shared a photo of Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales holding a giant check in his hands on Facebook last Saturday.

Velasquez-Morales was all smiles after winning a huge lot from the $2,000,000 50X Cashword game in East Boston. The lottery said it was his first time playing the $10 scratch-off and that he matched an impressive 11 words.

On Tuesday, Velasquez-Morales was arrested by ICE agents during operations in East Boston, the agency’s local field office said on X, alongside the same photo of the lotto winner holding his $1 million check.

“Looks like his luck ran out,” ICE Assistant Director of Public Affairs Micah Bock said in a press release about the arrest Wednesday.

ICE Boston said that Velasquez-Morales was from El Salvador and that he illegally entered the U.S. in May 2013. Nearly a year later, an immigration judge ordered his deportation in April 2014, according to the field office.

Velasquez-Morales attempted to flee arrest on Tuesday, Fox News reported. Three sources from ICE told the outlet that he ran when agents tried to take him into custody, but that he was quickly arrested.

In a follow-up post Wednesday, ICE Boston celebrated Velasquez-Morales’ arrest, writing, “Welcome to the ERO [Enforcement and Removal Operations] Boston lottery! Where illegal aliens and sanctuary politicians are out of luck, and the law-abiding citizens of New England are always the winners!”

Velasquez-Morales had chosen the cash option for his lottery prize, receiving a one-time lump sum of $650,000 before taxes, ICE said in Wednesday’s press release.

An official from the Massachusetts State Lottery told The Independent that anyone 18 years or older who is physically present in the state can buy lottery tickets at retail locations and win prizes. It’s unclear what will happen to Velasquez-Morales’ money now that he is detained.

Velasquez-Morales will remain in ICE custody until he is removed from the U.S., according to the agency.

“Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the United States and will be removed as quickly as possible,” the press release read. “Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin’s leadership, ICE is delivering on its mission to enforce our nation’s immigration laws, restore accountability and protect American communities.”

Earlier this month, ICE announced that it had broken the record for the highest number of immigrant arrests and deportations in agency history in the 2026 fiscal year with more than 491,000 arrests and more than 483,000 deportations.

“Thanks to President Trump’s leadership, ICE has been unleashed to target and remove illegal aliens so that we can save American lives,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said.

But many Americans find ICE’s tactics too aggressive, with the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens by federal immigration agents last January causing a huge wave of public outcry.

text:
At a recent immigration hearing at the Whipple federal building, 25 kids and a handful of attorneys packed into a court room. Benches filled up; kids ranging in age from 8 or 9 to older teens leaned against the wall and squeezed into corners. One by one, the kids joined their attorneys to talk through their case with a judge.

He appeared on a screen, video calling in from Houston, Texas.

Immigration attorneys say that’s a change. Until recently, a local immigration judge at Fort Snelling typically heard cases for unaccompanied kids — children who arrived in the United States without a parent. But earlier this month, a juvenile docket was assigned to Immigration Judge Jason Stern of the Houston – Greenspoint Park court.

Attorneys say the new judge is attempting to move cases through court faster, and has issued a removal order for a child who had already been granted legal protections.

Stern was first assigned a docket of kids in St. Paul in early November. He heard another on Tuesday. In several of those cases, he set deadlines in December and January for attorneys to file applications for asylum or other legal protections.

Attorney Meg Kaiser was in court Tuesday. She said the pace was unusual.

“It's not uncommon for judges to set deadlines… but it did seem to me like Judge Stern was setting deadlines a lot faster than some other judges would,” Kaiser said.

Stern asked some attorneys why those applications hadn’t been submitted already. One attorney — representing 9- and 12-year-old sisters — said she’s working to determine whether her clients are eligible to apply for asylum, but it’s taking time to work through traumatic memories with the kids.

Some of those kids have already been granted some legal protections — but they’re still seeing their cases sped up.

Several attorneys in court Tuesday told the judge that their clients have Special Immigration Juvenile Status — a legal protection that gives unaccompanied kids a path to get a green card. Many of those kids were still waiting for that green card. Judge Stern asked attorneys in several of those cases to also apply for asylum, or to submit evidence to the court that those cases were moving along.

Madeline Lohman is the advocacy director at the Advocates for Human Rights. She said that’s different than how the St. Paul judge usually handles kids with that legal status.

Lohman said some judges put those kids’ cases on pause while they wait to get a green card. But she said Stern is keeping up hearings and deadlines in those cases, and has ordered one child with that status removed from the country.

“I think it's something that the administration is trying to get judges all over the country to do. I don't think this was the first case ever in the country, but we hadn't seen one before,” Lohman said.

Attorneys also said Stern requires everyone to appear for court in person, while the St. Paul judge who typically hears those cases often allows people to appear via video call.

One attorney representing a teenage boy said his client lives 220 miles away. He asked Judge Stern if he could appear by video call for the next hearing date. An attorney for the Department of Homeland Security opposed. Stern asked for the request in writing, and said he’d rule on it later.

Attorney Kaiser squeezed into the courtroom’s entryway with her clients — a pair of brothers — since seats were full. She said it’s unusual for all of those video-call appearance requests to be rejected.

“I thought that was a bit surprising,” Kaiser said. “I think a lot of the judges at Fort Snelling would allow that in that circumstance.”

Lohman said that creates a barrier for many kids — especially those from North and South Dakota, which also fall under the St. Paul court’s jurisdiction.

“There were kids as young as 11 who were driving 11 hours to get to court, and he denied their request to do their hearing virtually. So that right there, that effort to really inconvenience kids and make it really difficult for them to get to all their court dates, that was different,” Lohman said.

And the stakes for missing a hearing are high. A judge can order a person immediately removed from the country.

Out-of-state judges have taken on cases from Minnesota before, but Lohman said this is the first she’s seen the juvenile docket switched to an out-of-state judge. She wonders if the court is attempting to schedule more kids’ cases more quickly. The change comes as President Donald Trump’s administration has shaken up immigration courts, firing many judges and encouraging deportations.

And, Lohman said, out-of-state judges sometimes have stricter records than those from Minnesota. A legal project tracking judges’ records indicates that Judge Stern grants relief at a lower rate than Judge Kalin Ivany, the St. Paul judge who typically hears juvenile cases.

“I don't know exactly what their rationale is, but the impact of the decision to have out-of-state judges hear Minnesota cases is that cases are being heard by less sympathetic judges who have very low rates of granting protection to children and to asylum seekers,” Lohman said.

In a statement, the Department of Justice said out-of-state judges are sometimes given hearings to reduce court backlogs.

“The Biden Administration allowed millions of unvetted migrants into our communities and intentionally turned a blind eye to hundreds of thousands of unaccompanied alien children in need of care,” a spokesperson said in a statement. “Reducing the immigration court backlog remains one of the highest priorities for this administration.”

Attorneys in Minnesota said they’re not sure whether the switch to an out-of-state judge will be long-term. For now, they’re awaiting more scheduling information while they work with the kids to meet deadlines.

text:
Port Isabel, Texas — On Nov. 17 at 6:30 p.m., agents assigned to the Brownsville Marine unit received information from U.S. Customs and Border Protection’s Air and Marine Operations Center regarding a civilian aircraft flying to Port Isabel, Texas.

Agents from AMO’s Brownsville Marine unit, Border Patrol, and Texas Game wardens responded to inspect the aircraft. The pilots were interviewed and gave consent to have the aircraft inspected - and as a result, eight adult males were discovered inside the airplane. All admitted to being unlawfully present in the United States and in possession of fraudulent identification documents.

“The successful apprehension of eight illegal aliens demonstrates the importance of the strong partnerships between Air and Marine Operations, the U.S. Border Patrol, and Texas Game wardens,” said Deputy Director of Marine Operations Robert Theriot. “This operation goes to show that collaboration, communication, and partnerships among agencies will always be essential as a force multiplier in combatting illegal activity.”

Immigration and Customs Enforcement responded to assist. A total of three male Honduran nationals, two male El Salvadorian nationals, and three male Guatemalan nationals were apprehended. Two adult male U.S. citizens, the pilots, were detained by ICE for questioning, and AMO Brownsville Marine unit seized a 2006 King B350.

Under the leadership of President Donald J. Trump and Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, the dedicated men and women of U.S. Customs and Border Protection, alongside our law enforcement partners, have arrested and removed thousands of criminal aliens from the country—including gang members, rapists, kidnappers, and drug traffickers—to make our communities safer.

text:
Kilmar Ábrego García, the Salvadorian national whose mistaken deportation turned him into a symbol of Donald Trump’s mass deportation efforts, has landed in Spain.

Ábrego García arrived in Madrid on Wednesday after leaving the United States of his own volition.

“I feel free of everything evil that has followed me up until this point,” he told reporters on a video call just hours after he touched down. “I’m happy … because this time I’m leaving with my freedom, not like before when they took me out inhumanely.”

He added: “The government does not decide where my story continues. My family and I will decide our future.”

Prior to his departure, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents met him at the airport and removed his ankle monitor, according to We Are Casa, a Maryland-based advocacy group.

As he made his way through the Madrid airport, Ábrego García did not speak to reporters, instead raising his fist in the air as he climbed into a waiting van.

Ábrego García became a lightning rod in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in 2025 after he was deported to El Salvador in what an official later called an “administrative error”.

The 31-year-old had been living in the US since 2019, after a judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador due to the dangers posed by a gang that had threatened his family. The judge allowed him to live and work in the US under ICE supervision, but he was not given residency status.

Married to an American woman, the Maryland resident was part of a group of more than 200 people sent by the US to Cecot, a notorious anti-terrorism mega-prison, in violation of the US immigration judge’s 2019 order.

Amid public outcry, he was returned to the US after a decision by the supreme court. Since then, Ábrego García has been fighting government efforts to deport him for a second time to a series of African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security officials.

On Wednesday, his lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said the Trump administration had wanted to deport Ábrego García “handcuffed, on an ICE flight bound for Liberia” on Tuesday.

“And what happened? He walked out a free man, without any restrictions, without shackles on his feet. He left for the country of his choosing, and he did so on a commercial flight, alongside everyone else,” Sandoval-Moshenberg added.

He described it as a “complete victory”, adding: “Instead of flying ICE Air, he flew United Airlines. Instead of being in shackles, he was in economy plus.”

He said Ábrego García had negotiated a deal with federal authorities in which they had agreed to allow him to leave the country, removing obstacles such as the ankle monitor and taking him off the no-fly list, as long as he left by 24 November. The Department of Homeland Security said on Tuesday Ábrego García had “self-deported” to Spain.

Sandoval-Moshenberg described Ábrego García’s departure from the US as temporary, saying that he would decide where to settle for the next two years as he waited out the remainder of the Trump administration.

“Mr Ábrego García has many options to return to the United States as the husband of a US citizen spouse and the father of a US citizen child,” he said. “We don’t expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritise reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland.”

On Wednesday, Ábrego García’s lawyer, Chris Newman, said his client had landed in Spain as a tourist and that he had no plans to meet with any politicians while in Spain. “I can confirm that he’s coming here with the intention of staying for just a few days and that he already has tickets, one could say, for his next appointment,” he told Spanish media.

His departure this week was celebrated by many who had sought to push back against the Trump administration’s pursuit of Ábrego García.

“They wanted to leave him there to rot for the rest of his life. Instead, we saw our judicial system work alongside a strong legal team to produce this outcome, where Kilmar Ábrego García is able to chart his own future,” said Senator Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland Democrat who traveled to Cecot to visit Abrego Garcia in April last year.

Van Hollen, who is vying to become Senate majority leader when Democrats regain control of Congress next year, has made Ábrego García’s case and opposition to the administration’s sweeping deportation crackdown central to his vision for the party.

“Ábrego García’s journey is an example of our constitution working despite the attacks of the Trump administration,” Van Hollen added. He said he had spoken with the Spanish ambassador to the United States, Ángeles Moreno Bau, and briefed her on “all the wrongs that have been committed by the Trump administration against Kilmar Ábrego García”, adding that he was pleased Ábrego García was now in Spain and “able to continue telling his story”.

House Republicans are optimistic that President Donald Trump could sign a bipartisan immigration reform bill before Democrats take control of Congress.

They warn that if the president waits until January it could result in legislation containing more "extreme" language that opens the door for amnesty.

"Yes, it's going to happen under this Congress," Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., told Fox News Digital, pointing to the country's labor shortages and Republicans' declining support among Hispanic voters as reasons to pursue immigration reform. "I think it's a win-win for a country, we get a much-needed workforce while providing some accountability for misbehavior."

Bacon's remarks come after Trump signaled during a recent "60 Minutes" interview that he would be open to immigration reform, potentially creating an opportunity for lawmakers to advance the Dignity Act, a bill introduced by Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, R-Fla., in 2025.

WHITE HOUSE DOUBLES DOWN AFTER TRUMP ANGERS BASE BY FLOATING ILLEGAL ALIEN DEAL WITH DEMS

The legislation, which now has over a dozen Republican co-sponsors, would provide certain undocumented immigrants who meet eligibility requirements with renewable legal status and work authorization, without establishing a direct pathway to citizenship.

However, Bacon warned that delaying the legislation until the 120th Congress, when Democrats will control both chambers, could result in a more expansive immigration package.

"Unfortunately, I think the Dems will make it more like an amnesty bill," Bacon told Fox News Digital. "They'll probably go to another extreme."

Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., added to Fox News Digital that "there is no better solution on the table that will get support from both parties while simultaneously standing in the way of the Democrats' looming amnesty-ridden citizenship-for-all alternative."

"The best way to see the work the administration is doing continue into the next two years while Democrats are in control of both houses is to pass a Republican-led immigration plan before January," Stutzman continued.

GOP INFIGHTING ERUPTS OVER IMMIGRATION BILL THAT WOULD SHIELD MILLIONS FROM DEPORTATION

Salazar previously told Fox News Digital that Trump's willingness to discuss immigration reform could create an opportunity to advance her legislation before Republicans lose control of Congress.

"I think that this is a very good window to concentrate on something that even the president said that he was willing to work with the Dems, which is immigration," Salazar said.

TRUMP ADMITS IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT MAY HAVE BEEN TOO 'TOUGH' IN FIRST INTERVIEW SINCE MIDTERMS

The bill's original sponsor also expressed hope that Trump could make immigration reform a defining part of his presidential legacy, comparing the opportunity to Abraham Lincoln's role in ending slavery.

Senate Democrats., like Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., told Fox News Digital that he would be willing to work with Salazar on pushing for the immigration bill.

text:
Kilmar Abrego García, a Salvadoran man whose wrongful deportation from the United States put him at the centre of a controversy over US President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, arrived in Madrid on Wednesday.

His case became a focal point in the debate over Trump's mass deportation policy in 2025, raising concerns about migrants' rights to challenge deportation orders and the administration's compliance with court rulings.

Wearing sunglasses and a baseball cap, Abrego García made his way to a vehicle at Madrid airport without speaking to reporters gathered at the scene, according to AFP journalists.

"While details remain private, Kilmar is planning on hosting various international speaking engagements, with stops planned in different countries," We Are CASA, a US immigrant advocacy group which has been supporting him, said in a statement.

The Salvadoran ultimately left the United States voluntarily on a commercial flight bound for Spain.

"I am leaving happy, I am leaving with my freedom," he said in a statement released by We Are CASA.

The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) confirmed his departure from the country in a statement, in which it labelled Abrego García a "trafficker, wife beater, gang member, and child predator."

"We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain," said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, quoted in the statement.

His lawyers, for their part, welcomed the fact that their client had been able to leave "on his own terms" after his long-running dispute with the US immigration authorities.

One of his legal representatives, Simón Sandoval-Moshenberg, said the departure brought an end to a deportation campaign he described as "retaliation". He also stressed that the move to Spain is temporary and that Abrego García, who is married to a US citizen, hopes to return to the United States once Donald Trump leaves the White House.

Deported "by mistake" to Bukele's mega-prison

His case began in March 2025, when federal agents arrested Abrego García in the street. Days later he was deported to El Salvador and sent to the Terrorism Confinement Centre (CECOT), a controversial maximum-security mega-prison built on the orders of President Nayib Bukele and intended to house alleged members of criminal gangs.

The deportation went ahead even though there was a court order expressly prohibiting his deportation to El Salvador, where he had received threats from armed groups before leaving the country. The US government itself later acknowledged that it had been "a mistake", although it initially resisted facilitating his return.

Back in the United States, Abrego García reported having suffered beatings, sleep deprivation and psychological torture during the almost three months he was held in CECOT.

The legal battle reached the US Supreme Court, which ordered the Trump administration to facilitate his return. The authorities eventually brought him back to the country, although they did so in the context of a criminal investigation that led to an indictment over his alleged involvement in a migrant-smuggling network.

However, a federal judge ultimately dismissed all the charges, ruling that the indictment was in fact motivated by a desire to retaliate against the Salvadoran for having opposed his deportation.

The Trump administration tried to deport him to Africa

As the criminal case progressed, the US government continued trying to deport him from the country. The authorities considered sending him to Uganda, Ghana and Eswatini, but failed to secure agreement from those countries to receive him. Meanwhile, Abrego García applied for asylum to prevent his deportation.

The dispute became one of the most high-profile cases under Trump's immigration policy and highlighted the differences between the executive and judicial branches over the limits of presidential powers regarding deportations.

Throughout the process, the US president and several members of his administration publicly accused the Salvadoran of belonging to Mara Salvatrucha, also known as MS-13, as well as of human trafficking and assaulting his wife, all allegations that were echoed in the statement published on Tuesday by the DHS announcing his departure from the country.

However, these accusations were called into question by the courts. In fact, federal judge Paula Xinis, who oversaw part of the litigation in Maryland, went so far as to open a contempt-of-court inquiry against some of the prosecutors involved in the case for allegedly repeatedly disobeying her orders.

Now, with Madrid as his first stop, Abrego García plans to travel to other countries to take part in various events and speak about his experience, according to Sandoval-Moshenberg.

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said on Tuesday that they’ve arrested 115 individuals in Indiana over “several weeks” in what they called a “targeted enforcement operation.”

In a press release from the agency, it said the arrests included undocumented or noncitizens and also involved individuals supposedly convicted of various crimes, but details on all of the arrestees were not provided in the release.

It was also unclear where the arrests occurred and the time frame in which they were made.

This announcement follows the five-day operation ICE conducted late this summer that resulted in 426 arrests, called “Operation Safe Community.” Most of those arrests happened in the Indianapolis metro area, but ICE also detained people throughout the state.

Among those recently arrested, the agency claims 18 had final removal orders from judges within the U.S. Department of Justice’s Executive Office for Immigration Review.

“This operation reinforces a fundamental principle: Federal immigration laws will be enforced in every American community, regardless of its size or location,” said ICE Chicago Assistant Field Office Director Raymond Hernandez.

Indiana falls under Chicago’s ICE operational jurisdiction.

ICE announced earlier this month that it had conducted 491,000 immigration arrests and more than 483,000 deportations in fiscal year 2026. That’s the most in the agency’s history, and more than last year’s record of around 442,000 deportations.

In its press release, the agency said enforcement operations “are highly targeted, and officers conduct due diligence.” They also said officers know who they are targeting in advance.

A new report from the immigration reform advocacy group FWD.us showed that the number of state and local officers working with ICE has doubled in the last eight months.

The report analyzes the federal ICE program, called 287(g), that deputizes state and local police for immigration enforcement.

Indiana lawmakers and officials have been pushing for more collaboration with ICE. Earlier this year the general assembly passed the FAIRNESS Act, which is meant to force local governments, including school districts, police departments and sheriff’s offices, to comply with federal immigration measures.

However, it looks like few sheriffs in the state have taken up the chance to join the 287(g) agreement.

In a September press release, Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita said only seven sheriffs across the state had entered into such an agreement with ICE.

“Agreements like these do not take away from local law enforcement; they only add to their ability to keep communities safe,” Rokita said. “They also open up opportunities to obtain federal funding to enhance public safety.”

title: How the Trump administration is evading oversight over last 2 weeks
description:
Then simply ignoring the courts, and finally immigration: a record 483,200 deportations, and new restrictions on legal immigration.

Avoiding oversight The Democrats won control of Congress, and from January they will be able to hold hearings, issue subpoenas and launch investigations.

text:
Here are some things you might have missed in last two weeks.

First, restricting oversight before the Democrats take over Congress in January. Then simply ignoring the courts, and finally immigration: a record 483,200 deportations, and new restrictions on legal immigration.

Every action, with sources, is on the Trump Action Tracker and subtitles are available.

Full text below.

***********************************

I want to cover three things today - the ways the administration is trying to avoid oversight since losing the midterms, then some more examples of how the Trump administration is simply ignoring the courts. And I’ll end on immigration, which I haven’t covered in a while. Everything here is from the last two weeks.

Avoiding oversight

The Democrats won control of Congress, and from January they will be able to hold hearings, issue subpoenas and launch investigations. The Trump administration’s response has been to hinder that oversight before it starts.

On the 21st November, Trump signed an executive order requiring companies that hold federal contracts to tell the White House before they share anything with Congress, and to withhold whatever the administration decides is confidential. So the firms that do business with the government are being told to clear it with the White House before they answer Congress.

The New York Times reported that the White House and Justice Department are coordinating to resist investigations, expanding claims of executive privilege and preparing to fight congressional subpoenas, while warning senior Democrats that their oversight could carry criminal consequences.

And those warnings are already going out. A US attorney, Aaron Reitz, told Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal he was under investigation for running a congressional inquiry into donations to Trump’s building projects. Days later Reitz sent a similar letter to Senator Elizabeth Warren, the likely incoming chair of the Senate Banking Committee, warning of significant legal consequences and telling her to preserve her records, without naming any crime she might be committing. Trump then posted the Warren letter publicly. Oversight is one of the constitutional jobs these senators were elected to do.

The administration is going after the courts too. On the 14th November, the Justice Department asked the Supreme Court to limit a key power of federal judges. At the moment, when a single judge determines that a government rule illegal, they can block it everywhere in the US, for everyone. The Justice Department wants that struck down, so that a ruling only protects the particular people who brought the case. In practice that would mean a rule a court has declared unlawful could carry on being enforced against everyone else, until everyone has gone to court separately. It is worth saying this is contested legal ground, and the Supreme Court already narrowed applicability of these nationwide rulings last year. But weakening this further would blunt the main way a single court can stop an unlawful policy in its tracks.

Sources

Executive order: federal contractors must notify the White House before giving Congress information (Reuters)

White House and DOJ coordinate to resist Democratic investigations and subpoenas (New York Times)

US Attorney Reitz tells Sen. Blumenthal he is under investigation over a congressional inquiry (PBS)

Reitz warns incoming Banking chair Sen. Warren of “significant legal consequences” (Reuters)

DOJ asks the Supreme Court to curb judges’ power to strike down unlawful regulations nationwide (Reuters)

Ignoring the courts

We keep seeing instances of a judge said no, and the administration doing it anyway.

Here are two on the environment from the last fortnight. On the 22nd November, the US Army said it would go ahead and detonate 68 barrels of a toxic explosive, lead azide, in Iowa, even though a federal appeals court had blocked its environmental permit over the risk of lead pollution. The Army invoked an emergency exemption, arguing the explosives were deteriorating and had to be destroyed.

Two days earlier, the administration auctioned off its first deep-sea mining leases near American Samoa, two areas totalling about 13 million hectares, for $3 million each, even though a judge had voided the environmental clearance for the sale because it breached the Endangered Species Act.

Here are two more examples from Immigration policy. In Colorado, a federal judge found ICE in contempt for re-arresting a man within minutes of the court ordering his release. The judge said the practice made a mockery of court orders, and reported that at least 18 people in Colorado had been held past their release dates or re-arrested straight after a judge freed them.

And in a separate case, a judge ruled that the administration had exceeded its authority in stripping Temporary Protected Status from more than 300,000 Venezuelans. Rather than restore it, the Justice Department went back to the Supreme Court, arguing that reinstating their protection would get in the way of deportations, and an appeals court has let the termination stand while the case runs. What this means is that the administration is free to detain and deport these people while the case drags on and thousands already have been deported. If you deport someone before the court has finally ruled, winning the case later does them no good. They’re already gone.

Sources

Army to detonate 68 barrels of lead azide in Iowa despite an appeals court blocking the permit (Reuters)

Deep-sea mining leases auctioned near American Samoa despite a judge voiding the clearance (Guardian)

Judge rules Rollins’ Christian emails to USDA staff unconstitutional; she vows to fight to the Supreme Court (Guardian; Reuters)

Judge finds ICE in contempt for re-arresting a man minutes after court-ordered release (Reuters)

TPS for 300,000+ Venezuelans kept terminated despite a judge finding the administration overstepped (New York Times)

Immigration

So on to immigration, which I haven’t covered in a while. ICE announced this month that it had deported almost half a million people in the year to the end of September 2026. That is more than in any 12-month period in the agency’s 23-year history, is 9% higher than the previous record set the year before and almost 80% higher than the final year of Biden’s administration.

And within these huge numbers are mistakes and attempts to bury them. The Justice Department has now admitted that Brian José Morales García, detained in Texas and deported to Mexico in April 2026, is a US citizen. Garcia says officers ignored his attempts to prove his citizenship and pressured him into signing deportation papers under threat of jail. The government had publicly called him an illegal immigrant; it now says he left voluntarily. He was let back into the US in August 2026 and is suing.

ICE meanwhile has been deleting its record. It deleted at least two of its own official posts that had defended its agents’ violent arrest of Aliya Rahman, an autistic US citizen with physical disabilities who was dragged from her car on the way to a medical appointment. The posts vanished just after she filed a lawsuit. Federal rules generally require those records to be kept.

Finally, there have also been new efforts aimed at deterring new immigration. On the 12th of November, Trump threatened to double tariffs on Mexico if it did not stop around a thousand migrants walking north towards the border.

It touches legal migration too. The administration is increasing restrictions on the 1 million or so international students in the US, with new rules and fees that would make it harder for them to work in the US. Universities say that these rules are deterring students from coming at all. And the Labor Department has proposed tightening the main route by which skilled foreign workers get a green card, extending it even to jobs long treated as shortages, including nurses and top scientists.

text:
The Sonoma County Commission on Human Rights expresses priority response and deep alarm regarding the immigration enforcement actions conducted by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) today in our county, which resulted in the detention of at least 13 individuals. These actions have immediate and lasting effects on families, children, and the broader community.

When community members are detained, children in particular face a sudden separation, loss of stability, emotional trauma, and disruption to schooling, healthcare, and daily life. Entire households can experience economic hardship as the main breadwinner is arrested, along with fear that ripples through our neighborhoods, workplaces, schools, and places of worship. Such outcomes undermine the social fabric and the well-being of Sonoma County residents.

Consistent with our mission to promote social justice, equity and safety among all people, to foster recognition of and appreciation for the diversity of our community, and to help ensure that marginalized and disadvantaged members enjoy the full range of human rights, we urge that enforcement being carried out stop and have a maximum regard for family integrity, due process, and the human dignity of all persons.

We stand in solidarity with the affected families and call for an immediate end to practices that inflict this level of harm on our community. Silence in the face of that fear would not be neutral; it would be a failure of our charge. The Sonoma County Commission on Human Rights rejects and condemns this active human rights violation of any enforcement that prioritizes mass disruption over family integrity and basic human dignity.

The Commission will continue to advocate for policies and actions that defend the rights, safety, and wellbeing of all Sonoma County residents.

—Sonoma County Commission on Human Rights

text:
The Justice Department’s new staffing order changes who defends ICE in court, not the rules a detainee’s petition must follow. Here is how those petitions work.

Attorney General Todd Blanche’s Nov. 24 memo directs lawyers from the department’s Antitrust, Civil, Civil Rights and Environment and Natural Resources divisions, along with the U.S. Trustee Program, to help U.S. Attorneys’ Offices answer habeas corpus petitions filed by people in ICE custody, CBS News reported. The memo counts more than 97,000 detainees who have filed such petitions since January 2025, about 10,000 of them since October 2026.

As reported earlier, the memo is a sign that the government intends to contest more of these cases rather than let them go unanswered. For families and detainees, the practical questions are more basic: what a habeas petition is, who can file one, where it goes, how fast it moves and what a judge can actually order.

What is a habeas petition for an ICE detainee?

A petition for a writ of habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. 2241 asks a federal district judge to decide whether a person’s detention is lawful. It is a civil case in federal court, separate from the removal case in immigration court. It does not decide whether the person can stay in the United States; it decides whether the government may keep holding them while that question is resolved.

Most of the recent petitions challenge the government’s position, adopted in July 2025 and endorsed by the Board of Immigration Appeals in Matter of Yajure Hurtado, that people who entered without inspection are “applicants for admission” subject to mandatory detention under 8 U.S.C. 1225(b)(2)(A), with no bond hearing before an immigration judge. Petitioners typically argue they fall under 8 U.S.C. 1226(a) instead, which allows bond, or that holding them without any hearing violates due process.

Who can file, where, and what does it cost?

Who signs it: Under 28 U.S.C. 2242, the petition must be signed and verified by the detained person or by someone acting on their behalf. Relatives sometimes file as a “next friend,” but courts examine whether that person qualifies, so most petitions are filed by an attorney.

Who is named: The petition must name the person who has custody of the detainee. In practice that usually means the warden of the facility and the ICE field office director, often with DHS officials added.

Where it goes: Petitions are generally filed in the federal district where the person is being held. That is why transfers matter: a move from one state to another can change which court, and which circuit’s law, applies.

The fee: Under 28 U.S.C. 1914(a), the court filing fee for a habeas application is $5, compared with $350 for most civil cases. Attorney’s fees are a separate matter and vary widely.

Finding the right facility first is often the hardest step. Our guide to locating someone missing from the ICE detainee locator covers what to do when the online system comes up empty.

How long does a habeas case take?

The statute is built for speed. Under 28 U.S.C. 2243, when a judge orders the government to show cause, the government’s response is due within three days unless the court allows more time for good cause, up to 20 days. A hearing is to follow within five days of that response, again subject to extensions for good cause.

Real timelines vary. Many judges grant extensions, some decide on the papers without a hearing, and busy districts move slower than the statute contemplates. The Blanche memo is aimed at precisely this pressure point: with more government lawyers available, fewer petitions should go unanswered or be resolved because the government could not respond in time.

What can a judge order?

In the mandatory-detention cases, the most common relief is an order requiring a bond hearing before an immigration judge within a set number of days, or release if no hearing is held. Some judges have ordered outright release. A habeas win does not end the removal case, and judges have recently had to address ICE re-arrests after release by writing conditions into their orders.

Does it matter which state the detainee is held in?

Yes, more than at any point in recent years. According to SCOTUSblog’s Nov. 17 summary, nine federal appeals courts (the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 6th, 7th, 9th, 10th and 11th Circuits) have rejected the government’s reading of Section 1225(b)(2)(A), while the 5th and 8th Circuits have accepted it. The 5th Circuit, sitting en banc on Oct. 23 in Sosnava Rodriguez, also held there is no due process right to a bond hearing for people never admitted, which practitioners at the National Immigration Project say leaves no bond-hearing right for that group in Texas, Louisiana or Mississippi.

Habeas remains available in those states on other grounds, such as whether a person is properly classified under the mandatory-detention statute at all, according to CLINIC and the National Immigration Project. But a detainee held in Texas faces a very different legal landscape from one held in New Jersey or Washington.

What the Supreme Court case could change

On Oct. 1, the Supreme Court agreed to hear Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, No. 26-104, a government appeal from a unanimous 2nd Circuit ruling for a Brazilian man who had lived in the U.S. for more than 20 years. No argument date has been set; SCOTUSblog expects argument in late winter or spring, which points to a decision by mid-2027. Our earlier coverage of the case heading to the Court explains the statutory dispute.

If the government wins, much of the current habeas volume could shrink, because the statutory argument behind most petitions would be foreclosed nationwide, leaving constitutional and individual classification claims. If the detainees win, bond hearings would be required in immigration court nationwide, and the 5th and 8th Circuit rulings on the statute would fall.

Quick answers

Does the DOJ memo change the law on ICE habeas petitions? No. It reassigns government lawyers. The legal standards and deadlines are the same.

Can a family member file a habeas petition for someone in ICE detention? The statute allows someone acting on the detainee’s behalf, but courts scrutinize next-friend filings, so an attorney is usually involved.

How much does it cost to file? The federal court filing fee is $5. Legal fees are separate.

How fast will a judge rule? The statute sets a three-day response deadline, extendable to 20 days, but actual timing varies by court.

Will winning stop deportation? No. Habeas addresses detention; the removal case continues in immigration court.

This article is for general information and is not legal advice.

title: Gov. Shapiro, Sec. Redding Hold Roundtable on Federal Immigration Enforcement
description:
It is clear that this nation needs comprehensive immigration reform that works with our farmers, not against them,” said Governor Shapiro.
From poultry and dairy to specialty crops, livestock, and food processing, the industry’s success depends on the people who make the entire food system work.
Industry sectors like mushrooms and poultry production have seen the biggest disruptions across various parts of their supply chains as a result.
The Pennsylvania State Police and Commonwealth agencies do not conduct immigration enforcement.
"Disruptions to our agricultural workforce are costly for our farmers and for the entire Commonwealth.
text:
Marietta, PA – Today, Governor Josh Shapiro and Pennsylvania Department of Agriculture Secretary Russell Redding held a roundtable discussion led by PennAg Industries Association at Hershey Ag(opens in a new tab) with farmers, agricultural organizations, and industry leaders from across the Commonwealth to discuss increased U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) activity across Pennsylvania and the effects those enforcement actions are having on the industry and its workforce.

Pennsylvania’s food processing, meat, poultry, mushroom, dairy, and agricultural sectors rely heavily on experienced immigrant workers and as a coalition of agricultural leaders wrote this week(opens in a new tab), recent federal immigration actions have resulted in substantial workforce losses across the Commonwealth. These losses result in sudden workforce disruptions which can have immediate animal-welfare, operational, and economic consequences that extend well beyond an individual business, ultimately affecting consumers and the nation’s food supply.

“For months, I’ve heard directly from farmers all across the Commonwealth who have raised their concerns about the way that the federal government’s cruel, chaotic immigration policies are making it hard for their workers. It is clear that this nation needs comprehensive immigration reform that works with our farmers, not against them,” said Governor Shapiro. “My Administration has repeatedly called on members of our federal delegation and the Trump Administration, urging them to listen to our farmers and work with them to develop comprehensive immigration reform that shows respect for our neighbors and keeps our border secure while creating legal, reliable pathways for agricultural labor. We will continue to shine a light on this issue and advocate for our farms and the workers who keep them running smoothly and help families across Pennsylvania and our country put food on the table.”

Pennsylvania is home to nearly 48,800 farms, and its agriculture industry contributes $132.5 billion to the Commonwealth’s economy and supports nearly 600,000 jobs. From poultry and dairy to specialty crops, livestock, and food processing, the industry’s success depends on the people who make the entire food system work.

“Farmers are asking for a system that recognizes the realities of running a farm and respects the essential people who make it possible,” said Secretary Redding. “When workers are afraid to come to work, or employers don’t know whether they can count on the people caring for their animals, harvesting their crops, and processing their products, the consequences reach far beyond the farm. Today’s conversation is about listening to our industry, standing with our agriculture community and the workers who deserve our support, and making sure Pennsylvania agriculture is part of the national conversation about immigration reform.”

The roundtable was held at Hershey Ag where agribusinesses in the company’s surrounding region — and all across the Commonwealth — have been targeted by ICE and impacted by Temporary Protected Status (TPS) terminations.

“While we have wonderful, efficient systems — that are, today, more sustainable and more efficient than ever — they also are highly interconnected and highly dependent on what happens with the people who are here every day. They are tightly managed and time-sensitive,” said Brent Hershey, Owner and President, Hershey Ag. “We need common sense here [to avoid] the destruction of the food system… We’re happy with secure borders, but we need a program that we can follow, and that program needs to be honored. We're playing by the rules, we're hitting the target — so don't take it away in the middle.”

Among the companies represented at today’s roundtable, more than 1,000 of their employees have lost legal status protection due to sudden changes in TPS, visas, and other legal pathways to live and work in the United States. Industry sectors like mushrooms and poultry production have seen the biggest disruptions across various parts of their supply chains as a result.

“In September, we met with the Governor to talk about this issue. Rather than he make a statement, he asked to stand with us instead, so here we are today, a room full of folks from all different segments of agriculture,” said Chris Herr, President of PennAg Industries Association. “We want a secure border — mission accomplished — we're happy about that, but we also believe it's important that Congress and the Administration in Washington fix this problem.”

Throughout the conversation, participants emphasized the need for an immigration system that strengthens border security, respects the rule of law, and recognizes the essential role immigrant workers play in the nation’s food supply. This also follows a joint letter(opens in a new tab) signed by 32 agricultural organizations and employers to the U.S. Secretaries of Agriculture Brooke Rollins and Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, expressing concern that employees with legal status have been detained during recent enforcement actions and that aggressive enforcement activity has caused other workers with legal status to miss work, out of fear.

“Our farm, along with several others, have had local workers detained and deported after traffic stops during their morning commute… And being here legally does not get you a get out of jail free card for harassment from ICE. We have H-2A workers, and they come on visas to pick seasonal fruit for us,” said Sarah Zost, President of the State Horticultural Association of Pennsylvania and fourth-generation fruit grower. “But there's a culture of fear and concern because you get targeted because of what you look like… and it causes lost time on all farms because workers, regardless of visa status, stay home. The immigrant workforce is a critical part of agriculture and we literally cannot grow and harvest fruit without them.”

While bipartisan solutions are pursued, industry leaders have continued urging local and federal officials to conduct enforcement actions that prioritize dangerous criminals rather than essential workers who provide much of the food Americans eat. Included in these appeals are calls for enforcement to be carried out lawfully, transparently, and with respect for due process, including clear communication with affected employers and communities. The Pennsylvania State Police and Commonwealth agencies do not conduct immigration enforcement.

“We've always had a good relationship with local law enforcement in the past, and when ICE has shown up in our facility, we've cooperated with them. We've helped them with any warrants that existed, and this year, just out of precaution, we went to local law enforcement and said ‘we want to reiterate that we want to be an open book. If there is a warrant for anybody in our organization, we want to cooperate with you,’” said Astin Melhorn, President of Paragon Poultry Management Group. “In August and September of this year, we had three of our crew vans stopped [by ICE], leaving company housing and heading towards our facility to get showered in for work. To our knowledge, there were no warrants and there was nothing presented, but in total, we lost 17 workers — some of which have work permits and others who were shipped as far as Oklahoma, and when they were released, they had to find their way back to Pennsylvania… That has very much rocked our world and our industry… and it’s a very frustrating thing when you’re an employer trying to do things correctly.”

Shapiro Administration’s Work to Strengthen Pennsylvania’s Agricultural Industry and Support its Workforce

Since taking office, the Shapiro Administration has worked to strengthen Pennsylvania’s agricultural workforce through investments in workforce development, agricultural education, and career pathways, while supporting an environment where agricultural businesses can grow and create opportunity.

This work has included additional steps to address critical workforce needs — and combat chaotic and cruel federal immigration policy:

In February 2025, Governor Shapiro signed legislation allowing permanent legal residents to become certified poultry technicians after completing a state-administered training course, helping expand the pool of qualified workers available to meet critical industry needs.

In July 2026, the Shapiro Administration confirmed(opens in a new tab) the federal government would not move forwardwith proposed ICE detention centers in Berks and Schuylkill counties, following administrative orders(opens in a new tab) issued by the PA Department of Environmental Protection.

In October 2026, the PA Department of Agriculture unveiled their Strategic Plan for Agriculture(opens in a new tab), recognizing that a robust and well-trained ag workforce is the backbone for a strong agricultural economy — prioritizing workforce development and recruitment as a key pillar of the Shapiro Administration’s work to ensure Pennsylvania agriculture remains profitable and globally competitive.

The Administration has also developed multilingual “Know Your Rights(opens in a new tab)” resources and regularly engages with immigrant advocates, service providers, and local officials to understand the impacts of changing federal immigration policies.

"Disruptions to our agricultural workforce are costly for our farmers and for the entire Commonwealth. Like every sector of our economy, agriculture depends on a reliable workforce. Farmers need workers to harvest crops, work in food processing plants and perform essential tasks that help put food on our tables,” said Senator Judith Schwank, Democratic Chair of the Agriculture & Rural Affairs Committee. “The indiscriminate and inhumane targeting of immigrant communities by the federal government is not only morally wrong, but it's also depriving Pennsylvania's agricultural industry of the hardworking individuals it relies on to sustain food production and support our economy."

title: A timeline of key events in Kilmar Ábrego García's fight with the Trump administration
description:
In a civil case in Maryland, Ábrego García challenged the Department of Homeland Security’s attempts to deport him to a series of African countries.
Here is a timeline of key events: Arrival: around 2011 Ábrego García flees El Salvador for the U.S. as a teenager.
Deportation: March 15, 2025 Ábrego García is mistakenly deported to El Salvador and held in a notoriously brutal prison.
In immigration custody: Aug. 25, 2025 Ábrego García reports to an immigration office in Baltimore and is taken into custody.
Self-deportation: Nov. 24, 2026 Ábrego García leaves the U.S. voluntarily for Spain, departing from Washington Dulles International Airport.
text:
Kilmar Ábrego García entered the news in March 2025 after he was deported to El Salvador despite a court ruling that should have prevented it. His complicated legal fight after that galvanized both sides of the debate over President Donald Trump’s immigration policies.

In a civil case in Maryland, Ábrego García challenged the Department of Homeland Security’s attempts to deport him to a series of African countries. A criminal case in Tennessee, where the government accused him of human smuggling, was dismissed after a judge found evidence of “vindictive prosecution” by the Justice Department. Months later, Ábrego García self-deported to Spain, potentially ending a defining saga of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

Here is a timeline of key events:

Arrival: around 2011

Ábrego García flees El Salvador for the U.S. as a teenager.

Arrest: March 28, 2019

Ábrego García is arrested outside a Maryland hardware store. Police accuse him of being a gang member and turn him over to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Immigration court: Oct. 10, 2019

A Maryland immigration judge rules that Ábrego García cannot be deported to El Salvador, where a gang has threatened his family. He is given a work permit and placed under federal supervision.

Detained by ICE: March 12, 2025

Ábrego García is detained by ICE in Maryland while driving home with his 5-year-old son.

Deportation: March 15, 2025

Ábrego García is mistakenly deported to El Salvador and held in a notoriously brutal prison.

Supreme Court: April 10, 2025

The U.S. Supreme Court says the Trump administration must work to bring Ábrego García back.

Senator visits: April 17, 2025

In defiance of Trump, Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland meets with Ábrego García at a hotel in El Salvador, helping to establish hope and momentum for Ábrego García’s family.

Criminal charges: June 6, 2025

Ábrego García is returned to the U.S. and charged with human smuggling, based on a Tennessee traffic stop from 2022.

Attempts at second deportation: July 23, 2025

ICE announces plans to remove him to a series of African countries, but is blocked by an injunction from a Maryland federal judge.

Released from jail: Aug. 22, 2025

Ábrego García leaves the Tennessee jail, where he has been since June, to return to his family in Maryland and await trial. Within minutes of his release, ICE sends notice that they intend to deport him to Uganda.

In immigration custody: Aug. 25, 2025

Ábrego García reports to an immigration office in Baltimore and is taken into custody.

Judge orders release: Dec. 11, 2025

A federal judge in Maryland orders ICE to immediately release Ábrego García.

No immigration detention: Feb. 17, 2026

A Maryland federal judge rules ICE cannot re-detain Ábrego García.

Judge dismisses criminal case: May 22, 2026

A federal judge in Tennessee dismisses the human smuggling case against Ábrego García after finding evidence that the government engaged in “ vindictive prosecution."

Prosecutors argue for reinstating criminal charges: Aug. 17, 2026

The Justice Department tells a federal appeals court that the federal judge in Tennessee erred in his scathing May ruling in the criminal case against Ábrego García.

Self-deportation: Nov. 24, 2026

Ábrego García leaves the U.S. voluntarily for Spain, departing from Washington Dulles International Airport. According to an unsealed Nov. 20 order, a federal judge said the government informed her that Ábrego García was free to self-deport “to any country that is willing to accept him.” The judge, in turn, set Nov. 24 as the deadline for his departure and ordered the removal of his GPS ankle monitor before he boarded the flight.

Arrival in Spain: Nov. 25, 2026

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detained a Princeton University doctoral candidate on Nov. 19 at an airport in Arlington, Virginia. Her colleagues, classmates, and lawmakers are calling for her immediate release ahead of Thanksgiving Weekend.

Eva Yi Xie, a Chinese national, was detained at the Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport as she departed from an annual conference of the Society for Neuroscience. Xie’s lawyers say that she was not presented with a warrant.

She was later taken to the Caroline Detention Center in Virginia, a court filing says. U.S. District Judge Anthony Trenga ordered the federal government to respond to a petition challenging Xie’s detention by 5 p.m. E.T. on Wednesday. In the meantime, he ordered ICE not to transfer or remove Xie from the Eastern District of Virginia.

According to court documents, Xie, 24, came to New York on a travel visa with her family in March 2016. Four months later, Xie’s mother applied for asylum. The family’s case is still pending, with a hearing scheduled for January 2028. Xie was granted work authorization and does not have any criminal history.

Kerry Doyle, a lawyer who represents Xie, tells TIME that Xie has received “unprecedented” support from Princeton, as well as the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where Xie earned her undergraduate degree in 2024. She says that there is an effort to collect letters of support in order to facilitate her release.

“We have this incredibly talented student—and by all accounts, an incredible person—who studies neuroscience. She has a very great future, and we're arresting her at the airport for no reason,” Doyle says.

In a statement shared with TIME, an ICE spokesperson says that a pending asylum application does not confer legal status and that Xie never held “valid authorization to study in the United States.”

“Xie was admitted to the United States on a temporary basis on March 16, 2016, but chose to violate our nation’s laws by refusing to depart by the required date of September 15, 2016,” the spokesperson says.

Democratic Senator Andy Kim of New Jersey, where Princeton is located, wrote on X on Monday that his office has been in touch with the school, Xie, and DHS in an effort to get more information and get her home.

“It's heartbreaking to see her detained and turned into another example of this administration's cruel immigration policies,” he said.

About 250 people showed up to a “Free Eva” rally at Princeton University on Monday in support of Xie. The organizers put together a phone bank to urge supporters to contact their federal representatives on Xie’s behalf.

Brody Lab, a neuroscience research group at Princeton, announced Xie’s arrest in a social media post last week and has since urged followers to contact congressional lawmakers to advocate for her prompt release. It says that Xie messaged the lab’s Slack channel for help when she got detained.

Rodney Priestley, the dean of the Graduate School at Princeton University, said last Friday that Xie’s detention was “distressing.” The university has provided legal counsel to Xie and remains in contact with Xie’s family.

Xie’s PhD adviser Carlos Brody told the Associated Press in an interview on Tuesday that Xie called into a weekly lab meeting to thank her coworkers for their support and is in “remarkable spirits.”

Adrian Bondy, a research scholar in the lab, told AP that even in detention, Xie “wants the science to continue and is thinking about scientific ideas.”

Xie is not the first researcher arrested by ICE. Science reported that Di Liu, a chemistry assistant professor at Arizona State University with a valid work visa, was detained by ICE in July at an airport on his way to a scientific conference in Nashville, Tennessee. A few days later, he was released without explanation. Last year, Tufts researcher Rumeysa Ozturk was detained by ICE in Cambridge, Massachusetts. She decided in April 2026 to voluntarily leave the U.S.

Two days after Xie’s arrest, ICE officers detained a father and daughter at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as passengers boarded an Alaska Airlines flight to Los Angeles. A viral video captured the moment when Mexican immigrant Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza and his daughter, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, were arrested. It showed Hernandez Mejia pleading for help before being dragged out of the jet bridge.

The recent arrests continue a trend seen throughout the Trump Administration’s second term. Stateline reported that there was a nationwide goal of 2,000 ICE arrests a day; a senior Department of Homeland Security (DHS) official told NBC News that officers were averaging 20 to 40 arrests a day at U.S. airports as of August.

Since May 2025, ICE has been obtaining traveler information through the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) through a previously undisclosed data-sharing program, according to records obtained by the watchdog group American Oversight. The New York Times reported that the program gives ICE access to the names and birth dates of passengers whom the TSA believes may be subject to arrest.

On July 21, two plainclothes ICE agents arrested Chantal Morales Rojas, a 27-year-old from Ecuador, at the jet bridge at Denver International Airport. The next day, ICE arrested Ethiopian Berhanu Kibret, a University of Maryland School of Pharmacy instructor returning from a conference where he received a teaching award, at the University of Maryland at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport.

The Trump Administration has also broadened its use of administrative warrants. Previous Administrations used such warrants to arrest people who were already in deportation proceedings. More recently, they have also been used in cases involving immigrants who are actively applying to renew their immigration status.

“In the past, people like that have never been prioritized for deportation if they pose no other public safety threat, given that they're taking steps to get into compliance with the law,” Gupta says.

“Our policy right now is to go after the worst of the worst,” DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said during a congressional hearing last week. “When we encounter someone here illegally, I am required to find out who they are.”

text:
Inundated by thousands of ICE detainee lawsuits, DOJ directs non-immigration attorneys to help with caseload

WASHINGTON, D.C. (CBS NEWS) — The Justice Department has directed attorneys from across its civil litigation divisions to help defend the Trump administration against a growing number of lawsuits filed by individuals in immigration detention.

More than 97,000 detainees have filed habeas corpus petitions challenging their detention since January 2025, including approximately 10,000 new petitions just since October 2026 alone, according to a Nov. 24 memo obtained by CBS News.

Habeas petitions are a legal mechanism through which individuals may challenge the lawfulness of their detention.

Prior to the second Trump administration, the federal caseload for habeas immigration detention petitions tended to be much lower — closer to a few hundred in an entire year.

It can take weeks or even months to resolve an immigration habeas petition.

The Justice Department says the litigation is straining resources at U.S. attorneys’ offices, which have been primarily responsible for handling the cases.

“Many of the Department’s U.S. Attorneys’ Offices have been overwhelmed by the influx of petitions and impracticable procedures set by the courts,” Attorney General Todd Blanche wrote in a three-page memo.

The memo directs attorneys from the department’s Antitrust, Civil, Civil Rights, and Environment and Natural Resources divisions and U.S. Trustees Program, to assist with the litigation — roughly 2,000 litigators across its civil components.

The memo doesn’t specify how many attorneys will be reassigned or how many cases they will be expected to handle.

Attorneys from the offices of the attorney general, deputy attorney general and associate attorney general will also take on additional cases.

Immigration-related habeas cases have skyrocketed since President Trump returned to office, as his administration has placed record numbers of individuals in ICE detention and narrowed the avenues for them to be released, including on bond.

Blanche characterized many of the habeas petitions as “frivolous” in his memo.

“The increase in habeas petitions resulted, in part, from the immigration bar’s attempt to thwart President Trump’s promise to the American people to prioritize their safety and security,” he wrote.

Last year, Stephen Miller, the architect of the Trump administration’s deportation policy and now the White House chief of staff, floated the idea of suspending the right of habeas corpus for those detained as part of Mr. Trump’s crackdown on illegal immigration.

The administration has not moved forward with the proposal, which would likely trigger swift legal challenges.

description:
Federal immigration officers came under fire in July after the deadly shooting of two immigrants, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine.
But those who want body-worn cameras say they're still waiting to see if the program is fully implemented, and if footage from incidents is publicly released.
Multi-year effort to push for cameras Money provided by congressional Republicans last year made ICE the highest-funded federal law enforcement agency.
ICE has been looking at how to equip its officers with body-worn cameras for at least five years.
President Joe Biden ordered federal law enforcement to wear body cameras and make other reforms in a 2022 executive order.
text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement says it now has enough body cameras to equip all its officers and agents. The update comes after years of immigration officials telling lawmakers and advocates that they did not have enough devices for a body-worn camera program to be implemented agency-wide. "Training required to equip individual officers remains ongoing and we expect to complete this training soon," an unnamed spokesperson told NPR in a statement. A DHS report from 2024 says ICE expected body cameras to be implemented agency-wide by September 2025; it's now been a year since that prediction. The initial effort was part of a broader Biden administration executive order to expand federal law enforcement use of body cameras.
