text:
By Diane Taylor

October 26, 2026

Tasks from determining asylum seekers’ ages to border surveillance now involve AI, says Open Rights Group.

AI has been embedded across the Home Office in near-total secrecy, reinforcing the so-called hostile environment for immigration, according to research.

Tasks from the detection of potential sham marriages to determining the age of asylum seekers and checking through the contents of phones of new arrivals now involve use of the technology, according to a report by Open Rights Group (ORG).

It is also being used to conduct surveillance of borders, through live facial recognition and AI-powered drones and satellites; to summarise asylum interviews and country policy information used as evidence in those interviews; and to prioritise and assess cases through the opaque Identify and Prioritise Immigration Cases (Ipic) tool.

Information for the report has been gathered from a mix of limited information published by the Home Office, freedom of information requests and questions from MPs. The report has cross-party support from Labour’s Bell Ribeiro-Addy, the Scottish National party’s Pete Wishart and the Green party’s Siân Berry.

The report, titled Automated Discrimination: Unpacking the Digital Hostile Environment, raises concerns about the use of AI in immigration, saying it is not neutral or accurate and can replicate bias and discrimination within society, particularly when a key driver for its use is anti-immigration policies and rhetoric.

It says AI is being trialled and tested in near-total secrecy, with officials routinely invoking national security to stonewall freedom of information requests and redact disclosures. Successive governments are criticised for pushing an ideology that reduces complex human cases to a technical problem that can be fixed.

The report raises concerns about “reducing people to data points” and replicating the hostile environment first envisaged by Theresa May as home secretary in 2012. “Relying on AI to decide who gets to stay here and who gets thrown back into danger is a deeply alarming move,” it states.

Open Rights Group is calling on the government to regulate AI and ban uses that are undemocratic and risk human rights violations, such as the use of ChatGPT tools in asylum applications.

It also wants more transparency and stronger freedom of information laws, a narrower definition of national security and a robust public register of government AI tools.

Ribeiro-Addy said: “In spite of questions and requests, the Home Office has been reluctant to publish the documents that would explain how AI is used in asylum processing, what the problems are and how they are being addressed. The department has not explained how it will ensure there is accountability when they fail or justified why some of the most vulnerable people, with the least power, should bear the greatest risks.”

Sara Alsherif, a programme manager at Open Rights Group, said: “Migration is a human phenomenon and experience, not a technical problem that can be fixed by artificial intelligence. We urgently need transparency, accountability and strict regulation to restrict how AI is used and to prevent its wider rollout.”

text:
On Tuesday morning, two elected officials with distinctly different general political ideals — Del. Sam Rasoul of Roanoke and Roanoke County School Board member Tim Greenway — joined together to denounce U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity in the region.

During a press conference at Roanoke’s Williamson Branch Library, they said that policy changes on the federal level need to be made and that conversations about immigration need to happen across the aisle.

There has been a “sharp increase” in ICE enforcement in the Roanoke Valley in the past two weeks, said Jaime McGuire, a Salem immigration attorney with Amaryllis Law. She said around 50 people have been detained in the Roanoke Valley, and another 40 have been detained in Lynchburg. She said ICE has also been active in Blacksburg and Christiansburg but was not able to elaborate.

She said because these numbers are only from community members who have witnessed the detainments, she expects the numbers are actually higher.

An ICE spokesperson, in an email response Tuesday to questions from Cardinal News about the recent activity, wrote that “for operational security and the safety of our officers, ICE will not disclose or discuss law enforcement operations. Every day, DHS enforces the laws of the nation across the country, including in Virginia.”

Included in that email were pictures with convictions listed for five people identified as “criminal illegal aliens” who were detained in Virginia — none in the Roanoke Valley or its general region. The charges range from drug distribution to sexual assault to murder.

The school board is a nonpartisan office. But Greenway, who was first elected to the county school board in 2015, is a Republican who has campaigned and voted as a conservative. Greenway is a “three-time Trump-voter,” according to a press release from Rasoul’s communications team announcing Tuesday’s press conference.

Greenway said Tuesday that the policies coming from the federal government now “do not reflect the Christian Conservative values” that he has “grown up believing in.”

“This is no way to live. This is not us. These are not American values. This is the difference between keeping our streets safe and simply terrorizing some folks,” he said.

Rasoul is a Democrat who is critical of the Trump administration and has built his political career on human rights and other issues such as support of a Green New Deal.

He said that he and Greenway have had open communication on various issues over the years, and the recent spike in ICE activity prompted this conversation.

“We have students who are not going to school, people who are not going to work, taxpaying, even citizens, who are worried about what will happen to me and my family,” Rasoul said. “I just want to thank my Republican colleague Tim Greenway here for saying we need to have a broader conversation. … We’ve gotta pull it out of the partisan sphere and say, how are we going to treat people the way we want them to be treated here in America that we know and love?”

Rasoul said he encourages people to have open conversations about immigration and to reach out to federal representatives. He said he and Greenway have not spoken with U.S. Rep. Ben Cline, R-Botetourt County, but have spoken with a number of other U.S. senators and officials.

“Too many families” are not feeling safe or are being “torn apart,” Rasoul said, “and it’s because of some policies that I believe have just clearly gone too far. Enough is enough.”

Greenway said he and Rasoul have had the opportunity to sit down with some families affected, and it “becomes real. You realize that these are folks trying to become legal who are having obstacles put in their way.

“I don’t want to demonize people, whether it be immigrants or whether it be the folks that are enforcing the policy,” Greenway said. “I feel more strongly that we need to demonize the policy.”

McGuire said in the last two weeks, “working fathers” are being detained in the middle of the workday, and that families are being given no information as to how to find their loved ones. McGuire said in an email Tuesday that in the past two weeks, she has only heard of men being detained.

“This is dramatically different from what I see in my practice everyday,” McGuire said. “Normally, individuals are detained on a random basis or more sporadically. This is very organized enforcement.” In an email, McGuire said her firm does not have an answer as to why this is happening.

She said ICE actions have been more rapid than usual in recent weeks, with individuals being moved outside of the locality or the state quickly. She said due process rights have been violated, but said she was not able to specify any cases due to attorney-client privilege.

Last Wednesday, Roanoke City Councilwoman Vivian Sanchez-Jones and council member-elect Danny Clawson — both Democrats — estimated around 30 people had been detained in three days. Both were connecting with a social media group that was verifying information throughout the week.

Community groups observed and kept track of activity last week outside of an ICE facility in Salem, where large SUVs were entering and leaving the fenced gate throughout the day. Agents at the facility were fully covered and masked, and protesters said there were an unusual number of vehicles outside of the facility. Cars were parked in the grass outside of the fence.

The number of ICE detainees in the Roanoke jail more than tripled in 2025 when compared to 2024, according to the jail’s invoice documents, which Cardinal News obtained from the city.

McGuire, the immigration attorney, said Tuesday that any families who are concerned, even with legal status, should create a plan for action in case of emergency. She said those who have had loved ones detained should reach out to legal counsel as soon as possible, within 24 hours.

Cardinal News staff writer Emily Schabacker contributed to this story.

name: Policy
title: Trump's new, dumb plan to stymie congressional subpoenas.
description:
It’s a transparent attempt to thwart congressional oversight into the administration’s numerous dealings, ranging from the White House ballroom project to violent immigration enforcement practices to the ongoing upheaval at Nvidia.
This executive order is a culmination of recent Trump administration attempts to mount a counterattack on the incoming Democratic-majority Congress.
Then, last week, White House counsel Will Scharf issued a directive to all federal agencies stipulating that they get “approval” from the White House before agreeing to appear before any congressional committee.
The last act came out Friday in the form of this new executive order.
Come January, we’ll be focused on highlighting critical oversight hearings, investigations, and how the Trump administration responds to accountability.
text:
Last week, President Donald Trump pulled out his favorite Sharpie to do what he does best: sign an executive order awarding himself unprecedented power that will result in a nasty legal fight. This latest order has to do with executive privilege and attempts to shield all communications between the White House and federal agencies and contractors from the incoming Democratic congressional majorities who have pledged to investigate the Trump administration. It’s a transparent attempt to thwart congressional oversight into the administration’s numerous dealings, ranging from the White House ballroom project to violent immigration enforcement practices to the ongoing upheaval at Nvidia. The order is classic Trump, setting up the legal groundwork to push back against Congress’ authority in order to protect himself and his allies. However, like many of the executive orders signed during his second term, this latest one tees up a larger constitutional question about the extent of executive branch privilege versus congressional control. Ultimately, the outcome is unlikely to favor the president.

“In order to protect and serve the American people, the executive branch must be able to work closely with its employees and contractors on sensitive matters without fear that confidential information will be released to unauthorized third parties,” is how the president kicked off his executive order. It goes on to claim that Congress can’t seek information from executive branch departments, agencies, employees, or contractors “without a valid legislative purpose that does not intrude on core Executive functions.” The order ends by demanding that federal employees and contractors notify and coordinate with the White House if they receive requests for information related to congressional investigations. If they don’t comply, they can expect contracts to be terminated and could even face debarment—a blacklist that prevents them from ever getting a government contract again.

This executive order is a culmination of recent Trump administration attempts to mount a counterattack on the incoming Democratic-majority Congress. It started when a U.S. attorney in Texas sent out a slew of letters to members of Congress accusing them of engaging in unlawful activity after they pledged to investigate the administration. Then, last week, White House counsel Will Scharf issued a directive to all federal agencies stipulating that they get “approval” from the White House before agreeing to appear before any congressional committee. The last act came out Friday in the form of this new executive order.

“This desperate Executive Order is totally unprecedented and blatantly unlawful. Federal contractors are paid with taxpayer dollars, not Trump’s personal billions (made illegally on the side),” the House Judiciary Committee account posted on X. “Public contractors have both a duty and a right to speak truthfully when Congress calls, and Congress has a duty to investigate and stamp out all the waste, fraud, kickbacks, shakedowns and corruption choking the government and driving up costs.”

While the White House is attempting to assert the doctrine of executive privilege over any and all communications between the executive branch and federal employees and contractors it hires, this isn’t historically how executive privilege has worked. It is a constitutionally protected right, defined as the president’s ability to withhold documents or information in their possession or in possession of the executive branch from the legislative or judicial branches of government. The Supreme Court has affirmed that it’s necessary in order to allow the president to carry out their duties and be free to discuss issues candidly without fear that the deliberations could be made public. Up until this point, as Joyce Vance, a former U.S. attorney for Alabama, recently noted, executive privilege has been understood to protect limited internal deliberations, “not commercial dealings between the government and contractors using public money.”

The extent of executive privilege was famously put to the test during the Watergate scandal, when former Republican President Richard Nixon’s White House faced a criminal indictment. Nixon argued that his recorded conversations with his staff should be covered by executive privilege, thereby shielding him from a federal subpoena. The Supreme Court disagreed, concluding that neither the doctrine of separation of powers nor the executive branch’s need for confidentiality justified absolute presidential privilege, with limited exceptions for military or diplomatic affairs. The United States v. Nixon decision has remained untouched ever since, with executive privilege understood to not supersede “the fundamental demands of due process of law in the fair administration of justice.”

While the White House is pressure testing executive privilege in the context of congressional investigations, it has also been using this strategy in the ongoing litigation over the future of the Kennedy Center. In that case, when lawyers for Ohio Rep. Joyce Beatty attempted to get the Trump administration to hand over dozens of emails and text messages between White House aides, the president’s legal team argued that its communications should be granted executive privilege in order to protect the White House’s ability to speak candidly and confidentially with staff. Judge Christopher R. Cooper, appointed by the Obama administration, is overseeing this case and has indicated an inclination to decide that some but not all of the president’s communications should be protected. It will come down to the context of the conversations: Were they about policy related to the Kennedy Center or about the “color of carpets”?

The administration’s right to executive privilege will weigh against Congress’ right to oversight, and there is plenty of case law and federal law that support Congress’ authority to check the executive branch. Consider the 1967 case Watkins v. United States, when the Supreme Court affirmed that Congress’ oversight power “comprehends probes into departments of the Federal Government to expose corruption, inefficiency or waste,” concluding that “motives alone would not vitiate an investigation which had been instituted by a House of Congress if that assembly’s legislative purpose is being served.”

There’s also the 1975 case Eastland v. United States Servicemen’s Fund, in which SCOTUS similarly concluded that “in determining the legitimacy of a congressional act we do not look to the motives alleged to have prompted it.” This all boils down to how the courts have long made clear that the relevant question isn’t why Congress is investigating a certain issue; “it’s solely whether the investigation has an objectively legitimate purpose,” Steve Vladeck, a law professor at Georgetown University, explained in his One First newsletter.

Last time we checked, investigating potential acts of executive branch corruption, like if donors to Trump’s ballroom project received deferential treatment, and violations of federal law, which include if the Epstein files were publicly released according to the Epstein Files Transparency Act, squarely fall under a legitimate legislative purpose.

It’s also worth mentioning that there are numerous federal laws that protect federal employees’ right to speak with Congress. The Lloyd–La Follette Act of 1912 guarantees federal employees the right to directly share information with Congress without interference or denial; Congress passed the act after the Roosevelt administration tried to ban federal employees from speaking with the legislative body unless they went through a federal agency department head. Without it, as Iowa Republican Sen. Chuck Grassley aptly explained back in 2018, “we would have an aristocratic government, one that would be dominated by the executive branch.”

Incoming chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee Maggie Hassan warned federal contractors that the president’s executive order “does not override their obligation to comply with congressional requests for information or subpoenas.”

We’ll have to wait and see how the fight over executive privilege plays out, at least until the new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3, 2027, and Democrats can officially begin their investigations and issue subpoenas. They’ll have two years to accomplish their accountability agenda, and now, with Trump’s latest order, they may need to bake in time for lengthy legal fights.

“This new EO, dressed up in fancy talk about executive privilege and enhancing efficiencies, is nothing but a naked ploy to try and protect the perpetrators of this corruption,” Lisa Gilbert, co-president of the consumer advocacy group Public Citizen, said in a statement. “It will not succeed. Sunlight is coming, and corrupt administration insiders and contractors, both, will have to face the American people.”

Elsewhere in Jurisprudence

On this week’s episode of Amicus, Dahlia Lithwick discusses how Congress can begin to rebuild the government after Trump took a sledgehammer to core institutions and practices. Dahlia is joined by K. Sabeel Rahman, a former Biden administration official, and their conversation connects DOGE’s slash-and-burn campaign to a longer, much-needed legal project that gets at future policymaking and the Supreme Court.

The Amicus bonus episode gets into the latest SCOTUS drama surrounding Justice Samuel Alito, who at a recent conservative dinner took a dig at attempts to overhaul the court’s composition. Madiba Dennie, of Balls and Strikes, joins the conversation and also discusses the GOP rush to confirm conservative judges.

Despite the heavy dose of hopium that came with this year’s blue tsunami, the Trump administration is barreling ahead with attacks on reproductive health by revealing plans to end workplace accommodations. Mary Ziegler, a law professor and abortion historian, explains in Slate how the end of accommodations for abortion, contraception, infertility treatment, and even miscarriage would weaken the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act while simultaneously endorsing sex discrimination.

Saul Cornell, of Fordham University, breaks down the big gun rights cases the Supreme Court will consider this term and how the legal argument for legalizing assault weapons nationwide rests on a misquote by Justice Antonin Scalia.

Now that Democrats have secured comfortable majorities in Congress, can America finally move away from the Electoral College and elect a president via national popular vote? I explain how it is in fact possible through the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an effort that’s been brewing since the early 2000s and could finally come to fruition.

Executive Dysfunction is going on a brief break over the winter holidays! Now that Democrats have secured majorities in both houses of Congress and intend to take up the gauntlet of accountability, this newsletter will be paused for the month of December as we plan to slightly shift gears in the new year. Come January, we’ll be focused on highlighting critical oversight hearings, investigations, and how the Trump administration responds to accountability. You’ll also be reading a new cast of voices for the first half of 2027, as I will be taking a step back to welcome my first child! We hope you continue to support Slate’s work and enjoy this newsletter, as we still plan to bring you the most important legal stories you may otherwise miss.

title: Immigration Protection as Labor Enforcement - Race, Racism and the Law
description:

text:
Abstract

Excerpted From: Mary Yanik, Immigration Protection as Labor Enforcement, 40 Georgetown Immigration Law Journal 1 (Fall 2025) (444 Footnotes) (Full Document).

Immigrant workers are a significant and growing share of the labor force in the United States and therefore crucial to effective labor policy: there are nearly eight million undocumented workers and over one million temporary guestworkers in the country, with foreign-born workers overall composing over eighteen percent of the civilian work force. Immigrant workers are in every industry, from construction, agriculture, and service to technology, health care, education, and beyond. They work in rural areas and in major cities at factories, farms, construction sites, and office buildings. They usually labor alongside U.S. citizens.

Formally, these immigrant workers enjoy the same labor protections as U.S. citizens. They are entitled to minimum wages, to organize and join unions without retaliation, to health and safety protections on the job, and to not face discrimination on the grounds of race, religion, disability, gender, or pregnancy. But behind this formal legal equality for immigrant workers lies the constant threat of immigration enforcement. Employers exploit immigrant workers because they can wield the threat of deportation against them. That powerful threat can effectively deter workers from complaining about labor abuse and from assisting labor agencies that seek to vindicate these formal labor protections. Some brave immigrant workers defy these threats, report labor violations, and cooperate with investigating labor agencies anyway. Most workers who defy these threats are not deported, but the constant threat lingers, in part because of the history of immigration enforcement in this country, which long targeted organizing workers. Because of this history and these legitimate fears, many more workers stay silent and accept the substandard conditions, because even an exploitive job is better than being ripped away from your home and family only to be permanently banished. Without the assistance of immigrant workers, who provide critical evidence in labor investigations, labor agencies have struggled to enforce the labor protections in their mandates, leaving both immigrant and citizen workers less protected.

Facing this reality, labor agencies charged with enforcing labor protections have tried to adapt. Labor agencies have hired bilingual investigators, reached out to immigrant rights groups and foreign consulates, and moved investigative interviews offsite to community spaces. Labor agencies now reassure immigrant workers that they investigate labor violations, that workers’ immigration status does not matter, and that they will not turn over workers’ information to immigration authorities. These assurances are true: immigrant workers are protected by all major labor laws and labor agencies no longer pass information on to immigration agents (though they did as recently as thirty years ago). But this has not done enough to allay fears because immigration status does matter: it matters to immigration enforcement agents, and therefore, it matters to workers who fear arrest and deportation. Immigration status also matters to employers, who can threaten to report a worker or call in a tip to encourage immigration enforcement against a troublesome worker. Against the backdrop of a long history of threats and actual immigration retaliation by employers, often facilitated by immigration agents, these fears are reasonable.

Knowing this, workers inevitably ask labor organizers, their attorneys (if they have them), or even the labor agencies themselves, “if I help in this labor investigation and then immigration arrests me or my employer calls ICE on me, will I be protected from deportation?”

For years, the answer to this question has been complicated and not exactly reassuring. In general, labor agencies do not have authority over immigration so they cannot grant any immigration protection themselves. Through an intergovernmental agreement, the immigration agencies have agreed to consider standing down from worksite raids where a federal labor agency has an open investigation, but this does not protect an individual worker from other immigration enforcement writ large. Through the same agreement, the immigration agencies screen their tips to generally not act if the source is obvious employer retaliation. But those intergovernmental measures do not offer any form of immigration protection, specifically status or work authorization, to even the most essential witness. Some labor agencies who detect certain crimes, like witness tampering or trafficking, can give the workervictim a pathway to applying for a U visa for certain crimes. Only some are eligible, and the pathway generally requires the help of an attorney with a waiting period longer than ten years for full adjudication of the application.

However, under a policy that was announced under the Biden administration, the answer to this essential question regarding workers’ fears in reporting labor abuse became more clear. On January 13, 2023, Biden’s Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced a “streamlined process” to consider applications for deferred action, or temporary protection from deportation, for immigrant workers. That process hinged on a request from a labor agency with an open labor investigation to protect workers who were potential witnesses to labor violations by their employer. Armed with this request, workers could then individually apply for the immigration protection as well as permission to work legally. Importantly, these protections were proactive and prophylactic: workers could request and win deferred action before employer retaliation occurred with the goal of enabling broad participation during the full course of the labor investigation, including to monitor and ensure compliance of any order or settlement.

Rosario Ortiz is one of the brave worker leaders who led the national campaign calling for these protections. Rosario worked as a painter in the Las Vegas region for Unforgettable Coatings Inc., a multi-state commercial painting company owned by Cory Summerhays. Ortiz and hundreds of other painters were not paid overtime wages and sometimes were required to work on the weekend for no pay. Rosario recorded this wage theft over two years and joined with others workers to report the company’s labor violations to the federal Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division in 2019, supported by the International Union of Painters and Allied Trades as well as the Arriba Las Vegas Worker Center. The Division sent investigators to worksites to confidentially interview workers, who reported that Summerhays had warned them of immigration consequences for talking to strangers, a thinly veiled threat of possible deportation to deter workers from cooperating in the investigation. Despite these terrifying threats, Rosario and other coworkers stepped forward and helped in the investigation.

Summerhays proved to be a recalcitrant and combative employer, and the Department of Labor filed suit in federal district court in March 2020, alleging wage theft, falsification of wage records, and intimidation of worker witnesses based on information provided by Rosario and other workers. The Department also sought and obtained a preliminary injunction ordering the company and its agents not to threaten or retaliate in any way against workers. But the company continued to resist, challenging this preliminary injunction and also refusing to turn over relevant records in discovery. This was an early sign that the litigation would become protracted, meaning that the cooperation of witnesses in the coming months and years would be essential to the case.

But Rosario and his coworkers, who were at the center of the case, were vulnerable. They had come forward during a virulently anti-immigrant administration, amidst immigration threats from the boss, and provided essential information and evidence to help the Department of Labor build and prosecute the labor case. Rosario and his coworkers therefore went public with their demand for immigration protection just a few months after President Biden assumed office with a bold pro-worker platform. Rosario organized his coworkers in Las Vegas via public rallies and also flew to Washington, D.C. to speak with Biden officials, including the Secretaries of Labor and Homeland Security. Worker rights organizations, unions, and immigrant rights groups rallied in support. They pressured the Department of Labor to push for immigration protections for worker-witnesses and the Department of Homeland Security to set up a process to receive these requests and to grant them. Rosario argued that his employer broke the law by stealing wages and also broke the law by threatening workers. He argued that the federal government was relying on him and other worker-witnesses to hold the company accountable and they therefore should receive immigration protections. In Rosario’s own words, “My coworkers and I have been fighting our case for more than three years, facing threats and intimidation on top of wage theft and health and safety risks as workers of Unforgettable Coatings Inc.”

These efforts eventually were successful and the Department of Labor issued a letter requesting immigration protections for current and former employees of Unforgetting Coatings, one of the first such letters in the country. With this letter, Rosario and other worker leaders applied for deferred action protection from the immigration benefits agency, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. In early 2022, these workers received some of the first approvals for deferred action based on labor enforcement under the Biden administration. With the work permit that followed, Rosario finally had legal permission to live and work in the U.S., his home for past twenty years. In the face of the immigration threats from his former boss, he could breathe a sigh of relief, with the reassurance that he was protected from deportation for at least the next two years.

Rosario’s victory paved the way for immigrant workers across the country to seek protections, leading to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announcement of its streamlined process in January of 2023. The announcement memorialized and publicized the process through which Rosario and his coworkers won protections. First, a labor agency issues a statement of interest to explain that agency’s enforcement interests in immigration protections for a group of workers. Then, second, immigration officials receive and adjudicate individual applications for deferred action from workers covered by the labor agency statement. Advocates coined the process Deferred Action for Labor Enforcement, or DALE. On the same day as this announcement, the Department of Labor announced a settlement with Unforgettable Coatings Inc. over their labor violations. Unforgettable Coatings Inc. agreed to pay $3. million in back wages and penalties to nearly six hundred workers in four states who had been victimized by its wage theft.

Rosario’s victories, winning immigration protections as well as broad remediation for labor violations from a company that exploited immigrant workers, built on decades of advocacy to protect immigrant worker rights. The conflict between immigration and labor enforcement stretches back even further, to early conceptions of immigration regulation as the principal tool for labor protection. And even after Congress enacted federal statutes with labor protections, and courts interpreted the laws to also apply to immigrants, employers used immigration enforcement to retaliate against immigrant workers seeking to organize, often with the acquiescence of federal immigration officials. From that dark history, and after Congress prohibited the employment of undocumented immigrants, labor agencies eventually shifted to agreements that sought limited neutrality from parts of immigration agencies to not interfere in active labor enforcement. But that claimed neutrality had its limits and failed to fully address the deep fears of immigrants who suffered labor violations. The announcement of DALE therefore broke new ground in, for the first time, using immigration protections to broadly facilitate labor enforcement rather than simply minimize immigration interference in labor investigations or narrowly protecting victims of certain crimes.

This article is the first scholarly analysis of the path to winning these laborbased immigration protections and their impact. This analysis builds on work by other scholars over the last several decades analyzing the increasingly important intersection of labor and immigration enforcement. Immigration scholars have long critiqued the “chronic imbalance of power between DHS and the DOL.” Scholarship in this field ranges from historical and sociological critique of racial capitalism, discussions of the challenge of immigration enforcement for labor enforcement, and critical analysis of major Supreme Court precedent in this area. Critiques of statutes, precedent and policy have resulted in a range of suggestions for reform, primarily through new legislation. Labor scholars have also analyzed the persistent problem of workplace exploitation of immigrant workers from a variety of perspectives. Some have explored state and local approaches to these issues, as well as lessons from innovative models of organizing and lawyering. Many scholars who have focused on how to prevent human trafficking have noted the persistent barrier of immigration enforcement. Finally, even beyond the intersection of labor and immigration, some scholars are turning to exploring public policy through immigration enforcement, with helpful insights on how the stakes of immigration policy extend beyond the border and beyond questions of humanitarian interests and belonging.

This article will proceed in three parts. The first part will review the deeply intertwined history of labor and immigration in the United States. This history begins with a focus on immigration restrictions as protection of labor markets, and then in fits and starts after federal workplace protections, eventually begins to acknowledge some protection of immigrant workers as critical to enforcing workplace standards. Building on this background, the second part tells the story of the final and successful push for affirmative immigration protections for workers under the Biden administration. This push included key immigrant worker leaders like Rosario Ortiz speaking out about high stakes labor violations and then demanding protection. This advocacy culminated in the January 2023 announcement of the DALE process. Following this announcement, and after some additional improvements, thousands of workers applied for and received protection before January 2025, when the second Trump administration moved to dismantle further DALE processing. Therefore, the third part will offer some preliminary reflections on what was accomplished through two years of DALE. Finally, the piece concludes that the announcement and implementation of this protection for two years has changed the landscape for immigrant workers, with implications for the advocates facing the current crackdown on immigration and future opportunities for immigration policy that serves a broader conception of the public interest and rule of law.

[ . . . ]

Throughout U.S. history, labor and immigration enforcement efforts have been deeply intertwined. This history reflects that the arc for immigrant workers has generally trended toward progress but in fits and starts with uneven advancement as well as periods of significant retrenchment, such as the advent of employer sanctions and the first Trump administration’s resurrection of mass worksite raids. The second Trump administration is another period of retrenchment. The end of DALE processing, aggressive worksite raids targeting day laborers, and targeting of immigrant rights defenders all serve to embolden exploitive employers, deter immigrant workers from reporting abuse, and hinder labor enforcement efforts. But the history also demonstrates that even in periods of retrenchment, political opportunity may be on the horizon.

Deferred action for labor enforcement was a particularly bright spot along that arc of progress for immigrant workers: it offered prophylactic protection from deportation that encouraged immigrant workers who were potential witnesses to come forward and assist labor enforcement. The two years of protections being available built constituencies committed to immigrant worker rights that have outlasted the administrative guidance: immigrant workers who have been granted DALE protection, state labor agencies committed to immigrant worker rights, and an expanded field of organizers, advocates, and attorneys with labor and immigration expertise and experience. These constituencies are serving as a bulwark against attacks on immigrant workers and also stand ready to resurrect affirmative protections for immigrant worker witnesses at the earliest opportunity.

Associate Clinical Professor of Law, Tulane Law School. Thank you to the Paul R. Verkuil Faculty Research Fund for its financial support for this project. I am also grateful for the helpful feedback of Kathleen Kim, Leticia Saucedo, Nickole Miller, Jennifer Gordon, Adam Feibelman, Ann Garcia, Bliss Requa-Trautz, Saru Matambanadzo, Jeremy Bock, and the participants in the Tulane Law Faculty Workshop and the Association of American Law School Section on Immigration Law’s New Scholars session. MADRID — Kilmar Ábrego García, a Salvadoran national who fought his mistaken deportation, arrived in Spain on Wednesday after voluntarily leaving the United States, potentially ending a defining saga of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.

Ábrego García was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and deported to a Salvadoran prison in what an official later called an "administrative error." His departure to Spain follows months of legal wrangling as he battled the administration's drive to deport him to Africa.

Ábrego García didn't speak to reporters after landing at Madrid's main international airport on Wednesday, and raised a fist as he entered a van.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said Tuesday night that he self-deported to Spain as part of a removal order and that he didn't receive any incentives and won't be allowed back into the U.S.

U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a post on X that he was "delighted" about Ábrego García's departure, listing a familiar litany of allegations for why he should be deported, including that he was a gang member, an accusation that Ábrego García has repeatedly denied.

Ábrego García's deportation in early 2025 came as the Trump administration was ramping up its immigration crackdown, promising to deport 1 million people annually.

Through an infusion of billions of dollars approved by U.S. Congress, the administration later supercharged its immigration enforcement capabilities, growing its cadre of immigration officers, expanding detention capabilities and pushing to deport an increasing number of people.

He was fighting against a second deportation to a series of African countries proposed by DHS officials.

text:
A seven-year-old girl who was arrested by federal immigration agents alongside her mother in suburban New Orleans – then sent to a family detention center in Texas – has written a letter asking Donald Trump to release her from custody, saying she wants to see her dad again and continue her academic education.

“Mr President Trump, I would like to visit my father and study at my school,” Charlotte Ortiz said in the letter she wrote in Spanish from inside the Dilley, Texas, immigration processing center after her and her mother’s detentions in late October.

The letter, a photograph of which was shared with the Guardian by independent reporting outlet Perdido Street News, also had hand-drawn figures of Charlotte; her “mama”, Karen; and her “papa”, Bruno.

Nonetheless, when recently asked about Charlotte and Karen’s detentions, a Trump administration spokesperson said there was a final order of removal for the mother after the family arrived from Venezuela seeking asylum in April 2024 through a humanitarian parole program that the president has since eliminated.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson suggested Karen Ortiz could secure her and her daughter’s release from custody by arranging “to self-deport now”.

Charlotte made her plea to Trump at what could be an inflection point for his second presidency, a main characteristic of which has been a mass deportation campaign. Tactics associated with that push, which much of the US public has come to see as cruel or overly aggressive, were widely considered to be a decisive factor in the 3 November midterm elections that cost Trump’s Republican party control of Congress for the last two years of his presidency.

Furthermore, Charlotte and her mother have been enduring their plight as Gina Hinojosa, the Texas governor-elect, recently told the New York Times that she would use the state’s licensing power to halt private prison companies such as the one contracted to run Dilley from holding children in detention.

Such detentions “should not be happening”, said Hinojosa, the first Democrat elected Texas governor since 1990 – and the only Hispanic person to ever win the office – in a social media video published on 19 November by Ms Rachel, the children’s YouTube star and activist. “It needs to stop.”

Wednesday marked Charlotte’s 29th day in detention at Dilley, exceeding the 20-day limit for detaining immigrant children set by a federal court in 1985 under a class-action lawsuit that accused the US government of mistreating children in immigration detention. A Texas Tribune analysis from August found that at least 60 children had been detained at Dilley for 100 or more days.

The DHS spokesperson did not provide an explanation for keeping Charlotte beyond the 20-day limit.

Attorney Kristin Etter of the Texas Immigration Law Council, who is representing Karen and her daughter, said Charlotte’s letter to Trump is something no child should ever have to write.

“We are calling on every leader at every level of government and in both parties to demand the release of Karen and Charlotte, close Dilley and end family detention for good,” said Etter, the council’s director of policy and legal services.

‘A nightmare’

As he put it in an interview with the Guardian and Perdido Street, Charlotte’s father said their family did not fit the profile of “dangerous criminals” whom the Trump administration once pledged it would focus its mass deportation efforts on.

The couple had been childhood sweethearts, began living together in 2018 and married in 2022. They financially supported themselves as delivery drivers for the retailer Walmart after arriving in Miami and settling in the New Orleans suburb of Gretna, said Bruno, 27, speaking in Spanish. Charlotte enrolled at William Hart elementary, a public school in Gretna, gaining a proficiency in English that Bruno was hopeful would serve her well.

Bruno said he and Karen, 25, became active in a local Pentecostal church, regularly attending services and retreats. They had no criminal record and paid their share of taxes, he said. And they were hoping to be granted asylum after government corruption, widespread criminal extortions and a general lack of freedom in Venezuela prompted them to try their luck in the US, Bruno recounted.

“We never came to this country illegally,” Bruno said, referring to his family’s arrival in the US seeking asylum under a Biden administration humanitarian parole policy. “We came here looking for a better opportunity, for our family to grow, to fulfill our dreams – and little by little we were [getting] it.”

But the second Trump administration discarded that policy. The US supreme court’s subsequent decision to uphold that termination then removed the temporary protected statuses of more than half a million people and exposed them to removal from the country.

A DHS spokesperson said an asylum application “does NOT confer legal status in our country”. And on 14 October, the spokesperson said, an immigration judge issued a final order of removal for Karen for “failing to show up for her mandatory immigration proceedings”.

Bruno blamed Karen’s absence from those proceedings on a noticing error.

In any event, on 26 October, after she dropped Charlotte off at school and went to the store, she was boxed in by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents in vehicles. “I thought they were going to crash into me,” Karen said in a statement provided by Etter.

She said the agents shouted at her to open the car, which she did. They then violently pulled her out of her car and handcuffed her.

“I thought it was a nightmare,” Karen’s statement said. She also recalled yelling, “my daughter, my daughter” – and unsuccessfully begging to be taken to Charlotte’s school.

Karen said the agents brought her to a garage for initial holding and allowed her a three-minute call to Bruno at about noon that day. Her abrupt silence until then had made Bruno worry that she had perhaps been abducted by kidnappers wanting a ransom – not that learning what had actually happened was a comfort, he said.

Ultimately, Karen’s statement said agents told her that she would suffer if she were detained alone. She said they told her they would bring Charlotte to her if she “signed a paper”.

Karen said she signed, and a family friend brought Charlotte to Karen at about 6pm that day. According to Karen, an officer told her that “if she did anything wrong”, she might not see Charlotte again until she was 21.

The mother and daughter were later put on a plane and did not arrive at Dilley until 3am the following day, going 10 hours without food, Karen said.

‘The most harrowing thing’

Bruno said he has been in as much contact as possible with Karen and Charlotte throughout their detentions at Dilley.

His loved ones’ experiences, as relayed to him, seem to be consistent with other previous reporting of life within the only family detention center in the US, which is operated by the country’s largest private prison contractor, CoreCivic.

According to Bruno, Charlotte loathes processed foods and has struggled with some of the dietary offerings at Dilley. He said she had dropped about 7lbs (3kg) halfway through her first week there, and was down about 15lbs more recently.

Bruno said he understood Karen, in desperation, at one point hid cereal in her and Charlotte’s quarters at the facility. But staff there found it and threw it away, he said.

“That was the most harrowing thing to hear,” Bruno said. “Over the course of a day, she might eat five spoonfuls of rice.”

Texas pastor Dianne Garcia has been visiting Dilley weekly since November 2025 and has had 41 members of her congregation detained there. She has found children losing weight and not eating to be “super common” at the family detention facility.

“It’s not just that they don’t like the food,” said Garcia, who leads the San Antonio-based church Roca de Refugio. Citing American Academy of Pediatrics research, Garcia said: “Any time in detention is harmful for children. It’s also an indicator of the stress that kids are going through.”

title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaves U.S. voluntarily for Spain - NPR
description:

Before Tuesday's move, Abrego Garcia and the Trump administration had been at an impasse about where he should go.

The legal battle Abrego Garcia has been living in the U.S. for over a decade.

text:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran immigrant who became a symbol of the pitfalls of President Trump's mass deportation campaign, has voluntarily left the U.S. after a legal battle that spanned nearly two years. He landed in Spain on Wednesday morning.

Abrego Garcia, who was arrested in 2025, mistakenly deported to El Salvador, and then brought back to the U.S., left for Spain on Tuesday, according to his lawyers and Trump administration officials.

He arrived on Wednesday morning in Madrid's international airport, Adolfo Suárez Madrid – Barajas Airport. There was no indication that he entered the country under any formal agreement with Spanish authorities.

Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, an attorney for Abrego Garcia, said he "left the United States a free man."

"The government wanted to deport him in shackles on an ICE Air flight to Liberia. Instead, he departed on a commercial aircraft, to a country that he chose, and able to move freely around the world," Sandoval-Moshenberg told NPR.

He called the move "a temporary departure" and said that Abrego Garcia, who has a wife and a child, both of whom are U.S. citizens, has many options to return to the U.S.

"We don't expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland," he added.

Sandoval-Moshenberg said Abrego Garcia will choose where "to settle in the next two years while he waits out the end of this administration."

Another lawyer for Abrego Garcia, Sean Hecker, confirmed Spain as his destination.

U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who played a leading role in championing Abrego Garcia's case, released a statement saying he "is traveling to a country of his choice, a free man, unharmed and with dignity."

Trump administration hails Abrego Garcia's "self-deportation"

Abrego Garcia's case became a flashpoint for Trump's mass deportation campaign. It raised serious questions about due process, third-country deportations and to what extent this administration is sending people to countries where they may face threats.

Before Tuesday's move, Abrego Garcia and the Trump administration had been at an impasse about where he should go.

Abrego Garcia said he'd be willing to move to Costa Rica if the government allowed it. According to his attorneys, Costa Rica offered him refugee status. But the administration did not support that plan and instead sought to deport him to Liberia. That attempt was ultimately blocked by the courts.

The Trump administration hailed Abrego Garcia's departure late Tuesday.

"We are DELIGHTED to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain," Markwayne Mullin, secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, wrote on X. He accused Abrego Garcia of being a gang member and a human trafficker, without evidence.

The legal battle

Abrego Garcia has been living in the U.S. for over a decade. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to his home country of El Salvador, after he made the argument that he would be tortured or persecuted there.

In 2025, immigration officers arrested Abrego Garcia and sent him to a notorious Salvadoran prison, where he claimed he suffered from beatings and sleep deprivation.

text:
Pregnant women spent an average of 43 days in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention during the first 16 months of President Donald Trump's second administration—750 percent longer than the average during the Biden administration, according to an analysis of ICE records.

The data was obtained by the Women's Refugee Commission (WRC) through a Freedom of Information Act request. It covered 733 pregnant women detained from January 2025 through April 2026, and ICE provided time-in-custody information for 557 of them. About 14 percent were held for at least 90 days, including one woman who spent 219 days in detention.

By comparison, Department of Homeland Security (DHS) reports cited by WRC show pregnant, postpartum and nursing women generally spent an average of about five to 12 days in ICE custody between 2021 and 2024. In the first half of fiscal 2024, 158 of 160 people in that group exited custody within an average of 11.65 days.

Read More on News

The Trump administration faces a new lawsuit alleging ICE has stopped following key parts of a 2021 directive intended to limit the detention of pregnant, postpartum, and nursing immigrants.

Newsweek contacted DHS for comment via email and awaits a response.

The plaintiffs argue that ICE's alleged change violates the Administrative Procedure Act and are asking the court to require the government to comply with the 2021 directive. The filing says the directive itself has not been formally rescinded and remains binding agency policy.

Six immigrant rights and advocacy organizations filed the lawsuit Tuesday in federal court in Washington, D.C. The plaintiffs include the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, Venezuelan Association of Massachusetts, Workers' Center of Central New York, Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition, Worker Justice Center of New York and Women's Refugee Commission.

Under the 2021 directive, ICE generally should not detain people known to be pregnant, postpartum, or nursing unless their release is prohibited by law or "exceptional circumstances" exist. Those circumstances include national security concerns or an imminent risk of death, violence, or physical harm. The policy also requires ICE to monitor those who are detained and review at least weekly whether continued detention is appropriate.

"Pregnant individuals and new mothers should not be subjected to dangerous detention conditions, denied critical medical care, or separated from their babies because this administration has decided to disregard its own rules," Skye Perryman, president and CEO of Democracy Forward, told Newsweek.

The WRC analysis also found ICE booked 124 women into detention when they were at least 20 weeks pregnant. They were detained for an average of 30 days, including 11 who remained in custody for at least 60 days and six for at least 90 days.

The number of pregnant women in ICE detention in the monthly data rose from nine in January 2025 to 128 in March 2026, a 1,320 percent increase, according to WRC. By comparison, the overall ICE detention population increased by about 71 percent over the period, the report said.

The report identified about 128 women with high-risk pregnancies or high-risk conditions. Only four were referred for a higher level of care, according to WRC. None of the 22 women identified with preeclampsia was referred for a higher level of care.

"Immigration detention has become a black box of impunity," said Zain Lakhani, director of migrant rights and justice at WRC, in a press release. "The data ICE provided to WRC shows shockingly high rates of pregnant women in detention, for substantial periods of time, without the care they urgently require to keep themselves and their babies safe. Pregnant women should not be detained."

WRC said some of the ICE records were incomplete or inconsistent, so it relied on records with clear booking and release dates and excluded possible duplicates from its analysis.

The new lawsuit characterizes ICE's alleged change as a "final agency decision" to stop applying the directive's presumption against detention and requirements involving notification, consultation, tracking, and weekly custody reviews.

The complaint also describes cases in which pregnant immigrants allegedly suffered medical problems while in ICE detention. In one case, a pregnant woman detained in Kentucky reported bleeding and later miscarried after being taken to a hospital, according to the filing.

Another woman with a high-risk pregnancy was allegedly detained into her third trimester before being deported during her eighth month of pregnancy.

The filing also alleges nursing mothers have been separated from their infants. One member of the Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition was taken while breastfeeding and had not been provided a breast pump while detained, according to the complaint.

Federal courts have separately ordered the release of some pregnant, postpartum, and nursing immigrants in cases involving the 2021 directive. The complaint cites decisions from courts in several states in which judges found ICE had failed to comply with the directive or the legal doctrine requiring agencies to follow their own rules.

He had previously been jailed for attempted rape, and was told at the time to expect deportation as soon as he was released, but he subsequently remained in the UK.

The Home Office declined to comment on individual cases, but said convicted foreign nationals were "referred for deportation at the earliest opportunity" and barred from returning.

Cardiff Crown Court heard that Meles had arrived in the UK in 2015 by hiding in a lorry from Calais to Dover, and later had claimed asylum.

In 2019, he was handed a five-year prison sentence for attempted rape, after attacking an unconscious woman at a house party.

At the time he was told by Judge Christopher Vosper KC that upon release he would "likely... be held in an immigration detention centre" and "the home secretary is likely to make a deportation order in your case".

But, following his release, he was not monitored and went on to assault another woman.

The court heard he had been working in a factory and was spending his wages on alcohol and visits to sex workers in Newport.

On 15 March 2026, he approached the victim and agreed on a price for sex, which was due to take place in a disused garage.

But, after she had performed a sex act on him, Meles, who was described as "tall and powerful", gripped the woman forcefully and raped her.

After she managed to push him off and face him, Meles slapped the woman hard in the face, and she ran away to raise the alarm.

On Friday, he was found guilty of rape and assault by beating following a five-day trial.

The judge, Recorder Andrew Hammond, said there were similarities between the rape and Meles's previous conviction for attempted rape.

"In both instances you seized the opportunity presented by your victim's vulnerability to satisfy your own sexual urges, displaying a wholesale disregard of the right of these women to choose and control what was done to their bodies," he said.

"I am sure you present a serious and imminent danger to any woman who has the misfortune to be alone with you in circumstances when they are vulnerable."

Meles was handed a nine-year sentence, extended by four years, with the judge adding he could make "no comment" on whether he would be deported after.

What is the law on deporting foreign criminals?

UK law includes automatic deportation for any foreign criminal given a sentence of at least 12 months' imprisonment, but it can also be issued for lesser offences at ministers' discretion.

Though individuals can appeal under human rights law, the government says that can be denied to those who are "convicted of a particularly serious crime [or] constitute a danger to the community".

When a foreign national is given a custodial sentence, the prison service will refer those cases to the Home Office to decide whether deportation is required.

However, it is unclear whether this process was initiated for Meles following his earlier release from prison.

The Home Office declined to comment on individual cases, but a spokesperson said: "Any foreign national who receives a prison sentence in the UK is referred for deportation at the earliest opportunity and will be barred from ever returning.

text:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — In its travel advisories, the U.S. State Department warns Americans not to visit Honduras' Gracias a Dios region, alerting them to violent crime, armed robbery, murder and active terrorist groups.

But for Hondurans, the message is less stark. “Overall, Gracias a Dios is a low-crime, functioning department,” says a State Department background report obtained by The Associated Press.

The report, and similar documents about Guatemala, Mexico and El Salvador, were prepared for use in immigration courts, where asylum denial rates have soared to 94% during President Donald Trump’s second term.

The reports use cherry-picked data, careful phrasing and in some cases facts that don’t stand up to scrutiny to create misleading depictions of countries that are in fact often plagued by violence, government corruption and police inaction.

They appear designed to make it easier for judges to deny asylum to people from those nations fleeing domestic violence and criminal gangs, painting pictures of life in their home countries that often clash with reality.

The reports have been "reverse-engineered,” said Elliot Young, a professor at Lewis & Clark College who analyzed the documents for the college’s Migration and Asylum Lab.

“They’re trying to hit the most frequent kinds of (asylum) cases that come up and provide counterevidence to the overwhelming evidence that these are dangerous places,” said Young, a scholar of Latin America and asylum law who has testified as an expert witness in more than 700 asylum cases.

In a statement, the State Department said that in line with U.S. laws and regulations it “may provide information about conditions in foreign countries” to immigration courts and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. The Justice Department, which oversees immigration courts, did not respond to a request for comment on what role the reports play in influencing asylum decisions.

A system in turmoil – and targeted

Cutting back on asylum has been a centerpiece of Trump’s immigration crackdown dating to his first term, when he dismissed migrants waiting in Mexico to get into the U.S. as “not legitimate asylum-seekers.”

Most asylum seekers, the Republican president said, were fleeing poverty.

“Asylum is a very special protection intended only for those fleeing government persecution based on race, religion and other protected status,” he said in a 2018 White House appearance.

Trump was years out of date. While asylum was largely seen after World War II as a way to protect people fleeing political persecution, the definition was expanded long ago, including to encompass some people fleeing domestic and criminal violence.

But he had a point about poverty.

Legal and illegal migration, particularly from Latin America, has exploded over the past two decades as people have sought more economic opportunity, with increasing asylum claims based on safety fears from domestic partners and criminal gangs.

Even during President Joe Biden's years, most asylum claims were rejected.

But denials have jumped from roughly 72% at the end of that Democratic administration to 94% in June under Trump, according to the data research nonprofit Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse.

Trump was elected to a second term in part by focusing on frustrated voters who had seen illegal immigration soar under Biden, with border arrests from Mexico reaching a record 250,000 in December 2023. The asylum system, meanwhile, faced a backlog of millions of cases.

The Trump administration has reshaped immigration courts as part of its push to increase deportations, organizing mass hearings, authorizing military lawyers as immigration judges, and giving judges more leeway to summarily dismiss claims.

A sanitized view of troubled countries

Immigration judges must weigh whether people seeking asylum based on domestic violence or criminal threats have a reasonable fear of persecution because of their race, religion, nationality, political views or an often-debated catch-all category, “membership in a particular social group.” They also have to show that their government can't or won't protect them and that they can't move elsewhere in their home country to escape persecution.

The reports offer what can sometimes seem like travel brochure descriptions of life in these countries.

They mention good schools, low crime, quality hospitals and constitutions that protect individual rights, with brief notes that “the availability of services” can vary across each country.

Take El Salvador, where the government of President Nayib Bukele has long faced accusations of widespread human rights abuses, including torture.

The State Department report takes a far more generous view of the situation, noting the government approach to rights abuses “is no different than that of developed countries in Europe and North America, including the United States itself,” and highlighting a handful of prosecutions tied to the civil war, which ended in 1992.

“In any country, a rogue official can mistreat those under their power,” it says.

For Honduras’ Gracias a Dios province, violent crime rates “compare favorably with rates of violent crime in many parts of the United States,” says the report.

Former officials and advocates say the six-page reports pale in comparison to traditional State Department human rights reports, lengthy dissections of more than 100 nations around the world, which under the second Trump administration have been truncated and delayed.

“These shorter reports clearly don’t address the full range of human rights issues that the country reports have traditionally addressed,” said Scott Busby, former deputy assistant secretary in the Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights and Labor at the State Department and now a senior adviser at the group Human Rights First.

They are “especially problematic given that the country reports themselves for last year have yet to be issued,” he said.

Looking at asylum-seekers’ ability to move elsewhere

In many ways, the reports appear aimed most directly at asylum regulations around a person's ability to escape persecution by simply moving.

Those regulations are key for anyone seeking asylum based on domestic or criminal violence.

The reports highlight specific parts of each country, mentioning places like an off-the-beaten track tourist destination in Guatemala and a province in El Salvador that has low crime and 24-hour emergency medical care.

But those mentions only tell part of the story.

“The fact that there may be pockets of a country that are relatively safe for some people doesn’t mean that everybody can just move to that part of the country,” said Neela Chakravartula, an asylum attorney with the Center for Gender & Refugee Studies at the University of California College of the Law, San Francisco.

If that were the case, Chakravartula said: “We’d all be living in Malibu.”

___

Associated Press reporter Joshua Goodman in Miami contributed to this report.

Former officials and advocates say the six-page reports pale in comparison to traditional State Department human rights reports, lengthy dissections of more than 100 nations around the world, which under the second Trump administration have been truncated and delayed.

“These shorter reports clearly don’t address the full range of human rights issues that the country reports have traditionally addressed,” said Scott Busby, former deputy assistant secretary in the Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights and Labor at the State Department and now a senior adviser at the group Human Rights First.

They are “especially problematic given that the country reports themselves for last year have yet to be issued,” he said.

Looking at asylum-seekers’ ability to move elsewhere

In many ways, the reports appear aimed most directly at asylum regulations around a person's ability to escape persecution by simply moving.

Those regulations are key for anyone seeking asylum based on domestic or criminal violence.

The reports highlight specific parts of each country, mentioning places like an off-the-beaten track tourist destination in Guatemala and a province in El Salvador that has low crime and 24-hour emergency medical care.

But those mentions only tell part of the story.

“The fact that there may be pockets of a country that are relatively safe for some people doesn’t mean that everybody can just move to that part of the country,” said Neela Chakravartula, an asylum attorney with the Center for Gender & Refugee Studies at the University of California College of the Law, San Francisco.

If that were the case, Chakravartula said: “We’d all be living in Malibu.”

___

Associated Press reporter Joshua Goodman in Miami contributed to this report.

text:
Seven months after Brian José Morales García was deported to Mexico, the Donald Trump administration has finally admitted that this young man of Mexican nationality was also a U.S. citizen, having been born in Denver, Colorado. “The plaintiff has dual nationality: United States and Mexico,” acknowledged U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons in the first line of a document filed Friday before a court in Austin, Texas, in which he requests the dismissal of a lawsuit by Morales for the damages caused by the deportation.

Morales García, 25, was detained on April 3, 2026, by officials from the Texas Department of Public Safety (DPS) and a state sheriff’s office who stopped the car he was traveling in as a passenger. He told them he was American, confirmed his immigration lawyer, who had access to the videos from the cameras installed in the police cars. But he did not have the documents proving his citizenship on hand, so the police officers called the immigration officers.

Since Trump took office in his second presidency, cooperation agreements between local and federal law enforcement have multiplied in the country, but especially in states that have been Republican strongholds, such as Texas and Florida.

Morales explained to a Customs and Border Protection (CBP) immigration agent that he had entered the country with his U.S. birth certificate, according to court documents. The official asked for it, as well as his social security number, but could not provide them immediately. After reviewing Mexican government databases, the CBP official confirmed Morales García’s Mexican nationality and classified him as an “illegal immigrant.”

“In response to his insistence that he was a U.S. citizen, the agents warned him that if he kept claiming it, he would face five years in prison for lying. He believed them and stopped insisting. He was coerced,” said Morales García’s immigration lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, in an interview with EL PAÍS.

Morales recalls the detention, according to his lawyer, as “a traumatic experience”: he suffered claustrophobia, and some officers pushed him and forced him to undress. After his deportation, he says, he lost his job in the air conditioning department. As a result, his family was left without income.

He was deported to Mexico four days later and remained there until August 30, 2026, when he was able to return to the United States. In that country, he lived with his relatives (his brother and grandmother) but did not find stable employment.

The lawyer asserts that the fact that the U.S. government recognized her client’s U.S. citizenship is “the bare minimum.” But after seven months and a lawsuit, it is not enough to repair the harm they caused him, she says. “They should have believed him from the start. They should never have deported him.”

Evidence for his return

Five months passed from Brian Morales’ deportation to his return home, to reunite with his newborn baby and his wife. Lincoln-Goldfinch said the judge in the case asked to present evidence to support his citizenship. Like many Americans, he did not have a passport, a document usually requested as a supplement to validate U.S. citizenship and which many cannot afford, since a new one costs $165.

The lawyers then gathered additional records from the hospital where Morales was born in Denver, medical records, affidavits from relatives who knew Brian Morales was born in Colorado, as well as expert reports that could analyze hospital documents.

“There came a time when we could tip the balance in our favor. There was enough evidence for the Government to agree to allow his return,” the lawyer recounts in the video call.

Lincoln-Goldfinch denounces that CBP agents did not verify Morales’s information in U.S. databases: “They had access to the information they needed, but they didn’t take the time to look for it.” And she adds that Brian Morales offered on several occasions to provide the documentation, which was at his home in Austin: “They refused to allow it to be delivered to them.”

EL PAÍS requested information from the Department of Homeland Security about the case and about the government’s request to dismiss this citizen’s lawsuit. They did not respond.

End of the story

When the government recognized that Morales was a U.S. citizen, it also called for the dismissal of the lawsuit filed by his lawyer demanding accountability from officials and agencies that proceeded with the arrest and deportation of a U.S. citizen. Among other things, government officials argue immunity to enforce immigration laws. The judge in charge of the case has not responded to that request, but Lincoln-Goldfinch says “they must be held accountable (...) And essentially, they are asking that this be the end of the story.”

“It was a very difficult and stressful time for him. He lived with the uncertainty of when he might return to the United States, while trying to make sure he had enough money to support his family,” says Lincoln-Goldfinch.

The lawyer states that in recent months she has received calls from three more U.S. citizens who were deported or whose documents were confiscated at the border and were not allowed to re-enter the country. An investigation by the media outlet ProPublica has documented at least 519 cases of U.S. citizens wrongly detained by immigration agents between January 2025 and October 2026.

Brian Morales, the lawyer says, remains nervous about the possibility of having new encounters with the police or immigration agents: “He is still processing the trauma of everything he went through.”
