text:
By ALANNA DURKIN RICHER, HALLIE GOLDEN and MICHAEL KUNZELMAN

WASHINGTON (AP) — Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national who fought his mistaken deportation, left the U.S. voluntarily for Spain on Tuesday, officials and his attorneys said, in what could bring an end to a defining saga of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

Abrego Garcia was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and deported to a Salvadoran prison in what an official later called an “administrative error.” His departure to Spain comes after months of legal wrangling as he battled the administration’s drive to deport him to Africa.

Abrego Garcia, his lawyers and the Trump administration sought to portray the departure as a victory.

“I am leaving happy. I am leaving with my freedom,” Abrego Garcia said in a statement. “I am leaving with the love of an entire community, with people who cared for me, believed in me, and joined my family in this fight.”

The Department of Homeland Security said Tuesday night that he self-deported to Spain as part of a removal order and that he didn’t receive any incentives and won’t be allowed back in to the U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a post on X that he was “delighted” about Abrego Garcia’s departure, listing off a familiar litany of allegations for why he should be deported, including that he was a gang member, an accusation Abrego Garcia has repeatedly denied.

But Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, an attorney for Abrego Garcia, called this a temporary departure as he “waits out the end of this administration.” He said Abrego Garcia has many options to return to U.S.

“We don’t expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland,” he said.

A judge told Abrego Garcia to self-deport by Tuesday, according to a person familiar with the matter, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the case.

Video posted by ABC News showed Abrego Garcia walking through Washington Dulles International Airport with his wife and others, including an official from We Are CASA, an advocacy group that has supported Abrego Garcia and his family.

Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who met with Abrego Garcia while he was pressing for his release from a Salvadoran mega-prison, described Abrego Garcia as a “free man” and said he is traveling to a country of his choice.

“I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free — including from this Administration’s constant persecution,” he said in a statement.

Abrego Garcia’s deportation in early 2025 came as the Trump administration was ramping up its immigration crackdown, promising to deport 1 million people annually. Through an infusion of billions of dollars approved by Congress, the administration later supercharged its immigration enforcement capabilities, growing its cadre of immigration officers, expanding detention capabilities and pushing to deport an increasing number of people.

He was fighting against a second deportation to a series of African countries proposed by DHS officials.

Abrego Garcia was mistakenly deported in March 2025

The 31-year-old Abrego Garcia has an American wife and child and has lived in Maryland for years, but he immigrated to the U.S. illegally as a teenager. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family. The judge allowed him to live and work in the U.S. under Immigration and Customs Enforcement supervision, but he was not given residency status.

His deportation in 2025 involved being sent to a mega-prison in El Salvador known as CECOT, which activists say is rife with abuses and where inmates are packed into cells and never allowed outside.

Facing public pressure and a court order, President Donald Trump’s administration brought him back in June 2025, but only after securing an indictment charging him with human smuggling in Tennessee.

A federal judge dismissed that case in May, finding that the Justice Department’s pursuit of criminal charges was designed to punish Abrego Garcia for challenging his deportation. The government is appealing.

The Trump administration vowed to deport him to a third country, threatening to send him to Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana, and, most recently, Liberia.

Abrego Garcia fought his deportation in court

Abrego Garcia had argued that if he were going to be deported, it should be to Costa Rica, which previously agreed to take him. But Todd Lyons, the former acting director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, said in a March 2026 memo that deporting Abrego Garcia to Costa Rica would be “prejudicial to the United States.”

Lyons wrote that Abrego Garcia should be sent to Liberia because the U.S. has spent governmental resources and political capital in negotiating for it to accept third-country nationals. The push for deportation to Liberia continued even after the U.S. signed an agreement with Costa Rica to accept deportees who cannot legally be returned to their home countries.

His case took an unusual turn on Oct. 6, 2026, when, five minutes before a hearing expected to determine whether U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement could detain and deport Ábrego Garcia to the West African country of Liberia, attorneys for both sides left the courtroom, along with Abrego Garcia.

When they returned 15 minutes later, it was announced the hearing was canceled. The two sides then gathered for another 90 minutes before leaving the courthouse without explanation. Abrego Garcia’s attorney said only the court case was not ready to proceed and he instructed reporters to watch the docket to learn the status of the case.

Associated Press reporter Rebecca Santana contributed.

title: Forget Congress. The Supreme Court will decide the future of Trump's immigration agenda
description: (CNN) — Democrats want to sideline President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda when they take control of Congress next year, but the real fight may take place across the street where
text:
(CNN) —
Democrats want to sideline President Donald Trump’s
immigration agenda
when they take control of Congress next year, but the real fight may take place across the street where the conservative Supreme Court is poised to uphold several of his most controversial policies.
The court will soon consider blockbuster appeals on the president’s
asylum ban
, his vast expansion of
mandatory detention
of migrants and his push to send certain people in the US illegally to countries other than their homeland — including some with
dubious human rights records
.
Decisions in those cases are expected by late June.
Though those three cases and several others are less flashy than this past summer’s blockbuster decision
upholding birthright citizenship
, the outcomes in the nuts-and-bolts disputes will have profound implications for policies the administration says are “indispensable” to its overall immigration crackdown.
“In all three of these cases, the Trump administration is trying to rewrite laws enacted by Congress, in service of a radical anti-immigrant agenda that has hurt not only immigrants, but the rule of law,” said Cecillia Wang with the American Civil Liberties Union, which is opposing the administration in two of those cases. “These Trump policies are not only illegal but also unpopular.”
Trump has had a mixed record on immigration at the 6-3 conservative court since returning to power last year. His unprecedented push to upend birthright citizenship was rejected. And the court limited his ability to use the
1798 Alien Enemies Act
to quickly remove certain migrants from the country.
On the other hand, six-justice majorities in June
allowed Trump to end
a form of humanitarian relief known as Temporary Protected Status and to limit asylum claims made at the border.
White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis dismissed Wang’s assertion that the court will find Trump’s immigration policies illegal.
“If the American Civil Liberties Union cares more about criminal illegal aliens than they do about American citizens, then they should change their name,” she said.
Some Democrats have framed the recapture of Congress as a rejection by voters of the administration’s immigration policies. Minnesota Sen.-elect
Peggy Flanagan
vowed to “rip ICE apart.” New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is all but certain to become the next House speaker,
told CBS
that Democrats would “put an end to Donald Trump’s violent mass deportation machine.”
But Republicans have
already frontloaded funding
for ICE for years. And Trump this month named Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, as White House
chief of staff
— a sign that the administration has no intention of slowing its immigration agenda.
“It stands to reason that hyper-aggressive immigration enforcement will continue to be one of the hallmarks of the Trump administration even as it faces Democratic majorities in both chambers of the legislature,” said Steve Vladeck, CNN Supreme Court analyst and professor at Georgetown University Law Center. “Whether the extremism of these policies will be allowed to continue is therefore going to be up to the Supreme Court.”
Conservatives who support the policies see a court that is prepared to back the president’s program.
“Over and over, judges in the district courts and the courts of appeals have interpreted the law contrary to clear congressional intent as evidenced by the text. And as a result, those decisions keep getting overturned,” Iowa Solicitor General Eric Wessan, whose state led briefs supporting the administration in two of the biggest cases, told CNN.
Wessan predicted that the justices will view lower court decisions on immigration against the administration with similar skepticism.
“Looking at the immigration cases the Supreme Court has taken this term,” he predicted, “I think it’s doing the same kind of cleanup.”
Human rights and arrests
The showdown will begin on December 9, when the justices will hear arguments in a case challenging Trump’s push to remove certain
migrants to countries
other than their homeland. In many cases, those removals are carried out without giving the migrant an opportunity to raise human rights concerns.
Federal law allows such “third country” removals in cases when a migrant’s home country refuses to accept them. The administration has used that provision to remove an Iranian national to Nicaragua, for instance, and Venezuelans to El Salvador, according to immigrants’ rights groups.
In some of those cases, immigrant rights groups say, migrants were sent back to their homeland from the “third country,” even when an immigration judge ordered that the administration not return to them to their native country.
Congress has also required the administration to ensure migrants won’t be tortured or persecuted once they land in a third country. That determination was previously made on a case-by-case basis. Under the second Trump administration, the government now accepts blanket assurances from a foreign country that no torture will take place, and migrants are often removed to that country without notice.
The Supreme Court, on its emergency docket,
three times allowed
the administration to pursue the policy while the case remained pending. It has not explained its reasoning.
Increase in arrests of migrants
Next year, the court will turn to the Trump administration’s decision to funnel not only recent border crossers into mandatory detention but also people who have been living within the United States for years.
That shift has permitted the Department of Homeland Security to dramatically increase the number of migrants arrested. And so if the court rejects that change, it will almost certainly jeopardize the administration’s ability to carry out massive sweeps for migrants that have played out in cities like Chicago and Minneapolis.
Immigrant rights groups say no prior administration, including Trump’s first, has interpreted federal law to require mandatory detention of so many migrants. But Justice Department officials told the Supreme Court that it is simply following the law that Congress enacted.
Asylum ban
And in the spring, the court will hear a challenge to Trump’s asylum ban. The president argues people crossing the border are making false asylum claims as a way to enter the country then stall the deportation process, since it can take years to resolve them.
US Solicitor General D. John Sauer, the administration’s top appellate attorney, warned the court of a “vicious cycle” that encouraged “illegal entry by millions of aliens, who (quite justifiably) inferred that even if they lacked meritorious asylum claims, they would ‘be released to live and work in the United States during their removal proceedings.’”
But the Immigration and Nationality Act specifically allows migrants to claim asylum, even as it leaves the decision about whether to grant safe harbor up to administration officials.
In stark language, the Justice Department has described its asylum policy as one of the “most important and effective” policies for stemming illegal immigration. A lower court order against the policy, the administration said, “threatens to revive the chaos along the southwest border that the proclamation has fended off for the past year and a half.”
The ACLU, representing 13 individuals and three immigrant rights groups that challenged the policy, said that if Trump wants to change the way asylum works, he should have passed a bill in Congress during the two years the chambers were in Republican hands.
Richard Caldarone, a senior litigation attorney at the National Immigrant Justice Center, said that the policies at issue in the cases had already put tens of thousands of people in harm’s way.
“These policies have been overwhelmingly rejected by lower courts across the country, and they flatly violate US immigration law as it has been understood for decades,” said Caldarone, whose group is fighting the administration in the asylum case.
“If the court validates the policies,” he said, “it will enshrine a new generation of internment camps, all but end the US asylum system as we have known it for almost half a century, and shatter our nation’s commitment to upholding human rights and democratic norms.”

Abrego Garcia had been ordered by a federal judge to leave the United States by Tuesday, a U.S. official confirmed to NBC News.

Abrego Garcia, wearing a dark hooded jacket, was seen at the Washington airport with his wife and brother, as well as lawyer Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, and representatives from immigrant rights group We Are CASA (Central American Solidarity and Assistance).

CASA said in a news release Tuesday that Abrego Garcia was expected to appear at a news conference later on Wednesday. He is also “planning on hosting various international speaking engagements, with stops planned in different countries,” the release said.

Before he boarded the flight, Sandoval-Moshenberg said his client was leaving the country his way instead of the way the administration wanted “in shackles” as an Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainee headed on a government plane to the West African country of Liberia.

Abrego Garcia would return to the United States to open arms and the reunification of his family here following the end of Donald Trump’s presidential term, the attorney said.

His client “has many options to return to the United States as the husband of a U.S. citizen and the father of a U.S. citizen child,” he added.

He added, “Where he goes from here, where he chooses to settle for the next two years while he waits out the end of this administration, will be his choice.”

The Salvadoran national became a central figure in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown last year after he was mistakenly deported to his home country.

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis late Tuesday hailed his departure as a win. “The El Salvadoran man chose to self-deport to Spain — a country that has been wrecked by open border policies. Good riddance,” she said.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin used similar language, calling this a matter of self-deportation, and characterized his presence in the United States as focused on an alleged life of crime.

“We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported,” he said. “Now, this El Salvadoran man cannot terrorize innocent Americans.”

The Washington Post reported earlier in the day that Abrego Garcia voluntarily agreed to leave the United States under an agreement with U.S. authorities who had sought his removal. The agreement, it said, would end those proceedings.

Court records in Maryland have yet to reflect such an order. There has been a handful of sealed filings in his civil case against the administration over the past several weeks, however.

The 31-year-old man immigrated to the U.S. illegally as a teenager, but has been in the United States for years, is married to an American and has a child with her.

He had lived and worked in Maryland for years under the regular supervision of Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from gang members.

He was deported there anyway in 2025 and sent to the Central American country’s CECOT megaprison. Activists have decried alleged abuses there and described inmates being packed into cells with no time outdoors.

Prison officials allowed Abrego Garcia a brief outside meeting with Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Maryland, who told reporters that Abrego Garcia had “experienced trauma” after an “illegal abduction.”

In a statement Tuesday evening, Van Hollen said Abrego Garcia was “traveling to a country of his choice, a free man — unharmed and with dignity.”

After Abrego Garcia was returned to the U.S. from El Salvador, ICE officials admitted in court filings that his deportation had been an “administrative error.”

But shortly after his return, Abrego Garcia was charged with human smuggling in a case stemming from a 2022 traffic stop for alleged speeding in Tennessee in which he was driving a van with multiple immigrant passengers.

Abrego Garcia told Tennessee Highway Patrol troopers he was taking the group of nine to a construction job. Authorities there did not pursue charges. A federal judge dismissed the 2025 Department of Justice case, saying the Trump administration failed to rebut the “presumption of vindictiveness.” The government appealed.

The administration continued to pursue Abrego Garcia’s removal, and he was fighting that in a lawsuit that was ongoing prior to today’s news.

Abrego Garcia has been fighting deportation to Liberia, as proposed by Department of Homeland Security officials. He wanted to go to Costa Rica, according to court records.

Trump and immigration officials alleged Abrego Garcia was an MS-13 gang member, something he denied.

In 2019 records from a loitering case in which he was picked up in a Home Depot parking lot, authorities in Prince George’s County said that Abrego appeared to be an MS-13 member.

They said they made that conclusion based on his clothing (including a Chicago Bulls hat) and tattoos, as well as a proven confidential informant. Abrego Garcia was not formally arrested that day, police said, and they did not have contact with him again. Abrego Garcia’s lawyers later called the evidence of his gang membership “hearsay.”

U.S. District Judge Waverly Crenshaw, who presided over the Tennessee smuggling case, warned top Trump administration officials to stop making statements about Abrego Garcia that were “exaggerated if not simply inaccurate” and could influence a potential jury.

text:
US Senators Jeanne Shaheen and Dick Durbin led colleagues in filing an amicus brief with the Supreme Court, challenging the administration’s policy and supporting plaintiffs in the case, D.V.D. v. DHS, according to a November 24 statement from the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

The lawmakers are asking the court to affirm the judgment of the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, which largely upheld a ruling restricting the policy. The Supreme Court had previously allowed the administration to resume the deportations while it considers the broader legal dispute.

The policy has involved cooperation from several African governments. Human Rights Watch has documented the deportation of third-country nationals from the United States to at least 12 African countries: Ghana, Cameroon, the Central African Republic, South Sudan, Sierra Leone, Uganda, Rwanda, Liberia, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Eswatini, Burundi and Equatorial Guinea.”

ADVERTISEMENT

Other countries involved in the wider programme include Costa Rica, Panama, El Salvador and Mexico.

The distinction lies between countries that have actually received deportees and those involved in agreements or attempted transfers. While 12 African countries have documented arrivals, the wider US deportation network covers 15 Africa countries, including three where transfers have not been publicly confirmed.

Lawmakers challenge blanket assurances for deportations

The senators argue that the Trump administration is failing to assess individually whether migrants face persecution or torture in countries to which they are being deported, rather than their countries of origin.

Facebook/Senator Dick Durbin

ADVERTISEMENT

The programme has faced resistance and controversy over the treatment of deportees. Human Rights Watch has documented cases of detention, ill-treatment and onward deportations to countries where migrants could face persecution or torture.

The senators' brief maintains that the policy violates protections under the Immigration and Nationality Act and the Foreign Affairs Reform and Restructuring Act of 1998, which prohibit sending people to countries where they face such dangers.

“The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) guidance at issue in this case has transformed a narrow and rarely used practice into a standing system of unchecked global removals,” the senators wrote.

They also challenged the administration's reliance on diplomatic assurances from receiving countries, arguing that broad promises of protection cannot replace individual assessments.

Citing a February 2026 investigation, the lawmakers said the State Department had failed to adequately monitor whether foreign governments honoured assurances on deportees' treatment. They further alleged that US officials had been instructed not to engage with migrants after handing them over.

“The inescapable conclusion is that the DHS Guidance enables the Administration to use third countries to carry out removals that U.S. law would otherwise prohibit while turning a blind eye,” they wrote.

name: Policy
title: This Should Be the First Target of the Democratic Congress | The New Republic
authors: Jonathan van Harmelen, Good Riddance Michael Tomasky, Ellie Quinlan Houghtaling, Malcolm Ferguson
description:
So the political commentariat has been abuzz over how Democrats will respond to—and rein in—the Trump administration.
Democratic victories are not just a rebuke of the Trump administration’s policies, they also send a clear signal from voters that Democrats can and should confront Trump and his enablers head-on.
The Trump White House responded to the midterm results with as much grace as a car crash in slow motion.
Now both private prison corporations are urging ICE officials to purchase their facilities at inflated prices, before Democrats take control of Congress in January.
Democrats in Congress have a busy year ahead of them.
text:
After one of the most historic victories in American political history, the Democrats will arrive in Congress next January with majorities in both the House and Senate—giving them legislative oversight of federal policy. So the political commentariat has been abuzz over how Democrats will respond to—and rein in—the Trump administration.

Democratic victories are not just a rebuke of the Trump administration’s policies, they also send a clear signal from voters that Democrats can and should confront Trump and his enablers head-on. Incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia caught the spirit of the moment when he sent a two-word tweet to the White House: “Lawyer Up.” Americans are feeling it, as well: According to Pew Research’s November 18 study, eight in 10 Americans are happy with the midterm results and believe Democrats will have a better plan for the future.

The Trump White House responded to the midterm results with as much grace as a car crash in slow motion. On November 9, White House counsel William O. Scharf sent Garcia and several other Democrats a preemptive warning letter stating that Trump “expects members of Congress to discharge their instigative [sic] functions within settled constitutional limits.” If the new Democratic Congress acts within the same kind of “settled constitutional limits” as the current administration, then buckle up for a dizzying 2027.

There are many issues for congressional Democrats to address: the unconstitutional war with Iran, tariffs, rampant inflation, executive overreach, the Supreme Court, and the future of AI. While all of these issues are pressing, Democrats should make investigating immigration officials a top priority. Among the many issues that pushed Democrats to victory this month, the Trump administration’s cruel persecution of immigrants and their families resonated greatly with voters.

Despite the election results, the Trump administration has continued arrests and deportations at its regular pace. Within the past days, a number of ICE arrests have grabbed headlines. On November 20, Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained Chinese-born neuroscientist Eva Yi Xie, a third-year Ph.D. student at Princeton, at Reagan Washington National Airport after she returned from a conference. Xie, who came to the U.S. from China as a child in 2016 and had applied for asylum and been assigned a court hearing in 2028, was detained on the grounds of overstaying a visa. An immigration judge, Anthony Trenga, has ordered ICE to comply with a petition of habeas corpus submitted by Xie’s attorneys, as reported on Friday by The Daily Princetonian.

Domestic flights at airports in other parts of the country have also become a new venue for Trump’s disturbing deportation scheme. In a more brazen act, ICE agents disrupted holiday travel at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday, November 21, when several unmarked agents seized a passenger waiting to board an Alaska Airlines flight. The Department of Homeland Security later confirmed that several agents detained Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, who they asserted had overstayed a visa. ICE then detained Mendoza’s daughter, who threw coffee at the agents as he was taken to custody, and charged her with overstaying a visa, as well. ICE’s actions led Washington Governor Bob Ferguson to call for ICE to be excluded from the state.

In places like California’s San Joaquin Valley, ICE agents continue to detain and deport lifelong residents like Luis Arreguin, who spent 49 of the 54 years of his life in California. For much of the two years since Trump returned to office, ICE and Customs and Border Protection have terrorized communities in the valley, leaving them with empty streets, shells of their former activity.

And, lest we forget, in many of the ICE and Border Patrol sweeps since January 2025, it is U.S. citizens who have been detained, with little thought given to their constitutional rights. ProPublica’s Nicole Foy, who last year broke the first story that ICE had detained 170 U.S. citizens, last month reported that the figure is now closer to 500.

The promotion of Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff is proof that, in spite of the midterm gains for Democrats, Trump will likely double down on immigration enforcement. Given Miller’s central role in DHS’s body count policy—arresting people to fill preestablished quotas, even if suspects turned out to be U.S. citizens—along with his documented obsession with pseudo-history and advocacy of the so-called “great replacement theory,” Miller’s new role is a strong signal of the administration’s priorities: Trump essentially views the Republicans’ midterm massacre as an occasion to double down on whatever policies he has in mind to deter future immigration and punish critics of ICE.

If Democrats want to honor their commitment to voters—and really demonstrate plans for a long-term solution for ethical immigration—they will prioritize investigations of the Department of Homeland Security in the coming year.

House and Senate Democrats have hardly been idle while in the minority. As I wrote a year ago, Representative Robert Garcia notably held hearings in Los Angeles regarding the unlawful deployment of the National Guard and the impact of ICE raids on California. On November 2 of this year, ProPublica reported on a letter submitted by a delegation of 40 House Democrats led by Representative Lou Carrera, who demanded that DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin release data on the number of U.S. citizens detained by ICE and CBP.

At the moment, Democrats are still developing a strategy for the new year. Politico reported that, despite Trump’s appointing Miller to chief of staff, many congressional Democrats see the midterm results as leverage with Trump to push immigration reform. Several Texas Democrats, including Representative Henry Cuellar and the newly elected Senator James Talarico, have stated they would be willing to work with the Trump administration on real immigration reform.

Much of that logic is rooted in a long-game strategy to push the White House to tone down mass raids and collaborate on new immigration legislation. Part of it is driven by the hope that Trump’s mind has changed, with some pointing to his statement during the recent 60 Minutes interview that his deportation agenda was “too tough” and promulgated the blue wave. Moderate Democrats are also worried about being portrayed as the “open-border” party—a fear going back to the 2024 election and before.

Nevertheless, calls for bipartisanship will not meet the urgent moment. The existing immigration system is so connected with the Trump machine that mere reforms are no match for the horrifying reality of the situation.

Between now and the 2028 election, Democrats have to work toward holding the current immigration bureaucracy, engineered by Donald Trump, accountable—not just for the sake of scoring political points but to repair the country and restore the rule of law. Despite Congress’s deference to the executive branch for the past two years, now is the time for Congress to flex its legislative power as described in the Constitution.

What steps should Democrats take? First, subpoena current and former Trump administration members involved in devising and enforcing immigration policy, as well as contractors affiliated with immigration projects.

We cannot ignore the urgent fact that there have been dozens of cases of people who have died in ICE detention due to poor condition and abuse from guards. “Start with the people who have died in ICE detention at a pace that is twice the historical average,” says Ann Garcia, senior staff attorney at the National Immigration Project. “Congress should subpoena every one of those records along with every detention center contract and assess where gaps led to death.” This inquiry should target agents who killed suspects during detention, such as David Brouillette, who shot immigrant Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero during a vehicle stop, along with agents Jonathan Ross, Raymundo Gutierrez, and Jesus Ochoa, who murdered protesters Alex Pretti and Renée Good.

Representative Jamie Raskin, who is slated to become chair of the House Judiciary Committee in January, has indicated that committee would prioritize restoring oversight over DHS. “Congressional Republicans wrote Trump’s ICE and CBP checks for $210 billion in taxpayer money with absolutely no oversight and no accountability,” says Raskin in a statement to The New Republic. “Predictably, we have seen zero oversight by Congressional Republicans on the killings of innocent people by immigration officers in our streets. We have seen zero oversight by Congressional Republicans on the inhumane treatment and deaths that are occurring in Trump’s mass detention centers around the country.”

Congress must also investigate the financial relationship between the deportation apparatus and the Trump family and its acolytes. It should begin with investigating the operation of Geo Group and CoreCivic, both of which maxed out their contributions to Trump’s campaign in 2024. It should also not be a surprise that the Trump family also owns stock in both companies.

Now both private prison corporations are urging ICE officials to purchase their facilities at inflated prices, before Democrats take control of Congress in January. For example, last month ICE paid CoreCivic $485.6 million for its Appleton, Minnesota, detention facility which, a year before, offered it to the state of Minnesota for $75 million. Last week, ICE purchased the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Washington, from GEO Group for a similar whopping $453 million. As Ann Garcia explains it: “Most of these jails are run by private companies like GEO Group, which put profit before people. The person now running ICE spent more than a decade as a GEO executive. And at a minimum, Congress has to strip ICE and CBP of the slush fund that has paid for all of their abuse against American communities.”

Raskin has signaled that finances would be a key issue of future hearings. “This system of financial irresponsibility, bureaucratic indifference, and medical negligence ends in January,” promised Raskin. “When Democrats take control of the House, we will launch all the congressional oversight and accountability work that Republicans have abandoned.”

Second, pass legislation that establishes clear guardrails on DHS, forces ICE and CBP to be transparent, and have both agencies take accountability for any illegal activity.

Already, current Democratic legislators have begun introducing legislation for the next cycle. Senator Andy Kim of New Jersey authored a bill to require the DHS to report any deaths within detention facilities within 30 days, and an immediate notice if a suspect is killed during enforcement operations like traffic stops. In the House, California Representative Lateefah Simon introduced a bill that would set final orders of removal to expire within 10 years for individuals who have been constantly present within the U.S. and have not committed any crime.

But there is more work to be done to protect the vast majority of aliens, who have never been accused of any crime. There is also a need to reform the rules for private bills with regard to the House and Senate Judiciary Committees. As I previously wrote for The New Republic, ICE and CBP have made the rules regarding private bills more restrictive with deportation cases.

Third, Democrats should invest in studying long-term immigration reform. Like Representative Robert Garcia’s hearings from last year, Democrats need to speak with those caught in the immigration system to understand how immigration policy is structured before the government can rebuild it. If Democrats can learn the lessons from failed policies like the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, it can create a better future that offers honest pathways to citizenship.

In the Senate, the main obstacle that awaits Democrats in the new year is the infamous filibuster. Already, as The Hill has reported, the filibuster is weighing on Senate Democrats who are hoping to avoid run-ins with their Republican colleagues on issues like immigration. Progressives, like Senator Jeff Merkley, have called for replacing the current filibuster rules with the talking filibuster—a continuous debate that ends when the filibustering part runs out of steam. More moderate voices, like Chuck Schumer, have urged caution. But, as political scientist Daniel Wirls noted in his 2021 study The Senate: From White Supremacy to Governmental Gridlock, keeping the filibuster has little to do with honoring political traditions: “It’s about political power, not constitutional principle. When push comes to shove, the vast majority of Senators prefer their individual and partisan power over better government.”

There are many questions that will confront Democrats in the coming months beyond the political calculus of winning in 2028. When pundits discussed immigration in 2024, they were happy to talk about it as an important issue but offered little insight on how it should be managed. What they got was an unchecked secret police that not only has detained and deported thousands of immigrants who have obeyed the law, but has even killed protesters and arrested U.S. citizens. They could articulate immigration as an issue but failed to foresee the rise of an ICE deportation machine, third-country deportations, and the Supreme Court legitimizing racial discrimination with Kavanaugh stops.

Democrats in Congress have a busy year ahead of them. Start by repairing the integrity of the nation’s immigration system.

name: Human Rights
title: Trump effectively ended asylum. Advocates look to the Supreme Court to restore it
description:
Now immigration advocates are looking to the Supreme Court to decide whether Trump has the authority to keep this once vital pathway closed.
VANESSA ROMO, BYLINE: For nearly two years, the Trump administration has prohibited asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border.
It's also canceled thousands of pending asylum applications and overhauled the immigration court system with mass firings of judges.
She says, taken together, the Trump administration's moves have gutted asylum in America and fundamentally restricted the job of immigration judges.
Combined, critics say the changes make much of the immigration court system a deportation arm of ICE.
text:
JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:

For decades, asylum offered protection for people fleeing persecution and danger. But under President Trump, that protection has been effectively shut down. Now immigration advocates are looking to the Supreme Court to decide whether Trump has the authority to keep this once vital pathway closed. Here's NPR's Vanessa Romo.

VANESSA ROMO, BYLINE: For nearly two years, the Trump administration has prohibited asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border. It's also canceled thousands of pending asylum applications and overhauled the immigration court system with mass firings of judges.

JENNIFER PEYTON: I got an email firing me when I was on vacation with my family.

ROMO: That's Jennifer Peyton, a former assistant chief immigration judge in Chicago who served on the bench for nine years. She says, taken together, the Trump administration's moves have gutted asylum in America and fundamentally restricted the job of immigration judges. Now, she's an immigration attorney who regularly appears before the judges that she helped train, though many of them have been fired too. Peyton says that's left scores of novice judges, some of whom, she says, are wreaking havoc.

PEYTON: The things I hear immigration judges say, they're, quite frankly, sometimes wrong. They're rash decisions and lack - or don't care that they lack - the training that we so rigorously put them through when I was on that team.

ROMO: President Trump has long claimed that asylum has been abused by people with, quote, "fake claims," which is why, within hours of retaking office, he issued the asylum ban along the southern border. The administration has also taken aggressive steps it says are intended to alleviate the crushing backlog of existing asylum cases. New Justice Department rules allow the government's lawyers to get claims more easily thrown out by arguing they're incomplete or insufficient.

Another tactic - get immigration judges to agree to send people to third countries and direct them to apply for asylum there, even when those third nations can't guarantee a person any protections. Combined, critics say the changes make much of the immigration court system a deportation arm of ICE.

MADHAVI NARAYANAN: As asylum attorneys trying to defend that right, all we can really do is try to keep fighting.

ROMO: That's Madhavi Narayanan, an immigration attorney with Human Rights First. She represents an Ethiopian man who's part of an ethnic minority facing repression from the ruling government. We're only identifying him by his initials, Z.G., because he fears retribution from the Ethiopian government. Narayanan says he fled Ethiopia following arrest and torture for his political views.

NARAYANAN: His ethnicity - they're very widely targeted, and it's very clearly documented, not only that he has corroborating evidence of his claim and statements from others who know what happened to him. And the torture that he underwent was extremely brutal. So in the past, he would have been granted asylum pretty quickly.

ROMO: Instead, Z.G. is one of thousands of asylum-seekers whose applications ICE successfully petitioned to be canceled. And like many others, he was given a removal order to a third country he's never stepped foot in - Uganda, a country that does not recognize the armed conflict in Ethiopia as a war and would likely send Z.G. back home. Narayanan says the judge hearing the case was troubled by that but said his hands were tied.

NARAYANAN: He was basically like, OK, I hear everything that you said, but I read this case, and I'm not allowed to consider this. And that was it.

ROMO: In coming months, the Supreme Court will decide whether sending asylum-seekers to other countries is legal, and it'll consider the question of the ban. But supporters of the president's restrictions are hoping the high court stays the course. Simon Hankinson is with the conservative Heritage Foundation, a think tank closely aligned with the president. Like Trump, Hankinson contends that most asylum applicants are exploiting the system and simply don't qualify for it.

SIMON HANKINSON: And even if they did, they've already passed through Mexico, which is a safe third country where they could claim asylum. So you have a population that overwhelmingly will not qualify under U.S. law for asylum. They're here because they want to get a job, essentially.

ROMO: Since the ban went into effect, Border Patrol apprehensions at the Southern border this year dropped to their lowest level in agency history. In the meantime, millions of people with active claims remain in limbo, like Z.G. He's desperately hoping to stay in the U.S. and hopes the high court reopens the asylum door.

Vanessa Romo, NPR News. Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

text:
The Supreme Court has agreed to review President Donald Trump’s effort to suspend access to asylum at the U.S.-Mexico border, setting up a major legal fight over the limits of presidential power and protections for people seeking refuge in the United States.

The administration is asking the justices to overturn lower court rulings that found Trump’s executive order unlawfully blocked migrants from applying for asylum. The order, issued on Trump’s first day back in office in January 2025, declared the situation at the southern border an “invasion” and sought to suspend entry and access to asylum for migrants covered by the policy.

Federal immigration law generally allows people physically present in the United States or arriving at the country to apply for asylum, regardless of how they entered. Applicants must still meet legal requirements to qualify for protection, including demonstrating they face persecution based on certain protected grounds.

The Trump administration argues the president has broad authority under federal immigration law to restrict entry and categorically deny asylum claims covered by the order. Officials say lengthy processing times contributed to border challenges and argue the policy has helped reduce crossings.

Immigrant rights groups challenge that interpretation, arguing Congress established protections and procedures that the president cannot unilaterally eliminate. They say the policy prevents people fleeing persecution from having their claims individually considered, as required by law.

The legal dispute centers in part on the president’s authority under Section 212(f) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which allows a president to suspend the entry of certain noncitizens when their entry is deemed detrimental to U.S. interests. The question is whether that authority also allows the administration to shut off access to the asylum application process.

The fight over asylum restrictions is not new. Previous administrations have also imposed limits on migrants seeking protection at the southern border. Trump’s first administration implemented policies including Remain in Mexico and restrictions on asylum eligibility. The Biden administration also introduced restrictions on asylum eligibility during periods of high border crossings.

The case also raises questions about the United States’ obligations under international refugee agreements, including protections against returning people to countries where they face persecution or torture.

The Supreme Court is expected to hear arguments in the case in the spring, with a decision anticipated by the end of June. name: Policy
title: Forget Congress. The Supreme Court will decide the future of Trump's immigration agenda
description:
“These Trump policies are not only illegal but also unpopular.” Trump has had a mixed record on immigration at the 6-3 conservative court since returning to power last year.
And the court limited his ability to use the 1798 Alien Enemies Act to quickly remove certain migrants from the country.
White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis dismissed Wang’s assertion that the court will find Trump’s immigration policies illegal.
Some Democrats have framed the recapture of Congress as a rejection by voters of the administration’s immigration policies.
Wessan predicted that the justices will view lower court decisions on immigration against the administration with similar skepticism.
text:
By John Fritze, CNN

(CNN) — Democrats want to sideline President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda when they take control of Congress next year, but the real fight may take place across the street where the conservative Supreme Court is poised to uphold several of his most controversial policies.

The court will soon consider blockbuster appeals on the president’s asylum ban, his vast expansion of mandatory detention of migrants and his push to send certain people in the US illegally to countries other than their homeland — including some with dubious human rights records.

Decisions in those cases are expected by late June.

Though those three cases and several others are less flashy than this past summer’s blockbuster decision upholding birthright citizenship, the outcomes in the nuts-and-bolts disputes will have profound implications for policies the administration says are “indispensable” to its overall immigration crackdown.

“In all three of these cases, the Trump administration is trying to rewrite laws enacted by Congress, in service of a radical anti-immigrant agenda that has hurt not only immigrants, but the rule of law,” said Cecillia Wang with the American Civil Liberties Union, which is opposing the administration in two of those cases. “These Trump policies are not only illegal but also unpopular.”

Trump has had a mixed record on immigration at the 6-3 conservative court since returning to power last year. His unprecedented push to upend birthright citizenship was rejected. And the court limited his ability to use the 1798 Alien Enemies Act to quickly remove certain migrants from the country.

On the other hand, six-justice majorities in June allowed Trump to end a form of humanitarian relief known as Temporary Protected Status and to limit asylum claims made at the border.

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis dismissed Wang’s assertion that the court will find Trump’s immigration policies illegal.

“If the American Civil Liberties Union cares more about criminal illegal aliens than they do about American citizens, then they should change their name,” she said.

Some Democrats have framed the recapture of Congress as a rejection by voters of the administration’s immigration policies. Minnesota Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan vowed to “rip ICE apart.” New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is all but certain to become the next House speaker, told CBS that Democrats would “put an end to Donald Trump’s violent mass deportation machine.”

But Republicans have already frontloaded funding for ICE for years. And Trump this month named Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, as White House chief of staff — a sign that the administration has no intention of slowing its immigration agenda.

“It stands to reason that hyper-aggressive immigration enforcement will continue to be one of the hallmarks of the Trump administration even as it faces Democratic majorities in both chambers of the legislature,” said Steve Vladeck, CNN Supreme Court analyst and professor at Georgetown University Law Center. “Whether the extremism of these policies will be allowed to continue is therefore going to be up to the Supreme Court.”

Conservatives who support the policies see a court that is prepared to back the president’s program.

“Over and over, judges in the district courts and the courts of appeals have interpreted the law contrary to clear congressional intent as evidenced by the text. And as a result, those decisions keep getting overturned,” Iowa Solicitor General Eric Wessan, whose state led briefs supporting the administration in two of the biggest cases, told CNN.

Wessan predicted that the justices will view lower court decisions on immigration against the administration with similar skepticism.

“Looking at the immigration cases the Supreme Court has taken this term,” he predicted, “I think it’s doing the same kind of cleanup.”

Human rights and arrests

The showdown will begin on December 9, when the justices will hear arguments in a case challenging Trump’s push to remove certain migrants to countries other than their homeland. In many cases, those removals are carried out without giving the migrant an opportunity to raise human rights concerns.

Federal law allows such “third country” removals in cases when a migrant’s home country refuses to accept them. The administration has used that provision to remove an Iranian national to Nicaragua, for instance, and Venezuelans to El Salvador, according to immigrants’ rights groups.

In some of those cases, immigrant rights groups say, migrants were sent back to their homeland from the “third country,” even when an immigration judge ordered that the administration not return to them to their native country.

Congress has also required the administration to ensure migrants won’t be tortured or persecuted once they land in a third country. That determination was previously made on a case-by-case basis. Under the second Trump administration, the government now accepts blanket assurances from a foreign country that no torture will take place, and migrants are often removed to that country without notice.

The Supreme Court, on its emergency docket, three times allowed the administration to pursue the policy while the case remained pending. It has not explained its reasoning.

Increase in arrests of migrants

Next year, the court will turn to the Trump administration’s decision to funnel not only recent border crossers into mandatory detention but also people who have been living within the United States for years.

That shift has permitted the Department of Homeland Security to dramatically increase the number of migrants arrested. And so if the court rejects that change, it will almost certainly jeopardize the administration’s ability to carry out massive sweeps for migrants that have played out in cities like Chicago and Minneapolis.

Immigrant rights groups say no prior administration, including Trump’s first, has interpreted federal law to require mandatory detention of so many migrants. But Justice Department officials told the Supreme Court that it is simply following the law that Congress enacted.

Asylum ban

And in the spring, the court will hear a challenge to Trump’s asylum ban. The president argues people crossing the border are making false asylum claims as a way to enter the country then stall the deportation process, since it can take years to resolve them.

US Solicitor General D. John Sauer, the administration’s top appellate attorney, warned the court of a “vicious cycle” that encouraged “illegal entry by millions of aliens, who (quite justifiably) inferred that even if they lacked meritorious asylum claims, they would ‘be released to live and work in the United States during their removal proceedings.’”

But the Immigration and Nationality Act specifically allows migrants to claim asylum, even as it leaves the decision about whether to grant safe harbor up to administration officials.

In stark language, the Justice Department has described its asylum policy as one of the “most important and effective” policies for stemming illegal immigration. A lower court order against the policy, the administration said, “threatens to revive the chaos along the southwest border that the proclamation has fended off for the past year and a half.”

The ACLU, representing 13 individuals and three immigrant rights groups that challenged the policy, said that if Trump wants to change the way asylum works, he should have passed a bill in Congress during the two years the chambers were in Republican hands.

Richard Caldarone, a senior litigation attorney at the National Immigrant Justice Center, said that the policies at issue in the cases had already put tens of thousands of people in harm’s way.

“These policies have been overwhelmingly rejected by lower courts across the country, and they flatly violate US immigration law as it has been understood for decades,” said Caldarone, whose group is fighting the administration in the asylum case.

“If the court validates the policies,” he said, “it will enshrine a new generation of internment camps, all but end the US asylum system as we have known it for almost half a century, and shatter our nation’s commitment to upholding human rights and democratic norms.”
