title: The Dairy Industry Is Quietly Building a More Exploitable Workforce - The American Prospect
description:
Most Americans have eaten food harvested by H-2A farmworkers, a binational migrant workforce who represent one-sixth of the nation’s farmworkers.
But the dairy industry is a notable exception, largely barred from recruiting H-2A farmworkers due to a regulatory barrier: The H-2A program is limited to seasonal jobs, which are uncommon in the year-round dairy industry.
If the dairy industry transitions to hiring H-2A visa holders, dairy workers could see pay cuts in almost every state that fits this definition.
And the seasonality requirement, the primary barrier for the dairy industry, would require Congress’s intervention.
What the memo does provide is very specific guidance on how the dairy industry could meet this requirement.
text:
This story was originally published by Sentient.

Jiménez has worked on New York dairy farms for nearly two decades, long enough to raise three children in the state and cultivate his own vegetable garden. Between 12-hour shifts tending calves, he finds pockets of time to organize with Alianza Agrícola, a collective of immigrant dairy farmworkers in New York state. This includes visiting nearby farms to educate workers on how to defend their rights, both as immigrants and agricultural workers with high-risk jobs. Sometimes this information can mean the difference between life and death.

There is one particularly vulnerable group of farmworkers he still struggles to reach: those on H-2A visas that allow them to live and work in the U.S. for up to 10 months per year.

Most Americans have eaten food harvested by H-2A farmworkers, a binational migrant workforce who represent one-sixth of the nation’s farmworkers. Yet their contributions to U.S. agriculture often remain out of sight for the same reason that Jiménez struggles to reach them: they live under the tight control of their employers who provide them with shared housing, limited transportation and their visa sponsorship.

“They tell me I cannot go to the house where they live because the supervisor is circling around and they do not want to have problems. They’re afraid,” says Jiménez, originally in Spanish that was later translated into English. He asked to only be identified by his last name.

Under New York law, farmworkers are guaranteed the right to receive visitors, including in employer-owned housing, but it’s still hard to enforce this under a system where, as Jiménez. put it, “the bosses have control over everything.”

On its current trajectory, the H-2A program looks increasingly like the future of farm labor in the United States. The number of H-2A visas issued annually has ballooned in recent years, surpassing 315,000 in 2024. These workers, largely from Mexico, South Africa and countries in Central America, have become indispensable to some of the most labor-intensive agricultural jobs, including harvesting crops that expose workers to poisonous residues in the process, like tobacco and sugarcane.

But the dairy industry is a notable exception, largely barred from recruiting H-2A farmworkers due to a regulatory barrier: The H-2A program is limited to seasonal jobs, which are uncommon in the year-round dairy industry. Dairy and other livestock farms are among the few agricultural industries that still rely almost exclusively on a local workforce, often made up of immigrants who permanently reside in the United States.

However, this could change as the dairy industry ramps up its lobbying effort to recruit H-2A farmworkers, a move that has the backing of the Trump Administration. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins has called the proposed H-2A expansion into the dairy industry her “utmost priority” while at the helm of the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

The H-2A program is being touted by the administration as a legal solution to farmworker shortages, but these shortages have also worsened under the administration’s mass deportation agenda and shuttering of the southern border, following the Biden administration’s near total ban on asylum.

These policy changes have left the H-2A program as a rare legal avenue into the U.S., hitting record-high recruitment levels under the Trump administration while poised to grow even further if the livestock industry is permitted to fully participate.

Meanwhile, farmworker advocates warn that scaling up the H-2A program could increase the risk of labor and human rights abuses, including human trafficking, while driving down farmworker wages across the livestock industry.

“We don’t have a philosophical objection to letting people come here to work and we’re not out to cause a labor crisis for no particular reason,” says Nathan Leys, a staff attorney at FarmSTAND. “What we’re worried about is workers being treated inhumanely, and just making life easier for agricultural employers without putting any additional safeguards into the program. That is something that worries me a lot.”

Catastrophic Wage Cuts Could Cause More Financial Strain for Workers

In October 2025, the Department of Labor changed how it calculates the hourly minimum wage for H-2A farmworkers, known as the Adverse Effect Wage Rate, or AEWR. This change immediately set into effect the most sweeping wage cuts in modern U.S. agricultural history. And these changes could go further: two bills pending before Congress seek to expand the H-2A program to livestock farms.

Sentient’s latest analysis shows how these wage cuts could significantly deepen if the H-2A program expands to include year-round jobs on hog, poultry and dairy farms. In many states, these livestock farmworkers could see their annual wages cut in half or more.

These wage cuts have taken a sharp toll on H-2A farmworkers hired for seasonal jobs on U.S. farms. Sentient previously interviewed an H-2A crop farmworker whose hourly wages dropped by 30 percent, from $16.16 in 2025 to $11.15 in 2026, jeopardizing his finances and health. Under pressure not to miss a day of pay, he worked even while exhibiting clear signs of heat illness, which can progress to death if untreated.

This is the bleak reality of what pay cuts mean for an already low-wage workforce, a level of financial strain that can quickly become life-threatening.

Following a methodology first developed by the Economic Policy Institute, Sentient compared average annual pay for hog, poultry and dairy farmworkers in 2025, based on Bureau of Labor Statistics data, with annual pay under the H-2A baseline wage rules for 2026-27. The analysis updates Costa’s figures and those in this Sentient story from January 2026, and only includes states with at least 100 employees per industry.

The findings are stark. If the dairy industry transitions to hiring H-2A visa holders, dairy workers could see pay cuts in almost every state that fits this definition. The sole exception is Puerto Rico—the only U.S. territory included in our analysis. In Georgia, the largest milk producer in the southeastern United States, the H-2A baseline wage is nearly 67% lower than the 2025 average state dairy industry wage—a difference of $39,892 per year.

For hog and poultry, farmworkers on year-round H-2A visas would earn pay below the 2025 industry average in every state. Poultry workers in Mississippi and Alabama would be hit especially hard, with a difference of more than 70%. In Alabama, it amounts to $54,233 per year. And in Iowa, the nation’s largest hog producer, which employed over 4,500 people in the industry in 2025, a workforce of H-2A workers would be paid 49% less than the previous average or $26,987.

H-2A workers would be paid much less almost everywhere, as projected H-2A wages are more than $10,000 lower per year than the average 2025 farmworker wage in all but a handful of states. In almost a third of states, the modeled wage gap exceeds $30,000 a year.

“The cuts are going to be so drastic that I think employers are going to be incentivized to just replace all those area workers with H-2A workers,” says Daniel Costa, the director of immigration law and policy research at the Economic Policy Institute.

The future of this wage is up in the air. In August, a federal judge ruled the new wage methodology unlawful and ordered the Department of Labor to develop a different way of determining the baseline pay of H-2A farmworkers by December 30. “We don’t know yet what the new rule will look like,” Costa told Sentient by email. “DOL could come back and do a similar rule, if they correct the procedural aspects of how they went about issuing the rule and their reasoning.”

Until the Department of Labor issues a new methodology, H-2A farmworkers are still being paid under this unlawful wage structure. Yet this wage structure could also become permanent through one of the pending bills seeking to expand the H-2A program, proposed by the House Agricultural Committee Chair Glenn Thompson. The bill would codify this wage rule into law, and therefore, override any new methodology issued by the Department of Labor.

“A Mathematically Guaranteed Subclass of Workers”

How is such a large projected wage cut possible? The answer hinges on how the new baseline wage for H-2A farmworkers is calculated.

The new rule divides farmworkers into two classes of wage earners, a system designed, in theory, to pay farmworkers based on skill level. Yet the entry-level class of wage earners, known as skill level I, is a sweeping category that includes 92% of H-2A farmworkers, according to the Department of Labor’s own projection. This tiered system allows the vast majority of H-2A farmworkers to be paid significantly lower wages than previous years—at the 17th percentile of farmworker wages in their region.

Cutting even further into hourly wages, this rule also allows employers to deduct housing costs directly from H-2A farmworkers’ pay. In Mississippi, when accounting for the housing deduction, the H-2A minimum wage at skill level I is just $8.84 per hour.

This structure establishes a “mathematically guaranteed subclass of workers,” according to Nathan Leys of FarmSTAND. So far, he has observed farmworkers being swept into this subclass without much apparent oversight. “A lot of positions are being certified as skill level I, and it doesn’t seem like DOL is doing a whole lot of double-checking to make sure that those positions really are appropriately classified as skill level I,” Leys tells Sentient.

There is also evidence of H-2A consultants pushing to classify employees as skill level I to lower wages. Back in November 2025, just a few weeks into the new wage rule, Daniel Ross, an attorney who specializes in H-2A labor law, hosted a virtual meeting to discuss this “celebratory moment.” Over Zoom, after stating “everything we say here today is meant to be general, high-level guidance,” he told an audience of labor contractors and employers to classify jobs as skill level I, rather than the higher-paid skill level II, even at the risk of this being flagged by a State Workforce Agency as a deficiency in the initial review of H-2A requests.

If a State Workforce Agency flags the skill level I classification for correction, “my advice would be don’t concede right away. Like, fight back. Tell them, ‘No, we’ll take this to the certifying officer,’” said Ross, who works for Seso Inc., a company that assists contractors and employers in recruiting H-2A farmworkers. He said this while presenting a slide with examples of State Workforce Agencies allegedly backing down from a stricter approach to broadening the skill-level 1 category to include more experienced workers. Sentient reached out to Mr. Ross but did not receive a response by the time of publication.

This meeting appeared to be attended by some of the largest H-2A labor contractors who are hired by farms to recruit and oversee farmworkers. Participants in the Zoom chat included representatives of Empire Farm Labor Contractor LLC, which has recruited over 4,000 H-2A farmworkers to date in 2026, and Overlook Harvesting, which has recruited over 3,500 H-2A farmworkers over the same period, according to federal H-2A data.

Sentient’s analysis is based on the skill level I wages, including the house reduction, which may reflect an even larger figure than the Department of Labor’s projection of 92%, given the push to widen the classification of this “subclass” of workers.

These Wage Cuts Would Create a Ripple Effect for All Farmworkers

These wage cuts depress the wages of all farmworkers, regardless of immigration status, including U.S. citizens and undocumented workers. This is due to a longstanding rule that requires farmworkers in “corresponding” positions—in other words, those who perform similar jobs on the same farm—be paid at least the H-2A wage, a legal obligation aimed at ensuring that H-2A farmworkers don’t displace the existing workforce.

Yet historically the H-2A minimum wage was higher than the state-level minimum wage, raising the wage floor for all farmworkers. Sentient’s calculations show how the current H-2A minimum wage does just the opposite, undercutting the wages of all livestock workers.

This is already playing out on some dairy farms. For instance, Riverview LLP’s controversial megadairy in Morris, Minnesota, recently received approval to hire H-2A farmworkers for 28 weeks for a rate of just $12.92, when including the housing deduction—the skill level I tier of wages for a job that may include repairing broken water lines, helping in the milking parlor with “cold stressed cows” and clearing snow from the feed alleys.

If local workers apply for this same job, they’d be paid the H-2A minimum wage, without the housing deduction: $14.60 per hour over 40 hours per week, according to the job order. This would amount to $16,352 over the course of the 28-week position (or $30,368 if this job were hypothetically extended to a year)—significantly less than the current annual wage of dairy workers in Minnesota of $53,896.

Wage cuts of this magnitude threaten to push farmworkers across the country into deeper financial strain, workers who are already struggling to afford rising food and housing costs. Jiménez currently makes $19.20 per hour, working nearly 80 hours per week, but this could be undercut if New York dairies hire H-2A workers at the skill level 1 rate of $13.62 per hour.

“It is a day-to-day struggle because we cannot send our children to college,” says Jiménez, elevating his voice above the din of farm machinery and mooing in the background of the phone call. “We still cannot advance to another level. We will always be workers.”

Pending Bill Would Expand Executive Power Over Labor

At the World Dairy Expo in September, Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins acknowledged the limits of her authority when asked about her plans for a “true, year-round H-2A program specifically for dairy” at a press conference. “The challenge is that this is a congressionally authorized program that very clearly states ‘seasonal,’” Rollins said before a crowd of dairy producers, agribusiness leaders and journalists gathered in Wisconsin.

She went on to explain that the USDA doesn’t write the rules for the H-2A program. “The Department of Labor, in partnership with USCIS and Homeland Security, they write the rules and the regulations,” said Rollins. And the seasonality requirement, the primary barrier for the dairy industry, would require Congress’s intervention.

Still, Rollins assured the crowd that “we are making progress” toward expanding the H-2A program while “we hopefully wait for Congress quickly to make some changes.”

In the future, Rollins could be given authority to expand the H-2A program to even more industries and rewrite many of its rules. Rep. Glenn Thompson’s proposed legislation, the Securing Agriculture’s Workforce Act, would give the Secretary of Agriculture the broad authority to “issue rules to define agricultural labor or services’’ opening the doors for more industries to be defined as agriculture at the discretion of the Agriculture Secretary, a presidentially appointed position.

The bill would consolidate the power of the executive branch over labor decisions, giving “both the Secretary of Agriculture, as well as the Secretary of Labor the authority that neither one of them has had in the past,” says Diego Iñiguez-López, the director of government affairs at the United Farmworkers Foundation, one of the signatories to a letter urging Congress to oppose this legislation in part because of its “executive overreach.”

The legislation would also give the Secretary of Labor authority to change protections established by Congress, allowing the Labor Secretary to “completely rewrite that and eliminate certain statutory protections,” Iñiguez-López tells Sentient. “So it’s essentially Congress giving its own authority to the executive branch for it to never receive it back again.”

If passed, this legislation would also automatically expand the definition of agriculture to include new sectors, including some meat processing and slaughtering jobs that are currently considered manufacturing. This would enable another H-2A expansion into a highly injury-prone line of work that currently employs many legal immigrants, including those with Temporary Protected Status targeted by the Trump administration.

Sidelining Farmworker Advocates for Livestock Industry Recommendations

The proposed Securing Agriculture’s Workforce Act is based on policy recommendations from the House Agriculture Committee’s Agricultural Labor Working Group, a bipartisan task force of 14 legislators that formed in June 2023.

Just a few weeks after its formation, the task force sought input from some of the largest meat industry trade groups. On July 19, 2023, the group of legislators hosted a discussion on how “panelists’ industries would benefit if the H-2A program is expanded,” according to the meeting summary.

Industry leaders from the Meat Institute, Livestock Marketing Association and the National Milk Producers Federation, along with the National Alliance of Forest Owners, made the case for extending the visa program to dairy farms, meat processors, livestock auctions and jobs in forestry. These recommendations went on to become central to Thompson’s legislative proposal.

On September 20, 2023, the subcommittee invited farmworker advocates and labor experts, including Costa of the Economic Policy Institute, to provide feedback on labor conditions. Costa tells Sentient he was surprised to learn that the legislators tasked with developing reforms for the H-2A program didn’t seem to know how federal oversight of H-2A farmworkers’ rights works.

“They didn’t know which federal agency was in charge of enforcing the wage and hour laws for farmworkers, which was something I explained to them,” says Costa.

“They also never heard of Operation Blooming Onion, one of the biggest trafficking cases in history that involved H-2A,” he says. This resulted in a landmark federal indictment in 2021, following a multi-year federal investigation exposing how a trafficking ring recruited over a hundred farmworkers on H-2A visas under false pretenses and then forced them to harvest Vidalia onions at gunpoint, under the threat of violence.

The roundtable panelists recommended that the Department of Labor strengthen its enforcement of labor protections. “Farm employers know they can violate the law and it is highly unlikely that they will ever be investigated,” Costa wrote in a follow-up letter to the Agriculture Labor Working Group sent in November 2023.

But unlike the concerns of industries, Thompson’s draft legislation doesn’t include any of the labor concerns raised during this discussion.

A Handshake Deal With the Trump Administration

There is also the potential for some dairy producers to expand recruitment of H-2A farmworkers in advance of any Congressional action. In June, the Trump administration issued guidance on the dairy industry’s recruitment of these workers, which some advocates and agribusiness leaders alike interpreted as a signal to the industry that the current administration will be more lenient.

This informal expansion, as it has been interpreted by some, came in the form of a memo issued by the Department of Homeland Security clarifying that “dairy can involve H-2A eligible temporary or seasonal labor, no matter that dairy cows can require milking or other types of work year-round.”

This reiterates what is already longstanding federal policy, raising more questions than answers.

“Frankly, I find the memo confusing because the memo itself doesn’t seem to change anything, and yet the way it’s been presented is almost as if ‘oh look, this is a change,’” says Maggie Gray, an associate professor of political science at Adelphi University whose research has focused on H-2A farmworkers. If the rules haven’t changed, this prompts the question, she says, of “what’s actually going on here?”

“It does seem that this policy memorandum is some sort of invitation,” says Gray. Reading between the lines, she ventures a speculation: “Perhaps what it’s saying is that the Department of Labor will be more liberal in considering the requests that come in,” she says, referring to the jobs orders that outline the terms and conditions of H-2A roles. Yet she is hesitant to commit to this interpretation, reiterating, “again, I find it confusing.”

Under the rules of the H-2A program, employers aren’t allowed to arbitrarily splice year-round jobs into seasonal positions. Instead, seasonal jobs must be tied to “a certain time of year by an event or pattern, such as a short annual growing cycle,” which is easy to define on most crop farms but harder to point to on a livestock operation.

What the memo does provide is very specific guidance on how the dairy industry could meet this requirement. “It’s almost a road map. The USCIS policy statement almost tells you what you have to say in your job description to already get approved,” says Greg Schell, a lawyer at Southern Migrant Legal Services. “Say this. Don’t say this. Don’t say milk the cows. That’s the wrong thing to say,” given that milking cows is a daily, rather than seasonal, task.

Agribusiness leaders appear to agree with this interpretation. On August 13, Cornell University’s agriculture workforce development program hosted a meeting for dairy farmers interested in the H-2A program and provided an update on the memo.

“There’s a legislative process ongoing, which would make a lot of those more wide open for dairy,” said Richard Stup, director of Cornell University’s Agricultural Workforce Development Program, in the meeting. “But right now, there’s a more narrow window.”

“The law isn’t changing, but the eyes that are looking at it are thinking about it a little bit differently,” said John Hollay, president and CEO of the National Council of Agricultural Employers and a panelist in the meeting.

The Future of Dairy Farmworker Organizing

As the H-2A visa program expands, it could not only result in the displacement of long-term dairy farmworkers but also their organizing efforts.

Alianza Agricola’s origin story is telling. About a decade ago, Jiménez and a group of around ten friends decided to educate themselves on how undocumented immigrants could obtain driver’s licenses in New York. They became leaders in the Green Light Driver’s License Campaign, knocking on doors in New York to make their case.

“We started to arrive at many universities and churches to convince people that having a driver’s license was necessary for immigrants and they believed in us. Many people joined us as allies to raise our voice too,” says Jiménez. “Little by little we were gaining strength and we came to form our group: Alianza Agrícola.”

A few years later, their organization landed a historic victory: the 2019 passage of a law guaranteeing driver’s licenses to all New Yorkers, regardless of immigration status—a win that has continued to matter. They rely on these licenses to travel to farms, workers’ housing and the state’s capitol building to push for legislative demands.

This victory required years of building support in New York communities, which was in some ways more feasible because of Jiménez’s long-term dairy job. This dangerous work comes with one distinct advantage: it can provide a level of geographic stability and steady wages that is increasingly rare in agriculture. As Costa observes, some year-round farmworkers can still have a “salary that is above the poverty line and that can sustain a family.”

If the dairy industry succeeds in its efforts to hire more H-2A farmworkers, it will likely make it harder for workers like Jiménez to organize. Yet Jiménez is not one to be deterred. He plans on continuing to look for a way “to spend time with H-2A farmworkers outside their houses,” he says. “It’s difficult to convince them to get together,” he adds, given that they “always have limitations to be able to go out as well.” But he hopes to bring them into his fold of organizing. After all, their lives and wages are bound up together.

title: Forget Congress. The Supreme Court will decide the future of Trump's immigration agenda - CNN
description:
“These Trump policies are not only illegal but also unpopular.” Trump has had a mixed record on immigration at the 6-3 conservative court since returning to power last year.
And the court limited his ability to use the 1798 Alien Enemies Act to quickly remove certain migrants from the country.

text:
Democrats want to sideline President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda when they take control of Congress next year, but the real fight may take place across the street where the conservative Supreme Court is poised to uphold several of his most controversial policies.

The court will soon consider blockbuster appeals on the president’s asylum ban, his vast expansion of mandatory detention of migrants and his push to send certain people in the US illegally to countries other than their homeland — including some with dubious human rights records.

Decisions in those cases are expected by late June.

Though those three cases and several others are less flashy than this past summer’s blockbuster decision upholding birthright citizenship, the outcomes in the nuts-and-bolts disputes will have profound implications for policies the administration says are “indispensable” to its overall immigration crackdown.

“In all three of these cases, the Trump administration is trying to rewrite laws enacted by Congress, in service of a radical anti-immigrant agenda that has hurt not only immigrants, but the rule of law,” said Cecillia Wang with the American Civil Liberties Union, which is opposing the administration in two of those cases. “These Trump policies are not only illegal but also unpopular.”

Trump has had a mixed record on immigration at the 6-3 conservative court since returning to power last year. His unprecedented push to upend birthright citizenship was rejected. And the court limited his ability to use the 1798 Alien Enemies Act to quickly remove certain migrants from the country.

On the other hand, six-justice majorities in June allowed Trump to end a form of humanitarian relief known as Temporary Protected Status and to limit asylum claims made at the border.

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis dismissed Wang’s assertion that the court will find Trump’s immigration policies illegal.

“If the American Civil Liberties Union cares more about criminal illegal aliens than they do about American citizens, then they should change their name,” she said.

Some Democrats have framed the recapture of Congress as a rejection by voters of the administration’s immigration policies. Minnesota Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan vowed to “rip ICE apart.” New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is all but certain to become the next House speaker, told CBS that Democrats would “put an end to Donald Trump’s violent mass deportation machine.”

But Republicans have already frontloaded funding for ICE for years. And Trump this month named Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, as White House chief of staff — a sign that the administration has no intention of slowing its immigration agenda.

“It stands to reason that hyper-aggressive immigration enforcement will continue to be one of the hallmarks of the Trump administration even as it faces Democratic majorities in both chambers of the legislature,” said Steve Vladeck, CNN Supreme Court analyst and professor at Georgetown University Law Center. “Whether the extremism of these policies will be allowed to continue is therefore going to be up to the Supreme Court.”

Conservatives who support the policies see a court that is prepared to back the president’s program.

“Over and over, judges in the district courts and the courts of appeals have interpreted the law contrary to clear congressional intent as evidenced by the text. And as a result, those decisions keep getting overturned,” Iowa Solicitor General Eric Wessan, whose state led briefs supporting the administration in two of the biggest cases, told CNN.

Wessan predicted that the justices will view lower court decisions on immigration against the administration with similar skepticism.

“Looking at the immigration cases the Supreme Court has taken this term,” he predicted, “I think it’s doing the same kind of cleanup.”

Human rights and arrests

The showdown will begin on December 9, when the justices will hear arguments in a case challenging Trump’s push to remove certain migrants to countries other than their homeland. In many cases, those removals are carried out without giving the migrant an opportunity to raise human rights concerns.

Federal law allows such “third country” removals in cases when a migrant’s home country refuses to accept them. The administration has used that provision to remove an Iranian national to Nicaragua, for instance, and Venezuelans to El Salvador, according to immigrants’ rights groups.

In some of those cases, immigrant rights groups say, migrants were sent back to their homeland from the “third country,” even when an immigration judge ordered that the administration not return to them to their native country.

Congress has also required the administration to ensure migrants won’t be tortured or persecuted once they land in a third country. That determination was previously made on a case-by-case basis. Under the second Trump administration, the government now accepts blanket assurances from a foreign country that no torture will take place, and migrants are often removed to that country without notice.

The Supreme Court, on its emergency docket, three times allowed the administration to pursue the policy while the case remained pending. It has not explained its reasoning.

Increase in arrests of migrants

Next year, the court will turn to the Trump administration’s decision to funnel not only recent border crossers into mandatory detention but also people who have been living within the United States for years.

That shift has permitted the Department of Homeland Security to dramatically increase the number of migrants arrested. And so if the court rejects that change, it will almost certainly jeopardize the administration’s ability to carry out massive sweeps for migrants that have played out in cities like Chicago and Minneapolis.

Immigrant rights groups say no prior administration, including Trump’s first, has interpreted federal law to require mandatory detention of so many migrants. But Justice Department officials told the Supreme Court that it is simply following the law that Congress enacted.

Asylum ban

And in the spring, the court will hear a challenge to Trump’s asylum ban. The president argues people crossing the border are making false asylum claims as a way to enter the country then stall the deportation process, since it can take years to resolve them.

US Solicitor General D. John Sauer, the administration’s top appellate attorney, warned the court of a “vicious cycle” that encouraged “illegal entry by millions of aliens, who (quite justifiably) inferred that even if they lacked meritorious asylum claims, they would ‘be released to live and work in the United States during their removal proceedings.’”

But the Immigration and Nationality Act specifically allows migrants to claim asylum, even as it leaves the decision about whether to grant safe harbor up to administration officials.

In stark language, the Justice Department has described its asylum policy as one of the “most important and effective” policies for stemming illegal immigration. A lower court order against the policy, the administration said, “threatens to revive the chaos along the southwest border that the proclamation has fended off for the past year and a half.”

The ACLU, representing 13 individuals and three immigrant rights groups that challenged the policy, said that if Trump wants to change the way asylum works, he should have passed a bill in Congress during the two years the chambers were in Republican hands.

Richard Caldarone, a senior litigation attorney at the National Immigrant Justice Center, said that the policies at issue in the cases had already put tens of thousands of people in harm’s way.

“These policies have been overwhelmingly rejected by lower courts across the country, and they flatly violate US immigration law as it has been understood for decades,” said Caldarone, whose group is fighting the administration in the asylum case.

“If the court validates the policies,” he said, “it will enshrine a new generation of internment camps, all but end the US asylum system as we have known it for almost half a century, and shatter our nation’s commitment to upholding human rights and democratic norms.”

text:
The Supreme Court has agreed to review President Donald Trump’s effort to suspend access to asylum at the U.S.-Mexico border, setting up a major legal fight over the limits of presidential power and protections for people seeking refuge in the United States.

The administration is asking the justices to overturn lower court rulings that found Trump’s executive order unlawfully blocked migrants from applying for asylum. The order, issued on Trump’s first day back in office in January 2025, declared the situation at the southern border an “invasion” and sought to suspend entry and access to asylum for migrants covered by the policy.

Federal immigration law generally allows people physically present in the United States or arriving at the country to apply for asylum, regardless of how they entered. Applicants must still meet legal requirements to qualify for protection, including demonstrating they face persecution based on certain protected grounds.

The Trump administration argues the president has broad authority under federal immigration law to restrict entry and categorically deny asylum claims covered by the order. Officials say lengthy processing times contributed to border challenges and argue the policy has helped reduce crossings.

Immigrant rights groups challenge that interpretation, arguing Congress established protections and procedures that the president cannot unilaterally eliminate. They say the policy prevents people fleeing persecution from having their claims individually considered, as required by law.

The legal dispute centers in part on the president’s authority under Section 212(f) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which allows a president to suspend the entry of certain noncitizens when their entry is deemed detrimental to U.S. interests. The question is whether that authority also allows the administration to shut off access to the asylum application process.

The fight over asylum restrictions is not new. Previous administrations have also imposed limits on migrants seeking protection at the southern border. Trump’s first administration implemented policies including Remain in Mexico and restrictions on asylum eligibility. The Biden administration also introduced restrictions on asylum eligibility during periods of high border crossings.

The case also raises questions about the United States’ obligations under international refugee agreements, including protections against returning people to countries where they face persecution or torture.

The Supreme Court is expected to hear arguments in the case in the spring, with a decision anticipated by the end of June. The ruling could help define how much authority future presidents have to restrict asylum and whether executive orders can override protections established under federal immigration law.

text:
Immigrants who had been released while their immigration processes were underway are being detained again by ICE, even when they attend their appointments and fulfill other obligations. This practice is at the center of a class-action lawsuit filed against the federal government, in which two North Carolina residents are participating.

The lawsuit, announced on November 13 by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), challenges a policy that, according to the organization, allows immigrants to be detained again without demonstrating that the circumstances that justified their release have significantly changed.

The case was filed in federal court in the Northern District of Georgia and seeks to protect immigrants from North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia. According to the ACLU, hundreds, possibly thousands, of people have been detained again since May 2025 under this practice.

Why can ICE re-arrest released immigrants?

For more than four decades, immigration authorities required an individual assessment demonstrating material changes in a person's circumstances before re-detaining them.

However, according to the lawsuit, DHS abandoned that practice in May 2025, allowing new arrests without that evaluation.

This means that those who had been released while their immigration cases were still pending could remain free, as long as they met requirements such as attending their court hearings and appearing periodically before ICE.

“Our clients have complied with the rules that the government imposed on them,” said Corina Scott, an attorney with the ACLU of North Carolina.

Scott explained that the plaintiffs attended his court hearings and immigration appointments while building their lives in the United States.

“Now, DHS is systematically depriving people of long-standing protections and arbitrarily detaining them again under difficult conditions,” he added.

A Greensboro father fears being arrested again

Livinton Sosa Martinez, a 41-year-old Nicaraguan resident of Greensboro, arrived in the United States in 2022 fleeing political persecution along with his wife and three children.

On March 19, 2026, he attended a routine ICE appointment in Charlottewhere he was arrested and later transferred to the Stewart Detention Center in Georgia.

After being detained for approximately three weeks, he regained his freedom through a $10,000 bail.

His arrest caused economic and emotional hardship for his family, according to testimony released by the ACLU.

“When I have to go to work, especially in Raleigh or Charlotte, my daughters cry because they’re afraid I’ll be arrested again,” Sosa Martinez said. “I know ICE can arrest me at any time, even if I follow all the rules,” she added.

Honduran mother fears being separated from her son

Raquel Mariona Ebora, a 39-year-old Honduran resident of Dunn, is also involved in the lawsuit.

Her husband, Kelvin López Espinoza, was detained during an immigration appointment in Charlotte on April 28, 2026, despite having a pending immigration application, according to the ACLU.

The couple has a three-year-old American son with autism who requires constant attention.

“I always dreamed of having a child, and now that I have one, even thinking about being separated from him is terrifying,” said Mariona Ebora.

“All I can do is pray to God that they don’t arrest me again like they did with my husband,” she added.

The immigrant fears being arrested during her next appointment with ICE, scheduled for March 2027.

What are the plaintiffs seeking?

The lawsuit also includes Álvaro Ibañez Cárdenas, a Venezuelan resident of Athens, Georgia, and Ambrosio Trujillo Zavaleta, a Mexican from Savannah.

ACLU lawyers argue that the policy violates the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) and Fourth Amendment protections against unreasonable detention.

The APA allows courts to overturn government policies when agencies make changes without a reasoned explanation, fail to consider the impact on people who relied on long-standing policies, or adopt policies that violate the Constitution and other laws.

The plaintiffs are asking the court to declare the policy illegal, suspend its implementation, and reinstate individualized assessment before ordering new arrests.

The case, titled Sosa Martínez et al. VUS Department of Homeland Security et al., remains in court. The charges have yet to be resolved by the court.

A federal district court has already declared the DHS's re-detention policy illegal and temporarily suspended its use in the area of ​​responsibility of the ICE Field Office in San Francisco, concluding that the agency radically departed from long-standing practice without providing the legally required justification.

text:
Outgoing Attorney General Ken Paxton has spent the past few weeks dismissing lawsuits as his term comes to a blue wave-induced end. The high-profile lawsuits range from gender-affirming care to immigration advocacy and the Council on American Islamic Relations.

Paxton lost his midterm election to James Talarico and will be replaced by Democrat Nathan Johnson, who won over Republican Mayes Middleton. Johnson has said he plans to review ongoing lawsuits and dismiss those he deems politically motivated to steer the AG’s office away from partisan politics when he takes office in January.

Here’s a rundown of the lawsuits Paxton’s office has already dismissed.

Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR)

Filed in February, Paxton’s lawsuit against CAIR sought to ban the group from operating in Texas. The petition alleged the group was working with the Muslim Brotherhood and asked a Collin County judge to declare the nation’s largest Muslim civil rights organizations as a foreign terrorist and transnational criminal organization.

Paxton’s lawsuit followed the terrorist designation Gov. Greg Abbott had already placed on the two groups. Abbott urged Paxton to take legal action against CAIR, as multiple Republicans ran campaigns on anti-Islamic rhetoric.

Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has already said she plans to remove the terrorist designation against CAIR when she takes office. The notice of nonsuit was filed Monday.

NCAA and transgender athletes

In December 2024, Paxton filed a lawsuit against the NCAA, alleging it falsely marketed events as women’s athletics and violated the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act.

Paxton accused the NCAA of marketing events as women’s competitions and then hosting “mixed sex competitions where biological males compete against biological females.”

“The NCAA is intentionally and knowingly jeopardizing the safety and well-being of women by deceptively changing women’s competitions into co-ed competitions,” Paxton said in a 2024 press release. “When people watch a women’s volleyball game, for example, they expect to see women playing against other women—not biological males pretending to be something they are not. Radical ‘gender theory’ has no place in college sports.”

Transgender athletes, which make up an extraordinarily small percentage of all athletes, have been a campaign point for many Republicans, including Paxton, in the past few years.

Gender Affirming Care

Paxton dropped multiple lawsuits against doctors who were accused of providing gender affirming care to transgender youth. Texas banned gender affirming care for minors in 2023 and was the first state to bring cases against health care providers. The lawsuits sought to impose fines and revoke the doctors’ medical licenses.

The cases against Dallas doctors May Lau and M. Brett Cooper were dismissed on Friday, Nov. 20. Lau has since moved her medical practice from Texas to Oregon.

The third doctor to have a suit against them dismissed was El Paso pediatric endocrinologist Hector Granados. The attorney general accused Granados of continuing to prescribe puberty blockers and other hormones to patients after the ban was in effect.

All three doctors said they had not violated state law and had asked the courts to dismiss the cases.

Immigrant advocacy groups

On Nov. 9, the AG’s office dropped its lawsuit to shut down FIEL, a Houston immigrant rights organization, for violating nonprofit restrictions by criticizing President Donald Trump and Abbott’s immigration policies. The lawsuit against FEIL, which stands for Familias Inmigrantes y Estudiantes en la Lucha and translates to Immigrant Families and Students in the Fight, was filed in 2024.

On the same day, Paxton dropped a petition to close an El Paso migrant shelter he accused of illegally harboring undocumented immigrants. Annunciation House is a network of shelters that houses immigrants processed and released by Border Patrol.

text:
LANSING – Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel this week joined a coalition of states and the District of Columbia in challenging a new U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) rule that would strip federal housing assistance from mixed-status families. Under the new rule, any household with at least one member who is not a U.S. citizen or eligible immigrant would be cut off from HUD assistance entirely, even though federal subsidies are already prorated to include only eligible individuals. The rule would also require all U.S. citizens in federal housing programs to take on the burdensome task of proving their citizenship or risk eviction. In a lawsuit filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, Attorney General Nessel and the coalition argue that the rule illegally reverses nearly 30 years of federal policy allowing mixed-status families to stay together and violates the Administrative Procedure Act by exceeding HUD’s authority to enact this arbitrary new restriction.

“For decades, the federal government has allowed eligible residents and citizens to access housing benefits for which they are qualified, without weaponizing the immigration status of another household member,” said Attorney General Nessel. “The prior prorated system is adequate to ensure benefits aren’t paid for non-citizen householders, and this new policy will push lawful immigrants and U.S. citizens out of their homes. The federal government should be helping states and local governments solve big problems, not creating entirely new ones.”

For nearly 30 years, federal housing programs have provided housing assistance to low-income families even if not every household member is eligible for assistance. Under this system, known as proration, HUD reduces the family’s subsidy so it covers only the eligible household members. Congress codified this protection in 1997, explicitly stating that families receiving prorated assistance “shall not” lose their benefits just because an ineligible family member lives with them. The new HUD rule eliminates this protection. Under the rule, a family can stay in HUD-assisted housing only if every household member is a U.S. citizen or an eligible immigrant. As a result, U.S. citizens and eligible immigrants who live with an ineligible relative will be forced to choose between maintaining their housing and keeping their family together.

HUD estimates that around 20,000 mixed-status families, totaling 78,100 people, will lose their housing assistance. This includes 55,000 people who are fully eligible for federal housing assistance, many of whom are children and seniors. The agency also acknowledges that the rule will lead to evictions and displacement, and that many of these families could become homeless.

The rule would also make it harder for millions of U.S. citizens to keep the housing they already qualify for. Under the new rule, every U.S. citizen would also need to provide their Social Security number and consent to have their citizenship status checked through the federal SAVE database. If SAVE cannot automatically confirm their citizenship, U.S. citizens would have to produce official documents to prove their status, such as an original or certified birth certificate, naturalization certificate, or passport. Nationwide, an estimated 3.8 million adult U.S. citizens lack a document proving their citizenship, and another 17.5 million face barriers to getting one.

The coalition asserts that the rule will increase homelessness and shift major costs onto state and local governments. By HUD’s own estimates, sheltering people displaced by the rule could cost governments between $20,000 and $50,000 per person each year. The rule would also shrink the supply of affordable housing more broadly. HUD acknowledges that losing rental assistance could leave many subsidized units vacant, reduce rental income for housing providers, and drive private landlords out of the Section 8 voucher program, making it even harder for eligible families to find a home.

Attorney General Nessel and the coalition argue that HUD’s new rule exceeds the agency’s authority and violates federal law, which expressly allows prorated assistance for mixed-status families and establishes different documentation requirements for U.S. citizens and eligible immigrants aged 62 and older. They argue that HUD also violated the Administrative Procedure Act by issuing an arbitrary and capricious rule. The coalition is asking the Court to declare the rule unlawful, strike it down, and block HUD from implementing or enforcing it against the plaintiff states, their local governments, and their public housing authorities.

Joining Attorney General Nessel in filing this lawsuit, which is led by the attorneys general of New York, California, and Massachusetts, are the attorneys general of Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Hawai’i, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, and Wisconsin, and the governor of Pennsylvania.

Habeas corpus petitions also have the effect of moving immigration cases out of immigration court, where they are supposed to be handled, and into federal court, where judges are appointed by presidents and typically don’t have experience or expertise in immigration law.

The staffing crunch had already forced one U.S. attorney’s office to pull back. He suggested judges email release orders directly to the detention center when no government lawyer was assigned. The office reversed course in November after reaching an agreement with judges on new procedures.

Still, the habeas petitions have continued to climb as Immigration and Customs Enforcement has held record numbers of people in custody and the administration has narrowed avenues for release, including on bond. **The amicus brief draws on Senate Foreign Relations Committee Democrats’ investigation earlier this year that called into question whether the Administration’s deportation agreements sufficiently protect deportees from torture and persecution**

WASHINGTON – This week, U.S. Senators Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Ranking Member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, led their colleagues in filing an amicus brief with the Supreme Court challenging the Trump Administration’s third-country deportation policy and urging the Court to affirm the judgment of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit.

The brief, filed in support of the plaintiffs in D.V.D. v. DHS, argues that the Administration’s third country policy violates longstanding protections established by Congress under the Immigration Nationality Act and the Foreign Affairs Reform and Restructuring Act of 1998—specifically that the Administration is failing to carry out case-by-case determinations as to whether an individual may be persecuted or tortured in a third country. The brief notes that the Administration’s approach is a departure from State Department practice which included post-transfer monitoring. It draws from findings from a February 2026 report released by Senate Foreign Relations Committee Democrats which found that Administration has failed to meaningfully monitor whether foreign governments are complying with diplomatic assurances regarding the treatment of individuals deported to third countries.

“The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) guidance at issue in this case has transformed a narrow and rarely used practice into a standing system of unchecked global removals,” wrote the Senators. “The statutory and regulatory framework of the Immigration and Nationality Act ('INA') and Foreign Affairs Reform and Restructuring Act of 1998 ('FARRA') does not allow for blanket diplomatic assurances to serve as a green light for large-scale third-country deportations but instead contemplates an individualized, case-by-case analysis.”

“Congressional fact-finding has also revealed that the State Department is not meaningfully monitoring foreign government compliance with diplomatic assurances or enforcing agreement terms, even where evidence suggests foreign governments are violating their commitments,” continued the Senators. “Indeed, during an investigation by the Senate Foreign Relations Committee Minority staff, staff learned that the Administration had instructed U.S. officials not to engage with deportees once they were handed over to a foreign government.”

“The inescapable conclusion is that the DHS Guidance enables the Administration to use third countries to carry out removals that U.S. law would otherwise prohibit while turning a blind eye,” wrote the Senators.

You can read the full amicus brief HERE.

The brief was also signed by Senators Gary Peters (D-MI), Ranking Member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, Chris Coons (D-DE), Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Mazie Hirono (D-HI), Tim Kaine (D-VA), Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), Jacky Rosen (D-NV), Alex Padilla (D-CA) and Adam Schiff (D-CA).

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national mistakenly deported as part of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, was leaving the U.S. voluntarily for Spain on Tuesday, according to a person familiar with the matter.

Abrego Garcia’s departure, which would come after months of legal wrangling over his case, could bring to a conclusion what has become a defining saga of the second Trump administration’s mass deportations agenda. A judge told Abrego Garcia to self-deport by Tuesday, according to the person familiar with the matter, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the case.

Abrego Garcia was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and deported to a Salvadoran prison in what an official later called an “administrative error.” He was fighting against a second deportation to a series of African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security officials.

Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who met with Abrego Garcia while he was pressing for his release from a Salvadoran mega-prison, described Abrego Garcia as a “free man” and said he is traveling to a country of his choice.

“I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this Administration’s constant persecution,” he said in a statement.

Abrego Garcia’s deportation in early 2025 came as the Trump administration was ramping up its immigration crackdown, promising to deport 1 million people annually. Through an infusion of billions of dollars approved by Congress, the administration later supercharged its immigration enforcement capabilities, increasing its cadre of immigration officers, expanding detention capabilities and pushing to deport an increasing number of people.

Attorneys who represented Abrego Garcia in both the Maryland immigration proceedings and his criminal case in Tennessee didn’t immediately respond to messages seeking comment. A spokesperson for We Are CASA, an advocacy group that has supported Abrego Garcia and his family, declined to comment.

“Our priority continues to be keeping the family safe,” said the spokesperson, Jossie Flor Sapunar.

DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Abrego Garcia was mistakenly deported in March 2025

The 31-year-old Abrego Garcia has an American wife and child and has lived in Maryland for years, but he immigrated to the U.S. illegally as a teenager. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family. The judge allowed him to live and work in the U.S. under Immigration and Customs Enforcement supervision, but he was not given residency status.

Facing public pressure and a court order, President Donald Trump’s administration brought him back in June 2025, but only after securing an indictment charging him with human smuggling in Tennessee. A federal judge dismissed that case in May, finding that the Justice Department’s pursuit of criminal charges was designed to punish Abrego Garcia for challenging his deportation. The government is appealing.

The Trump administration vowed to deport him to a third country, threatening to send him to Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana, and, most recently, Liberia.

Abrego Garcia fought his deportation in court

Abrego Garcia had argued that if he were going to be deported, it should be to Costa Rica, which previously agreed to take him. But Todd Lyons, the former acting director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, said in a March 2026 memo that deporting Abrego Garcia to Costa Rica would be “prejudicial to the United States.”

Abrego Garcia should be sent to Liberia because the U.S. has spent governmental resources and political capital in negotiating for it to accept third country nationals, Lyons wrote. The push for deportation to Liberia continued even after the U.S. signed an agreement with Costa Rica to accept deportees who cannot legally be returned to their home countries.

The case took an unusual turn Oct. 6, 2026, when, five minutes before a hearing expected to determine whether U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement could detain and deport Ábrego Garcia to the West African country of Liberia, attorneys for both sides left the courtroom, along with Abrego Garcia.

When they returned 15 minutes later, it was announced the hearing was canceled. The two sides then gathered for another 90 minutes before leaving the courthouse without explanation. Abrego Garcia’s attorney said only the court case was not ready to proceed and he instructed reporters to watch the docket to learn the status of the case.

Footage captured exclusively by ABC News shows Abrego Garcia boarding a flight to Madrid, Spain, from a Washington, D.C.-area airport.

The Salvadoran national, who was returned to the United States after being mistakenly deported to El Salvador’s notorious CECOT prison, opted to leave voluntarily. The New York Times reported that his decision came as he faced the prospect of being deported to Liberia.

His departure marks “a major development” in his deportation saga, ABC News’ Laura Romero wrote. It also prompted a wave of reactions online.

“Kilmar Abrego Garcia humiliated the Trump admin because he exposed their failures and beat them in court; even all the way to the Supreme Court,” wrote Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, a senior fellow at the American Immigration Council.

“For that, they tried everything to punish him,” he added. “And they lost, again and again. Now, they lose a final time: he leaves as a free man.”

“How many millions of tax dollars did the Trump administration squander trying to save face after they mistakenly sent him to CECOT?” asked political analyst Anthony LaMesa. “Do any MAGA supporters want to defend this shameful saga?”

Journalist Michael McGough suggested Abrego Garcia’s departure wasn’t the end of scrutiny over the administration’s handling of his case.

“Presumably the new Congress can still investigate how he was treated,” he wrote.

Meanwhile, Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) celebrated the new development.

text:
Geoff Bennett:

Hundreds of thousands of immigrants living illegally in the U.S. recently lost their Medicaid coverage under a provision of President Trump's signature tax and spending law. The law is projected to reduce federal Medicaid spending by $900 billion over the next decade.

Deema Zein reports now on what that loss of coverage means for some of those affected.

Deema Zein:

These days, 46-year-old Hasan Al-Omar takes every opportunity to get outdoors near his apartment in Columbus, Ohio. Just last month, Al-Omar lost his Medicaid coverage, and, with it, the caregivers that helped him leave his home and live more independently.

Hasan Al-Omar (through interpreter):

If I'm not able to get back on Medicaid, what will happen to me? Who will help me with the bathroom, with eating, with drinking, with medical treatment? I can't afford to buy medical supplies or fix my wheelchair if it's broken, or get a new bed if it breaks. Medicaid helped me with all of those things too.

Deema Zein:

Now getting through the day requires relying entirely on his family to care for him.

Hasan Al-Omar (through interpreter):

My wife works to pay the rent and bills. And my children are in school. Just recently, I had an accident because I couldn't hold it anymore. I called my boys to come home from school, and the three of them, they took me to the bathroom and they gave me a bath.If they don't return my Medicaid, death is better for me.

Deema Zein:

In 2012, Al-Omar fled war in Syria. After more than a decade living in a tent in Lebanon, his family of seven entered the country in 2024 through the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program.

Hasan Al-Omar (through interpreter):

I said to myself that I will go there and live in safety and stability and dignity. But, right now, my life is at risk because there is no one to consistently take care of me.

Deema Zein:

He's one of 100,000 more immigrants the Congressional Budget Office estimates will be uninsured by 2034. But a KFF Health News report found more than 280,000 immigrants were expected to lose Medicaid coverage in October alone.

That includes refugees, asylum recipients, and survivors of human trafficking and domestic violence. Undocumented immigrants are not eligible for federally funded Medicaid coverage. In an e-mail to PBS News, the White House pointed to two memos listing examples of Democrats expanding health care access to undocumented immigrants, alleging the Biden administration and some Democratic-led states had -- quote -- "abused their power."

President Trump also has repeatedly made false claims that undocumented immigrants exploit taxpayer-funded health care in large numbers, including Medicaid.

President Donald Trump:

But our country can't handle people that come into our country illegally, and they want to give them full health care benefits.

Jimmy Carter, Former President of the United States: Ours is a nation of refugees, a nation of immigrants.

Deema Zein:

It was Jimmy Carter's 1980 Refugee Act that created a federal framework for refugees to access medical care. And even in 1996, when Congress barred many legal immigrants from Medicaid for five years, it exempted refugees and asylums from that waiting period.

Dr. Alan Bock:

To have so many patients suddenly lose access to health insurance, I mean, this is new. We're -- it affects the work that we're trying to do to help the vulnerable population, and ultimately affects these families significantly.

Deema Zein:

Dr. Alan Bock is a physician at Lower Lights Health in Columbus. He says many of his refugee patients are now struggling to pay for medical visits out of pocket. And he says he's had multiple patients who mistakenly had their Medicaid coverage cut.

Dr. Alan Bock:

When these patients feel like they can no longer get care, they're just less likely to have controlled blood pressure, controlled diabetes. And so, in the short term, that can lead to complications. These patients will end up in the E.R. more.

If they're not getting the regular even simple cholesterol medications because they're not seeing their primary care doctor, that increases their risk.

Deema Zein:

It's a fear 79-year-old Hawo Jimale has lived with since losing her insurance. Now a doctor's visit is up to $150 out of pocket. She relies on a community member to cover that cost and buy blood pressure medication. Originally from Somalia, Jimale lived in an Ethiopian refugee camp for 20 years before coming here in 2024 via the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program.

Hawo Jimale, Refugee (through interpreter):

I am asking the government to give back what they used to give me, my Medicaid. They were the ones who brought us here as refugees.

Steve Camarota:

This is a way of the administration, you might, say nibbling at the edges, trying to curtail welfare use, in this case Medicaid, among a subpopulation.

Deema Zein:

Steve Camarota is the director of research at the Center for Immigration Studies, a think tank that supports lower immigration levels. He said cutting Medicaid for legal immigrants isn't cost-effective.

Steve Camarota:

And the best solution would be to have an immigration system that selects people who are unlikely to need welfare. So the way you do that is have a system more based on education and skills and earnings potential, rather than our current system, which is very, very heavily weighted towards just whether you have a relative here. And so that's how you can address it, I think, most effectively.

Deema Zein:

But for refugees already in the U.S., there's a backlog for permanent residency, nearly 150,000 pending green card applications.

And Alvare Tyunibyan is one of them. She has been waiting for her green card for over a year. During that time, she was diagnosed with bone marrow cancer. Last month, she received the same letter as thousands of others, saying her Medicaid coverage had been revoked.

Alvare Tyunibyan, Refugee (through interpreter):

I was in shock. With such a disease and with my financial means, if my chemotherapy treatment stops, my doctors say my life will be shortened.

Deema Zein:

Tyunibyan entered the U.S. in 2024 through a program that accepts minority groups from former Soviet Union countries, including her home country of Armenia. She's able to continue blood transfusions for now with financial aid from her university hospital. But her chemotherapy has been postponed.

Alvare Tyunibyan (through interpreter):

I hope that the insurance will be restored, because I have no other opportunities. And there is hope in God. We hope that God will arrange everything for us.

Deema Zein:

And, for now, Hasan Al-Omar is holding on to hope too.

Hasan Al-Omar (through interpreter):

I hope to get Medicaid back and to return to doing physical therapy, and to one day get back to walking and working. I hope that my children will continue to study and will not be stopped from going to school to take care of me. And I hope that government officials will consider my health and financial situation and return my Medicaid coverage.

Deema Zein:

For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Deema Zein in Columbus, Ohio.

After dropping her 5-year-old son off at school on the morning of October 10, 2025, Dayanne Figueroa—a single mother and US citizen by birth—suddenly had her car rammed on West Hubbard Street by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents.

Video shows that agents pointed guns at Figueroa, then 31, dragged her out by her legs, threw her onto the pavement, and pinned her face down using their knees. According to the complaint, one of the agents placed a knee near an incision from a recent kidney surgery, which she said “caused acute and severe pain.”

Despite repeatedly identifying herself as a US citizen, Figueroa was detained without a warrant. She said agents put her phone into airplane mode, preventing her friends and family from contacting her. They then spirited her away in an unmarked red van with other detainees.

While en route to Broadview Detention Center in suburban Chicago, Figueroa suffered a panic attack, according to the complaint.

As she shook, cried, and gasped for air, agents photographed her, and one told her: “You’re a criminal. No one will help you.” Figueroa had no prior criminal record and was never charged with a crime.

While at Broadview—an ICE processing facility that became notorious for overcrowding and conditions described as "dehumanizing" after it became a de facto detention center during Midway Blitz—Figueroa said she was subject to “invasive body searches and to sexualized and degrading comments, mockery, and coercive questioning.”

The complaint alleges that before being permitted to use a restroom, she was subject to another purported search involving an agent “touching her private parts.” She said she was eventually allowed to use the restroom under surveillance, without any privacy.

She said agents knew she was recovering from recent major kidney surgery but withheld water and medical assistance until she began urinating blood.

After several hours in custody and a transfer to another facility in Lombard, Figueroa was released and transferred to a hospital for emergency evaluation.

When Figueroa’s boyfriend, mother, and family lawyer arrived at the Lombard facility in search of her, an agent informed them that she was “fine.”

In fact, the complaint said the force used by the officers had broken one of her dental crowns and caused internal bleeding. Meanwhile, her surgical wounds were aggravated, and the denial of medical care exacerbated her underlying kidney condition and delayed her recovery.

The damage to Figueroa went beyond the physical. The lawsuit says the ordeal "destroyed her sense of safety, security, and peace," and that she "suffers from severe emotional and psychological trauma, which continues to affect her ability to live her life as she did prior to the incident."

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) blamed Figueroa for the collision, accused her of assaulting federal officers, and described her as an “agitator," who "violently resisted arrest," claims contradicted by video evidence.

An investigation by the Illinois Accountability Commission released this April found that there was "no credible evidence suggesting that Figueroa intentionally rammed her vehicle into the agents’ vehicle."

The report concluded that agents “may have falsified the narratives” in their report to justify forcefully detaining Figueroa. It cites multiple glaring inaccuracies—including the claim that Figueroa kicked officers using black high-heeled shoes, when in fact her shoes had fallen off as she was dragged out of her vehicle.

In December 2025, Figueroa was one of five US citizens who testified about their mistreatment by federal immigration agents at a congressional forum convened by Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.).

Figueroa, a first-generation Mexican American, described her experience as "violence, blatant racial profiling, and a shocking abuse of federal authority."

Last week, while confronting DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.), a Chicago native who is seeking to chair the House Homeland Security Committee’s oversight subcommittee next year, described Figueroa’s case as an example of how federal agents have abused their power under President Donald Trump.

"They don’t respect the civil rights of our neighbors or the rule of law; they terrorize our communities; they act with impunity," Ramirez said.

The assault of Figueroa fits into a much broader pattern of documented abuse during the Trump administration's mass deportation campaign, including the violent detention of US citizens, warrantless arrests, racial profiling, denial of medical care, and official accounts of confrontations that have been contradicted by video evidence.

During Operation Midway Blitz, federal agents shot US citizen Marimar Martinez five times and falsely accused her of ramming their vehicle, dragged US citizens from their homes and detained them for hours during a military-style apartment raid, and denied medical care to a man after an agent repeatedly punched him in the head.

As of October, ProPublica had identified at least 519 US citizens who had been detained by federal immigration agents since Trump returned to office, and said the real number was likely higher.

“What happened to me is what happens to people when our government is allowed to act with impunity and trample our Constitution,” Figueroa said in a statement on Tuesday. “A badge—or in my case, a police Velcro patch that looks like it was bought off Amazon—is not a free pass to intimidate, terrorize, or mistreat people.”

"These reckless federal agents are an insult to every legitimate law enforcement officer and a complete and utter embarrassment from the very top all the way down,” she added. “They have made a mockery of everything this country claims to stand for, and I hope this lawsuit helps hold those responsible for my attack accountable, and puts an end to this horrific abuse.”

The lawsuit includes claims of false arrest, false imprisonment, assault, battery, negligence, and the intentional infliction of emotional distress under Illinois law. She is being represented by Democracy Forward, a nonprofit legal advocacy organization, and the California-based Carrillo Law Firm.

“Ms. Figueroa has endured one of the most horrifying experiences imaginable—having her personal safety attacked by masked ICE agents who took the law into their own hands,” said Luis Carrillo of the Carrillo Law Firm. “Ms. Figueroa had broken no laws when she was savagely attacked while on her way to work. But today is the first step in her fight for justice. She is tremendously courageous for speaking out not just for herself, but for the voiceless who cannot speak. We look forward to joining the fight for justice for her.”

"More nuclear weapons, particularly lower-yield weapons that leaders may perceive to be more 'usable,' will only increase the risk of a catastrophic nuclear war," wrote the senators, who co-chair the Nuclear Weapons and Arms Control Working Group.

"Tactical nuclear weapons are the gateway drug to nuclear destruction, and we urge you to drop these plans immediately," they added.

The letter comes amid reports that the Pentagon is revising US nuclear guidance to emphasize tactical weapons and limited nuclear options in conflicts, possibly including the increasingly protracted Iran War.

The push aligns with Hegseth's doctrine of "maximum lethality," which—when paired with his embrace of autonomous warfare and stated disdain for “stupid rules of engagement” designed to minimize civilian harm—risks treating the mass slaughter of noncombatants as the unfortunate but acceptable price of battlefield success.

Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby has defended the mainstreaming of tactical nukes as necessary to provide the president with more options in any war against a nuclear-armed adversary.

"We want to be able to give the president and secretary credible, rational nuclear options," Colby said at an August conference hosted by US Strategic Command.

While Trump’s own intelligence agencies have concluded that Iran does not have and is not trying to build nuclear weapons, in addition to the United States, China, France, India, Israel, North Korea, Pakistan, Russia, and the United Kingdom possess such arms.

Arms control advocates warn that the very idea of a limited nuclear war is dangerously misleading. A weapon's smaller explosive yield does not guarantee that a nuclear-armed adversary will respond in a similarly restrained fashion, or that a catastrophic escalation could be avoided, as the 1983 "Proud Prophet" war game chillingly demonstrated.

Whitley Strieber and James Kunetka's bestselling 1984 novel Warday recounts in an investigative journalistic style a "limited" nuclear exchange between the United States and the Soviet Union that lasts less than an hour, destroying just a handful of cities on each side. Yet tens of millions of people are killed in the United States alone on the day of the war and in the following years, and five years on, much of the world has been transformed almost beyond recognition.

Recalling that perilous era of hair-trigger tensions and nuclear near-misses, Markey and Merkley noted that during the Cold War, the US military maintained thousands of tactical nuclear weapons, including torpedoes, artillery shells, short-range missiles, and even portable atomic "backpack" devices designed for soldiers to carry behind enemy lines on suicide missions.

"Any use of nuclear weapons carries with it the high and inescapable risk of escalation into catastrophic nuclear war, which no one would win."

As the Cold War wound down, the US eventually abandoned much of that arsenal. In 1991, then-President George HW Bush announced plans to eliminate virtually all US tactical nuclear weapons, and the country's stockpile of such weapons has since declined by more than 90%, according to the senators' letter.

But the Trump administration has been moving in the opposite direction. Trump's first term saw the deployment of the lower-yield W76-2 warhead on submarine-launched ballistic missiles, and the president is currently pursuing a new nuclear-armed sea-launched cruise missile and an accelerated weapons development initiative known as the Rapid Capabilities Program.

"If President Trump perceives the use of lower-yield weapons as more credible, their deployment increases the risk of nuclear war," Markey and Merkley wrote.

A September analysis by the Centre for International Security and Economic Strategy warned that expanding the role of tactical nuclear weapons risks normalizing their use in military conflicts and potentially triggering a renewed nuclear arms race.

The rise of lethal autonomous weapons systems, popularly called killer robots, has added an unprecedented level of risk—and urgency—to the equation.

Markey and Merkley urge Hegseth to abandon plans to expand the development and potential use of tactical nuclear weapons, while demanding answers about the Pentagon’s nuclear strategy, weapons programs, and whether it believes a limited nuclear exchange could avoid escalating into all-out thermonuclear Armageddon.

"Any use of nuclear weapons carries with it the high and inescapable risk of escalation into catastrophic nuclear war, which no one would win," the senators wrote. "The clear firebreak against such a worldwide disaster is to draw a bright line between nuclear weapons and all other weapons. We must strive to keep that firebreak wide and strong."

"Blurring the line by developing more tactical nuclear weapons is deeply unwise and increases nuclear risk," they added. "We urge you to abandon these plans immediately."

At a press conference on Tuesday, the Army sought to quell rising public fear about the explosion.

EPA Associate Administrator Tom Croci said the agency had “created a blanket of sampling teams and testing teams that... will be there during detonation with air monitoring systems and then after detonation to all of the places within the affected area that need to be sampled.”
