The revelations suggest that the use of Palestinians to shield Israeli troops from potential attacks was not confined to isolated incidents or a single theater of operations. Haaretz called the practice "widespread" at the start of Israel's genocidal assault on Gaza. Accounts from Israeli soldiers, Palestinian survivors, and human rights organizations have repeatedly described a tactic that appears to have become embedded in military operations.

First-hand accounts from IDF troops and veterans, Palestinian survivors, and human rights groups have repeatedly described Israeli soldiers' use of civilians, including women and children, to shield them from potential attacks by Palestinian resistance fighters. For years, the IDF whistleblower group Breaking the Silence has published testimonies from soldiers describing the use of Palestinians to search buildings, tunnels, and suspected explosive sites before Israeli troops entered.

"He's like a dog in Oketz," one Israeli soldier told Breaking the Silence of Palestinians used as human shields, referring to the IDF's canine unit. "He looks for things like explosive devices. If there's one, he'll set it off, and that's how we find out."

"It's terrible, just terrible. I think that's one of the reasons I wanted to speak out," the soldier said. "After I left Gaza, and following conversations with other people, I realized this was a widespread phenomenon—it wasn't happening just in our unit. It became clear to me then that this is a broader pattern, and that it was obvious we weren't the only ones doing this."

Using human shields is prohibited under international humanitarian law, including Article 28 of the Fourth Geneva Convention and Article 51(7) of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions. The practice is a war crime under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court. It was also outlawed by Israel's Supreme Court in 2005 in an explicit repudiation of the erstwhile long-standing practice.

While Israel and its supporters often accuse Palestinian resistance groups including Hamas—which led the October 2023 attack on Israel—of using human shields, United Nations investigators and international human rights groups have found little evidence that Palestinians are intentionally doing so.

Meanwhile, a May 2025 Associated Press investigation found that Israeli soldiers had systematically used Palestinian civilians as human shields in Gaza, citing survivors of the practice and Israeli military personnel. One Israeli officer told the AP that by the end of his nine-month deployment, nearly every infantry unit was using Palestinians to clear buildings before troops entered.

"Once this idea was initiated, it caught on like fire in a field," the officer said. "People saw how effective and easy it was."

Dubbed the "mosquito protocol," the practice involved forcing detained Palestinians to enter potentially booby-trapped buildings and tunnels ahead of Israeli soldiers. Some were dressed in IDF uniforms, fitted with cameras, bound, and threatened with death if they refused.

In one case, a Palestinian man said Israeli soldiers attached a camera to his forehead and forced him to enter homes to check for explosives and Palestinian fighters. He was passed between military units for more than two weeks, spending nights bound in a dark room before being sent out again.

"These are not isolated accounts," Breaking the Silence executive director Nadav Weiman told the AP. "They point to a systemic failure and a horrifying moral collapse."

Haaretz has also reported testimony from Israeli soldiers indicating that commanders knew about the practice. One soldier said that after seeing Al Jazeera footage documenting the use of Palestinians as human shields, he recognized the tactic immediately.

"There's pride in it," another soldier reportedly said, while describing the attitude among troops toward using Palestinians to protect Israeli personnel.

Women, children, and elders have not been spared from the practice.

In the occupied West Bank, Palestinian mother Hazar Estity told the AP that Israeli soldiers took her from her home in the Jenin refugee camp in November 2024 and forced her to enter and photograph apartments before troops went inside.

Estity pleaded with soldiers to let her return to her 21-month-old son, but they refused.

"I was most afraid that they would kill me," she told the AP. "And that I wouldn't see my son again."

Multiple IDF soldiers told Israeli investigative journalist Illy Pe'ery last year about an incident in which "a senior officer in the Israeli army’s Nahal Brigade tied an explosive cord around the neck of an 80-year-old Palestinian man and forced him to serve as a human shield, ordering him to scout out abandoned houses under threat of having his head blown off."

"After he had served this purpose, the soldiers ordered the man to flee with his wife, but upon being spotted by another battalion, they were both shot dead on the spot," Pe'ery wrote.

Defense for Children International-Palestine has documented Israeli forces using Palestinian children as human shields, including forcing minors to walk ahead of soldiers during dangerous military raids.

Accountability has remained extraordinarily limited. According to Haaretz, none of the soldiers implicated in the 16 investigations opened since October 2023 have been prosecuted.

Israeli soldiers who have confronted superior officers about using human shields say they have been rebuffed.

“We talked to our commander, and we asked him to stop doing it,” one soldier told CBS News last year, “but we were ordered to continue. He told us it was policy.”

“It's fucked up, you know," he added, "to use citizens as your human shield like a dog.”

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national who fought his mistaken deportation, left the U.S. voluntarily for Spain on Tuesday, officials and his attorneys said, in what could bring an end to a defining saga of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.

Abrego Garcia was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and deported to a Salvadoran prison in what an official later called an “administrative error.” His departure to Spain comes after months of legal wrangling as he battled the administration's drive to deport him to Africa.

Abrego Garcia, his lawyers and the Trump administration sought to portray the departure as a victory.

“I am leaving happy. I am leaving with my freedom," Abrego Garcia said in a statement. "I am leaving with the love of an entire community, with people who cared for me, believed in me, and joined my family in this fight.”

The Department of Homeland Security said Tuesday night that he self-deported to Spain as part of a removal order and that he didn't receive any incentives and won't be allowed back in to the U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a post on X that he was “delighted” about Abrego Garcia's departure, listing off a familiar litany of allegations for why he should be deported, including that he was a gang member, an accusation Abrego Garcia has repeatedly denied.

But Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, an attorney for Abrego Garcia, called this a temporary departure as he “waits out the end of this administration." He said Abrego Garcia has many options to return to U.S.

“We don’t expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland," he said.

A judge told Abrego Garcia to self-deport by Tuesday, according to a person familiar with the matter, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the case.

Video posted by ABC News showed Abrego Garcia walking through Washington Dulles International Airport with his wife and others, including an official from We Are CASA, an advocacy group that has supported Abrego Garcia and his family.

Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who met with Abrego Garcia while he was pressing for his release from a Salvadoran mega-prison, described Abrego Garcia as a “free man” and said he is traveling to a country of his choice.

“I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free — including from this Administration’s constant persecution,” he said in a statement.

Abrego Garcia's deportation in early 2025 came as the Trump administration was ramping up its immigration crackdown, promising to deport 1 million people annually. Through an infusion of billions of dollars approved by Congress, the administration later supercharged its immigration enforcement capabilities, growing its cadre of immigration officers, expanding detention capabilities and pushing to deport an increasing number of people.

He was fighting against a second deportation to a series of African countries proposed by DHS officials.

Abrego Garcia was mistakenly deported in March 2025

The 31-year-old Abrego Garcia has an American wife and child and has lived in Maryland for years, but he immigrated to the U.S. illegally as a teenager. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family. The judge allowed him to live and work in the U.S. under Immigration and Customs Enforcement supervision, but he was not given residency status.

His deportation in 2025 involved being sent to a mega-prison in El Salvador known as CECOT, which activists say is rife with abuses and where inmates are packed into cells and never allowed outside.

Facing public pressure and a court order, President Donald Trump’s administration brought him back in June 2025, but only after securing an indictment charging him with human smuggling in Tennessee.

A federal judge dismissed that case in May, finding that the Justice Department’s pursuit of criminal charges was designed to punish Abrego Garcia for challenging his deportation. The government is appealing.

The Trump administration vowed to deport him to a third country, threatening to send him to Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana, and, most recently, Liberia.

Abrego Garcia fought his deportation in court

Abrego Garcia had argued that if he were going to be deported, it should be to Costa Rica, which previously agreed to take him. But Todd Lyons, the former acting director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, said in a March 2026 memo that deporting Abrego Garcia to Costa Rica would be “prejudicial to the United States.”

Lyons wrote that Abrego Garcia should be sent to Liberia because the U.S. has spent governmental resources and political capital in negotiating for it to accept third-country nationals. The push for deportation to Liberia continued even after the U.S. signed an agreement with Costa Rica to accept deportees who cannot legally be returned to their home countries.

His case took an unusual turn on Oct. 6, 2026, when, five minutes before a hearing expected to determine whether U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement could detain and deport Ábrego Garcia to the West African country of Liberia, attorneys for both sides left the courtroom, along with Abrego Garcia.

When they returned 15 minutes later, it was announced the hearing was canceled. The two sides then gathered for another 90 minutes before leaving the courthouse without explanation. Abrego Garcia’s attorney said only the court case was not ready to proceed and he instructed reporters to watch the docket to learn the status of the case.

___

Associated Press reporter Rebecca Santana contributed.

title: Facing 97000 Immigration Detention Lawsuits, Justice Department Mobilizes 2000 Lawyers
description:
More than 97,000 habeas petitions have been filed since January 2025, according to the memorandum.
“Each new habeas petition results in a direct diversion of resources from the Department’s U.S. Attorneys’ Offices,” the memorandum states.
It says several U.S. attorneys’ offices have been overwhelmed by the volume of petitions and court procedures, diverting attorneys from other responsibilities.
Attorneys from the department’s civil litigation divisions will now assist in defending the government against detention challenges.
The administration argues that many of the petitions are frivolous and that immigration attorneys have used them to circumvent the administrative immigration process established by Congress.
text:
The Justice Department is mobilizing approximately 2,000 attorneys from across its civil litigation divisions to help defend the federal government against a growing number of lawsuits challenging immigration detentions, expanding the administration’s legal response to a sharp increase in habeas corpus petitions.

In a memorandum dated Nov. 24, 2026, Attorney General Todd Blanche directed four civil litigation divisions — Antitrust, Civil Rights, Civil, and Environment and Natural Resources — as well as the U.S. Trustees Program, to assist U.S. attorneys’ offices in handling the cases.

More than 97,000 habeas petitions have been filed since January 2025, according to the memorandum. Approximately 10,000 additional petitions have been filed since October 2026 alone.

Habeas corpus petitions allow individuals to challenge the legality of their detention in court. In immigration cases, detainees commonly use them to contest the government’s authority to hold them in custody.

In a statement posted on X on Tuesday, Blanche said the department was increasing its legal resources to respond to what he described as an influx of frivolous petitions.

“The Department of Justice is surging resources to double down on fighting the onslaught of frivolous habeas petitions used by corrupt judges to release criminal aliens back into communities and avoid deportation,” Blanche wrote.

“Thousands of petitions have been filed since @POTUS took office, which fall hardest on U.S. Attorney’s offices. So, we are surging main justice resources to help them fight these because criminals should not be given a free pass for being in our country illegally,” he added.

Civil Litigation Divisions to Assist Prosecutors

The memorandum says the growing number of cases has placed significant pressure on U.S. attorneys’ offices, whose assistant U.S. attorneys have primarily handled the litigation since January 2025.

“Each new habeas petition results in a direct diversion of resources from the Department’s U.S. Attorneys’ Offices,” the memorandum states.

It says several U.S. attorneys’ offices have been overwhelmed by the volume of petitions and court procedures, diverting attorneys from other responsibilities.

The directive extends the administration’s response beyond prosecutors who have been handling immigration-related cases. Attorneys from the department’s civil litigation divisions will now assist in defending the government against detention challenges.

Blanche’s office, along with attorneys in the offices of the deputy attorney general and associate attorney general, will also take on habeas matters until the overall number of petitions begins to decline.

U.S. attorneys’ offices will continue participating in the litigation.

New Assignments and Training for Attorneys

Under the memorandum, each participating litigation division must designate a point of contact for habeas cases in the coming weeks.

The director of the Executive Office for U.S. Attorneys will coordinate with offices facing the largest caseloads to arrange additional legal support.

The department said it would consider requests for attorneys in specific geographic areas, where practical, based on existing court admissions and other factors. The process will be introduced gradually across the participating divisions. Travel expenses will be covered when necessary.

Attorneys will also receive jurisdiction-specific resources, including contact information for civil division chiefs and Department of Homeland Security personnel.

The department plans to provide training on habeas litigation, covering the different types of legal challenges immigrants have raised since the beginning of the Trump administration.

Blanche also directed several senior Justice Department officials to develop recommendations for a more aggressive appellate strategy in habeas cases.

The attorney general’s Advisory Committee, the Executive Office for U.S. Attorneys, the Civil Division, and the offices of the solicitor general, associate attorney general and deputy attorney general must submit their recommendations within 30 days of the memorandum’s issuance.

Administration Defends Immigration Enforcement

The memorandum attributes the increase in habeas petitions partly to the administration’s immigration enforcement policies and efforts to detain and deport immigrants.

It references President Donald Trump’s Jan. 20, 2025, executive order, titled “Protecting the American People Against Invasion,” and says the Justice Department has since prosecuted thousands of immigration-related criminal offenses while defending against a growing number of detention challenges.

The administration argues that many of the petitions are frivolous and that immigration attorneys have used them to circumvent the administrative immigration process established by Congress.

The memorandum also criticizes the previous administration’s immigration enforcement policies, claiming that its failure to enforce immigration laws contributed to an immigration crisis.

It says the Trump administration has removed more than 1.2 million immigrants who were in the country illegally and that the Department of Homeland Security continues to detain nearly 2,800 immigrants daily for deportation.

The attorney general acknowledged that the participating divisions are already facing substantial workloads, particularly following personnel reductions. He also noted that many attorneys have already volunteered or offered to assist with habeas litigation.

The memorandum says assignments should be limited to the number of cases each attorney can adequately and effectively defend.

title: Standing with our Immigrant Neighbors - The San Francisco Foundation
description:
We are witnessing what immigrant families across the Bay Area have been living with for more than a year, mostly out of view.
When our neighbors can be detained and arrested without explanation by masked federal agents, none of those rights are secure.
Donate to the Stand Together Bay Area Fund, which provides direct emergency grants to trusted, local nonprofit organizations.
These organizations help our immigrant neighbors pay their rent, put food on the table, and cover basic needs.
For example, several Bay Area counties have limited the use of public property for immigration enforcement.
text:
Like many of you, I watched the video of immigration agents pinning a teenager to the ground in East Oakland, as he screamed, “I am a 17-year-old boy.” Two days earlier, about a dozen people were arrested in a single morning in Sonoma County – one of which resulted in a two-year-old child being left alone in a car. And ICE has arrested at least 37 people in San Mateo County in November.

We are witnessing what immigrant families across the Bay Area have been living with for more than a year, mostly out of view. These are not isolated incidents; they are tactics that have been used for far too long to violate people’s constitutional and human rights.

No family should have to live with this kind of fear. And the harm reaches far beyond the people arrested. About 150,000 Bay Area children live in households with an undocumented family member. When a parent is detained, those families can lose more than two-thirds of their income overnight.

These are our neighbors. They work every kind of job, pay taxes, raise families, and build this region alongside everyone else who calls it home. They are us. Standing with them is about honoring our shared humanity. It is about securing the rights we all count on. When our neighbors can be detained and arrested without explanation by masked federal agents, none of those rights are secure.

Values are tested in moments like this one. As I wrote at the end of last year, the antidote to fear isn’t silence. It’s community and action. Here are three things you can do now:

Help families stay stable. Check in on families who may be afraid to leave home. Donate to the Stand Together Bay Area Fund, which provides direct emergency grants to trusted, local nonprofit organizations. These organizations help our immigrant neighbors pay their rent, put food on the table, and cover basic needs. Click here to donate.

Know your rights. Save your county’s rapid response hotline. Learn what to do if agents come to a home or workplace, and pass it on to neighbors, coworkers, and your children’s schools. We have collected some resources here.

Show up for your neighbors. Let your local officials know you want them to protect immigrant residents. For example, several Bay Area counties have limited the use of public property for immigration enforcement.

The Bay Area has always been at its best when we stand together, and when we stand up for what is right even when it’s hard. If we believe in the dignity of every person who calls this place home, this is the moment to live it.

title: President Trump Orders Federal Contractors to Route Congressional Requests Through the ...

He has also publicly suggested that executive privilege may extend to company executives who worked with the President.
This EO desperately orders contractors to get White House permission before complying with congressional oversight.

text:
On November 20, 2026, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14438, Protecting the Executive’s Privileges and Enhancing Efficiencies in Federal Contracting (the “EO”). The EO directs all federal contractors and subcontractors to immediately notify the White House and their contracting agencies of any “pending or future congressional request respecting the contractors’ communications or work with the executive branch,” and to “abide by any instructions received from the White House and contracting agency related to the withholding of communications” that the White House or the agency has determined are protected by executive privilege. Agencies are directed to consider contract termination or cancellation, suspension, and debarment for contractors that fail to comply.

The EO was issued less than three weeks after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections, and it is the latest in a series of steps the Administration has taken in anticipation of an increase in congressional oversight when Congress convenes on January 3, 2027. Following weeks of escalating warnings and competing claims of authority between the White House and incoming congressional leadership, the EO pushes the Administration’s effort to control the flow of information to Congress out to the private companies that perform the government’s work. Its practical effect is to place federal contractors, and their subcontractors, squarely between two co-equal branches of government, each with its own leverage, leaving contractors not only at risk of becoming instruments in a broader political struggle, but also exposed to legal jeopardy: withholding information from Congress can invite subpoena enforcement and potential contempt or obstruction exposure, while disregarding executive branch instructions can invite adverse contract action. This Legal Update summarizes the EO, places it in its political context, assesses the significant questions about its enforceability, and offers practical steps contractors should consider now.

What the Executive Order Requires

The EO rests on the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act (the “Procurement Act”) and the President’s constitutional authority. It states a policy of “preventing and prohibiting uncoordinated disclosures of information pursuant to congressional requests,” and asserts that Congress “cannot seek information from executive branch departments and agencies…, employees, or Federal contractors without a valid legislative purpose that does not intrude on core Executive functions.” Its operative provisions address:

Notification: Contractors must immediately notify the White House and the contracting agency of any congressional request concerning their communications or work with the executive branch. The obligation expressly reaches requests that were already pending when the EO took effect.

Withholding: Contractors must follow White House and agency instructions to withhold communications that either has determined are protected by executive privilege.

Coordination: Agencies must coordinate with the White House and contractors on “appropriate responses” to congressional requests, “including the application or assertion of any relevant privileges.”

Subcontractor flowdown: The requirements also apply to subcontractors on federal contracts, and agencies are to make prime contractors responsible for subcontractor compliance.

Implementation: Agencies must promptly inform contractors of their obligations, and the Office of Management and Budget (“OMB”) must issue guidance on monitoring compliance and coordinating among agencies, contractors, and the White House. The EO is silent on when that guidance must issue and on how long the executive branch may take to complete its privilege review.

Enforcement: Agencies “shall consider whether to take all appropriate actions, consistent with applicable law”—including termination or cancellation of contracts and suspension or debarment—where a contractor or subcontractor fails to comply with EO requirements. The EO, like most, also states that it creates no enforceable right against the United States and must be implemented consistent with applicable law and subject to appropriations.

The EO does not define a congressional request, does not distinguish between informal staff inquiries, committee letters, and subpoenas, and does not address existing whistleblower protections for contractor employees. Nor does the EO define “federal contractor.” On its face, the EO could reach any company that holds a federal contract or subcontract, regardless of the size of work relative to the company’s overall business or whether the congressional request relates to it at all. Large companies with diversified operations that hold some federal contracts, and that face congressional scrutiny for reasons unrelated to that work, should therefore not assume they fall outside its scope. OMB guidance may clarify this point.

The Context: A New Congress and an Administration Bracing for Oversight

The EO is best understood as one piece of a broader, and escalating, interbranch confrontation that began almost immediately after the midterm elections:

White House Counsel correspondence: Earlier this month, White House Counsel Will Scharf wrote to Representative Robert Garcia, the likely incoming Chair of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, warning that certain anticipated investigative tactics could “cross the line into blatant criminality” and that the Administration “will not be extorted and will not be cowed by unlawful process.” In separate letters to Democratic ranking members, Mr. Scharf took the position that their preservation and document demands are not requests of a committee because they do not yet hold the gavel. Rep. Garcia responded that Congress’s authority “comes from Article I of the Constitution, not from permission of the White House.”

Testimony clearance: On November 16, Mr. Scharf directed agencies to obtain approval from the White House Counsel’s Office and the Office of Legislative Affairs before employees agree to testify before Congress. He has also publicly suggested that executive privilege may extend to company executives who worked with the President.

Privilege and “private advisers”: The groundwork was laid months before voters went to the polls. An August 10, 2026 opinion of the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel concluded that executive privilege can extend to certain communications with “private advisers,” a position whose legal footing has been disputed by commentators and that bears directly on communications between companies and senior officials. The EO, notably, sweeps more broadly than the OLC opinion because it reaches any congressional request concerning a contractor’s “communications or work with the executive branch,” and applies to all federal contractors and subcontractors (which is not defined)—without regard to whether they have any advisory relationship with the President or senior officials.

Congressional preservation demands: For their part, incoming Democratic chairs have already begun laying groundwork. Representative Garcia sent document preservation notices to a dozen current and former officials and Trump family members, and Senator Richard Blumenthal, who is expected to chair a key Senate investigative panel, has already sent letter to contractors working on the White House ballroom construction project, questioning them about their participation in the project and the terms of their involvement, as part of a planned inquiry. Federal contracting, including DHS procurement and alleged pay-to-play arrangements, has been identified as a top investigative priority.

In an accompanying fact sheet, the White House framed the EO as “protecting executive privileges from congressional overreach.” The EO itself contends that, absent coordination, the executive branch may be forced into duplicative litigation over the same requests, and that agencies will be “chilled from sharing sensitive information with contractors,” including on national and homeland security matters.

Congressional Reaction

Democratic leaders reacted swiftly and signaled that they intend to test the EO once they assume control in January:

Representative Robert Garcia (Ranking Member, House Oversight and Government Reform): “Today’s executive order is the latest in the Trump Administration’s blatant attack on Congress’ constitutional right to conduct oversight. This EO desperately orders contractors to get White House permission before complying with congressional oversight. What is the White House trying to hide? Donald Trump wants to stop us from exposing the rampant waste, fraud, and corruption by his Administration, but we’re just getting started.”

Representative Jamie Raskin (expected incoming Chair, House Judiciary): The EO is “unprecedented and blatantly unlawful.” “Federal contractors are paid with taxpayer dollars … Public contractors have both a duty and a right to speak truthfully when Congress calls, and Congress has a duty to investigate and stamp out all the waste, fraud, kickbacks, shakedowns and corruption choking the government and driving up costs.”

Contractors should expect incoming chairs to respond not only with letters and subpoenas directed at contractors, but potentially with appropriations riders and legislation aimed at the EO. Congressional requests are also likely to seek information about contractors’ coordination with the White House and their contracting agencies under the EO, including what contractors have been directed to withhold. Contractors should also expect litigation challenging the EO’s enforceability and constitutionality.

Is the Executive Order Enforceable Against Contractors?

The EO stands on materially different footing depending on which obligation is at issue. Its notification requirement is the most defensible; its withholding requirement, and the threat of contract penalties for responding to Congress, are the most vulnerable.

1. The EO is not self-executing as a matter of contract

Executive orders direct agencies; they do not by themselves amend existing contracts with federal contractors (much less subcontractors, which do not have contractual privity with the Federal government). Procurement Act orders have generally been upheld where they bear a sufficiently close nexus to economy and efficiency in procurement, but they are typically implemented through FAR clauses, class deviations, or bilateral modifications. Until an agency incorporates a clause, a contractor’s obligation to comply arises, if at all, from agency instruction rather than from the contract itself, and unilateral changes to existing contracts raise familiar questions about consideration and the Changes clause. The EO’s efficiency rationale will also be tested against the reality that its principal purpose, as framed by the White House, is to protect executive privilege from congressional inquiry.

2. An EO cannot displace a valid congressional subpoena or federal criminal law

The EO does not, and cannot, relieve a contractor of its obligation to respond to a valid congressional subpoena. Willful default on a subpoena is a federal misdemeanor under 2 U.S.C. § 192, which carries a five-year statute of limitations—well beyond the current Administration’s term. Former senior advisers Steve Bannon and Peter Navarro both served sentences for contempt of Congress. Separately, 18 U.S.C. § 1505 criminalizes corruptly obstructing “the due and proper exercise of the power of inquiry” by either House of Congress. While the current Justice Department is unlikely to bring such charges, the limitations periods extend beyond 2028, and a future Administration may take a different view. What’s more, criminal prosecution is not the only potential enforcement route. House Democrat Representative Robert Garcia expressly discussed going directly to federal court to compel compliance with congressional subpoenas, rather than relying on the Justice Department to prosecute criminal contempt. As a result, a contractor cannot treat compliance with the EO as a safe harbor—nor does the EO purport to provide one.

3. Executive privilege belongs to the President—and courts decide disputes

The presidential communications privilege is real and is constitutionally grounded, as the Supreme Court recognized in United States v. Nixon, but it is qualified and is ultimately adjudicated by the courts. In affirming Mr. Navarro’s conviction, the D.C. Circuit emphasized that the power to withhold information on the basis of executive privilege is “vested in the President and no one else.” A contractor that declines to produce documents on the strength of an agency’s view that material “may be” privileged, without a formal presidential assertion, may have little to stand on if a committee pursues enforcement. And under Trump v. Mazars USA, LLP (2020), disputes over congressional subpoenas to third parties for presidential information are resolved through a balancing framework applied by courts—not by instruction to the third party. The more routine the records (pricing, performance, invoices, subcontracting decisions), the weaker any privilege claim is likely to be.

To understand the EO, it is important to understand what executive privilege does and does not cover. “Executive privilege” is an umbrella term for several distinct doctrines. The strongest is the presidential communications privilege, which protects communications made in the process of shaping presidential decisions, and courts have extended it to communications authored or solicited and received by senior White House advisers with broad and significant responsibility for advising the President. The deliberative process privilege, which can extend more broadly across the executive branch, protects pre-decisional and deliberative agency material, but it is a weaker, common-law privilege that does not cover purely factual material, and is more readily overcome by a showing of need. The executive branch has also invoked protection for national security, foreign relations, and sensitive law enforcement information. The privilege’s established core concerns confidential executive branch decision-making; it does not automatically extend to exchanges with private companies. The Administration’s effort to protect White House conversations with private-sector advisers advances a contested extension of that core.

Critically, the EO is not limited to communications with the President or the White House: it reaches any congressional request concerning a contractor’s communications or work with any part of the executive branch. Most of that material—contract files, pricing and invoicing records, performance data, internal company communications, and routine correspondence with agency contracting personnel—falls well outside the presidential communications privilege and, at most, could implicate the weaker deliberative process privilege, if any privilege at all. Material that could more plausibly be covered includes, for example, a contractor’s communications with senior White House officials concerning advice sought by the President or presidential decision-making, or classified or sensitive national security information.

As a practical matter, if the executive branch seeks to prevent a contractor from producing particular materials, it has several tools available. The President could formally assert executive privilege over specific documents or testimony and so advise the committee and the contractor. The Justice Department could seek to intervene in, or initiate, litigation to block enforcement of a subpoena, as occurred in Mazars, and could decline to prosecute a contempt referral. Agencies could also invoke contractual confidentiality terms, classification or controlled unclassified information restrictions, or other statutory limits on disclosure. Each of these mechanisms shifts the burden of the dispute onto the executive branch—where it belongs—rather than onto the contractor, and a contractor instructed to withhold should consider pressing for the executive branch to use the formal mechanisms available to it.

4. Statutory whistleblower and anti-gag protections

Under 41 U.S.C. § 4712, contractor and subcontractor employees are protected from reprisal for disclosing information they reasonably believe evidences gross mismanagement, waste, abuse, or violations of law to, among others, a Member of Congress or a congressional committee. Contractors are also generally prohibited from requiring employees to sign confidentiality agreements that restrict lawful reporting of waste, fraud, or abuse (see FAR 52.203-19). The Lloyd-LaFollette anti-gag provision, carried in annual appropriations acts, shields federal employees who communicate with Congress, but its protections extend to government personnel and do not extend to contractors or insulate their disclosures. A contractor that disciplines or restricts employees in an effort to comply with the EO could face reprisal claims and congressional scrutiny of its own.

5. Suspension and debarment require a cognizable cause

Suspension and debarment are designed to protect the government from non-responsible contractors, not to punish; they require a recognized cause and due process. A debarment premised on a contractor’s responding to a lawful congressional subpoena would be highly susceptible to challenge, including on First Amendment and retaliation grounds, and the EO’s own “consistent with applicable law” caveat would likely feature prominently in any such challenge.

6. Discretionary contract actions are the more likely enforcement tools

Discretionary contract actions are likely to be the more practical levers for enforcing compliance with the EO. Section 4 of the EO directs agencies to consider “all appropriate actions,” and many of the actions available to an agency require no finding of contractor default or non-compliance. An agency may terminate a contract for convenience when the contracting officer determines that termination is “in the Government's interest,” a deferential standard that does not require any contractor default. A contractor challenging a convenience termination would have to overcome a strong presumption that the government acted in good faith. An agency may also decline to exercise an option or extend the period of performance, decline to renew or recompete a contract, or withhold new task or delivery orders under indefinite-delivery contracts. Contractors should therefore not assume that the absence of an implementing contract clause insulates them from adverse action. A termination for default, by contrast, requires an actual failure to perform or to comply with a contract term, which makes a clause or modification implementing the EO a significant development to watch.

7. Beyond privilege: limits on congressional inquiry into the President’s exclusive powers

Apart from executive privilege, the Administration is likely to argue, relying on the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Trump v. United States, that Congress cannot investigate presidential actions within the President’s “conclusive and preclusive” constitutional authority at all. The Court in that case suggested that such authority includes the pardon power, the removal of executive officers, and the President’s decisions regarding the investigation and prosecution of federal crimes. Whether, and to what extent, that reasoning applies to congressional investigations is likely to be contested. The decision addressed presidential immunity from criminal prosecution, not Congress’s authority to investigate potential executive branch malfeasance—a materially different question. Congress may seek information to determine whether legislation is needed to address misconduct by third parties, rather than to restrict the President’s exercise of an exclusive constitutional power. For example, it might investigate whether to enact criminal penalties for people who pay intermediaries to obtain pardons, or adopt other prophylactic safeguards against corruption, without purporting to invalidate or condition the pardons themselves. The constitutional validity of any particular measure would present a separate question. Congress also has distinct constitutional powers of impeachment and removal, which provide an additional basis for investigating alleged abuses of presidential authority, even where criminal liability may be unavailable. Accordingly, the Administration’s anticipated reliance on Trump v. United States should not be treated as establishing a categorical bar to congressional inquiry into these subjects. The boundaries are likely to be litigated, with potential implications for contractors whose work touches those areas.

Bottom line: A requirement that contractors promptly notify their agencies of congressional requests, giving the executive branch an opportunity to assert privilege through proper channels, is likely to be viewed as reasonable, and many contractors may choose to provide notice regardless of its ultimate enforceability. By contrast, an instruction to withhold information from Congress in the face of compulsory process, or to coordinate the substance of a response with the White House, carries meaningful legal risk for the contractor that follows it. Contractors thus face competing risks: withholding information from Congress may expose them to legal proceedings, while producing it over executive branch objections may trigger adverse contract action. Court challenges to the EO, its implementing clauses, and specific privilege assertions are likely, though when they will be resolved, and how, remains to be seen.

Next Steps and Client Considerations

While the appropriate response to the EO should be determined on a case-by-case basis, contractors should not wait for OMB guidance or a congressional subpoena to prepare. We recommend the following:

Inventory pending requests now. Because the notification duty extends to pending requests, identify any open congressional letters, staff inquiries, or preservation notices, including those received from current ranking members. Document the date and manner of any notice provided to the contracting agency and the White House, if the company determines to provide notice.

Establish a single intake and escalation process under the direction of counsel. Route all congressional contacts—including informal calls to government relations staff and business personnel—to a designated legal lead. Assign clear decision-making authority across the functions that will be involved in any response, with appropriate governance visibility for significant matters.

Preserve documents. Implement or refresh legal holds covering records relating to the subject of any request, including messaging platforms and personal devices. Nothing in the EO alters preservation obligations, and spoliation would compound exposure on every front.

Distinguish notice from withholding. Providing notice to the contracting agency generally presents less risk than withholding from a committee, though the analysis will depend on the request and the company’s circumstances. A contractor that receives an instruction to withhold should consult counsel about its independent obligations to Congress before taking any action. That includes assessing whether the instruction is in writing, identifies specific documents, and reflects a formal presidential assertion of privilege..

Engage strategically with the executive branch. Following any notice, a contractor may need to understand whether the executive branch intends to assert a privilege over specific materials and, if so, by what formal mechanism. Any privilege belongs to the President, and any assertion is for the executive branch to make and defend directly with the committee. The contractor’s own obligations to Congress remain unchanged. Where the executive branch indicates it may seek to protect information, the company should consider whether to engage with the relevant agency to raise and defend that position directly with the committee.

Engage early with committee staff. Congressional investigations are frequently resolved through negotiated accommodations on scope, timing, and format. Where appropriate, being transparent with committee staff about the company’s process and timing, producing responsive material on a rolling basis, and identifying any material withheld and the basis for withholding it can reduce the risk of escalation to subpoenas and contempt.

Monitor contract actions closely. Watch for agency notices, class deviations, and proposed modifications implementing the EO. Evaluate whether to accept bilateral modifications, whether consideration or equitable adjustment is warranted, and what flowdown and certification obligations will attach. Avoid making certifications of compliance that the company cannot support.

Manage subcontractor flowdown. Primes should consider how they will communicate the EO’s requirements to subcontractors and how they will track subcontractor requests, without assuming responsibility for decisions they cannot control.

Protect employee rights. Review internal policies, confidentiality agreements, and training to ensure they do not restrict protected disclosures to Congress, and confirm that managers understand anti-retaliation obligations. Assess early whether individual employees or executives who may be asked to testify need separate counsel.

Prepare witnesses and messaging. Companies whose work is likely to draw congressional interest—including those involved in high-profile projects, DHS and immigration enforcement contracting, and defense procurement—should consider preparing potential witnesses for transcribed interviews and hearings, and align public and internal communications so that the company is seen as responding to its legal obligations, rather than aligning with either branch.

Consider parallel exposure. Information produced to Congress is not protected by attorney-client privilege as a matter of course, may become public, and can prompt referrals to the Justice Department, state attorneys general, and plaintiffs’ counsel. Responses should be prepared with that broader exposure in mind.

Mayer Brown’s bipartisan Congressional Investigations, Government Contracts, and Global Investigations & White Collar Defense teams include former senior officials from the White House, the Department of Justice, the Department of Homeland Security, and Capitol Hill. Please contact the authors or your Mayer Brown contact with questions about the EO or for assistance responding to congressional or agency inquiries. This Legal Update is general in nature; each contractor’s response should be tailored to its specific circumstances.

name: Human Rights
title: Trump effectively ended asylum. Advocates look to the Supreme Court to restore it - KALW
description:
Now immigration advocates are looking to the Supreme Court to decide whether Trump has the authority to keep this once vital pathway closed.
VANESSA ROMO, BYLINE: For nearly two years, the Trump administration has prohibited asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border.
It's also canceled thousands of pending asylum applications and overhauled the immigration court system with mass firings of judges.
She says, taken together, the Trump administration's moves have gutted asylum in America and fundamentally restricted the job of immigration judges.
Combined, critics say the changes make much of the immigration court system a deportation arm of ICE.
text:
JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:

For decades, asylum offered protection for people fleeing persecution and danger. But under President Trump, that protection has been effectively shut down. Now immigration advocates are looking to the Supreme Court to decide whether Trump has the authority to keep this once vital pathway closed. Here's NPR's Vanessa Romo.

VANESSA ROMO, BYLINE: For nearly two years, the Trump administration has prohibited asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border. It's also canceled thousands of pending asylum applications and overhauled the immigration court system with mass firings of judges.

JENNIFER PEYTON: I got an email firing me when I was on vacation with my family.

ROMO: That's Jennifer Peyton, a former assistant chief immigration judge in Chicago who served on the bench for nine years. She says, taken together, the Trump administration's moves have gutted asylum in America and fundamentally restricted the job of immigration judges. Now, she's an immigration attorney who regularly appears before the judges that she helped train, though many of them have been fired too. Peyton says that's left scores of novice judges, some of whom, she says, are wreaking havoc.

PEYTON: The things I hear immigration judges say, they're, quite frankly, sometimes wrong. They're rash decisions and lack - or don't care that they lack - the training that we so rigorously put them through when I was on that team.

ROMO: President Trump has long claimed that asylum has been abused by people with, quote, "fake claims," which is why, within hours of retaking office, he issued the asylum ban along the southern border. The administration has also taken aggressive steps it says are intended to alleviate the crushing backlog of existing asylum cases. New Justice Department rules allow the government's lawyers to get claims more easily thrown out by arguing they're incomplete or insufficient.

Another tactic - get immigration judges to agree to send people to third countries and direct them to apply for asylum there, even when those third nations can't guarantee a person any protections. Combined, critics say the changes make much of the immigration court system a deportation arm of ICE.

MADHAVI NARAYANAN: As asylum attorneys trying to defend that right, all we can really do is try to keep fighting.

ROMO: That's Madhavi Narayanan, an immigration attorney with Human Rights First. She represents an Ethiopian man who's part of an ethnic minority facing repression from the ruling government. We're only identifying him by his initials, Z.G., because he fears retribution from the Ethiopian government. Narayanan says he fled Ethiopia following arrest and torture for his political views.

NARAYANAN: His ethnicity - they're very widely targeted, and it's very clearly documented, not only that he has corroborating evidence of his claim and statements from others who know what happened to him. And the torture that he underwent was extremely brutal. So in the past, he would have been granted asylum pretty quickly.

ROMO: Instead, Z.G. is one of thousands of asylum-seekers whose applications ICE successfully petitioned to be canceled. And like many others, he was given a removal order to a third country he's never stepped foot in - Uganda, a country that does not recognize the armed conflict in Ethiopia as a war and would likely send Z.G. back home. Narayanan says the judge hearing the case was troubled by that but said his hands were tied.

NARAYANAN: He was basically like, OK, I hear everything that you said, but I read this case, and I'm not allowed to consider this. And that was it.

ROMO: In coming months, the Supreme Court will decide whether sending asylum-seekers to other countries is legal, and it'll consider the question of the ban. But supporters of the president's restrictions are hoping the high court stays the course. Simon Hankinson is with the conservative Heritage Foundation, a think tank closely aligned with the president. Like Trump, Hankinson contends that most asylum applicants are exploiting the system and simply don't qualify for it.

SIMON HANKINSON: And even if they did, they've already passed through Mexico, which is a safe third country where they could claim asylum. So you have a population that overwhelmingly will not qualify under U.S. law for asylum. They're here because they want to get a job, essentially.

ROMO: Since the ban went into effect, Border Patrol apprehensions at the Southern border this year dropped to their lowest level in agency history. In the meantime, millions of people with active claims remain in limbo, like Z.G. He's desperately hoping to stay in the U.S. and hopes the high court reopens the asylum door.

Vanessa Romo, NPR News. Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

text:
PORTLAND Ore. (KPTV) - Portland Police body camera video shows officers responding to a Jan. 8 shooting in which Customs and Border Protection officers shot two people in the parking lot of Adventist Hospital during an attempted immigration arrest.

The video shows a CBP officer picking up a shell casing and putting it in his back pocket. Portland Police officers must follow local, state and federal protocols, but Department of Homeland Security agencies largely regulate themselves.

CBP officers shot Luis Nino-Moncada and Yorlenys Zambrano-Contreras in their car during the attempted arrest. Responding PPB officers are heard saying they were caught in an awkward position.

DHS said its agents were targeting Zambrano-Contreras and alleged she had connections to the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua. Nino-Moncada, also a non-citizen, was driving. Nino-Moncada later said court he saw masked agents approaching his car, got scared and tried to get away. He hit a CBP vehicle and allegedly struck one agent in the chest with his truck.

Agents fired as he drove away and said they feared for their lives. The shots hit Nino-Moncada in the arm and Zambrano-Contreras in the chest.

Nino-Moncada tells first responders, “ICE, fué ICE,” which translates to “ICE, it was ICE.”

At the scene of the shooting, another officer’s body camera captured the moment a CBP officer picked up a shell casing, put it in his back pocket and turned away.

“That’s a casing right there, leave it,” Officer Afdup commands. “The one you just picked up. In your back pocket. Just put it down. Thanks, buddy. Don’t pick up any casings. Just leave them there.”

Portland Police were tasked with securing the scene for the FBI, which was on its way to take over the official investigation.

DHS followed its own protocol. A team leader said agents would wait for a supervisor but did not specify the protocol.

“We’re going to separate him from everybody else and then we’ll follow our procedures,” the team leader says on the video.

After they were released from the hospital, Zambrano-Contreras was taken to an ICE detention facility in Tacoma. In September, Nino-Moncada was sentenced for damaging federal property. The U.S. Attorney’s Office said he will be deported to Venezuela.

DHS has not responded to requests for comment on the tampering of evidence.

title: Local officials discuss ICE activity in Roanoke - WDBJ7
description:

text:
ROANOKE, Va. (WDBJ) - Roanoke Democratic Del. Sam Rasoul and Republican Roanoke County School Board member Tim Greenway held a joint news conference Tuesday calling out ICE for the way it has detained people in Roanoke over the past two weeks.

The local elected officials called on the federal government to change its approach.

Rasoul said the news conference was intended to start a conversation in the Roanoke Valley across party lines.

“We are coming here today on a bipartisan basis to open up the conversation,” Rasoul said.

Rasoul said the community has been torn apart by the way ICE has treated the people it has detained. He said ICE has terrorized the Hispanic community in Roanoke, including people who are in the country legally.

Rasoul described his own background as the child of immigrants.

“As a child of immigrants who watched my family work in their Roanoke corner store seven days a week, morning, noon, and night, I am a true product of that American dream,” Rasoul said.

He said he and Greenway share some beliefs about the country.

“We both believe this is a nation of laws that need to be respected, and we are a nation that is embracing people,” Rasoul said.

The officials said people are afraid to go to work and school because of federal policies.

Rasoul said a third of Roanoke City Public Schools students are Hispanic, and that students are afraid to come to school. He said the fear is affecting families across the valley.

“Right now, when our communities are terrorized, … these kids are afraid to come to school. People are afraid to go to work. This is not the way we should be handling immigration law,” Rasoul said.

Rasoul said the federal policies raise constitutional concerns.

“We are concerned that there are constitutional violations where you have people who are lawfully going through the process and just being snatched off the streets,” said Rasoul, a Democrat who represents the 38th District.

Rasoul said he has heard that U.S. citizens and people in the middle of an application process are being taken off the streets and sometimes cannot be found for weeks. Rasoul said he considers that treatment inhumane.

Rasoul said the Bill of Rights was meant to protect individual rights, and that the Supreme Court has ruled that many of those rights apply to people regardless of their status. He said people seeking asylum have a right to be heard in court.

Asked whether he had spoken with Ben Cline about the concerns, Rasoul said he had not, but that he has raised them with a number of federal officials, including U.S. senators. Mark Warner and Tim Kaine.

Rasoul said the expansion of ICE in the region has left people feeling unsafe.

“The way we’ve just exploded ICE all across the region, it’s a federal policy that unfortunately has left too many people feeling unsafe, especially with the practices that we are seeing,” Rasoul said.

Asked about action at the state level, Rasoul said Virginia has enacted some policies and is looking into more, including around 287(g) agreements. He said he wants the federal government to change course.

“And we would ask our President, our Congress, to immediately change these policies,” Rasoul said.

Greenway said he has lived in Roanoke County his entire life and has represented the Vinton District on the Roanoke County School Board for over a decade. He said he has not seen as much confusion over a policy as he has over immigration policy.

Greenway echoed Rasoul’s concerns.

“I voted for Trump three times, 2016, 2020, and 2024. As a lifelong conservative Republican, I’m standing here to say enough is enough. The policies on immigration coming from the federal government right now are not the America I grew up in, nor the place I want my grandkids to see. When we start grabbing law-abiding citizens from the streets, we’re snatching a member of our community from all of us. Many of these people are seeking to be legal immigrants,” Greenway said.

Greenway said the people being detained include parents.

“They could be a parent with children at home waiting for them. People are even scared to leave their homes because of what we’re seeing in the streets,” Greenway said.

He said he sees a difference between public safety and the current approach.

“This is the difference between keeping our streets safe and simply terrorizing some folks,” Greenway said.

Greenway said he supports law enforcement.

“I believe our communities and our schools must be safe from all criminals. And I support our law enforcement, state police, and FBI, doing what they can to keep the valley safe, to keep our neighborhoods safe,” Greenway said.

Greenway said his faith informs his position.

“But the policies coming from the federal government right now do not reflect the Christian conservative values that I’ve grown up believing in,” Greenway said.

Asked how he would like to see the federal approach change, Greenway said he does not want to blame immigrants or the people enforcing the policies.

“I don’t want to demonize people, whether it be immigrants, or whether it be the folks that are enforcing the policies. I feel more strongly that we need to demonize the policy,” Greenway said.

Greenway said meeting with families affected by immigration enforcement has shaped his view. He said he and Rasoul have held those conversations a couple of times.

“When you have the opportunity to sit down with these families, it becomes real,” Greenway said. “You realize that these are folks trying to become legal who are having obstacles put in their way.”

Greenway said people in both parties and at every level of government have trouble speaking with each other and that needs to change.

“I just think conversation has been lost in our society,” Greenway said.

Rasoul and Greenway called on the federal government to carry out immigration enforcement in a more humane way and to ensure the constitutional rights of those being detained are protected.

title: USC freshman blinded in one eye by DHS at 'No Kings' rally files lawsuit
authors: C.J. Ciaramella, Matthew Petti, Jacob Sullum, Aaron Tropper
description:
A Los Angeles teenager who was blinded in one eye at a March "No Kings" protest after a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officer shot him in the face with a projectile filed a civil rights lawsuit Monday.
According to his lawsuit, Collins "will need ongoing prosthetic and ophthalmologic care, and possibly cosmetic and reconstructive surgery, for the rest of his life."
In January, a 21-year-old protester in Santa Ana, California, was permanently blinded in one eye after a DHS officer shot him in the face with a less-lethal weapon.
Another 23-year-old in Los Angeles was blinded by a Los Angeles Police Department projectile in March.
DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Collins' lawsuit.
text:
A Los Angeles teenager who was blinded in one eye at a March "No Kings" protest after a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officer shot him in the face with a projectile filed a civil rights lawsuit Monday.

Tucker Collins, an 18-year-old freshman at the University of Southern California, was photographing a March 28 "No Kings" protest outside the Metropolitan Detention Center in downtown Los Angeles when he was struck in the face with a less-lethal projectile. Multiple videos showed Collins was standing well behind a line of officers and holding a large camera in his hand when he was shot in the face, instantly crumpling to the ground. Doctors had to surgically remove Collins' right eye.

Collins' suit against the U.S. government and several unidentified DHS officers seeks damages for inflicting catastrophic physical injuries and emotional distress, in violation of his Fourth Amendment right to be free from excessive force and First Amendment rights to free speech and assembly.

"Tucker never posed a threat to anyone," V. James DeSimone, a civil rights attorney representing Tucker, said in a press release. "No one around him was throwing anything, no one ordered the crowd to disperse, and still an officer fired a projectile into his eye. The Constitution protects the right to peacefully assemble and to document what our government does in public, and simply recording what is happening in plain view should not cost anyone their sight."

According to his lawsuit, Collins "will need ongoing prosthetic and ophthalmologic care, and possibly cosmetic and reconstructive surgery, for the rest of his life."

The suit states that Collins wants to keep attending protests but is afraid of being injured again. "It feels safer to climb a mountain than to exercise my First Amendment rights," Collins says in the lawsuit.

DHS agents have been repeatedly documented retaliating against videographers, protesters, and legal observers. Collins' case is only one example of people being harassed, assaulted, and seriously injured by federal agents for activities that courts say are squarely protected speech.

In January, a 21-year-old protester in Santa Ana, California, was permanently blinded in one eye after a DHS officer shot him in the face with a less-lethal weapon. Another 23-year-old in Los Angeles was blinded by a Los Angeles Police Department projectile in March.

Last year, the Justice Department paid $7.65 million to settle a lawsuit by a Portland man who was shot in the head with a crowd-control munition by a U.S. marshal, fracturing his skull.

In response to a lawsuit accusing DHS of First Amendment retaliation against protesters and journalists, a federal court in California issued a preliminary injunction in September 2025 banning DHS agents from using crowd-control weapons on reporters, legal observers, and protesters who didn't pose a threat of imminent harm to a law enforcement officer or others.

Another federal judge issued a similar injunction in 2020 ordering federal agents to stop assaulting and arresting protesters and legal observers in Portland, Oregon.

A deeper problem is that "less-lethal" police projectiles frequently maim and can even kill people. Police departments are well aware of these dangers, but continue to maintain lax oversight and rules about their use.

In 2020, The Miami Herald obtained body camera footage showing police officers in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, laughing as they shot protesters with rubber bullets, fracturing one woman's eye socket.

"Did you see me fuck up those motherfuckers?" one of the officers said, mistakenly under the impression that his body camera was turned off.

DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Collins' lawsuit.

text:
Batavia, N.Y. (WHAM) — After spending nearly six weeks in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody, Germán Machado is back home with his family, reflecting on his time in detention as he continues to navigate the asylum process.

BACKGROUND: SUNY Brockport community rallies for release of employee detained by ICE | Family fears for future after ICE detains SUNY Brockport employee outside home | SUNY Brockport employee detained by ICE outside home, union says

The SUNY Brockport IT technician returned home from work late Monday afternoon — his first shift since being taken into custody. Machado was released Saturday on $25,000 bond from the Buffalo Federal Detention Facility, where he had been held since Oct. 13.

"Losing your freedom is a bad thing, in your mind, in your heart," Machado reflected. "That's something that — you only realize how it feels when when you lose your freedom."

Machado sat beside his wife, Maria (Miji) Velázquez, in their Batavia home, revealing an electronic monitoring device attached to one of his ankles.

Velázquez worked as a freelance investigative reporter in their home country of Venezuela.

"You as a journalist need to be impartial. Both sides of the story. You have to report and that's it," Velázquez said. "In Venezuela, you couldn't do that."

She reflected on the hazards of her work, including threats and, at times, violent retaliation for her reporting.

"My wife, covering a visit of the opposition leader in our city, she received — some people attacking her, punching her, and they tried to steal her camera and recording — everything. And she fought, and she didn't allow them to take her stuff," Machado said.

Velázquez and Machado recalled one frightening incident involving their children.

"My eldest went to the garage to open the gate. And when my son was getting inside the driveway, a motorcycle with two guys approached them with guns. And they told them that, tell your mother if she doesn't stop talking, you know what, we are going to kill you both," Machado said.

Machado's family fled Venezuela in 2016, seeking political asylum in the United States. The Department of Homeland Security said Machado had permission to stay until the following year, but the family said he continued to receive work authorization while awaiting a decision on their asylum case.

That wait stretched nearly a decade before Machado was suddenly arrested.

Machado recalled being pulled over during his morning commute Oct. 13. DHS said he was arrested during a targeted enforcement operation.

"I thought that I was going to receive a ticket for speeding too fast in, oh, I don't know what," he chuckled. "I asked them what's going on, and they told me that they stopped me because I had stayed I was illegally living here so I told them that I wasn't — that I was legal because I was told that wait until receiving a resolution or an appointment for an (asylum) hearing."

In a statement, DHS said, "To be clear: work authorization or a pending application does not confer legal status in the U.S."

Machado’s union representatives said he has a valid federal employment authorization document that expires in 2029.

Machado likened his time in federal custody to being an animal in a cage. He recalled spending hours in a crowded room with other detainees and sleeping on the floor in cold conditions.

"I felt very, very small, little. That was the moment when I started feeling lost and afraid and threatened in the sense that I wouldn't be able to defend myself since the things that I was saying — nobody — nobody listened, nobody pay attention," Machado said.

His arrest prompted protests and calls for his release, including from Gov. Kathy Hochul. Machado recalled learning about the news coverage of his case from officers inside the detention facility.

"They mentioned to me that they had seen me in the news and that there were some protests outside," Machado said.

"I think it was two or three days without any communication," Velazquez said of her husband's time in custody. "And all of a sudden, people from everywhere. (People) started to text through Facebook, Instagram, started to ask one another about me, how to connect to me, and how to contact me."

The family's focus now is moving forward as they continue navigating the asylum process in hopes of remaining in the United States.

Machado, who is due back in court next month, told 13WHAM he feels free and happy, but his experience in detention has left him with lingering fears.

"Still I feel afraid, even though I was released, but still I don't trust completely that I can be everywhere for free — of my choice," he said.

In a statement, a spokesperson for DHS said in part: "In violation of our nation’s laws, he overstayed his welcome by almost a decade and failed to depart. He has been released from ICE custody pending his removal proceedings. He will continue to receive due process."

Velázquez said she's awaiting a written decision following her asylum hearing earlier this month. She said once a decision is made, the family can appeal to have Machado included in her case.

"We are deeply grateful to everyone who stood beside our family," said Velázquez. "During some of the most difficult weeks of our lives, we discovered that compassion is not simply something people express; it is something they put into action. People showed up, made phone calls, wrote letters, organized support, visited Germán, offered transportation, helped us navigate the legal process, and reminded us that we were not alone. We will never forget that."

text:
WEST HUMBOLDT PARK — A West Humboldt Park cafe abruptly closed Monday when its employees walked off the job after allegations that its co-founder works as an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent surfaced online.

Tasa Coffee Roasters, 4136 W. North Ave., was closed by its staff after rumors began to swirl online that Pierre Marquez, who helped start the business with his wife, works as a supervisory detention and deportation officer for ICE.

The accusation stems from a post on Reddit that states a Pierre Marquez appears on the website Ice List, an unofficial database of ICE agents and employees.

UPDATE: Humboldt Park Coffee Shop Announces It’s Permanently Closed After Fallout Over ICE Allegations

The post quickly went viral, leading to swift condemnation online and in the majority Latino neighborhood, before employees walked out and the storefront was egged.

In a handwritten message taped to the door Monday, Tasa baristas and roasters said they found out about the allegations through the Reddit post and closed the shop because of it.

“We do not stand beside, condone, support or accept anyone or any org associated with ICE,” baristas and roasters said in their statement. “As the baristas, we are discussing what steps will be necessary for us. We intend to do our best as employees to be as honest and transparent as we can be.”

Tasa was opened in 2022 by Pierre Marquez and his wife, Jackie Marquez. While its business license and city records only list Jackie Marquez as owner, the couple previously described the business as a joint effort, with Pierre Marquez telling Block Club in 2022 the idea for the business started after he bought a $200 at-home roaster during the pandemic lockdown.

The business, which has a “Hands Off Chicago” sign on its front door, also landed a $230,000 grant from the city’s Neighborhood Opportunity Fund in 2021 and has hosted events geared toward the Latino community, including fundraisers and DJ pop-ups.

In a 2025 Block Club article, Pierre Marquez said he bought a year’s worth of Colombian coffee in an effort to dodge President Donald Trump’s global tariffs.

Jackie Marquez posted a statement on Tasa’s Instagram Monday saying she is the cafe’s sole owner but did not address questions about her husband’s employment.

“I personally disagree with current immigration policy and I believe in civil dialogue and mutual respect, even when we disagree,” she said in the statement. “I ask that my employees not be targeted or held responsible for matters outside their control.”

Pierre Marquez and Jackie Marquez did not reply to requests for comment. Questions sent to an email address of an individual named Pierre Marquez who works for Homeland Security did not bounce back and were not responded to Monday.

Relative Shows Gun

A man who identified himself as Jackie Marquez’s relative, however, arrived to the cafe around 2 p.m. Monday and said neighbors “misunderstood” the situation.

When asked if Pierre Marquez is an ICE officer, he said he did not know if it was true but that Pierre Marquez “works for us.”

He then defended his daughter before telling a Block Club reporter that he has a gun, lifting his shirt to show a gun in his waist band. As a few neighbors arrived on the scene, he again lifted his shirt to show his silver gun. He then went inside the business and took down the handwritten statements baristas posted in the shop’s windows.

Neighbors called police and two officers arrived after a few minutes, taking the man’s gun and detaining him for about 20 minutes, a Block Club reporter observed. The man was released after witnesses declined to file a complaint. Officers said he had a legal right to carry a gun but did not answer if the man had a FOID card.

Video of the man being placed in handcuffs is in the below Instagram post:

Esme Segura and Felipe Lopez, Humboldt Park neighbors who saw the incident and heard about the ICE allegations, were shocked by the sight of the man’s gun.

“He was very upset that we were recording, and then he just started banging on the wall or the window, and flipping us off, and then showing us his gun,” Segura said.

Neighbors React To The Allegations

Neighbors walked by the business Monday afternoon, taking photos and telling passersby “They work for ICE.” Some have also taken to social media to express frustration over the allegations and rapid responders have alerted others of the business’s possible ties to ICE.

Some neighbors, like Lopez and Segura, now plan to boycott the business and told their friends not to go there anymore.

“I’m really proud of the community, the way that they responded to this so quickly [since] there’s not a lot that we can do right now with just defending each other and our neighbors from ICE,” Lopez said. “If we’re able to at least drive some of these people out of here and and make it clear that it is unacceptable to be an ICE agent and operate in our community, that could benefit us.”

Neighbors and social media commenters also ripped Jackie Marquez‘s statement on the business’s Instagram. Lopez said it does not matter if Jackie Marquez is Tasa’s sole owner because of her husband’s documented involvement in the business.

“They’re all responsible,” Lopez said. “I mean, there’s no way that she didn’t know that he was an ICE agent. Is he like Batman sneaking out in the middle of the night?”

Ald. Jessie Fuentes (26th) said her political coalition is “no longer supporting, promoting, or partnering with this establishment” in light of the allegations.

“As our immigrant neighbors are living with the fear that someone they love could be taken into detention, we reject any and all businesses that profit from or enable ICE’s terror,” Fuentes said in a statement.

The outcry comes a year after Operation Midway Blitz, when ICE and Homeland Security agents conducted unprecedented immigration enforcement campaigns in the Chicago area that saw thousands detained, a man killed, tear gas deployed on city streets and people brutalized.

An ICE spokesperson declined to confirm or deny if Marquez is an employee of the agency, said in a statement that “doxxing our officers put their lives and their families in serious danger.”

As federal employees, however, Homeland Security agents’ names are a matter of public record, and their identities have been disclosed through Freedom of Information Act requests and court documents.
