text:
Source:

Read a PDF of our statement here.

On Monday, the Legal Defense Fund (LDF), Muslim Advocates, the Black Alliance for Just Immigration (BAJI), and the Haitian Bridge Alliance (HBA) filed an amicus brief in the U.S. Supreme Court case, U.S. Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D.

The brief argues that the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS’s) policy of mass deportations of immigrants to “third countries,” countries that are not their country of origin, fails to comply with the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment. The policy relies on either blanket diplomatic assurances that deportees will not be persecuted or tortured without any process at all, or, in the absence of such assurances, the policy provides a perfunctory procedure that robs people of a fair opportunity to stop their deportation. In either case, the Trump Administration is violating the Constitution’s due process requirements. As a result, people who are deported to third countries are vulnerable to persecution or torture because the Trump Administration’s policy fails to ensure their safety or prevent them from being sent to their country of origin where, because of dangerous conditions, the United States was barred from sending them back to.

The Trump Administration’s disregard for due process protections disproportionately harms and targets Black immigrants and other immigrants of color. More than half of the people deported to third countries are Black people or people of color. People deported to third countries describe inhumane detention conditions, beatings, food deprivation, and total restriction on outside contact. Many are later sent back to their countries of origin or face no other choice but to return there due to untenable conditions in the third countries.

“The Trump administration has unlawfully deported people to countries where they may face torture and death. But the Constitution is clear: people, regardless of immigration status, are afforded due process rights and cannot simply be deported to an unsafe and unfamiliar country based on the whims of the Administration and without proper procedural safeguards,” said Kacey Mordecai, Senior Counsel at LDF. “Black immigrants and other immigrants of color are more likely to be removed to third countries and face persecution and torture as a result. Permitting this unconstitutional policy will encourage this Administration’s discriminatory immigration enforcement and undermine the Constitution’s fundamental norms of equality and fairness.”

###

Founded in 1940, the Legal Defense Fund (LDF) is the nation’s first civil rights legal organization. LDF has been completely separate from the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) since 1957, though it was founded under the leadership of Thurgood Marshall while he was at the NAACP. LDF’s Thurgood Marshall Institute (TMI) is a division of LDF that undertakes innovative research and houses LDF’s archive. In all media attributions, please refer to us as the Legal Defense Fund or LDF (do not include NAACP) and refer to the Institute as LDF’s Thurgood Marshall Institute or TMI.

text:
A federal appeals court has upheld new Virginia laws restricting agreements between local law enforcement agencies and immigration enforcement.

The ruling in the Fourth Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals yesterday (Monday) kept in place legislation patroned earlier this year by Del. Alfonso Lopez (D-3) and Sen. Saddam Azlan Salim (D-37), prompting celebration from both lawmakers.

The bills, passed largely on party-line votes and signed into law by Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D), restrict the ability of Virginia law enforcement agencies to enter into or renew 287(g) agreements with the federal government, unless a slew of specific criteria are first met.

The 287(g) agreements are formal partnerships between local law enforcement agencies and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which allow deputized officers to perform functions typically undertaken by immigration agents.

The state laws restricting interactions went into effect on July 1, but in late August, U.S. District Court Judge Robert Payne issued a temporary injunction, putting the legislation on hold until the matter played out in court. On Nov. 23, a three-judge panel of the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals voted unanimously to lift the injunction.

The ruling allows the state’s restrictions on ICE interactions to stay in place while litigation moves forward. It concluded that the federal government is “not likely to succeed” on at least some of its arguments challenging the new laws.

“Just as the commonwealth’s former leaders could empower its agencies and political subdivisions to assist with federal immigration enforcement efforts in the past, its current leaders may alter the conditions of that authorization going forward,” noted the opinion.

Lopez praised the action:

“Local and state police have no obligation to assist in civil immigration enforcement, especially when their time and resources can be used keeping our communities safe. For now, Virginia will not be forced to participate in increasingly dangerous and unprofessional actions by ICE agents that disregard due process and the rule of law. If the legislation faces additional appeals, I stand ready to continue defending it.”

Added Salim: “The federal government cannot conscript our local officers into its mass deportation machine, and the General Assembly has every right to set the terms on which our own agencies cooperate.”

Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones said the ruling, while just one step in a longer process, represents a “significant victory … against federal overreach.”

The ruling “reaffirms the commonwealth’s authority to determine whether and under what conditions state and local resources may be used to assist federal immigration enforcement efforts,” said Jones, whose office is handling litigation for the state government.

Among provisions of the state legislation, agreements between local agencies and ICE cannot be authorized if federal officials act without valid judicial warrants or conduct enforcement activities at schools.

The advocacy organization We Are CASA also celebrated the ruling, saying it “protects community trust.”

“Today is a huge win for our families and the autonomy of our Commonwealth,” We Are CASA said in a press release. “For years, our members have fought to make sure Washington can’t force local police and sheriffs to do ICE’s work, and yesterday, the court backed us up. text:
NEW YORK -- Children's educator and YouTube personality Ms. Rachel visited federal youth immigration court in New York City on Monday where she met children facing deportation proceedings and called attention to what advocates describe as a lack of legal representation for immigrant youth.

Among the children she met was 9-year-old Angel, who now lives in the Bronx with his mother after traveling alone from Mexico. Angel was among the children appearing in court without an attorney as they navigate immigration proceedings.

"It's heartbreaking. I care so much about every child and I just want to see every child thriving in school and my heart goes out to anyone going through this," Ms. Rachel said.

The former Bronx public school teacher toured the court alongside Congressman-elect Brad Lander, who said he wanted to see firsthand how immigrant children are being treated in the system.

"I think about how that makes a child feel whether or not you are removable...I don't want any child to hear that word associated with them," Ms. Rachel said.

Lander criticized what he described as reduced support for legal representation for immigrant youth.

"There has been an aggressive assault on the system of providing legal representation and services for young people," he said.

Nonprofit organizations such as Safe Passage Project provide pro bono legal representation to children who appear in immigration court without attorneys. Legal Director Tania Cohen said her organization has seen an increase in removal orders and a decline in funding.

"The issuance of removal orders which are deportation orders has significantly increased for immigrant children who are eligible for a green card," Cohen said.

While at the courthouse, Ms. Rachel spoke with Angel about his Christmas wish list.

"I told him to write down some things he wants for Christmas, in conversation because I wanted to get him some Christmas presents and then he came and gave me this and it says the first thing he wants is an immigration lawyer," she said.

Angel said meeting Ms. Rachel was "Good."

According to the report, a judge gave Angel's mother until Dec. 15 to obtain legal representation.

Lander said he plans to push for restored funding and increased oversight once he takes office in Congress.

"We're going to have oversight hearings and we're going to show up ourselves and we're going to push to make sure the legal funding is restored," he said.

Ms. Rachel said policymakers should focus more on the needs of children.

"I think our problems would really be a lot less if we all just focus on taking care of kids and centered kids in policies," she said.

text:
On Monday, California and 21 other states filed a lawsuit against a Trump administration policy that would deny federal housing assistance to qualifying families if one or more relatives don’t qualify because of their immigration status. This rule would affect approximately 1,700 families in L.A. with mixed immigration status that live in federally subsidized housing, and approximately 7,000 households statewide.

For the past 30 years, families with mixed immigration statuses have been allowed to live in federally subsidized housing, with proportionally reduced financial assistance for families with one or more ineligible residents. But in a Nov. 12th ruling from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, the Trump administration is trying to block all households with mixed immigration statuses from applying for and participating in Housing and Urban Development programs, like federally subsidized housing and Section 8.

According to the rule, the new restrictions will go into effect starting Dec. 14, and mixed immigration status households will have until March 14, 2027, to submit proof of continued eligibility.

The lawsuit, co-led by California, Massachusetts, and New York, argues that the Housing and Urban Development program does not have the jurisdiction to rewrite the law created by Congress. Furthermore, the lawsuit argues that the existing program expressly protects prorated assistance to families with mixed immigration status.

In addition to this lawsuit, L.A. based nonprofit Public Council has filed a lawsuit on behalf of L.A. County residents, and L.A. and San Francisco housing authorities have filed an additional lawsuit against the new rule arguing that it violates federal housing law and would increase administrative costs to cities.

In a statement on Monday, Mayor Karen Bass said, “Los Angeles is a city of immigrants. I’m proud that we have joined other cities from across the country to fight back against the Trump administration’s proposed rule change that threatens every mixed-status household with the loss of the federal housing assistance they rely on to stay afloat.”

title: LGBTQ people face stark dangers under the Trump admin's third-country removal policy
description:
This week, amicus briefs supporting the challengers’ position that the policy violates the Administrative Procedure Act were submitted in the case.
As the Justice Department argued to the Supreme Court: The Guidance also comports with due process.
The Supreme Court in Abrego Garcia blessed precisely this remedy in precisely this context.

text:
On December 9, the U.S. Supreme Court is set to consider the legality of the Trump administration’s policy of quickly deporting people to countries where they had no prior connection — and whether people can even bring a wholesale challenge to the policy.

Although the Trump administration relies upon so-called “diplomatic assurances” from the governments where it is sending people to justify its claim that it is not committing human rights violations when it sends people to these countries without any real opportunity to challenge the deportation, a brief filed on Monday on behalf of LGBTQ organizations highlights the emptiness of that claim by looking to their clients.

“No assurance about the safety of LGBTQ refugees is credible from a government that criminalizes LGBTQ people, persecutes them, or is unable or unwilling to protect them from persecution by others,” the brief from Lambda Legal and Immigration Equality argued to the Supreme Court.

The implementation of the Trump administration’s third-country removal policy — under which one report showed more than 25,000 people had been deported by August of this year — has been made possible by a series of Supreme Court shadow-docket orders over the past year and a half.

The policy has led to widespread condemnation, as reports have circulated about the emptiness in practice of the “diplomatic assurances.”

In one case involving a gay man who had received protection against being sent back to Egypt, Ahmed Soliman was sent under the third-country removal policy to Equatorial Guinea, where, Gillian Brockell reported for The American Prospect, he was “repeatedly beaten, held at gunpoint, threatened, and deprived of food, water, and medical care.“

Share

Now, however, the full arguments over the policy — challenged in Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D. — are set for the Supreme Court’s December oral argument sitting. When amicus briefs were due on October supporting the Trump administration’s position, only three briefs were filed: two from right-wing organizations and one from a multistate group of Republican attorneys general led by Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird. She would lose her re-election bid four days later.

This week, amicus briefs supporting the challengers’ position that the policy violates the Administrative Procedure Act were submitted in the case. In contrast, 15 briefs were submitted on Monday. They were representing a diverse range of organizations — like the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, Human Rights Watch, the ACLU, and the NAACP — and immigrant groups — like the National Immigrant Justice Center and American Immigration Council — as well as individuals who currently or previously had roles in the executive branch, the legislative branch, and the United Nations.

The brief led by Lambda Legal and Immigration Equality was filed on behalf of “nonprofit organizations that assist lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and queer (LGBTQ) refugees through legal representation, advocacy, and other forms of community support“ and highlighted the inherent impossibility of the Trump administration’s arguments that its third-country removal policy is lawful under the Foreign Affairs Reform and Restructuring Act (FARRA) and Convention Against Torture (CAT).

As they explained:

A country’s willingness to accept deported people says nothing about whether it is safe for them. Some of the destination countries criminalize same-sex intimate relationships or nonconforming gender expression outright; others tolerate violence against LGBTQ people by state and non-state actors, exposing them to persecution and torture that withholding and CAT protection exist to prevent.

This is not speculation, either. “The Government knows many of these countries are dangerous for LGBTQ people because its own State Department has documented it,“ they wrote. “Beyond persecuting LGBTQ people directly, many of these governments also fail to protect them from violence by others.“

This has led to the absurd — and dangerous — reality that there are people in the U.S. who were granted asylum or refugee status due to the conditions for LGBTQ people in a country where the U.S. is now deporting LGBTQ people under the Trump administration’s third-country removal policy:

Specifically, the brief continued, “the records of a single amicus, Immigration Equality, show that at least 775 of its clients from the 37 countries with which the U.S. has entered [third-country removal] agreements have received asylum, withholding of removal, or CAT protection.”

The blunt reality, they explained, is:

The Government is now deporting LGBTQ people to many of those same countries, including people who have already proven to a U.S. adjudicator that they would likely be persecuted or tortured in their home countries because they are LGBTQ.

The Trump administration relies on the “diplomatic assurances” against human rights violations that it has received to justify sending anyone to the third countries. As the Justice Department argued to the Supreme Court:

The Guidance also comports with due process. It ensures that any alien will either be sent to a country where the United States has secured a credible assurance that no alien will be tortured or persecuted, or will be given actual notice and an opportunity for a prompt review as to any affirmative fear of removal. Whatever the Due Process Clause may require in this context involving immigration and foreign affairs—where the Executive is entitled to the greatest deference—it demands no more than that.

In addition to the boilerplate, generic nature of the language — as detailed at Law Dork previously — the Lambda Legal and Immigration Equality brief focused on how inadequate that is.

Noting the Trump administration’s argument that “the countries designated for third-country removals ‘are ones where an alien is particularly unlikely to have a viable claim of torture or persecution,’” the brief answered: “This misstates both law and fact.“

In part, they noted:

[T]he Government is well-aware of country conditions for LGBTQ people in countries selected for third-country removals, as evidenced by State Department human rights reports and other materials discussed above. Violence rising to the level of persecution and torture is inflicted on members of the LGBTQ population in those countries, and “lack of prior connections” does not insulate anyone from those harms ….

This, ultimately, led them to the conclusion that “[a] blanket promise cannot answer the question the law requires—whether this person, given who they are, will be safe in this country. Only an individualized determination can.”

The Supreme Court will be hearing arguments on December 9 as to whether a federal district court has jurisdiction to hear this case, whether such a court can issue classwide relief by vacating the policy, and whether the policy is legal.

One person’s case

In the meantime, and almost certainly because of the Supreme Court’s shadow-docket order allowing the policy to remain in effect while it is considering the case, Ahmed Soliman remains in Equatorial Guinea.

Despite the efforts of U.S. District Judge John Hinderaker, a Trump appointee, since October 6 to get Soliman back to the U.S., a pair of orders from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit — in apparent reliance on the Supreme Court’s stay in D.V.D. — has blocked Hinderaker’s efforts. The first, November 3, order was styled as an “administrative[] stay,” referring the motion for a stay pending appeal to the merits panel — and blocking what had been Soliman’s imminent scheduled return under orders from Hinderaker. That administrative stay was issued by Judges William Fletcher (Clinton), Roopali Desai (Biden), and Ana De Alba (Biden).

On November 20, on a 2-1 vote, the merits panel granted the stay pending appeal — keeping Hinderaker’s efforts on hold and Soliman in Equatorial Guinea. The unsigned order granting the stay only stated the factors for granting a stay and concluded that “we find that they support the issuance of a stay.” It was issued on behalf of Judge Mark Bennett (Trump) and Holly Thomas (Biden).

Judge Susan Graber (Clinton) wrote an opinion “dissenting in large part from the order granting a stay.“ Although she would have found that Hinderaker went too far into the details — itself a ruling that shows the removal that appellate judges have from the Trump administration’s behavior on the ground — she would have denied the stay request to the extent it ordered the government “facilitate the return” of Soliman as the Supreme Court had OK’ed in Kilmar Abrego Garcia’s case.

Calling the government’s irreparable harm claims “wholly unpersuasive,” Graber explained, “The district court’s order requires the government to facilitate the return of a single individual from a single country. The Supreme Court in Abrego Garcia blessed precisely this remedy in precisely this context. There is no possible irreparable harm here from permitting Plaintiff’s return to safety while his legal challenges are resolved.”

The Trump administration had, however, argued that the stay in D.V.D. “squarely controls” the consideration of Soliman’s case. As Graber explained it, “The government reasons that, because the Court found irreparable harm in D.V.D., irreparable harm necessarily will result here. I strenuously disagree. Particularly when assessing irreparable harm to the government, the government’s equivalence of this case and D.V.D. strains credulity.”

Specifically, she continued:

Whatever harm could result from arranging a flight for one passenger, none of the harms described in D.V.D. is present. Denying a stay here would not affect thousands of persons; upend international agreements; indefinitely disturb all third-country removals; create an unworkable morass; impose massive operational burdens; impose massive costs on the government; require new rounds of diplomatic engagement; or affect any current or future flight involving other deportees. Instead, a stay would require merely the facilitation of the return of a single person from a single country. As noted, the Supreme Court in Abrego Garcia blessed precisely this remedy in precisely this context. There is no possible irreparable harm here. In my view, it is not even a close call.

But, for now — and against the vote of that one Clinton appointee backing a Trump appointee — Soliman remains in Equatorial Guinea because of the votes of three Biden appointees, a different Clinton appointee, and a different Trump appointee in the wake of the Supreme Court’s order allowing the third-country removal policy to remain in effect during litigation.

After Soliman’s deportation to Egypt was blocked under the Convention Against Torture because he “faced a clear probability of torture in Egypt“ in part due to his sexuality, as Graber noted, he is now in Equatorial Guinea — a country that the Lambda Legal and Immigration Equality brief highlighted “criminalize[s] same-sex intimacy” and in which “police or security forces abuse LGBTQ people or fail to protect them” and “serious anti-LGBTQ societal violence“ is present.

This is not just a policy and numbers. These are real people, facing real consequences each day this policy remains in effect.

The oral arguments on the Ninth Circuit appeal in Soliman’s case, meanwhile, are not even scheduled to take place until January 12 — and those arguments will be before the same panel that just blocked his return to the U.S.

title: Fact Check Team: Supreme Court to review Trump's bid to suspend asylum at southern border
authors: MORGAN STEPHEN S| Fact Check Team, MORGAN STEPHEN S, Fact Check Team
description:
The administration is asking the justices to overturn lower court rulings that found Trump’s executive order unlawfully blocked migrants from applying for asylum.
The order, issued on Trump’s first day back in office in January 2025, declared the situation at the southern border an “invasion” and sought to suspend entry and access to asylum for migrants covered by the policy.
The question is whether that authority also allows the administration to shut off access to the asylum application process.
Trump’s first administration implemented policies including Remain in Mexico and restrictions on asylum eligibility.
The Biden administration also introduced restrictions on asylum eligibility during periods of high border crossings.
text:
The Supreme Court has agreed to review President Donald Trump’s effort to suspend access to asylum at the U.S.-Mexico border, setting up a major legal fight over the limits of presidential power and protections for people seeking refuge in the United States.

The administration is asking the justices to overturn lower court rulings that found Trump’s executive order unlawfully blocked migrants from applying for asylum. The order, issued on Trump’s first day back in office in January 2025, declared the situation at the southern border an “invasion” and sought to suspend entry and access to asylum for migrants covered by the policy.

Federal immigration law generally allows people physically present in the United States or arriving at the country to apply for asylum, regardless of how they entered. Applicants must still meet legal requirements to qualify for protection, including demonstrating they face persecution based on certain protected grounds.

The Trump administration argues the president has broad authority under federal immigration law to restrict entry and categorically deny asylum claims covered by the order. Officials say lengthy processing times contributed to border challenges and argue the policy has helped reduce crossings.

Immigrant rights groups challenge that interpretation, arguing Congress established protections and procedures that the president cannot unilaterally eliminate. They say the policy prevents people fleeing persecution from having their claims individually considered, as required by law.

The legal dispute centers in part on the president’s authority under Section 212(f) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which allows a president to suspend the entry of certain noncitizens when their entry is deemed detrimental to U.S. interests. The question is whether that authority also allows the administration to shut off access to the asylum application process.

The fight over asylum restrictions is not new. Previous administrations have also imposed limits on migrants seeking protection at the southern border. Trump’s first administration implemented policies including Remain in Mexico and restrictions on asylum eligibility. The Biden administration also introduced restrictions on asylum eligibility during periods of high border crossings.

But the current policy goes further by seeking to suspend access to asylum for migrants covered by the order, raising questions about whether the president can override protections Congress enacted.

The case also raises questions about the United States’ obligations under international refugee agreements, including protections against returning people to countries where they face persecution or torture.

The Supreme Court is expected to hear arguments in the case in the spring, with a decision anticipated by the end of June. The ruling could help define how much authority future presidents have to restrict asylum and whether executive orders can override protections established under federal immigration law.

Specifically, the brief continued, “the records of a single amicus, Immigration Equality, show that at least 775 of its clients from the 37 countries with which the U.S. has entered [third-country removal] agreements have received asylum, withholding of removal, or CAT protection.”

The blunt reality, they explained, is:

The Government is now deporting LGBTQ people to many of those same countries, including people who have already proven to a U.S. adjudicator that they would likely be persecuted or tortured in their home countries because they are LGBTQ.

The Trump administration relies on the “diplomatic assurances” against human rights violations that it has received to justify sending anyone to the third countries. As the Justice Department argued to the Supreme Court:

The Guidance also comports with due process. It ensures that any alien will either be sent to a country where the United States has secured a credible assurance that no alien will be tortured or persecuted, or will be given actual notice and an opportunity for a prompt review as to any affirmative fear of removal. Whatever the Due Process Clause may require in this context involving immigration and foreign affairs—where the Executive is entitled to the greatest deference—it demands no more than that.

In addition to the boilerplate, generic nature of the language — as detailed at Law Dork previously — the Lambda Legal and Immigration Equality brief focused on how inadequate that is.

Noting the Trump administration’s argument that “the countries designated for third-country removals ‘are ones where an alien is particularly unlikely to have a viable claim of torture or persecution,’” the brief answered: “This misstates both law and fact.“

In part, they noted:

[T]he Government is well-aware of country conditions for LGBTQ people in countries selected for third-country removals, as evidenced by State Department human rights reports and other materials discussed above. Violence rising to the level of persecution and torture is inflicted on members of the LGBTQ population in those countries, and “lack of prior connections” does not insulate anyone from those harms ….

This, ultimately, led them to the conclusion that “[a] blanket promise cannot answer the question the law requires—whether this person, given who they are, will be safe in this country. Only an individualized determination can.”

The Supreme Court will be hearing arguments on December 9 as to whether a federal district court has jurisdiction to hear this case, whether such a court can issue classwide relief by vacating the policy, and whether the policy is legal.

One person’s case

In the meantime, and almost certainly because of the Supreme Court’s shadow-docket order allowing the policy to remain in effect while it is considering the case, Ahmed Soliman remains in Equatorial Guinea.

Despite the efforts of U.S. District Judge John Hinderaker, a Trump appointee, since October 6 to get Soliman back to the U.S., a pair of orders from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit — in apparent reliance on the Supreme Court’s stay in D.V.D. — has blocked Hinderaker’s efforts. The first, November 3, order was styled as an “administrative[] stay,” referring the motion for a stay pending appeal to the merits panel — and blocking what had been Soliman’s imminent scheduled return under orders from Hinderaker. That administrative stay was issued by Judges William Fletcher (Clinton), Roopali Desai (Biden), and Ana De Alba (Biden).

On November 20, on a 2-1 vote, the merits panel granted the stay pending appeal — keeping Hinderaker’s efforts on hold and Soliman in Equatorial Guinea. The unsigned order granting the stay only stated the factors for granting a stay and concluded that “we find that they support the issuance of a stay.” It was issued on behalf of Judge Mark Bennett (Trump) and Holly Thomas (Biden).

Judge Susan Graber (Clinton) wrote an opinion “dissenting in large part from the order granting a stay.“ Although she would have found that Hinderaker went too far into the details — itself a ruling that shows the removal that appellate judges have from the Trump administration’s behavior on the ground — she would have denied the stay request to the extent it ordered the government “facilitate the return” of Soliman as the Supreme Court had OK’ed in Kilmar Abrego Garcia’s case.

Calling the government’s irreparable harm claims “wholly unpersuasive,” Graber explained, “The district court’s order requires the government to facilitate the return of a single individual from a single country. The Supreme Court in Abrego Garcia blessed precisely this remedy in precisely this context. There is no possible irreparable harm here from permitting Plaintiff’s return to safety while his legal challenges are resolved.”

The Trump administration had, however, argued that the stay in D.V.D. “squarely controls” the consideration of Soliman’s case. As Graber explained it, “The government reasons that, because the Court found irreparable harm in D.V.D., irreparable harm necessarily will result here. I strenuously disagree. Particularly when assessing irreparable harm to the government, the government’s equivalence of this case and D.V.D. strains credulity.”

Specifically, she continued:

Whatever harm could result from arranging a flight for one passenger, none of the harms described in D.V.D. is present. Denying a stay here would not affect thousands of persons; upend international agreements; indefinitely disturb all third-country removals; create an unworkable morass; impose massive operational burdens; impose massive costs on the government; require new rounds of diplomatic engagement; or affect any current or future flight involving other deportees. Instead, a stay would require merely the facilitation of the return of a single person from a single country. As noted, the Supreme Court in Abrego Garcia blessed precisely this remedy in precisely this context. There is no possible irreparable harm here. In my view, it is not even a close call.

But, for now — and against the vote of that one Clinton appointee backing a Trump appointee — Soliman remains in Equatorial Guinea because of the votes of three Biden appointees, a different Clinton appointee, and a different Trump appointee in the wake of the Supreme Court’s order allowing the third-country removal policy to remain in effect during litigation.

After Soliman’s deportation to Egypt was blocked under the Convention Against Torture because he “faced a clear probability of torture in Egypt“ in part due to his sexuality, as Graber noted, he is now in Equatorial Guinea — a country that the Lambda Legal and Immigration Equality brief highlighted “criminalize[s] same-sex intimacy” and in which “police or security forces abuse LGBTQ people or fail to protect them” and “serious anti-LGBTQ societal violence“ is present.

This is not just a policy and numbers. These are real people, facing real consequences each day this policy remains in effect.

The oral arguments on the Ninth Circuit appeal in Soliman’s case, meanwhile, are not even scheduled to take place until January 12 — and those arguments will be before the same panel that just blocked his return to the U.S.

authors: MORGAN STEPHEN S| Fact Check Team, MORGAN STEPHEN S, Fact Check Team

The Biden administration also introduced restrictions on asylum eligibility during periods of high border crossings.
text:
The Supreme Court has agreed to review President Donald Trump’s effort to suspend access to asylum at the U.S.-Mexico border, setting up a major legal fight over the limits of presidential power and protections for people seeking refuge in the United States.

The administration is asking the justices to overturn lower court rulings that found Trump’s executive order unlawfully blocked migrants from applying for asylum. The order, issued on Trump’s first day back in office in January 2025, declared the situation at the southern border an “invasion” and sought to suspend entry and access to asylum for migrants covered by the policy.

Federal immigration law generally allows people physically present in the United States or arriving at the country to apply for asylum, regardless of how they entered. Applicants must still meet legal requirements to qualify for protection, including demonstrating they face persecution based on certain protected grounds.

The Trump administration argues the president has broad authority under federal immigration law to restrict entry and categorically deny asylum claims covered by the order. Officials say lengthy processing times contributed to border challenges and argue the policy has helped reduce crossings.

Immigrant rights groups challenge that interpretation, arguing Congress established protections and procedures that the president cannot unilaterally eliminate. They say the policy prevents people fleeing persecution from having their claims individually considered, as required by law.

The legal dispute centers in part on the president’s authority under Section 212(f) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which allows a president to suspend the entry of certain noncitizens when their entry is deemed detrimental to U.S. interests. The question is whether that authority also allows the administration to shut off access to the asylum application process.

The fight over asylum restrictions is not new. Previous administrations have also imposed limits on migrants seeking protection at the southern border. Trump’s first administration implemented policies including Remain in Mexico and restrictions on asylum eligibility. The Biden administration also introduced restrictions on asylum eligibility during periods of high border crossings.

But the current policy goes further by seeking to suspend access to asylum for migrants covered by the order, raising questions about whether the president can override protections Congress enacted.

The case also raises questions about the United States’ obligations under international refugee agreements, including protections against returning people to countries where they face persecution or torture.

The Supreme Court is expected to hear arguments in the case in the spring, with a decision anticipated by the end of June. The ruling could help define how much authority future presidents have to restrict asylum and whether executive orders can override protections established under federal immigration law.

text:
An Immediate Response

Hours after the arrests, as the video ricocheted across social media, OneAmerica and MLK Labor held a joint press conference at the United Food and Commercial Workers Local 3000 office in Des Moines. Ferguson attended.

Throughout the press conference, audience members spoke up about ICE's access to driver data held by the Washington State Department of Licensing. Researchers at the University of Washington's Center for Human Rights documented 406 cases from August 2025 through Nov. 11, 2026, in which immigration arrests followed federal agents' searches of Washington license plate records through Nlets, a national data-sharing network.

An elementary school teacher who attended the press conference said they had witnessed the arrest of a coworker on school property. They questioned Ferguson about driver data, asking what more the state is doing to protect school safety. According to Ferguson, Washington state currently does everything within its power to keep ICE from accessing driver data.

"For data that the state has, ICE has been disconnected from all of it, including license plates. What happens, however, is other federal actors don't care what the rules are and get that information. We cut those individuals off each individual time that they do that," said Ferguson.

"The Trump administration and ICE are so annoyed by us cutting them off that we've been sued by the Trump administration," he added.

Ferguson also called for the abolition of ICE and its banishment from all airports, arguing that ICE is beyond reform. He said he would ask Alaska Airlines to request ICE have no presence at the airport. "And I'm going to be reaching out to every airline that operates out of Sea-Tac and [request] that statement be made to ICE," he said.

Following the press conference, three activists from Superfamilia KC, a grassroots organization that organizes mutual aid and advocates for King County's undocumented communities, entered the room with a bullhorn. They accused Ferguson of being complicit in ICE's continued use of DOL data to make arrests in Washington state. As attendees left the room, the activists chanted through a bullhorn that "the governor collaborates with ICE."

After the demonstration, Superfamilia KC posted a statement on its Instagram account that described the press conference as "performative."

text:
Los Angeles (AP) — A federal appeals court on Monday approved the Justice Department’s bid to dismiss its own lawsuit that sought to stop California from counting roughly 20,000 ballots until officials could verify the immigration statuses of recipients it alleged were noncitizens.

The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals decision marked the official end to a flurry of litigation in California immediately preceding the competitive and high-stakes November midterms. Federal prosecutors who brought the lawsuit previously said that their efforts would become moot after Election Day, since local officials would no longer be able to prevent ballots from being counted.

The contested ballots were at the heart of a protracted legal battle between the Trump administration and California over the eligibility of voters in the heavily Democratic state, and came amid broader federal scrutiny of local elections nationally.

The Trump administration also issued a raft of subpoenas in Alaska in a spoiler candidate controversy, but moved to drop those efforts two days after former Rep. Mary Peltola won an outright majority in the race to become Democrats’ 56th senator, as part of a Democratic midterm blowout.

A related lawsuit filed against the Justice Department by the labor unions and pro-voting groups was also dismissed this month.

The lawsuit came after the federal government threatened to charge California state election workers who counted the contested ballots and issued criminal grand jury subpoenas to clerks in Los Angeles and Orange counties. It argued that the Justice Department’s efforts risked interfering with the lawful administration of state and federal election law, since ballot processing was already underway when the federal government issued the subpoenas.

text:
Attorneys general for 21 states, Washington, D.C., and Pennsylvania's governor filed a lawsuit against the Department of Housing and Urban Development over a rule that would deny housing aid to families with members who lack eligible citizenship or immigration status.

The lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts on Monday and claims that the rule, which takes effect on Dec. 14 and would require people to verify their citizenship or eligible immigration status to receive federal housing assistance, could split up families or evict U.S. citizens from public housing, The Associated Press reported.

The attorneys general of California, New York, and Massachusetts led the lawsuit and were joined by Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, the District of Columbia, and the Democratic governor of Pennsylvania.

More than 30 years ago, Congress authorized prorated federal housing assistance for families whose members have different citizenship or immigration statuses. The families receive less assistance if a household member is ineligible because of their immigration status, but HUD's new rule would ban mixed-status families from receiving any aid.

“No child should lose their home over a parent’s immigration status,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) said during a press conference on Monday. “This rule is cruel, and it’s unlawful.”

“Picture a mom with two kids in public housing. All U.S. citizens. Their dad is not eligible. Under this rule, all four of them lose their home,” he added.

HUD's rule would affect more than 7,000 mixed-status households in California, according to Bonta's office, "potentially displacing thousands of U.S. citizen children from their homes and imposing financial and administrative burdens on state and local agencies forced to fill in the gaps for families who will lose their homes as a result of the rule’s implementation."

Also, the rule would require private landlords and public housing authorities to report tenants who fail verification to the Department of Homeland Security.

“Congress never gave HUD the power to throw mixed-status families out of their homes or turn private landlords into immigration enforcement. But that’s exactly what this rule does,” Bonta said.

HUD Secretary Scott Turner told the AP on Monday, “HUD’s final rule fully implements the 1980 Housing and Community Development Act and ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars. This rule guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing. This change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist.”

Turner first announced the proposed rule in January, but HUD just finalized it last week.

text:
Some people arrested and detained for civil immigration warrants in Alaska have been placed in extended solitary confinement, subjected to strip searches after visits with attorneys and denied regular access to phone calls, showers, recreational time and medical care while held in the state-run Anchorage Correctional Complex, Alaska lawmakers heard on Friday.

The House Judiciary Committee held an investigatory hearing on U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity in Alaska and conditions of confinement for people held in state prisons. ICE detainees are held in state custody while awaiting civil immigration proceedings or before being transferred to federal detention facilities in the Lower 48.

It was the third such hearing on state detention policies under the Alaska Department of Corrections since the start of the Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda in 2025. The committee held a similar hearing following the transfer of 41 men in ICE custody to Alaska which raised similar concerns of punitive conditions of detention, violations of due process and criminal confinement.

Rep. Andrew Gray, D-Anchorage, chair of the Judiciary Committee, criticized the department for its treatment of ICE detainees. People arrested by ICE are under administrative custody, and not charged or convicted of any criminal offense, Gray noted.

“Lockdowns, strip searches, missing medications, lawyers who cannot access their clients — those are the same things documented at our June 2025 hearing, where we were assured that DOC would do better,” he said. “Seventeen months later, it appears that little has changed.”

No DOC officials were present at the hearing. Officials with DOC declined to participate, but would answer written questions from the committee, Gray said.

Officials with DOC did not respond to a list of questions Monday on the department’s policies for placing ICE detainees in solitary confinement, subjecting them to strip searches and allowing access to regular phone calls, visits, showers and recreational time. Officials did not respond to questions about lawmaker concerns that DOC has violated federal standards of confinement.

Gray said Alaska and the Legislature need to do more to strengthen oversight and protections for ICE detainees in state custody. He said they should review cooperative agreements between DOC and the federal government, and potentially ban ICE arrests in state courthouses, schools and other public facilities.

Alaska has seen a surge in the number of people arrested and detained by ICE with the Trump administration’s nationwide immigration crackdown, rising from 13 people in 2024 during the Biden administration to 99 people in 2025, according to DOC data compiled by the ACLU of Alaska. That is a 662% increase.

This year, from January through Oct. 19, DOC has detained 130 people. The majority of people have been detained at the Anchorage Correctional Center. DOC has an agreement with ICE to hold federal detainees at a cost of $243.24 per person per day.

One of the people detained this year was Latyr Barreto, who shared his experience being incarcerated at ACC with the committee.

He told lawmakers he came to Alaska in 2020 after marrying a U.S. citizen, and has worked as a certified nursing assistant, including in home care and hospice, in Anchorage and the Matanuska-Susitna Valley for the last six years.

Barreto was arrested by ICE for a civil violation, not criminal charges, he said. He was jailed at ACC for the first 11 days with two other ICE detainees in a cell with only two beds, where he slept on the floor. They experienced frequent lockdowns, which prohibited calls with his attorney, showers and leaving the cell. One day after he complained, he was transferred to solitary confinement.

He remained there for the next four months, while fighting his case.

“I spent 117 days in solitary confinement. I was alone in my cell approximately 23 hours a day. I was allowed one hour of recreation and would shower every other day. This was my daily routine for nearly four months,” he said. “The restrictions affected my ability to maintain relationships, communicate with people outside, access legal resources and participate in ordinary daily activities.”

He could make calls through a phone that was passed through the food slot in his cell, which was physically difficult, he said. Calls and visiting hours were restricted to certain times.

After in-person visits with his attorney, he was routinely strip searched in a public area.

“A dozen times, every one of those strip searches took place in a room where a camera was pointed directly at me. Staff also left the door open. People walking through the area, including detainees, being escorted and other staff members could see me naked, male or female. I repeatedly asked staff to provide privacy,” he said. “My requests were never honored.”

He urged lawmakers to examine DOC standards of detention, use of solitary confinement and policies for detainees to access basic services, including communication with their attorneys — “because the next person who finds themselves in that situation might not have the opportunity to tell the story. I do,” he said.

Anchorage Republican Rep. Mia Costello thanked Larreto for his testimony and said it was “disturbing.”

“Your testimony today is meaningful and will most likely result in changes from this committee or future legislatures,” she said. “I appreciate your courage and coming forward and speaking with us in person.”

Costello lost her re-election bid earlier this month to Democrat Denny Wells.

Another unidentified 55-year-old ICE detainee submitted an affidavit to the committee with a similar experience of being held in solitary confinement, routinely strip searched and denied access to services including medical care, which resulted in physical and mental health effects.

“Being treated like a criminal is dehumanizing and demoralizing,” they wrote.

Kristine Quint, an immigration attorney with Cascadia Cross Border Law Group who is representing Barreto, told lawmakers she was shocked to learn her clients were strip searched after seeing her. “I find that absolutely abhorrent,” she said.

“I’ve since learned that it’s standard procedure at the ACC for criminal inmates as well,” she said. “Every time there’s a contact visit with an attorney, everybody is strip searched, and it is just so normal that nobody really comments on it anymore.”

“But I do believe it is avoidable, especially when meeting with an attorney to review necessary legal documents,” she added. She said she and Barreto did not get an answer from ACC officials on why he was kept in solitary confinement for so long.

Nicolas Olano, another immigration attorney with the Nations Law Group, told lawmakers strip searches are not standard practice for detainees meeting with their attorneys in other federal immigration facilities.

According to ICE’s policy for standards in non-dedicated facilities, detainees should be searched “in the least intrusive manner as appropriate.” “Absent reasonable suspicion that a detainee is concealing contraband, detainees shall not be strip searched,” it says.

Anchorage Democrat Genevieve Mina asked why ICE detainees in administrative custody for immigration issues appear not to have the same access to basic amenities as prisoners in the general population, and whether Alaska could be held liable for violating state and federal standards.

“My thinking just revolves around this same conversation that we had last summer,” she said. “That No. 1 — the conditions that people have been experiencing are unconstitutional and unjust. But number two, we have a contract with the federal government, and what liability do we risk as a state, knowing that people are still under terrible conditions over a year later? And I want to make sure that we are going to change and we have good state safeguards.”

Challenges to communication between immigration attorneys and clients

Quint testified that it’s difficult for those arrested by ICE in Alaska to contact and hire an immigration attorney, and in turn, it’s logistically difficult for attorneys to reach clients in DOC custody due to constraints to visitation and phone hours. ICE detainees can be transferred quickly out of state with no notice, she said.

“So if I schedule an appointment today to see somebody tomorrow, it’s possible they will be gone, and I won’t actually get in to see them. That’s obviously a huge concern,” she said.

Quint said there’s no public record of how many people have been arrested by ICE in Alaska and not held in DOC custody, but transferred immediately out of state. “I do believe that the number of arrests that are occurring here are probably much higher than we are aware,” she said.

A spokesperson for ICE responded to a request for information about the number of people arrested by ICE in Alaska with a link to a White House dashboard that reports 107 people were arrested in Anchorage from Jan. 2025 to May 2026.

Quint recounted several stories she had heard about from colleagues doing immigration work in Alaska.

“An Indigenous man from Mexico was detained here this summer. He has a wife and child here in Alaska. He was swiftly deported to Mexico and disappeared, and is now presumed dead,” she said.

Quint and other immigration attorneys told the committee that they are filing more habeas corpus petitions to challenge ICE detentions. Additionally, they said a change in August in the immigration court process prohibiting attorneys from representing clients virtually over WebEx video streams is barring Alaska-based attorneys from representing clients detained in Tacoma, Washington. That is the location of the nearest ICE detention facility.

Olano said generally Alaska attorneys now have to turn down clients detained in the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, due to prohibitive costs to fly there to represent them in person.

“It’s extremely unfair in the sense that these people chose their attorney here, they chose him because it was somebody that can contact their family, get the documents needed — work with Kotzebue, work with Juneau, work at a local level to get them out,” he said. “And now they cannot have that.”

Fear of ICE has reverberating effects

Laura Nations, an immigration attorney with the Nations Law Group, said Alaska families are living in fear of ICE, and the effects are reverberating through communities, schools and places of employment, as well as the criminal justice system.

She said that means they aren’t reporting crimes because they are fearful of ICE involvement if they contact the police.

“I have done a lot of work, particularly in the labor trafficking space over the years, and I have seen since January of 2025 a real breakdown in the ability to seek justice for people who have been the victims of crimes,” she said. “And also just the extreme fear that folks in our community and across our state are experiencing that is causing them not to make reports.”

Nations emphasized its a public safety issue for all Alaskans when perpetrators are not held accountable. “When people are not being held accountable for criminal behavior, they continue to do that, and that causes harm beyond just the immediate impact,” she said. “It also makes all of us and everyone in our state less safe.”

People are particularly fearful of traveling and risking arrest at airports, she said, as the U.S. Transportation Security Administration coordinates with ICE and can flag people who have immigration warrants or deportation orders.

“That curtails both obviously personal travel, but also business,” she said. “And those are costs that we are all bearing in various ways because all of those things end up having a ripple effect.”

While the state does not have jurisdiction over federal immigration enforcement, Nations urged lawmakers to take action where the state has authority, including reviewing state cooperative agreements with ICE and ensuring protections of due process rights.

“None of this is inevitable, and we don’t have to bear some of these costs,” she said.

Lawmakers pledge to take legislative action, increase oversight

Members of the House Judiciary Committee from across the political spectrum called the testimony “shocking” and “disturbing” and said legislative action was needed.

Gray, chair of the committee, closed the hearing by outlined some of the policy areas the Legislature could take up beginning in January.

“We need independent routine oversight of conditions for everyone held in state custody,” he said. “Second, we need minimum protections written into statute for civil civil immigration detainees, protecting them from things like unnecessary strip searches.”

Gray said the state should prohibit taking custody of ICE detainees from other states, as DOC officials agreed to do in June 2025. He said Alaska also should follow other states in banning ICE arrests at courthouses, schools and other public facilities.

Additionally, DOC has a Warrant Service Officer Program agreement with ICE, signed in 2020, to deputize correctional officers to serve immigration warrants on people in state custody, prior to their release on state charges. The ACLU of Alaska estimates 31%, or 40 of 130 people have been detained under the agreement since January 2025.

Gray said legislators should review those agreements, “and decide whether or not we should continue any of them.”

In an interview Monday, Gray said there should be accountability for what ICE detainees have endured in Alaska, and he’s hopeful for new leadership under the Kreiss-Tomkins administration.

“My hope for the hearing this close to a new administration coming in, is that whoever comes in knows that this happened, and makes sure that nothing like this ever happens again,” he said. “Look at what has been happening — this is not who we are. We are not going to allow this to happen. We are not going to do this to people.”

title: European court rules against Poland and Latvia over migrant pushbacks at Belarus border
description:
The ruling covers separate cases dating back to 2021, when irregular migrants used by Belarus as a tool of political pressure were intercepted at the border and summarily turned back.
It could set a precedent for similar cases of state-sponsored pressure, such as the mass arrival of irregular migrants in Ceuta from Morocco last July.
The first case concerned two Afghan nationals who crossed the Polish border from Belarus illegally and were left stranded in a makeshift camp on Polish territory between August and October 2021, before being pushed back across the border into Belarus.
In the second, 19 Iraqi nationals of Kurdish origin, including six children, accused Latvia of pushing them back into Belarus after an irregular border crossing in August 2021.
ECHR judgments are legally binding under the Convention, with their implementation overseen by the Council of Europe, a separate organisation from the EU that brings together 46 European countries.
text:
The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) ruled on Tuesday that Polish and Latvian authorities subjected individuals from Afghanistan and Iraq who tried to enter their territory from Belarus to inhuman or degrading treatment, potentially setting a precedent against summary pushbacks by EU countries.

The ruling covers separate cases dating back to 2021, when irregular migrants used by Belarus as a tool of political pressure were intercepted at the border and summarily turned back.

The decision was highly awaited, as it is the first to address the protection of people caught up in the instrumentalisation of migration. It could set a precedent for similar cases of state-sponsored pressure, such as the mass arrival of irregular migrants in Ceuta from Morocco last July.

The first case concerned two Afghan nationals who crossed the Polish border from Belarus illegally and were left stranded in a makeshift camp on Polish territory between August and October 2021, before being pushed back across the border into Belarus.

In the second, 19 Iraqi nationals of Kurdish origin, including six children, accused Latvia of pushing them back into Belarus after an irregular border crossing in August 2021.

Both situations occurred in the context of hostile actions by the Belarusian authorities, described as "instrumentalisation of migration". Minsk had encouraged, facilitated or forced the movement of migrants across its borders with EU countries to destabilise neighbouring states.

The Court held that countries have the right to control the entry of foreign nationals into their territory, and that removing irregular migrants to the instrumentalising state would not, in itself, violate Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment.

However, national authorities must identify people who are particularly vulnerable to ill-treatment, including elderly, disabled or sick individuals, as well as anyone facing a clear and immediate risk of such treatment.

As a result, the court found violations only in the cases of some applicants: one Afghan national who entered Poland, and all the children who crossed into Latvia, along with their accompanying family members.

The Court stated that children must be treated as an extremely vulnerable group with specific needs and therefore cannot be pushed back, even in cases of instrumentalisation.

Another case against Lithuania, concerning four Cuban nationals who repeatedly crossed the Lithuanian-Belarusian border in 2022, was rejected. The Court found no violation of Article 3.

ECHR judgments are legally binding under the Convention, with their implementation overseen by the Council of Europe, a separate organisation from the EU that brings together 46 European countries.

text:
The revelations suggest that the use of Palestinians to shield Israeli troops from potential attacks was not confined to isolated incidents or a single theater of operations. Haaretz called the practice "widespread" at the start of Israel's genocidal assault on Gaza. Accounts from Israeli soldiers, Palestinian survivors, and human rights organizations have repeatedly described a tactic that appears to have become embedded in military operations.

First-hand accounts from IDF troops and veterans, Palestinian survivors, and human rights groups have repeatedly described Israeli soldiers' use of civilians, including women and children, to shield them from potential attacks by Palestinian resistance fighters. For years, the IDF whistleblower group Breaking the Silence has published testimonies from soldiers describing the use of Palestinians to search buildings, tunnels, and suspected explosive sites before Israeli troops entered.

"He's like a dog in Oketz," one Israeli soldier told Breaking the Silence of Palestinians used as human shields, referring to the IDF's canine unit. "He looks for things like explosive devices. If there's one, he'll set it off, and that's how we find out."

"It's terrible, just terrible. I think that's one of the reasons I wanted to speak out," the soldier said. "After I left Gaza, and following conversations with other people, I realized this was a widespread phenomenon—it wasn't happening just in our unit. It became clear to me then that this is a broader pattern, and that it was obvious we weren't the only ones doing this."

Using human shields is prohibited under international humanitarian law, including Article 28 of the Fourth Geneva Convention and Article 51(7) of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions. The practice is a war crime under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court. It was also outlawed by Israel's Supreme Court in 2005 in an explicit repudiation of the erstwhile long-standing practice.

While Israel and its supporters often accuse Palestinian resistance groups including Hamas—which led the October 2023 attack on Israel—of using human shields, United Nations investigators and international human rights groups have found little evidence that Palestinians are intentionally doing so.

Meanwhile, a May 2025 Associated Press investigation found that Israeli soldiers had systematically used Palestinian civilians as human shields in Gaza, citing survivors of the practice and Israeli military personnel. One Israeli officer told the AP that by the end of his nine-month deployment, nearly every infantry unit was using Palestinians to clear buildings before troops entered.

"Once this idea was initiated, it caught on like fire in a field," the officer said. "People saw how effective and easy it was."

Dubbed the "mosquito protocol," the practice involved forcing detained Palestinians to enter potentially booby-trapped buildings and tunnels ahead of Israeli soldiers. Some were dressed in IDF uniforms, fitted with cameras, bound, and threatened with death if they refused.

In one case, a Palestinian man said Israeli soldiers attached a camera to his forehead and forced him to enter homes to check for explosives and Palestinian fighters. He was passed between military units for more than two weeks, spending nights bound in a dark room before being sent out again.

"These are not isolated accounts," Breaking the Silence executive director Nadav Weiman told the AP. "They point to a systemic failure and a horrifying moral collapse."

Haaretz has also reported testimony from Israeli soldiers indicating that commanders knew about the practice. One soldier said that after seeing Al Jazeera footage documenting the use of Palestinians as human shields, he recognized the tactic immediately.

"There's pride in it," another soldier reportedly said, while describing the attitude among troops toward using Palestinians to protect Israeli personnel.

Women, children, and elders have not been spared from the practice.

In the occupied West Bank, Palestinian mother Hazar Estity told the AP that Israeli soldiers took her from her home in the Jenin refugee camp in November 2024 and forced her to enter and photograph apartments before troops went inside.

Estity pleaded with soldiers to let her return to her 21-month-old son, but they refused.

"I was most afraid that they would kill me," she told the AP. "And that I wouldn't see my son again."

Multiple IDF soldiers told Israeli investigative journalist Illy Pe'ery last year about an incident in which "a senior officer in the Israeli army’s Nahal Brigade tied an explosive cord around the neck of an 80-year-old Palestinian man and forced him to serve as a human shield, ordering him to scout out abandoned houses under threat of having his head blown off."

"After he had served this purpose, the soldiers ordered the man to flee with his wife, but upon being spotted by another battalion, they were both shot dead on the spot," Pe'ery wrote.

Defense for Children International-Palestine has documented Israeli forces using Palestinian children as human shields, including forcing minors to walk ahead of soldiers during dangerous military raids.

Accountability has remained extraordinarily limited. According to Haaretz, none of the soldiers implicated in the 16 investigations opened since October 2023 have been prosecuted.

Israeli soldiers who have confronted superior officers about using human shields say they have been rebuffed.

“We talked to our commander, and we asked him to stop doing it,” one soldier told CBS News last year, “but we were ordered to continue. He told us it was policy.”

“It's fucked up, you know," he added, "to use citizens as your human shield like a dog.”

DAWN and Taxpayers Alliance Against Genocide (TAAG) sued over Trump's February 2025 Executive Order 14203, which allows sanctions against foreigners who support ICC probes into US and Israeli nationals, and bars the provision or receipt of "services by, to, or for the benefit of" a targeted entity or person.

Under the order, the administration has sanctioned the ICC as well as its prosecutors and judges; the groups Al-Haq, al-Mezan, and the Palestinian Center for Human Rights (PCHR); and Francesca Albanese, the UN special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Palestinian Territory occupied since 1967.

Last month, Judge Jesse Furman, appointed to the Southern District of New York by former President Barack Obama, found that the "services" ban violates the First Amendment to the US Constitution and blocked the Trump administration from enforcing that prohibition against DAWN and TAAG—which convinced the judge to expand his injunction on Monday.

"The court holds that plaintiffs are entitled to an injunction that bars enforcement of the services prohibition against anyone who provides or receives speech-based services, thereby engaging in First Amendment-protected speech and association," Furman wrote, noting that the government tried to use a 2025 US Supreme Court decision to prevent the expansion.

In Trump v. CASA, the majority "held that a federal court generally may grant injunctive relief only to the parties before it," but that "does not necessarily overrule its earlier precedents approving of broader injunctions where, as here, a First Amendment facial overbreadth challenge succeeds," the judge explained.

Earlier this month, after Furman's first ruling, TAAG held a press conference during which American taxpayers, including human rights activists and lawyers, formally submitted video footage, firsthand eyewitness accounts, and other evidence to the ICC, and called on the court to issue arrest warrants for Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and other top US officials over their alleged complicity in Israel's ongoing genocide in the Gaza Strip.

"We challenged Trump's executive order on the ICC because we refused to let his regime intimidate us into silence while it used our tax dollars to fund crimes against humanity," Anna Marie Stenberg of TAAG said Tuesday. "This victory means that others can join us in challenging these crimes without fear of punishment for exercising their First Amendment rights."

"Ordinary people have a right to seek justice, and our government cannot take that right away," she added. "We must always stand up to a bully!"

DAWN said Tuesday that it will "hold a press conference in The Hague on December 1, 2026 to announce its next steps as ICC member states meet there under a US ultimatum to rein in the court."

Whitehouse, Heinrich, and other supporters of the bill have argued the legislation, which passed in the Senate last week with 15 members of the Democratic caucus joining 47 Republicans in approving it, would speed the construction of renewable energy infrastructure.

The bill would limit federal courts' authority to block a variety of energy projects due to environmental protections, and could stop future administrations from rolling back approvals of projects that have previously been permitted. BAAJA could potentially speed up the modernization of electric grids and transmission lines for solar and wind energy projects.

But with international climate experts warning in recent months that continued fossil fuel emissions have all but eliminated the possibility of avoiding a global temperature rise surpassing 1.5°C over preindustrial levels—and more of the catastrophic, deadly extreme weather that such warming causes—the climate scientists emphasized on Monday that the benefits to renewable energy industries won't outweigh the dangers embedded in the bill, which would also speed up approvals for oil and gas projects and pollution-causing data centers.

The bill would "prevent the rapid and nearly total phaseout of coal, oil, and fossil gas from the US and global energy systems," reads the letter. "Without this phaseout, and the subsequent reduction of emissions to (net) zero, the world will be unable to halt global heating. BAAJA represents a step away from the transition to a (net) zero economy."

The scientists noted that under the "Disparate Treatment" standard in the bill, which creates a right for developers to challenge project delays and denials, "even if Congress passes climate legislation in the future, fossil-energy companies can sue federal agencies and win the full cost of their projects, plus attorney fees and economic damages," to be paid with public funds.

"This means that agencies may be required, by law, to continue permitting fossil fuel projects, lest they be sued and the government be subject to massive penalties," wrote the scientists, including Michal Mann of the University of Pennsylvania, Michal Oppenheimer of Princeton University, and J. Timmons Roberts of Brown University. "This Disparate Treatment standard will be, moreover, measured against the collective decisions of six years of the Trump administrations and four of the Biden administration, when clean energy met new demand but did not yet replace fossil energy."

The legislation, therefore, would create "a regulatory regime that makes the current balance of energy sources permanent" and "runs counter to what science shows we need to do to resolve climate change."

Along with climate scientists, energy experts have acknowledged in recent years that the world must transition away from fossil fuels to avoid the worst impacts of planetary heating, which has already been linked to deadly heatwaves, flooding, and wildfires.

The scientists questioned an analysis frequently cited by proponents of BAAJA, in which the Rhodium Group projected that the legislation could prevent up to 1.5 billion metric tons of US emissions through 2040.

"But that represents roughly 1/36th of current annual emissions, a tiny fraction of the reductions we need to achieve (net) zero emissions," they wrote. "In Rhodium’s high-emissions scenario US emissions rise between 2033-2040."

"Moreover, the Rhodium Group estimate is based primarily on the transmission provisions of BAAJA, and does not take into account what the bill does to the [National Environmental Policy Act] and other environmental laws," the scientists added, referring to the bill's exemptions for projects including pipeline expansions from environmental reviews.

The experts urged members of Congress to instead consider modeling from Purdue University engineering professor Kevin Kirchner, who found "that BAAJA likely increases domestic greenhouse gas emissions outright and also increases domestic mortality attributable to air pollution," and a report from Columbia University’s Center for Global Energy Policy, which warned that "the emissions effects of the bill are 'highly uncertain.'"

"It is our opinion as climate and Earth scientists that, even if BAAJA reduced emissions to the degree modeled above, those reductions would not offset the bill’s codifying of coal, oil, and natural gas in the US energy mix," the experts said. "Even reduced emissions continue to make global warming worse so long as they are ongoing."

In recent weeks, journalist and lawyer Aaron Regunberg said, the public has heard "lots of back-and-forth about whether BAAJA, backed by both the clean energy industry and Big Oil, is good or bad for climate."

"Climate scientists just weighed in with a very loud 'BAD,'" he said.
