Reich argued that primarily, Trump’s push to restore Huang as CEO of the chipmaking giant despite an embarrassing scandal regarding an extramarital affair, which raised questions about possible export violations and risks to US national security, “was because of money.”

"[Artificial intelligence] is too important to the US stock market and, evidently, Huang is too important to AI," Reich said. "And Nvidia has become too important an ally to the Trump regime."

Trump personally stood to benefit from his intervention to protect Huang. The CEO is a close personal friend and ally of the president, and as Nvidia shares rebounded Monday, Trump made up to $15 million on his holdings in the company. Since Huang gained White House access near the start of Trump's term in January 2025, CNBC has reported, accounts connected to the president have traded up to $97.5 million in the company's shares.

But Huang's fate also had dramatic implications for the entire stock market. In October, before the Huang scandal broke, Nvidia alone accounted for an astonishing 8% of the S&P 500—an index that underpins the personal accounts and retirement plans of tens of millions of Americans.

University of Michigan economist Justin Wolfers estimated that the initial fallout from the revelation of Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy wiped out roughly $240 billion in American household wealth—equivalent to nearly $2,000 per household—even before the chipmaker's stock suffered its most dramatic losses.

In all, the Financial Times reported that as of Friday, before Trump sprang into action to restore Huang to his throne, the company had shed $1.5 trillion in market value. Applying the rough assumption Wolfers used for the initial decline would put the corresponding US household loss at about $1.2 trillion—or roughly $9,200 per household—within less than two weeks.

By the time markets closed Monday, after Trump directly intervened to pressure Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang and heavily implied he'd be protected from prosecution for possible export-control violations, the company regained $952 billion in market value, with shares surging over 31%—marking the largest single-day market cap gain on record for a US company.

"Do you see the problem here?" Reich said. "There are no rules, no standards, no accountability, no protections for the public. There are just stock prices, quid pro quos, and elite impunity."

Axios political reporter Zachary Basu on Tuesday described Trump's extraordinary intervention as "a de facto bailout of the AI industry." It was reportedly conceptualized that way within the president's inner circle, according to one source, who told the outlet that "Jensen is too big to fail."

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said the upheaval caused by Huang's improprieties provided a preview of the disaster that could befall the country if AI-linked companies—which together now account for nearly half of the S&P 500's market value, according to JPMorgan—were to suffer a crash. He said the companies' executives, who command personal fortunes of over a trillion dollars collectively, must be held responsible, not taxpayers.

“We have an extremely volatile economy and a stock market that is increasingly dependent on the whims of a handful of Big Tech oligarchs who have bet trillions of dollars on artificial intelligence,” Sanders wrote on social media Tuesday.

In the case of Huang, he said, "The fate of one man caused the stock market to lose and then regain trillions of dollars in value," but "it's not just Nvidia."

"One day, the value of Anthropic, a company that has never made a profit and is deeply in debt, skyrockets to over $2 trillion. The next day, the value of that same company is cut by more than a quarter based on Wall Street fears that its massive debt will be rated as junk," he said, describing the wild swings in the AI company’s valuation following its stock market debut last week.

"What will happen tomorrow? Nobody knows," said Sanders, who has introduced legislation calling for broad government intervention to regulate the breakneck development of AI and a ban on so-called "superintelligent" models that can outperform human intelligence.

"One thing must be made certain: If the AI bubble bursts, taxpayers will not bail out Big Tech oligarchs," the senator added. "Not tomorrow. Not next year. Not ever."

“If AI companies fail, Big Tech oligarchs must bail them out, not taxpayers,” he said. “Our message to these multi-billionaires is simple: If you take out a loan, pay it back. Don’t come begging to taxpayers to bail you out.”

“We hold the [Israeli] occupation fully and directly responsible for the epidemic outbreak," the ministry said.

Bahaa al-Sous, the father of newborn twin girls, told The New Arab Tuesday that he had discovered his daughter Ilat was sick 10 days ago after the storm.

Nvidia's stock price surged more than 30% on Monday after news of Huang's reinstatement broke. The news also sparked a broad share price rally in the tech sector, which had sold off sharply in the wake of Huang's exit and amid news that the semiconductor giant was facing a Securities and Exchange Commission probe over its accounting practices.

The Financial Times, which first reported Trump's $15 million estimated gain from the Nvidia rally, noted that Trump "applied pressure" to the corporation's board over the weekend "after watching what was once America’s most valuable company as well as the wider tech sector hemorrhage value last week."

"Just to be clear: the president of the United States called into a private company’s board meeting and pressured them into reinstating a fired CEO whose actions his own government is investigating, and personally made 15 million dollars in the process," wrote Zeteo's Mehdi Hasan in response to FT's reporting. "In any other era, a monumental political scandal for the president. But not in ours, apparently."

Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) called Trump's intervention "psychotically crooked," arguing that the president once again put "private gain above the national interest."

"He is attempting to grant functional immunity to Nvidia and declare Huang 'exonerated' even though ongoing investigations continue to reveal national security risks and a seeming contempt for the law," Beyer wrote. "And the leaders of the tech industry are all too eager to exploit Trump's corruption for their own ends, regardless of the consequences."

A BBC analysis of Trump's financial disclosures for the last two years found that the president's investment accounts "purchased shares of Nvidia worth between $23 million and $86 million," and that "he has bought Nvidia stock 85 separate times through a number of investment accounts."

"Trump has also sold some of his stake in Nvidia since returning to the presidency," BBC added. "Over 19 sales, Trump gained between $3.5 million and $10.2 million, according to his government disclosures."

"We need to investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement," US Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) said on Monday. "This White House is the most corrupt in history."

“We are mindful of the very real risks presented by the Army’s planned detonation,” the judges wrote in their ruling. “However, we must acknowledge the realities of the situation: The degraded explosives present a risk of an uncontrolled and unplanned explosion," unless they are destroyed.

The decision followed a legal challenge by Earthjustice on behalf of the Iowa Environmental Council and the state chapter of the Sierra Club that argued that the federal government had failed to adequately consider alternatives to the detonation and protect public health.

The US Army is set to detonate 68 drums containing approximately 9,773 pounds of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near Middletown on Wednesday.

Lead azide is a highly sensitive explosive used in the manufacture of ammunition and other military munitions. The material became increasingly unstable after water evaporated from its storage containers, allowing crystals to form. An April inspection reportedly found crystallization on 58 of the 68 drums.

Army officials contend that moving or chemically treating the deteriorating explosives might trigger an accidental explosion that could kill or wound workers and people nearby. They argue that a controlled detonation under carefully selected weather conditions is the least dangerous option.

However, green groups warn that the consequences could extend far beyond the immediate blast site. Earthjustice said the lead plume could travel up to 100 miles from ground zero, depending on the weather.

“The EPA itself admits that there is no safe level of lead exposure for humans,” said Michael Schmidt, general counsel for the Iowa Environmental Council, when the lawsuit was announced.

Iowa's Department of Health and Human Services acknowledges that the explosion will create a dust plume containing lead particles that could travel beyond the military installation and settle on surrounding surfaces. The agency warned of two main exposure pathways: inhalation of airborne lead particles and ingesting or even touching contaminated dust deposited on soil, playgrounds, vehicles, buildings, and other surfaces.

Children and pregnant women are particularly vulnerable. Lead exposure can cause serious neurological and developmental damage, including impaired brain development in children. Unlike some airborne pollutants, lead deposited on farmland, soil, and household surfaces can remain a source of exposure long after the initial explosion.

State health officials have told residents in potentially affected areas to stay indoors, keep their windows and doors shut for 24 to 48 hours, use indoor air filtration, and wet-clean potentially contaminated surfaces after the airborne exposure period ends.

In addition to environmental groups, elected officials from around the region vehemently oppose the planned detonation.

"The Army still has failed to explain to the public why this detonation needs to happen this way—and too many people fear for their family’s health and safety," Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), an Army veteran, said Sunday on social media. "This is an extreme failure of communication, planning, and leadership. And they must be held accountable for the harm done."

Earlier Monday, Trump said he had ordered the Army to hold off on the detonation until the Eighth Circuit ruled on the matter, and made the operation contingent on approval from Democratic sIowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand.

The president said on his Truth Social platform that if the court gave the green light, "we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and long-term, situation."

Sand stated that the Trump administration should be the one to "make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago."

Area residents, including many farmers, are scrambling to protect their families, homes, fields, and livestock.

"We’re feeling less confident that anybody knows what they’re doing,” retired school teacher Jim Plate, who lives with his wife Krys Plate two miles south of the Army installation, told The New York Times. “We’re getting very frustrated by whatever the heck is going on.”

Krys Plate said that she is "terrified."

"Everybody knows," she told the Times, "that the acceptable level of lead is zero."

text:
A father and daughter detained by masked immigration officers on an airport jet bridge in Seattle, causing chaos in front of other passengers, were heading to a family baptism ceremony in California, their lawyer said Sunday.

Other passengers boarding the Alaska Airlines flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday used their cellphones to film the father and daughter being detained by the officers, who were wearing unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The recordings were widely viewed on social media.

The videos show the officers struggling with someone on the ground. The flight, bound for Los Angeles, was delayed.

The father and daughter were traveling to attend a baptism ceremony in California and are seeking asylum in the U.S., where they have lived since 2015, their lawyer, Olia Catala, told The Associated Press in a telephone interview. They have no criminal record, Catala said.

“They’ve done everything correctly, and these are educated people,” Catala said of the father and daughter. “She went to college, to university, she worked for a nonprofit. No criminal history (for) any of them. So it’s just heartbreaking.”

Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers detained Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who it said had overstayed his visa “in violation of our nation’s laws.”

During the confrontation, another passenger “hurled hot coffee on the officers,” the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the U.S. illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

Mejia, in her mid-20s, had married a U.S. citizen and filed paperwork for adjustment of her status, her attorney said. Mejia’s husband was accompanying Mejia and her father when they were detained Saturday, Catala added. The husband was not detained, the attorney said.

Both were being held at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Catala said.

She said Mejia was carrying a cup of coffee when the confrontation occurred.

“When somebody’s charging at you, you’re going to drop a cup of coffee,” Catala said.

“It was just a lot of commotion, and honestly, if somebody is running at you or charging at you and they’re not wearing a uniform, you don’t know who they are,” Catala said. ”There was a lot of panic, chaos, not knowing what’s going on.”

“They just lunged forward. They didn’t identify themselves and then sort of hit this family from behind,” John Gaedeke, who was in line waiting to board the flight and filmed part of the confrontation on his cellphone, said of the officers.

Gaedeke said passengers on the jet bridge were screaming or crying “because it was just so emotional, and just to see the pain and anguish and then the speed and violence with which it happened.”

Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people it says have overstayed visas.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns “directly with the appropriate authorities.”

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would “engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred.”

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE’s tactics were “deeply un-American” and called for the agency’s abolition.

“The video is horrific and it is chilling,” Ferguson said at a news conference Saturday with labor leaders and local elected officials.

title: “Only Path Forward Is to Abolish”: Outcry After Masked ICE Agents Arrest Family at Seattle Airport
description:
SOFIA LARRONDO HERNANDEZ MEJIA: Sofia Larrondo.
SOFIA LARRONDO HERNANDEZ MEJIA: We have a work permit.
AMY GOODMAN: Both Alaska Airlines and the Port of Seattle said ICE agents carried out the operation without their participation or knowledge.
This is one of, unfortunately, many thousands of detentions that is happening not only in Washington state, but across the country.
We see that this is not the first time that ICE agents have shown up unannounced to Sea-Tac Airport, as well as other airports across the country.
text:
AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan González.

In Washington state, Democratic officials have denounced federal immigration agents after they were filmed violently arresting a father and his daughter boarding a flight at the Seattle-area airport, known as Sea-Tac, on Saturday. Video of the arrests shows ICE officers holding down a passenger and dragging her through the door of an Alaska Airlines jet bridge, which — while she screams loudly. Another passenger who tries to intervene is shoved by a masked officer.

SOFIA LARRONDO HERNANDEZ MEJIA: No! No!

ICE AGENT 1: Hey! Hey! You’re coming with us!

ICE AGENT 2: Get back.

PASSENGER 1: What’s your name?

SOFIA LARRONDO HERNANDEZ MEJIA: Sofia Larrondo. I’m getting arrested by ICE.

ICE AGENT 2: Come on. Get back.

PASSENGER 2: What is your name?

SOFIA LARRONDO HERNANDEZ MEJIA: We are Americans.

PASSENGER 1: Identify yourselves!

SOFIA LARRONDO HERNANDEZ MEJIA: We have a work permit.

ICE AGENT 2: ICE.

SOFIA LARRONDO HERNANDEZ MEJIA: We have a work permit.

AMY GOODMAN: Both Alaska Airlines and the Port of Seattle said ICE agents carried out the operation without their participation or knowledge. At least two people were arrested: Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza and his daughter, Sofia Hernandez Mejia. The father and daughter don’t have criminal records. ICE later said that Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, who’s originally from Mexico, was targeted for overstaying his tourist visa. ICE said the daughter would be charged with assault for allegedly throwing hot coffee at an agent. Witnesses say the coffee went flying after agents, who were dressed in plainclothes, lunged at the family from behind without identifying themselves. Sofia Hernandez Mejia has been in the U.S. since she was 14 years old and is married to a U.S. citizen. The father and daughter are now being held at Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma.

Washington Governor Bob Ferguson spoke hours after their arrests on Saturday.

GOV. BOB FERGUSON: Look, ICE is completely and totally out of control. And today we are confronted with yet more evidence of this. The video is horrific, and it is chilling. Masked agents, who do not identify themselves, drag screaming individuals off a jetway as they’re about to do something very ordinary in our country: board a flight. There is no justification for this brutality. I spoke a couple hours ago with representatives from Alaska Airlines. I made my view very clear to Alaska Airlines. They need to call on ICE to get out of our airports.

SUPPORTER: That’s right. That’s right.

GOV. BOB FERGUSON: I’ll be making that request — I’ll be making that request of every other airline that operates in Sea-Tac Airport, as well. They need to — they need to speak up. … It is time to abolish Donald Trump’s ICE. It’s time. It is — it is beyond — it is beyond changing a culture. OK? The culture of ICE is bankrupt. It lacks morals. It lacks any decency. It is un-American.

AMY GOODMAN: Well, for more, we go to Seattle, Washington, where we’re joined by Josefina Mora-Cheung, director of organizing for La Resistencia.

Josefina, thank you so much for being with us. Can you explain what we just watched on this video that has horrified the nation, to say the least, also traumatized not only the passengers, but the whole flight crew, which had to be delayed because they were so upset.

JOSEFINA MORA-CHEUNG: Good morning, Amy. Thank you for having me.

Unfortunately, as you mentioned, it is a really horrific and heartbreaking video to watch. We see that two people are dragged away from the jet bridge, and, in that, causes chaos, in order to be able to have people around understanding what is going on. As you mentioned, they are unidentified agents. They were also wearing masks, which is against Washington state law. And, you know, we see that people — the evidence that came out of this was really documented by the community members. We’re at a point in which community members are now training and being the bystanders to know what happens in this situation, because it’s so commonplace.

This is one of, unfortunately, many thousands of detentions that is happening not only in Washington state, but across the country. And this is one of the very, you know, extreme examples that has not only happened this year, but has happened in many years previous. And we see this as a very clear escalation and continued violence that is being perpetuated on our immigrant communities by ICE. And it’s only a glimpse of the violence that we are able to see in the public that happens behind closed doors in places like where Ricardo and Sofia are detained currently, at the Northwest ICE Processing Center.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: But, Josefina, I wanted to ask you about this whole issue of what local authorities can do in situations like this, because, clearly, if these agents got to actually the spot where passengers were boarding the flight, they must have passed through Alaska Airlines checkpoints. And also, how much control can local authorities have, given the fact that federal agencies, like the TSA and U.S. Customs, are so present at every airport and don’t have to necessarily listen to local agents, local law enforcement?

JOSEFINA MORA-CHEUNG: That’s right. We see that this is not the first time that ICE agents have shown up unannounced to Sea-Tac Airport, as well as other airports across the country. But the airlines and, you know, the agencies at the airports have responsibilities to maintain passenger safety. As we see in that particular video, not only were the people that were kidnapped violently detained, but in addition there was bystanders that were very violently shoved.

Again, this is a clear example that there is no kind of accountability, and that ICE is incredibly emboldened under this new administration to have free rein over our communities. And if this continues to happen, this is a clear example that the only path forward is to abolish ICE. Governor Ferguson of Washington state has called for ICE to get out of Sea-Tac Airport, but that should extend to all airports in Washington, including the airport where deportation flights happen, at King County Airport in Seattle.

AMY GOODMAN: Earlier this month, the Government Accountability Office, or GAO, released a report titled “Immigration Detention: ICE Should Determine Cost Effectiveness of New Initiatives Before Continuing.” It found ICE wasted, to say the least, millions of taxpayer dollars in its rush to expand detention capacity significantly, to say the least, overpaying for warehouses. On Saturday, The Seattle Times ran a piece headlined “Congrats, you paid Manhattan prices for a jail on the Tacoma Tideflats.” The article notes, quote, “the federal government’s purchase of the immigration detention center in Tacoma this past week defies economic gravity. The Department of Homeland Security paid more than six times the assessed value for the Northwest ICE Processing Center, a [more than 1,600-bed] immigrant detention center. At $453 million, it’s believed to be the largest real estate transaction by dollar value in Pierce County history.” GEO Group — that’s what the article said — expects to make $340 million from the sale after taxes and fees. And we’re seeing this across the country, paying many times more than originally even these for-profit prison companies asked. Where is this money going? And talk about what’s happened in Tacoma.

JOSEFINA MORA-CHEUNG: Well, so much of this money, you know, is being pocketed by GEO, as has been mentioned. And one of the really big concerns, as well, is that these sales are not shocking, but the shocking part is that many of it has to do with trying to skirt accountability on a state law level. The Northwest Detention Center, the Northwest ICE Processing Center, has been involved in various litigations. GEO Group is still in litigation with Washington state over their dollar-a-day program, work program that they used to have for almost 10 years now, and has recently been involved with the Washington state Department of Health on denying inspections of the facility, after a state law was passed in 2023. So, it’s clear that although ICE has the budget to make these, you know, wild purchases, it is also in great part to avoid accountability in places like Washington, where groups like La Resistencia have been pushing for much stricter regulations and accountability at levels that we don’t get on a federal level.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: Well, Representative Pramila Jayapal has criticized the failure of accountability for these private detention corporations. There’s been 62 immigrants who have died in detention under GEO Group and CoreCivic. What kind of accountability have you seen?

JOSEFINA MORA-CHEUNG: Very little, very little accountability. Here in Washington in the Northwest ICE Processing Center, we’ve seen at least three deaths since 2018, and two of those happened nearly back to back in 2024. Very little actual accountability or answers came from either ICE or our congressional representatives, who were not able to stand up against these deaths that happened.

And so, you know, the accountability doesn’t just come from ICE or at the federal level, but our congressional delegation also has a huge responsibility to play. Especially as we see this new, quote-unquote, “Democratic blue wave,” it is incredibly important that these representatives are able to follow through with what voters expect, which has been bigger calls to abolish ICE and end this incarceration system for immigrants across the country, not only here in Washington.

AMY GOODMAN: Josefina Mora-Cheung, I want to thank you so much for being with us, Josefina, director of organizing for La Resistencia. We’re going to do an interview with you in Spanish after the broadcast, post it at democracynow.org.

But coming up, we’re going to look at the movement to free jailed immigrants who went on hunger strike on this side of the country, at Delaney Hall in New Jersey, the ICE jail there, owned by GEO Group. We’ll hear exclusive audio from one of the hunger strikers who remains locked up. Back in 15 seconds.

text:
Why It Matters

The House Committee on Homeland Security's Nov. 18 hearing, Worldwide Threats to the Homeland: 25 Years After 9/11, turned into an oversight fight over administration conduct as Democrats pressed three Trump administration officials on outages, immigration enforcement and domestic terrorism. ​

Witnesses defended the administration's record, with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin telling the panel, "I paid for it personally," when challenged over a government flight to a football game. For lobbyists and congressional staff, the exchanges preview the oversight the committee's ranking member said Democrats will pursue when they take control of the House in January.

The Big Picture

The committee scheduled the hearing as its annual threat review, marking 25 years since 9/11. Events in the preceding days shifted its focus: PBS NewsHour reported on flight delays, website outages and concerns about a possible Iranian dirty-bomb plot, and lawmakers questioned officials about all three.

Committee Chair Rep. Andrew Garbarino (R-NY) presided. He said Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director Kash Patel did not appear despite his office being notified in August. FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia testified instead. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton was the third witness.

The administration's May 6 counterterrorism strategy, as Reuters reported, prioritizes threats in the Western Hemisphere, including cartels. The committee held previous Worldwide Threats hearings on Nov. 20, 2024, and Dec. 11, 2025.

What They're Saying

One of the sharpest exchanges came when Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-MS), the ranking member, asked Raia to name a right-wing organization that meets the FBI's criteria for domestic terrorism. "Just name one," Thompson said. Raia named 764 and Antifa, then said the FBI does not deal in organizations but "the people in those organizations."

Thompson opened by accusing administration officials of having "weaponized DHS." Mullin said DHS had answered 21 of 36 letters from Thompson's office. Asked whether the president directed FBI investigations, Raia answered, "Absolutely not."

Rep. Seth Magaziner (D-RI) asked whether every immigration agent deployed in the field had completed a background check. Mullin said yes, adding that those without one were on administrative leave. Asked how many untrained agents had been deployed, he said he would "have to get back to you."

Rep. Dan Goldman (D-NY) pressed Clayton on whether internal upgrades caused an outage. Clayton said there was "no indication" of state-sponsored actors. Goldman replied that Clayton was "clearly not answering." Rep. LaMonica McIver (D-NJ) told Mullin, "You are killing people," during an exchange over deaths in immigration custody at Delaney Hall. Mullin responded, "That's your opinion."

Political Stakes

Mullin faced questions from Thompson about a government flight and a visit to a company's suite at a football game. The company held a $2.2 billion DHS contract, according to Thompson. Mullin said he reimbursed the government for travel. Thompson closed by saying "Accountability is coming" once Democrats take control of the House in January.

Clayton and Raia advocated for the reauthorization of Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act. Clayton said the surveillance authority "should not expire" and that more than 60% of critical information in the president's daily brief comes from it. Raia said the FBI "fully supports" the president's request to reauthorize it. Rep. Michael McCaul (R-TX), speaking at his final hearing, called failure to reauthorize the provision "political malpractice."

The Bottom Line

No follow-up hearing has been announced. Mullin agreed to provide figures he did not have, including statistics on immigration agent training and hiring at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). He also said he hopes the Senate confirms the agency's director.

Thompson's pledge to intensify oversight in January and the administration's push to reauthorize Section 702 emerged as two issues for the incoming Congress.

title: Immigration Is Not a Fringe Issue - Yahoo
description:
As if one were a political liability and the other a path back to working families.
Voters rejected an administration whose immigration policies have made life more expensive and less secure for working families.
And in the last two years, 60 people have died in immigration enforcement custody or encounters, according to The Guardian.
An investigation by ProPublica revealed that more than 500 U.S. citizens have been caught up in immigration enforcement practices.
Strongly worded letters, congressional investigations, and modest cuts to immigration enforcement funding will not be enough in this new Congress.
text:
At a Senate forum on ICE violence, I listened to the sons of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo describe the morning their father was shot dead by ICE agents while on his way to work. Besides them sat and wept the families of Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti.

Next to me were clergy wearing t-shirts that said "Connected Americans" and whispering prayers as they listened to the testimony of families whose loved ones had been killed in the streets. While a number of elected officials sat in the front of the room, they were not the center. The families and those of us there to bear witness were.

The demands made that day by people like Lorenzo's sons were not unfamiliar to me. They're the demands I hear from people every day: swift justice that remedies what our communities have been forced to endure and a future where all working people can live with safety, stability, and dignity. It takes courage to speak out when your voice breaks. These families did it anyway.

Meanwhile, throughout the midterms, Democratic candidates were advised by centrist think tanks and commentators to talk less about immigration and more about the economy. As if one were a political liability and the other a path back to working families. No one in that Senate room was living a separate problem.

The failure of both Democrats and Republicans to deliver a path to citizenship has pushed economic security further out of reach for working people, leaving millions of workers vulnerable to deportation, family separation, and a future defined by instability and uncertainty. Multiply that across every workplace where someone has been killed, detained, deported, or stripped of their ability to work, and the consequences are anything but abstract. They affect us all. Immigrants sustain the industries, workplaces, and communities we all depend on. And those who insist we must choose between a path to citizenship or supporting working families have yet to stand with the families bearing the cost of that false choice.

The midterm results should make it impossible to ignore the truth: there is no such thing as a functioning economy for working people without immigrants. Voters rejected an administration whose immigration policies have made life more expensive and less secure for working families. Even the President admitted what those families already knew. In an interview with 60 Minutes, Donald Trump said that his mass deportations "might have been too tough," costing both him and Republicans control of Congress. "I get hurt because we also took people who had good jobs."

Soon after the episode aired, Trump named Stephen Miller, the central architect of the deadly raids, family separations, and mass deportations, as his next White House Chief of Staff. A president who acknowledges the cost of mass deportations went on to promote the man who built it. This is a warning to every member of the incoming Congress, newly elected and returning: the election did not end this fight. It's likely they will escalate it. We will be organizing so that Members of Congress defend the people they were elected to represent.

What Americans are up against is formidable. The numbers describe the mass deportation machinery Congress has helped fund. ICE's detention population grew by more than 70% between January 2025 and April 2026. Congress still approved approximately $75 billion in additional ICE funding, including $45 billion for immigration detention, despite polling showing that 58% of Americans believe ICE's enforcement actions have gone too far. And in the last two years, 60 people have died in immigration enforcement custody or encounters, according to The Guardian.

The harm does not stop with immigrants. An investigation by ProPublica revealed that more than 500 U.S. citizens have been caught up in immigration enforcement practices. Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti amongst them. Our broken, violent immigration system impacts neighborhoods, workplaces, and families across the country. No one is left out of its reach. And our economy suffers when the millions of working people whose labor helps sustain it are left vulnerable without a path to citizenship.

My home state of Texas shows what it looks like when a candidate refuses to treat immigration, human rights, and the economy as separate issues. Salgado Araujo lived and worked in Texas for 35 years, putting his three sons through college as a proud, hardworking father. As James Talarico campaigned for his Senate seat, he spoke of his death and committed to ICE accountability and citizenship. Four months to the day after the shooting, the now senator-elect visited Salgado's memorial in Houston, pledging to seek justice and adding his "I voted" sticker, alongside many other fellow Texans, to the memorial site where Salgado Araujo was shot and killed.

The sticker can be seen as a promise; an oath to use every tool available to protect communities against the terror that has stolen the lives of fathers, mothers, workers, and loved ones across our communities. The organizers, voters, community leaders, and ordinary Americans who made it possible for Talarico to win are now watching whether he and other newly-elected Members of Congress will honor that oath in January.

Strongly worded letters, congressional investigations, and modest cuts to immigration enforcement funding will not be enough in this new Congress. Democrats must pursue a fundamental change in direction, starting with a pathway to citizenship and ensuring immigrants are protected in every legislative priority the new Congress advances.

Voters want leaders willing to confront an enforcement agenda that is tearing families apart, destabilizing workplaces, and wasting billions of their taxpayer dollars, while they're left struggling simply to make ends meet. And they want leaders who understand that protecting immigrant workers is essential to building an economy that works for everyone.

Electoral wins alone will not protect the millions of people—both citizens and immigrants—whose livelihoods and futures remain at risk. We cannot afford another Congress that recognizes the issue but fails to deliver a solution.

Voters, especially Black, Latino, young, and working-class people, have done their part by rejecting Trump's agenda at the ballot box. Now Democrats must do theirs. With Stephen Miller's ability to escalate the administration's cruelty, the incoming Congress cannot settle for symbolic resistance or half measures. A pathway to citizenship is the floor of what Congress must deliver. Millions of working people will be organizing to make it so, because the people we love belong here for good.

description:
California, along with 21 other states and Washington D.C., filed a lawsuit on Monday challenging a Trump administration rule that would bar tens of thousands of low-income households from receiving federal housing assistance, including more than 7,000 in California.
The new rule would terminate aid for all of these households on Dec.14.
Undocumented immigrants have been banned from receiving federal housing subsidies for decades.
“California won’t stand idly by while the Trump administration forces families to choose between staying together and keeping a roof over their heads,” said Attorney General Rob Bonta in a press conference announcing the suit.
They also warn that housing agencies will be squeezed financially as they evict lower-cost mixed status households and replace them with households entitled to full benefits.
text:
By Ben Christopher, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California, along with 21 other states and Washington D.C., filed a lawsuit on Monday challenging a Trump administration rule that would bar tens of thousands of low-income households from receiving federal housing assistance, including more than 7,000 in California.

Earlier this month the Trump administration finalized a rule to bar all households with “mixed” immigration status — meaning, those with some members who are citizens or legal residents and others who live in the country illegally — from receiving housing vouchers or living in public housing.

The new rule would terminate aid for all of these households on Dec.14. The states’ lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for Massachusetts argues that the Trump administration overstepped its authority in overriding a congressional statute and asked the federal court to freeze the new rule from going into effect.

Undocumented immigrants have been banned from receiving federal housing subsidies for decades. But starting during the Clinton administration, Congress has required the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development to provide assistance in proportion to the share of members who have legal status. A family with two undocumented parents and two citizen children, for example, would receive half the eligible aid.

“California won’t stand idly by while the Trump administration forces families to choose between staying together and keeping a roof over their heads,” said Attorney General Rob Bonta in a press conference announcing the suit.

In a written response, the HUD press office said the rule “ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars.”

“This rule guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing,” the statement, attributed to Secretary Scott Turner, continued. “This change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist.”

Since the Trump administration published the final version of the rule earlier this month, local public housing agencies have been racing to figure out how to comply while minimizing the eviction of residents and financial collateral damage for the agencies themselves. Some warn that many U.S. citizens and legal residents may struggle and ultimately fail to comply with the more stringent requirements to prove eligibility. They also warn that housing agencies will be squeezed financially as they evict lower-cost mixed status households and replace them with households entitled to full benefits.

text:
Four immigrants who were detained at a Louisiana ICE facility accused staff of subjecting them to a “monthslong nightmare” of sexual and physical abuse in a new federal complaint.

The lawsuit, filed Monday in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Louisiana, alleges that two former officials at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center threatened the detainees with death, solitary confinement and deportation to coerce them into performing “physical and sexual labor.”

By extracting labor from detainees, the lawsuit says the defendants — a former assistant warden named Emmanuel Reyes and a former guard named David Courvelle — helped enrich the private prison firm that runs the facility, the GEO Group.

The alleged abuses began in 2023 and continued until last year, says the lawsuit, in which a group of civil rights and immigrant advocates represent the plaintiffs. Reyes and Courvelle could not be reached for this story. Spokespeople for the GEO Group and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not immediately respond to inquiries.

The legal filings come after another civil complaint filed last year, adding to a list of criticisms about guards’ behavior inside the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center. One of 10 ICE detention or processing facilities in Louisiana, the facility is located in Basile and is the nation’s largest immigration lockup for female detainees.

Courvelle separately faced a criminal FBI investigation for sexually abusing a detainee. A federal judge sentenced him in June to three years in federal prison.

He and Reyes are accused of primarily targeting transgender and nonbinary detainees. In one instance, Reyes allegedly forced detainees to move metal cabinets and cinder blocks back and forth across the facility through the night. His aim was to punish people “who think they are men” by “treating them like men,” the lawsuit says.

The plaintiffs include two transgender men from Mexico, 38-year-old Luis Renteria-Gonzalez and 43-year-old Mario Garcia-Valenzuela. A third plaintiff, 38-year-old Kenia Campos-Flores, is from El Salvador and identifies as nonbinary. A fourth plaintiff is identified in the complaint as Jane Doe.

Renteria-Gonzalez and Garcia-Valenzuela are currently in Mexico while Campos-Flores remains in federal custody, court records show. A spokesperson for the National Immigration Project, one of the groups representing the plaintiffs, said that attorneys for the plaintiffs are not releasing Jane Doe’s location to protect her safety.

The lawsuit describes how Reyes operated an off-the-books “forced work program” in which women would be forced to perform jobs late at night without any official recording of the work, the lawsuit says. Tasks included “heavy-duty cleaning work” and repairs that relied on machinery.

Reyes would refuse the detainees’ requests for protective equipment, the lawsuit says. When Garcia-Valenzuela asked for protective equipment during one job, Reyes allegedly responded: “Aren’t you a man? Can’t you do manly work?”

Reyes would randomly “pay” the defendants by adding small amounts to their commissary accounts, which ICE detainees often use to buy food. Detainees have complained about the poor quality of facility meals.

Over a four-month period, Reyes is accused of forcing Jane Doe to repeatedly perform oral sex on him.

While Reyes has not been criminally charged, the lawsuit appears to signal that an FBI probe that later yielded criminal charges against Courvelle also prompted agents to look at Reyes.

FBI and DHS agents sat down with Renteria-Gonzalez in August 2024 as part of that probe, the lawsuit says. The suit says that during the discussion, the detainee told agents about alleged sexual and physical abuse by Reyes as well as Courvelle.

Courvelle was later convicted of one count of sexual abuse of a ward, a federal felony. Prosecutors said he had sexually abused a detainee from Nicaragua with whom he developed “a personal relationship,” and enlisted other detainees — including Renteria-Gonzalez and Garcia-Valenzuela — to act as “lookouts” to avoid detection while he committed the abuse.

text:
President Donald Trump signaled potential areas of cooperation with a Democratic Congress during a Nov. 20 press conference, notably on immigration policy.

His comments came just a few days after key Catholic bishops said they would continue to encourage lawmakers in both parties to work toward humane immigration policies, during the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops’ fall plenary assembly in Baltimore on Nov. 17.

In the aftermath of Republicans losing control of both chambers of Congress in a Democratic landslide, Trump offered mixed signals about the degree to which he would be willing to work with the new Congress on the issue, at first suggesting his approach may have been “too tough” and that he was open to working with Democrats, before his administration indicated its deportation policy would continue. Trump also named Stephen Miller, seen as a main architect of his immigration policy, as his chief of staff.

In response to a question on the subject of immigration policy, Trump did not rule out working with Democrats.

“You know, what’s happened is, I’ve been called by a lot of Democrats, I will tell you, you’ll have to figure out who,” Trump said, adding, “They want to talk to me about healthcare, and they want to talk to me about immigration.”

Trump said he was potentially interested in working with Democrats on immigration policy that would allow him to continue to deport “the worst of the worst” but suggested potential cooperation on avenues for “very hardworking people that came in.”

But Trump did not eschew his hardline immigration policy, also saying, “We are not going to let immigration destroy our country.”

Citing a recent phone call with Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, D-Texas, Trump said he may be able to work with Democrats on border security.

“It was a very productive call, and she wants to have a strong border, and we’ll be able, I think we’ll be able to work something out,” Trump said.

Previously, Hinojosa told The Texas Tribune, “He understands my commitment to keeping a secure border.”

“I reached out to him to make sure that he had a direct line to me, and it was a very positive conversation,” Hinojosa said. “He indicated his desire to help Texas, and any friend of Texas – anybody who wants to help Texas – is a friend of mine.”

In response to a question about how the bishops planned to navigate the new political environment in their advocacy for humane immigration policies, Archbishop Paul S. Coakley of Oklahoma City, president of the USCCB, told reporters at a Nov. 17 press conference, “Many of our concerns will remain the same.”

“We are concerned about treating migrants with respect and dignity. We’re concerned about the policies of mass deportation, to try to rein that in,” the archbishop said. “We’re concerned about conditions in detention centers and providing adequate pastoral and spiritual care in those settings. So those are some of the things that are kind of low-hanging fruit. We’ll just continue to try to advocate as we have been.”

Bishop Daniel E. Flores of Brownsville, Texas, USCCB vice president, pointed to the special pastoral message on immigration the conference approved at its previous fall plenary assembly, saying, “I think we continue to have the concerns that we raised.”

In Nov. 18 remarks to the assembly, Bishop Brendan J. Cahill of Joliet, Illinois, chair of the USCCB’s Committee on Migration, said a year after that message, “much of what we addressed at that time continues to be relevant today,” identifying family separation and the ability to provide pastoral care to those in detention centers as among the conference’s key concerns.

Catholic social teaching on immigration balances three interrelated principles: the right of persons to migrate; the right of a country to regulate its borders and control immigration; and a nation’s duty to regulate its borders with justice and mercy.

RICHMOND, Va. — A federal appellate court on Nov. 23 ruled against Virginia’s ICE mask law, but upheld a law restricting local cooperation with immigration officials, the Courthouse News Service reported.

U.S. District Judge Robert Payne blocked both laws over the summer after the General Assembly passed them in the spring. The case then went to the Fourth Circuit.

| DOWNLOAD: 5 officer safety conversations to have with your team

The panel agreed with Payne that the masking law, which required ICE officials to wear identifiable items on their clothing and prohibited facial coverings, violates the intergovernmental immunity doctrine, Courthouse News reported.

“We question neither the sincerity nor the reasonableness of the commonwealth’s objections to masked and otherwise-unidentified law enforcement activities, and we emphasize that states may limit or forbid such conduct by their own state and local officers,” said U.S. Circuit Judge Toby Heytens, who authored the opinion. “But just as Congress may not ‘issue orders directly to the states,’ states may not issue orders directly to the federal government.”

On the second law, the court disagreed with Payne’s conclusion that restrictions on 287(g) agreements violate the contracts clause and the intergovernmental immunity doctrine.

The Virginia partnership law allowed agencies to continue working with ICE under the condition that they do not perform immigration enforcement in certain locations, like schools and churches, refrain from using “mass surveillance technology” and assist with immigration operations without a judicial warrant.

“The intergovernmental immunity doctrine does not apply because the 287(g) law neither directly regulates the federal government nor prevents private parties from contracting with it,” Heytens said. “Its arguments get basic federalism principles backward.”

Heytens also said the law doesn’t violate the contracts clause because it restricts future agreements rather than existing contracts.

text:
[Episcopal News Service] The Episcopal Church’s two presiding officers have joined other Christian leaders in signing a “friend of the court brief” in support of immigrants who sued to stop the Trump administration from deporting them without due process to countries other than their countries of origin.

The immigrants’ class-action lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security is scheduled for oral arguments before the U.S. Supreme Court on Dec. 9.

“Protecting the persecuted and providing fair judgment for each individual person is a fundamental part of Christian traditions, which recognize that every person is made in God’s image and therefore has God-given dignity,” the Christian leaders said in their Nov. 23 filing. It was signed by Episcopal Church Presiding Bishop Sean Rowe and House of Deputies President Julia Ayala Harris, as well as the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, the United Church of Christ, the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America, the United Methodist Church, the Cooperative Baptist Fellowship and several churches in the Anabaptist and Pentecostal traditions.

“Israelites and Christians – including Jesus himself – were welcomed as migrants and have long welcomed the stranger and the persecuted,” the Christian leaders said. “This longstanding practice of providing refuge to those who need it most is reflected in Christian doctrine today, and requires that each individual receive fair process before judgment.”

For the past two years, the Trump administration has aggressively pursued immigration enforcement, detentions and deportations to fulfill President Donald Trump’s campaign promises to sharply reduce both legal and illegal immigration. Many of those policies have prompted a political backlash, as enforcement actions have disrupted communities and often have targeted immigrants with little or no criminal record.

Some of the enforcement actions that have generated the most outcry are “third country removals,” or cases in which immigrants, including asylum-seekers, have been deported to countries where they have no previous ties but may face renewed threat of persecution and violence.

Human Rights First, one of the groups that filed the lawsuit on the immigrants’ behalf, called it an “egregious policy” that provided the immigrants no chance to challenge their removal. Homeland Security authorities have “removed or sought to remove individuals to war-torn countries, countries in which they have been imprisoned, and to countries that have effectuated ‘chain refoulement’ by subsequently returning them to countries in which they face persecution or torture,” Human Rights First said.

The Christian leaders cited numerous religious texts in their “friend of the court brief,” from Bible passages to The Episcopal Church’s Book of Common Prayer, as well as resolutions adopted by the church’s General Convention related to humane treatment of migrants.

Christianity “teaches that vulnerable persons facing persecution are uniquely deserving of protection and hospitality,” the brief says. “Sovereign nations have a legitimate authority to regulate migration but a corresponding obligation to respect each person’s God-given dignity through humane and proportional immigration policies.”

The filing comes one month after The Episcopal Church and its ecumenical and interfaith partners prevailed in a separate federal lawsuit that they filed to strengthen protections from the Trump administration conducting immigration enforcement actions at houses of worship. The church and 26 other plaintiffs in that case have argued that intensified enforcement has driven some worshippers to stay home.

A lower court judge ruled in April 2025 that The Episcopal Church and other plaintiffs had not sufficiently demonstrated an imminent threat. Last month, the Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit reversed that decision, sending the case back to the U.S. District Court to rule on the merits of the plaintiff’s arguments.

And earlier this month, the Diocese of San Joaquin in California’s Central Valley filed its own “friend of the court” brief in another federal lawsuit. The diocese expressed its support for seven immigrants who sued the Trump administration over the conditions of their confinement in the biggest immigrant detention facility in California.

General Convention has long supported immigration policies that treat migrants with dignity. Episcopalians interested in ways of supporting immigrants in their communities and nationally are encouraged to review the Immigration Action Toolkit produced by the church’s Washington, D.C.-based Office of Government Relations.

In a recent press release, GEO states that the company expects to receive approximately $340 million in net proceeds. The Office of Inspector General must investigate this egregious waste of taxpayer dollars, which serves to enrich a private detention contractor to maintain unsafe conditions in immigration detention.”

Senator Murray noted that the GEO Group has been awarded a 10-year contract with ICE without any plan to improve the NWIPC’s cruel conditions—and explained that the acquisition of the facility is a clear attempt to evade oversight. This scheme is a blatant attempt by ICE and the facility’s operator, GEO Group, to block Washington state from enforcing a state law that allows public health officials to inspect private detention facilities to ensure detainees are treated with basic dignity.”

In Washington state, Senator Murray has conducted consistent oversight of NWIPC, despite the Trump administration’s efforts to block Congressional oversight of federal immigration detention facilities. After a protracted legal battle over Washington state’s ability to enforce health and safety standards at NWIPC, a federal appeals court ruled in August 2025 that the state should be allowed to enforce such standards at the detention center, and that failure to comply could result in fines of up to $10,000 per violation. In December 2025, Senator Murray led Members of the Washington state Congressional delegation in a letter to ICE, expressing grave concerns with conditions at NWIPC and demanding answers to a long list of questions regarding overcrowding and lack of access to medical services, food, and legal counsel for individuals detained at the facility.

Senator Murray has spoken out forcefully and consistently against the Trump administration’s cruel and counterproductive mass deportation campaign and the egregious treatment by ICE and DHS of American citizens, legal immigrants, and undocumented immigrants. As Vice Chair of the Appropriations Committee, she led Democrats’ efforts fighting tooth and nail to secure meaningful reforms in law to rein in ICE and Border Patrol—which Republicans ultimately refused altogether and chose to skirt Democrats by delivering another massive blank check for the agencies with no accountability. Earlier this year, at a Senate Appropriations Homeland Security Subcommittee hearing on the FY27 budget request for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS)—Murray pressed Secretary Markwayne Mullin on the conduct of ICE and Border Patrol and Republicans’ refusal to enact reforms into law. Senator Murray also joined dozens of her Senate colleagues in calling for stronger accountability measures for ICE officers, and urging DHS to fulfill its previous commitments to deploy and expand the usage of body-worn cameras, strengthen officer identification requirements, and review enforcement protocols.

In July 2026, Senator Murray released a video calling for an independent investigation in response to the fatal shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo by ICE, and demanding ICE release all of the footage of the tragedy. In March, Senator Murray released a video about the numerous violent shootings we are seeing from Trump’s reckless ICE and CBP agents across the country—and the urgent need to rein in these rogue agencies. Senator Murray highlighted the stories of Marimar Martinez, Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, Carlos Jimenez, Francisco Longoria, and Carlitos Ricardo Parias—all of whom were shot by ICE or CBP agents. Throughout the video, Senator Murray calls out the egregious use of force from federal agents, their lies that don’t hold up in court, and the extreme danger they are putting families and communities in by recklessly using firearms. Senator Murray also called out Republicans for refusing to negotiate serious and common sense measures to rein in ICE and CBP.

In July 2026, Senator Murray called on ICE to stop the deportation of a small business owner, Eduardo Aguirre Esparza, who has lived in Seattle for 23 years and is the husband of an American citizen. Eduardo was forcefully detained and in the process of being deported before courts could consider emergency relief. In December 2025, Murray called attention to the violent assault of Wilmer Toledo-Martinez in Vancouver, Washington and she successfully advocated for his release from the Northwest ICE Processing Center (NWIPC). Wilmer was lured out of his home under false pretenses, violently detained by federal agents, and mauled by an attack dog despite not resisting arrest or attempting to flee. Not long after, Murray also called attention to the case of Jose Paniagua Calderón, whose foot was run over by agents in Vancouver.

In February 2025, Senator Murray signed onto a letter demanding that DHS end wrongful searches and interrogations of Tribal members, and continued to push for answers from DHS on the matter last December. In March 2025, Murray also reintroduced her Stop Shackling and Detaining Pregnant Women Act. In September 2025, Senator Murray and Senator Richard Blumenthal led 27 of their Senate colleagues in a letter expressing concern with prevalence and the treatment of pregnant, postpartum, and nursing women in ICE detention. In November 2025, Senator Murray joined 48 of her colleagues in the Senate and House of Representatives in introducing the Restoring Access to Detainees Act, which would mandate that DHS allow people who have been detained to contact their legal counsel and families.

Senator Murray also met with farmworkers, advocates, and community members in Burlington last year to listen to their concerns amid a recent spike in ICE activity—including large-scale raids and the detention of local activists and leaders—in Northwest Washington, particularly in Whatcom and Skagit counties.

Murray has been outspoken against the Trump administration’s inhumane immigration agenda from the start, strongly opposing passage of the Laken Riley Act. Murray was one of the few Senate Democrats to take to the floor to speak out forcefully against its passage.

Dear Mr. Cuffari:

I write to request an immediate investigation into the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) pending acquisition of the Northwest ICE Processing Center (NWIPC) in Tacoma, Washington from the GEO Group, Inc. (GEO), a private prison operator with a record of mistreatment and abuse of people detained in its custody. The NWIPC, assessed by the City of Tacoma to be valued at $72.6 million, is reportedly being sold for $453 million. In a recent press release, GEO states that the company expects to receive approximately $340 million in net proceeds. The Office of Inspector General must investigate this egregious waste of taxpayer dollars, which serves to enrich a private detention contractor to maintain unsafe conditions in immigration detention.

I call on you to examine the details of the acquisition agreement, particularly how the parties arrived at a sale price more than six times the City’s assessed land value for the NWIPC. Additionally, I urge you to investigate whether ICE fully complied with the Federal Acquisition Regulation and other relevant laws, regulations, and policies, including procurement and conflict-of-interest requirements. I further urge you to investigate whether ICE had developed a strategic plan in line with GAO’s September 2026 report’s recommendation prior to their decision to purchase the Tacoma facility.

This waste and abuse of taxpayer dollars to pursue President Trump and Stephen Miller’s cruel and extreme immigration agenda deserves immediate attention before the sale is finalized.

Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Sincerely,

Patty Murray

Dive Brief:

A coalition of local governments and public housing authorities filed a lawsuit Monday to halt a U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development rule that would block households with mixed immigration statuses from receiving federal housing assistance.

The rule, scheduled to go into effect Dec. 14, is “callous, ill-conceived, and illegal,” and a violation of the Administrative Procedure Act, the lawsuit states.

HUD’s rule change could displace at least 15,500 mixed-status families, according to the suit, placing additional burden on localities’ already-strained homeless shelter and support systems.

Dive Insight:

Households with mixed immigration statuses have for decades been able to receive federal housing assistance, prorated based on the number of household members who verify they are U.S. citizens or have eligible immigration status, according to plaintiffs.

On Nov. 10, HUD announced all recipients of federal housing aid would be required to provide proof of eligibility for all household members. “The final rule includes any tenants currently living in ‘mixed status’ households that have exploited regulatory loopholes by enabling illegal aliens and ineligible noncitizens to latch on to those with eligible status,” the agency stated.

The coalition filed their lawsuit Monday in the U.S. District Court of Massachusetts. Other lawsuits challenging the rule have also been filed by states and Los Angeles-area tenant organizations and housing advocacy groups.

“HUD’s Final Rule is a radical departure from the law and decades of past practice and regulations,” San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu, representing the city in the Nov. 23 lawsuit, said in a news release. “Cities across the country are coming together to fight this callous and illegal change that is designed to push immigrant families into homelessness.”

Along with San Francisco, plaintiffs include Boston; Chicago; the City and County of Los Angeles; King County, Washington; New York City; Providence, Rhode Island; San Diego; Santa Clara County, California; Seattle, and eight public housing authorities.

text:
A former private prison in western Minnesota that just reopened as a detention facility for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is sparking pushback.

The detention facility in Appleton, three hours west of Minneapolis, opened Nov. 9 after the Department of Homeland Security purchased it for nearly $500 million from CoreCivic, which still manages the site. It was formerly Prairie Correctional Facility, which closed in 2010.

Immigrant rights advocates say 70 people are currently in custody at the site, which can hold up to 1,600 detainees. In response to an inquiry from WCCO News, ICE said the number of detainees is "subject to change" and not publicly released.

The agency in a statement on Nov. 12 said the facility "gives ICE immediate capacity to detain and remove those who have no legal right to remain, protecting American communities and restoring the integrity of our borders without waiting years for new construction."

Dozens of people gathered at the Minnesota State Capitol in St. Paul on Monday, calling for oversight and its closure. In 2023, the Minnesota Legislature passed a law banning the use of private prisons for people incarcerated in the state system.

"Whether it's civil or criminal, the Constitution protects everyone. Due process matters. Access to the court matters. Human dignity matters, and that's why we're here today," said Julio Zelaya, director of advocacy for the ACLU of Minnesota.

Protestors held signs with messages like "abolish ICE now," "close the camps" and "due process, not profits."

In a letter to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, DFL U.S. Rep. Betty McCollum questioned why the federal government paid what it did for the facility when the state was offered the site for a fraction of the price just a year earlier.

"The facility opened during the deadliest period for people in ICE custody in more than two decades. It is also the product of a costly and hasty detention expansion that jeopardizes local property tax dollars and that Congress's own watchdog has found is wasting taxpayer money," McCollum and others wrote.

In a statement, a spokesperson for CoreCivic said that the federal government determined the sale price "following its assessment process."

The ICE detention center's opening comes 10 months after the thousands of federal immigration agents descended on Minnesota in Operation Metro Surge, an unprecedented operation during which two American citizens were shot and killed.

Democrats are set to take back total control of the State Capitol — the House, Senate and governor's office — after November's election, and they promise future action on ICE accountability measures that passed the Minnesota Senate earlier this year but didn't clear the tied House.

Those measures include banning face masks for federal agents and prohibiting them from making arrests at schools, hospitals and courthouses. Republicans have questioned if the Legislature has the authority to implement those rules since ICE is a federal agency. State lawmakers have little power to restrict the facility's operation, as protestors demand.

"I want to say it is our priority to make sure that what happened in Minnesota last winter never happens again," said Rep. Samantha Sencer-Mura, the newly elected majority whip for the DFL-led House, at the Monday rally.

But not everyone is opposed to the Appleton detention site. Sen. Torrey Westrom, a Republican from Alexandria, Minnesota, who represents the town, praised the federal purchase of it. In a statement, he said it creates 450 new jobs and provides an economic boost to the region.

"Although this is a lost opportunity for the state of Minnesota, this is a practical solution that puts an existing facility back to use, brings back good jobs for rural Minnesota, and represents a wise use of taxpayer resources," Westrom said in August at the time of the announcement of the sale.
