text:
Summary

Haliah M., age 12 when she spoke to Human Rights Watch in March 2026, fled Afghanistan with her parents, three older brothers, and two older sisters in 2021 after the Taliban took power. Her father had worked for the previous government, she explained, and some of his colleagues had been killed. “As soon as the Taliban took control, they started looking for everyone working for the prior government,” she said. Her parents were also concerned about what life would be like for the three girls under the Taliban, and she agreed with their decision to leave. “As you well know, under the Taliban a woman can’t go anywhere by herself. There is no access to university for women. It would even be difficult for my sisters and me to finish our secondary education,” she told us.

The family travelled to Pakistan, Iran, and then Türkiye, where they spent three years. When her parents started to worry that Türkiye would return them to Afghanistan, they moved on, transiting Greece, North Macedonia, and Serbia before reaching Bosnia and Herzegovina.

They entered Croatia in February 2026. “We walked for hours, nearly the whole day,” Haliah said. Officers dressed in Croatian police uniforms apprehended the family as they crossed a road and ordered them to hand over their phones. She and her 14-year-old sister Roya are the only ones in the family who spoke English, which they learned at their school in Afghanistan, so she talked to the police on behalf of her family:

I tried to explain why we had left Afghanistan, but they didn’t say anything about applying to stay in Croatia. Then I asked them to give us back even one phone. I said we needed to be able to contact our relatives. I explained that we had photos of our documents on our phone. One of those police pulled out his gun and shot our phones in front of me.

The police drove the family back to the border and ordered them to return to Bosnia and Herzegovina. “They hit one of my brothers with a baton. They hit him on the leg right by the foot, and now he can’t walk well. He’s 17,” she said.

She and her family were at a migrant reception center in northwest Bosnia and Herzegovina when we spoke in March 2026. Located some 25 kilometres from Bihać, the nearest city, the camp has faced water shortages. There is no local bus service; infrequent buses from Sarajevo to Bihać often only let passengers disembark at a stop along the highway about 30 minutes by foot from the reception center. In the winter, snowfall can reach people’s waists, making it difficult to move between the buildings where people are housed and the canteen.

Haliah and Roya would have liked to be in school, but only younger children were able to attend classes when we visited the center. Authorities had made arrangements for a single bus to take no more than six children to and from an elementary school, meaning that not even every child of elementary school age could attend. The center itself offered no classes.

The family was not sure where they hoped to end up. Not Croatia, Haliah said, not after the way the Croatian police had treated them. She was urging her parents and older siblings to consider Switzerland even though they knew nobody there. “It’s very beautiful, and the government doesn’t tell people what to believe,” she said. She was especially interested in Geneva. “I want to work for the United Nations, for UNHCR. There are lots of people in the situation I am now, and I want to be able to help them,” she explained.

Pushbacks by Croatian police—operations intended to physically prevent people from reaching, entering, or remaining in a territory and which lack any or only summary screening for protection needs and have no legal basis or oversight—are a longstanding, ongoing practice that has persisted despite consistent reports by human rights and humanitarian groups, media investigations, international condemnation, and regional court rulings. In 2023 Human Rights Watch published “Like We Were Just Animals”: Pushbacks of People Seeking Protection from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina, which documented the practice up to that time. Monitoring arrangements have not succeeded in eliminating the practice. Indeed, the Croatian authorities continue to demonstrate official tolerance for these persistent unlawful pushbacks by police through inadequate oversight, ineffective investigations and a lack of meaningful accountability, and repeated minimization—and often denial—of the existence of the practice.

Croatian police typically carry out pushbacks at or near the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina or Serbia, forcing people to return to those countries. Human Rights Watch and other groups have also documented pushbacks from elsewhere in Croatia, including in and around Zagreb and in some instances near the border with Slovenia. Many people described experiencing repeated pushbacks by Croatian police.

Croatian police often inflict violence during pushbacks: beating people with fists or truncheons, kicking them after ordering them to lay face down on the ground, firing weapons in the air. People subjected to pushbacks regularly report that Croatian police take all the money they have and confiscate or destroy phones. In some cases, people also recount having documents seized, backpacks burned, or being forced to remove their shoes and other clothing or even to strip to their underwear before being pushed back. Researchers for a 2025 Save the Children study heard consistent reports of “violent and degrading treatment by border police, especially Croatian authorities” and observed, “for many refugees and migrants passing through the [Western Balkans], violent pushbacks and numerous rights violations have become inseparable from their journey.” The Western Balkan route connects Türkiye and Greece to Croatia and, less frequently in recent years, Hungary, with Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina serving as the points of entry to these countries.

Until August 2025, Haliah and her family would have stayed in a dedicated facility in Bihać for families with children. That facility, the Borići transit reception center, was a short walk from the city center, giving families easy access to schools, health clinics, shops, and parks. Borići was renovated with EU funding of more than 2 million Bosnian marks (€1 million) and then closed in August 2025. Despite the European Union’s substantial investment in the facility and the ongoing need for accommodation suitable for children, and the remoteness and unsuitability of Lipa for children, including the adverse impact on access to education, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said in November 2025 that the facility was “[n]o longer required for hosting migrants” as “reception capacities have been consolidated at TRC Lipa near Bihać.” According to local government officials, the arrangement to use Borići as a family migrant center was intended from the outset to be temporary. Bosnia and Herzegovina’s only other dedicated migrant center for families and unaccompanied children, the Ušivak transit reception center, near Sarajevo, closed in February 2026.

The European Union has promoted—and funded—increased external border control by Croatia at the expense of addressing the international protection needs of people on the move. In doing so, it has largely turned a blind eye to reports that Croatian police regularly carry out pushbacks with impunity. An EU-funded Croatian border monitoring mechanism has done little effective monitoring due to access and other limitations, and Croatian authorities have used the mechanism to justify limiting the oversight role of Croatia’s independent ombuds office despite its authority under Croatian law to investigate reports of human rights violations. Frontex, the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, has cooperated with Croatian border police in border monitoring operations, and in September 2026 Croatia’s interior minister suggested that Frontex should also strengthen its presence in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Croatia should immediately end pushbacks at its borders, including those to Bosnia and Herzegovina and to Serbia, and instead afford everybody who expresses an intention to seek international protection the opportunity to do so. Croatia should also ensure that its new border monitoring mechanism is a robust and independent safeguard against pushbacks and other official abuse.

Through enforcement of EU law and as a condition of funding, the European Commission should require Croatian authorities to end pushbacks and other human rights violations at its borders and provide concrete, verifiable information on steps taken to investigate reports of pushbacks and other human rights violations against migrants and asylum seekers. In the absence of such evidence, the European Commission should withhold migration management funding and assess Croatia’s fulfillment of its obligations under the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum, including its compliance with international and EU legal obligations against non-refoulement. The European Union and its member states should also fundamentally reorient their migration policy to create pathways for safe, orderly, and regular migration.

Recommendations

To the Croatian Ministry of the Interior

End pushbacks and other collective expulsions of migrants and asylum seekers.

Direct police not to use informal detention facilities, including vans and other vehicles used as informal detention sites.

Allow and facilitate people to exercise their right to claim international protection at the border or upon arrival in the country.

Provide effective free legal aid for, and take proactive steps to safeguard the right of, every person to challenge decisions relating to their detention or deportation before a competent, impartial, and independent tribunal in an individualized, prompt, and transparent proceeding that affords essential procedural safeguards.

Ensure that people who experience torture or other ill-treatment—whether in their home countries or en route—are identified as early as possible, have access to health care, including rights-respecting mental health care and psychosocial support, and receive redress.

Require video recording of all border enforcement operations and the preservation of video footage to assist in investigating allegations of ill-treatment.

Issue clear and unequivocal directives to police that ill-treatment, including any excessive use of force, contravenes Croatian and EU law and will not be tolerated, and require police to undergo training on relevant human rights norms.

Refer any reports of excessive use of force, other ill-treatment, or other improper conduct by police to an independent authority for prompt, effective, and impartial investigation and, if appropriate, prosecution.

To the Croatian Police Directorate

Require police to record every “interception” and “diversion” operation involving migrants, which at a minimum should include the time, precise location and a brief description of actions taken, the officers involved, the means used to “intercept” or “divert” people, the number of people “intercepted” or “diverted,” whether any means of restraint or use of force was applied and to how many people, and the outcome of the operation.

To the State Attorney’s Office

Promptly and thoroughly investigate reports of pushbacks and of ill-treatment made by nongovernmental organizations or referred by the Croatian ombudsperson or the border monitoring mechanism.

To the Government of Croatia

Ensure that the border monitoring mechanism is independent in law and in practice, has sufficient resources and a robust mandate to monitor border-related operations anywhere on the territory of Croatia, is empowered to investigate cross-border violations even when victims are no longer on Croatian territory, and takes into account information provided or made publicly available by non-governmental organizations, media, and EU or UN agencies.

Explicitly ensure that the border monitoring mechanism can refer reports of pushbacks and other human rights violations to the State Attorney’s Office for prompt and thorough investigation.

Encourage the border monitoring mechanism to focus on conducting unannounced visits, which should pay particular attention to verifying respect for fundamental rights in the application of the Schengen acquis (the EU rules that govern the Schengen Area), and take into account evidence from the Croatian ombudsperson and nongovernmental and international organizations in the programming and design of evaluations.

Cooperate with human rights oversight bodies of the United Nations and the Council of Europe, including UN special rapporteurs and the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT).

To the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina

Provide adequate staffing and other resources and the necessary political support to enable the Ministry of Security’s Sector for Asylum to register asylum claims and make refugee status determinations within the six-month period provided in the Law on Asylum.

Ensure that conditions in temporary reception centers for asylum seekers meet essential standards of habitability and provide food and other services that are appropriate for the age, health and disability needs, and culture of the people housed there. Temporary reception centers should be accessible by public transit and should not be unreasonably far from shops, schools, hospitals, and other essential services.

Move families with children and unaccompanied children from the Lipa reception center to other facilities that are appropriate for the needs of children. As with centers for adults, facilities for children should be accessible by public transit and should not be unreasonably far from shops, schools, hospitals, and other essential services.

To European Union Member State Governments

All countries in the European Union should suspend the return of asylum seekers to Croatia under EU regulations that require that the first EU country of arrival is responsible for a person’s asylum claim, until Croatia definitively ends pushbacks and other collective expulsions, and ensures meaningful access to asylum as required by EU law.

All countries in the European Union should create pathways for safe, orderly, and regular migration.

To the European Commission

In line with the recommendation of the European ombudsperson, require Croatian authorities to provide concrete and verifiable information on steps taken to investigate reports of collective expulsions and mistreatment of migrants and asylum seekers and evidence of steps taken to hold Croatian police accountable for violent pushbacks and other ill-treatment of asylum seekers and migrants.

Press Croatia to end its violations of fundamental rights at its borders and provide solid evidence of thorough investigations of allegations of collective returns and violence against migrants and asylum seekers at its borders. In the absence of such evidence, the European Commission should assess Croatia’s fulfilment of its EU obligations with a view to possible legal action against Croatia for violating EU law, including by engaging in collective expulsions and failing to provide access to asylum.

Actively review and assess the border monitoring mechanism to ensure that Croatian authorities have in place a system that can credibly monitor border operations and a wide scope of potential rights abuses and provide political and financial support only to a system that meets these conditions.

Withhold migration management funding until Croatia demonstrates meaningful and sustained progress in ending pushbacks and abuses at its borders and make any future funding contingent on full and unhindered access of EU staff and other independent observers who monitor border operations.

To the EU Council and the European Parliament

Strengthen scrutiny over border monitoring practices and ensure that national mechanisms are empowered to address all alleged fundamental rights violations by national border management authorities or during border control activities, are independent from border control or law enforcement institutions, proactively take into account information from other relevant sources, are designed to be capable of ending abuses and ensuring accountability at the domestic level, and publicly report on their findings and conclusions.

To Frontex, the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, and the European Commission

Frontex should ensure that its operations in Croatia are consistent with its human rights obligations under the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights and all applicable international human rights law, including the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (the European Convention on Human Rights), and that it complies with its duty to avoid complicity in abuse. The Frontex mandate review and foreseen substantial upgrade in the agency’s standing corps and resources should result in greater accountability in the agency’s operations.

Frontex’s Fundamental Rights Officer (FRO) should monitor and publicly report on Croatian security forces’ compliance with European and international human rights and refugee law, as well as compliance by Frontex’s officers and those contributed by member states. The Frontex mandate review should strengthen the role and resourcing of fundamental rights monitoring along with accountability for noncompliance.

The Frontex executive director should escalate the prospect of triggering article 46 of its regulation, under which the agency has a duty to suspend or terminate operations in case of serious abuses, if no concrete steps are taken by Croatia to end these abuses within three months from the publication of this report.

In considering whether to trigger article 46 of Frontex’s regulation on Croatia, or when examining concerns brought by the FRO, the executive director should consider allegations of abuse and reports from international and regional organizations, nongovernmental groups, civil society, and the media.

Methodology

Two Human Rights Watch researchers interviewed 87 people—all refugees, asylum seekers, and other migrants—in and around Bihać, Bosnia and Herzegovina, in April and August 2025 and March and August 2026. Seven identified themselves as unaccompanied children. Six were parents travelling with children under age 18, and four were children travelling with their parents or other family members. Their countries of origin included Afghanistan, Algeria, Cameroon, Gambia, Ghana, India, Iran, Morocco, Palestine, Pakistan, the Republic of Congo (Congo-Brazzaville), Somalia, Sudan, Syria, and Türkiye.

Human Rights Watch also interviewed 15 aid workers, lawyers, health professionals, volunteers, and activists who distribute food, provide medical or legal services, or offer information and other support to asylum seekers and migrants.

Human Rights Watch researchers conducted interviews in English, French, or Bosnian. In some cases, interviewees used translation apps to provide additional details as they responded to our questions. We explained to all interviewees the purpose and public nature of our reporting, that the interviews were voluntary and confidential, and that they would receive no personal service or benefit for speaking to us. We also obtained oral consent from each adult interviewee and oral assent from each child interviewee.

This report uses pseudonyms for all migrant or asylum-seeking children and adults. In some cases, additional identifying information such as the precise location of the interview has also been withheld. Moreover, Human Rights Watch has withheld the names and other identifying information of some humanitarian workers who requested that we not publish this information.

On April 2, 2025, Human Rights Watch requested access to Dugi Dol, an unofficial place of detention near the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina which numerous interviewees reported is used by Croatian police to hold people prior to pushing them back. Croatian authorities did not reply to our request. Human Rights Watch also sought and received access from authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina to the Borići family accommodation center in Bihać in April 2025, the Sarajevo Immigration Detention Center in April 2025, and the Lipa reception center in April 2025 and March 2026.

Human Rights Watch sought comment from Croatia’s Ministry of the Interior, Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Ministry of Security, and the European Commission on the findings of this report. The Croatian Ministry of the Interior’s reply is reflected in this report and appears in full in the annex. The other agencies had not replied as of November 18, 2026, the date this report was finalized for publication.

In line with international standards, the term child refers to a person under the age of 18. As the United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child and other international authorities do, we use the term unaccompanied children in this report to refer to children “who have been separated from both parents and other relatives and are not being cared for by an adult who, by law or custom, is responsible for doing so.” Separated children are those who are “separated from both parents, or from their previous legal or customary primary caregiver, but not necessarily from other relatives,” meaning that they may be accompanied by other adult family members.

This report uses refugee to mean a person who meets the criteria in the 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol. Under the 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol, a refugee is a person with a “well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion,” who is outside of the country of nationality and is unable or unwilling, because of that fear, to return.

The term migrant is not defined in international law; our use of this term is in its “common lay understanding of a person who moves away from his or her place of usual residence, whether within a country or across an international border, temporarily or permanently, and for a variety of reasons.” It includes asylum seekers and refugees, and the term migrant children includes asylum-seeking and refugee children.

The report uses the term pushback to mean operations aimed at physically preventing people from reaching, entering, or remaining in a territory, and which employ no or merely summary screening for protection needs and has no legal basis or oversight. These operations may be conducted by state authorities or by individuals or groups acting at the behest of state authorities or under colour of law. This use follows the practice of international and regional experts. The Committee on the Rights of the Child uses pushback interchangeably with forced return.

The Balkan Route to the European Union

Official data suggest that in 2025 and 2026, fewer people compared to earlier years are travelling via the Balkan route, the name given to what is in fact a combination of routes through one or more of the countries of the Western Balkans, with Bosnia and Herzegovina often the last stop before people attempt to enter the European Union. These statistics likely understate the number of people travelling through Bosnia and Herzegovina to Croatia and onward to other EU countries.

In fact, in 2024 and 2025, “significantly more people appear to have passed through Western Balkan countries than indicated by official statistics,” Save the Children has concluded based on an analysis of discrepancies among data for transit through Bosnia and Herzegovina and other countries in the Balkans, the number of irregular border crossings in Slovenia, and first-time asylum applications in destination countries. Aid workers interviewed by Human Rights Watch agreed that official numbers substantially underestimate the number of migrants who attempt to enter Croatia from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Moreover, the International Rescue Committee and Diaconia Valdese found that the number of people who entered Italy in and around Trieste after transiting through Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and other countries in the Western Balkans may be higher than indicated by official data.

The European Commission considers Croatia one of 12 EU member states “at risk of migratory pressure.” Croatia received nearly €150 million in EU funding between 2015 and 2020 “to better manage migration and borders.” For 2021 to 2027, the European Union has allocated nearly €200 million to Croatia under its Border Management and Visa Instrument (BVMI) funding.

The European Union Migration and Asylum Pact, a package of regulations adopted in 2024 that took effect in June 2026, overhauls how the European Union manages its external borders, processes asylum applications, and addresses responsibility-sharing among member states. In July 2026, the European Union adopted a Return Regulation with new rules on deportations and a framework for creating “return hubs”—deportation centers—in countries outside the European Union.

The Croatian government has in turn taken steps to restrict access to asylum and to limit the rights of asylum seekers at the same time that asylum applications in Croatia have decreased. The Ministry of the Interior’s 2030 Migration and Asylum Management Plan notes:

We want to effectively return all persons who do not meet the conditions for staying in the Republic of Croatia to the safe third countries from which they came to the Republic of Croatia, and whenever possible, to their countries of origin. Therefore, this Plan focuses on strengthening partnerships with third countries, particularly with countries closer to the region, in order to successfully carry out returns.

Legislative amendments that came into force in June 2026 allow the establishment of “special centers for asylum seekers, who will not be able to move freely throughout Croatia.” In March 2026, Croatian authorities announced plans to open a reception center in Željava, about 10 km northwest of Bihać. News accounts have variously described the proposed center as a migrant reception center, an asylum processing center, and a detention center. As of November 2026, Croatian authorities had not confirmed whether the center was in operation.

In line with the European Union’s focus on the externalization of migration control, the European Union struck an agreement with Bosnia and Herzegovina in June 2025 to conduct joint immigration enforcement operations “in a bid to curb irregular migration.” “Frontex officers have been present on the ground since November 2025 and have brought expertise and equipment to support border surveillance, border checks and the detection of fraudulent documents,” the Brussels Times reported in May 2026. Frontex increased its deployment of officers to Bosnia and Herzegovina in early 2026, with the aim of eventually placing 116 officers in the country.

As the European Union has focused on migration enforcement, it has reduced its funding for protection activities in the Western Balkans. Save the Children has noted that “a sharp decrease in the protection budget in Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina since 2023 and security-focused border control have increased the reliance of children on the move on unsafe routes and therefore reduced visibility and access to identification, support, and services.”

The United Kingdom has also provided financial support for migration enforcement in the region. In October 2025, then-Foreign Secretary Yvette Cooper met with foreign ministers from the governments of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, and other countries in the Western Balkans to discuss migration policy, among other issues. At the meeting, Cooper announced that the United Kingdom would contribute £10 million toward efforts to combat people smuggling in the region.

Unlawful, Violent Pushbacks by Croatian Police

When the [Croatian] police caught me, they beat me severely and we went back to the Croatian border in a police van. . . . When we told them that we didn’t want to cross the cold river, they beat us and forced us into the river. They made us strip to our underwear before we crossed, and we were cold. We had to run to the river and swim through the cold water, and the water was sometimes over our heads. I was scared.

—Jamal A., a 17-year-old Moroccan boy interviewed in Bihać, Bosnia and Herzegovina, April 7, 2025

They [the Croatian police] forced us to take off our clothes and laughed at us. They forced us to swim in the river, and the river was very rough. It was 1 Celsius that day. They stole our money. They stole 100 euros from me, and they beat us a lot. They broke my phone, and I can’t call my mom anymore.

—Aziz K., also 17 and from Morocco, describing the pushback he and Jamal A. faced in March 2025, interviewed in Bihać, Bosnia and Herzegovina, April 7, 2025

Nearly every one of the migrants interviewed by Human Rights Watch for this report described experiencing at least one violent pushback by Croatian police. Between August 2024 and October 2025, Save the Children recorded 1,811 accounts of individuals pushed back from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina, including 276 affecting children, numbers that the organization cautions very likely understate the continued prevalence of pushbacks.

According to these accounts, Croatian police regularly take money and phones, as well as backpacks with documents and medicine, clothing, and sometimes glasses, crutches, and other essential items before pushing people back into Bosnia and Herzegovina, practices Human Rights Watch documented in 2023 and in earlier years. In August 2026, a health provider with a humanitarian organization estimated that 20 to 30 percent of the population they treat for injuries are unaccompanied children whose injuries were sustained during pushbacks.

The fear and distress caused by pushbacks cause accumulating psychological harm, mental health professionals have observed. “Children are visibly stressed after pushbacks,” said an aid worker with another group.

Most pushbacks occur near the border, but we also heard accounts of pushbacks of people who had reached the Croatian capital, Zagreb. For instance, Yassine I., a 36-year-old man from Morocco, said police apprehended him at the bus station in Zagreb, took him to one of the rivers that mark the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina, and ordered him to cross. Similarly, an aid worker with a third group told us, “Even if people are close to Zagreb, maybe 25 kilometres away, the Croatian police transport them to a container camp near the border” before pushing them back at points along the border far from populated areas. Such accounts are consistent with the findings of the Center for Peace Studies, a human rights group based in Zagreb, which observed in 2025 that “recent developments indicate that pushbacks are now occurring further inland.”

Lack of Access to Asylum in Croatia

People reported that Croatian police ignored their requests for asylum. For instance, Vivek S., a 24-year-old man from India, said, “I have tried to cross three times. I asked for asylum and to go to Zagreb. They say no. They don’t reply to our requests.” Yuusuf B., from Somalia, told us, “They released the dogs on us to chase us into Bosnia. We say, ‘Asylum, center Zagreb.’ They just say, ‘No, go to Bosnia.’”

Some people who asked for asylum said police appeared to single them out for beatings. Aid workers told us they had heard similar accounts. “The guys are saying Croatian police beat them with batons because they’ve asked for asylum . . . . They face more violence if they ask for asylum,” one aid worker said.

In a 2025 judgment, the European Court of Human Rights found that Croatian authorities had removed an asylum seeker to a third country (in that case North Macedonia) without examining his asylum claim on its merits or without allowing him any access at all to the asylum procedure. The accounts we heard and the reports of other groups indicate that this case is not an exception but is part of a pattern of denial of the right to seek asylum by Croatian police.

Moreover, the removal of people without examining their individual circumstances amounts to collective expulsions, as discussed more fully in the “Legal Standards” chapter, and violates EU and international law.

Violence During Pushbacks

We heard repeatedly from people who told us that Croatian police beat them, took all the money they had, destroyed phones, and forced them to wade or swim across rivers to return to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Summarizing the most common practices during pushbacks, a caseworker told us:

[The Croatian police] steal from them. They take their money, burn their belongings, take their phones. People are forced into the river. They come back with visible injuries on their arms, face, and legs. Police sometimes shoot guns in the air. . . There is a bridge at the river, but people are still forced to wade across the river. People report being pushed into deep water intentionally.[44]

For instance, Rami M., 17, and Zayd D., 16, both from Morocco, told us Croatian police pushed them back in April 2025. “They beat us on the legs with their sticks and took our phones,” Rami said. “We had almost reached Slovenia when we were pushed back. They treated us very badly. I don’t know why they did this.”

When we spoke with three men from Sudan who said they had just been pushed back by Croatian police, one of them, 25-year-old Mustafa S., told us, “The [Croatian] police caught us. They took everything and beat us. . . . They hit us on our feet, arms, and back with their batons.”[46]

Croatian police beat boys, particularly teenagers, as well as men, we heard. An aid worker in Bosnia and Herzegovina told us in early March 2026, “One week ago I identified a group of eight boys, all about age 15, who had just been pushed back. The Croatian police caught them near the border and beat all of them, hitting them with batons and the butts of their guns.” In another such case, an aid worker with another group told us in July 2026 that they assisted a group of 22 unaccompanied children who said Croatian police beat them, denied them access to asylum procedures, and detained them in Dugi Dol, an unofficial detention center.

“Sometimes police make us kneel and sometimes they force us to lay down on our stomachs” before carrying out beatings, Mustafa said.

Among the accounts we heard of violence by Croatian police against children:

Rasul S., a 31-year-old from Pakistan, told us Croatian police hit all of the men and boys in his group during a pushback in February 2026. “There were maybe 12 underage boys with us, about 16 or 17 years old. The police hit all these underage boys, same as the adult men,” he said.

Cemal H., from Türkiye, told us Croatian police hit his 10-year-old son on the head during a pushback in 2025, during which they also beat him and held lit cigarettes to his leg. After the boy was attacked by Croatian police, he stopped talking for months, a health professional told us.

The same health professional also described an incident in which police fired their weapons in the air after catching three teenage boys between 14 and 16 years of age, saying, “The boys were scared and traumatized from this incident.”

We heard many accounts of Croatian police hitting people’s legs and feet. For instance:

“They hit me on the shoulder, feet, and legs. . . . They put a weapon to my head to force me back to Bosnia,” said Hamid M., a 23-year-old from Morocco.

“They hit my legs and broke our phones. The police were beating us, laughing and filming us with their phones,” 20-year-old Ali D., also from Morocco, told us.

Zalmai B., age 27, showed us his swollen ankle, saying, “Croatian police hit my legs with a baton near Kladuša. My ankle has hurt for many days.”

Another man, Haider M., said he saw Croatian police kick a woman who was in a wheelchair.

Some people said Croatian police punched them in the face, sometimes with brass knuckles, which they called “the box.” Nadim S., a 24-year-old from Afghanistan, said Croatian police had hit him with the “box,” pointing to visible swelling and bruising on his face and head. Luqman F. said Croatian police had hit him in the face, cracking a tooth, before forcing him into a river marking the border between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Faraz T., from Afghanistan, also described being hit with the “box” as well as batons and said Croatian police kicked him in the crotch.

In some cases, as with the group of boys in the incident described by the health professional, we heard that police fired their weapons in the air as they ordered people to return to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Franck A., 47, from Congo-Brazzaville, told us that when Croatian police caught him in early 2025, “They pointed us toward Bosnia and shouted, ‘Go, go, go, Bosnia’ in English and shot in the air.”

Accounts collected by Save the Children, other groups working in Una Sana Canton, in northwest Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Croatian ombuds office also describe beatings and other violence by Croatian police during pushbacks. “My mother was hit by a Croatian police car and broke her arm; now she has a cast. The Croatian police were terrible—they beat us, broke our phones, and sent us back,” a 16-year-old boy told Save the Children in 2025.

Aid groups told us they were seeing more injuries from dog bites than in previous years. In August 2026, a health provider said, “The number of dog bites we are treating has at least doubled this year. Police almost regularly have dogs with them now.”

By some accounts, pushback tactics have become somewhat less violent compared with previous years. “In the past there were broken ribs and a lot of blood,” one aid worker told Human Rights Watch. “The police mainly hit people in the legs now.”

Nonetheless, as her description indicates, Croatian police continued to inflict cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment as they carried out pushbacks. In addition to frequent beatings and other physical violence, “verbal and emotional abuse is strong,” an aid worker with another organization told Human Rights Watch.

An outreach worker with a third group said, “Nearly everybody who is pushed back has a similar experience of violence. There is mostly no difference in the treatment of men, women, and children. . . . Cases where people don’t experience violence [during pushbacks] are rare.”

“Where are the human rights?” asked Anwar M., a 40-year-old from Syria. “Here they will bring a case against somebody for mistreating animals, but with migrants, you can do anything. This treatment we are facing is against the European Convention and all of the human rights conventions.”

Theft of Money

We heard repeated, consistent accounts of Croatian police taking all the money people had on them before pushing them back to Bosnia and Herzegovina. For instance, Saraj R., a 17-year-old boy from Afghanistan, said that when Croatian police caught him in March 2025, “they took my phone, money, shoes, and coat” before pushing him back. “It was very bad,” he said, beginning to shake as he recalled the experience. Marwan B., a 43-year-old man from Palestine, said that before Croatian police forced him to return to Bosnia and Herzegovina in March 2025, “They took 120 euros from me, and they took my wallet and put it in the fire.”

Hasan R., a 24-year-old man from Pakistan, listed the amounts he could recall Croatian police taking from him during various pushbacks between January and March 2026, saying, “The first time the police took €150. Then €80. The next time €70. Another time they took €100, another time €120. Each time they caught me, they took all the money I had.”

The following accounts were among the many others we heard of Croatian police taking money from people before pushbacks: Mounir A. (€100 taken in February 2026), Mustafa S. (€150, March 2026), Omar S. (€150, April 2025), Khaled O. (€150, March 2025), Khalil R. (€150, early 2025), Behrooz P. (€300, February 2026), Sami T. (€300, March 2025), Darwesh S. (€400, February 2026), Wahid A. (€700, February 2026), and Ali D. (€700, March 2025).

In some instances, Croatian police have issued bills or receipts for costs purportedly incurred in detention. “Sometimes people get receipts for food or drinks they didn’t receive. The receipts are always in the amount the person had on them,” an aid worker told us. Officials with Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Service for Foreigners’ Affairs (SFA) also described this practice by Croatian police.

Confiscation or Destruction of Phones and Other Property

Similarly, the accounts we heard indicate that Croatian police continue to confiscate or destroy mobile phones, a practice Human Rights Watch and other groups have previously documented. “They [the Croatian police] took everything; they took phones, chargers, money, and forced us back,” said Mohammed A., from Bangladesh, describing a pushback by Croatian police in March 2025. Mustafa S., a 25-year-old from Sudan, told us that when Croatian police caught him and three other men, “They took everything . . . smashed all of our phones.”[86] In separate interviews, 10 men we interviewed in August 2026 also said police took their phones, sometimes destroying them, during each of the several pushbacks each man had faced in the previous month.

Rashid D., from Afghanistan, who said that Croatian police had pushed him back to Bosnia and Herzegovina five times in early 2025, explained:

The first time they broke our phones so that they couldn’t be fixed. The second time they destroyed the SIM card slot and the charging port. And the third time they took our phones along with money, credit cards, and everything we had in our pockets. And they beat us with the [batons] they had in their hands and sent us to Bosnia.

He did not take a phone with him on his two subsequent attempts to enter Croatia, he said.[88]

We also heard numerous accounts of police forcing people to hand over shoes or clothing before returning them to Bosnia and Herzegovina. “They put everything in one bag and didn’t give it back when we asked to give us what’s in the bag,” Vivek S., a 24-year-old man from India, said.

Mounir A. told us Croatian police made him give them his jacket and trousers, along with €100, before pushing him back in early 2026. Jamal A. and Aziz K., whose accounts appear at the beginning of this chapter, said Croatian police made them strip to their underwear prior to a pushback in March 2025. Ibrahim B., a 20-year-old from Morocco, told us Croatian police made him give them his shoes in addition to his phone and money before they pushed him back in April 2025. Omar S., a 20-year-old man from Algeria, also said Croatian police made everyone in his group remove their clothes before pushing them back in early 2025.

An outreach worker with an aid organization in Bosnia and Herzegovina that assists people who have been pushed back from Croatia confirmed that she has spoken to children who were barefoot and shirtless who said they had walked overnight to Bihać after Croatian police took their shoes, jackets, and shirts before pushing them back to Bosnia and Herzegovinia. “On Saturday we identified 14 children who arrived without shoes, cold, sick. One boy fainted from exhaustion,” she told us in April 2025.

“Croatian police smash and burn asthma inhalers and medications people are carrying,” a health provider with another aid group told us in August 2026.

In some instances, Croatian police also seized or destroyed items such as glasses, crutches, and other assistive devices.

Forcing People Across Rivers

As with the accounts of Jamal A. and Aziz K., the 17-year-old boys whose cases appear at the beginning of this chapter, we heard that Croatian police ordered some people to wade or swim across rivers, including the Korana, to return to Bosnia and Herzegovina. “They took our stuff, phones, and stripped us from our clothes and forced 7 of us into cold river,” said Omar S., a 20-year-old man from Algeria, describing a pushback in March 2025.

Yassine I., a 36-year-old man from Morocco, said Croatian police had done the same to him in early 2026: “When they caught us, they threw us in the river. This happened to me twice.”

Mustafa S., 25, from Sudan, said that after Croatian police caught him and three other men in March 2026, “They threatened to set their dogs on us to force us into the river to cross back into Bosnia. We were cold and wet. We had to walk back to Bihać.[99]

Similarly, Tariq A., from Pakistan, said that Croatian police had forced him and others into the river in early 2026 even when the water level was high after heavy rains. Bilal O., a 36-year-old man, who was travelling with Tariq, added, “It was very cold.”

Humanitarian groups working in Bosnia and Herzegovina also told us that they received frequent accounts of Croatian police forcing people to cross rivers.

Detention in Abusive Conditions Before Being Pushed Back

Harun C., a 17-year-old Kurdish boy from Türkiye, told us Croatian police held him, his 15-year-old brother, their 2-year-old sister, and their parents in the back of a parked van for two days without access to food or water before pushing them back to Bosnia and Herzegovina in April 2025.

Other people also described being held in vans for a day or longer before Croatian police pushed them back. For instance, Yassine I., a 36-year-old man from Morocco, said prior to one pushback in early 2026 he was held in a Croatian police van for one day with seven other people. “There were children with us—16, 17 years old,” he said. Between February and October 2025, Save the Children also documented accounts of people detained for hours or days in poorly ventilated Croatian police vans without water or food.

In addition, we heard several accounts of Croatian police detaining people for days in overcrowded cells resembling shipping containers, often without adequate food or water, in a remote location near the border, a description that matches the unofficial detention center Dugi Dol. For instance, Yassine, the man from Morocco, told us Croatian police held him for 72 hours before pushing him back to Bosnia and Herzegovina in February 2026. “The station was in a small, abandoned village,” he said. One man, Luqman F., said he was held for 17 days. “There were many people in the cell. They kept bringing more and more people in,” said 25-year-old Khalil R.

Save the Children has also reported that children and adults apprehended near Velika Kladuša are often detained in Croatia in abusive conditions before being pushed back to Bosnia and Herzegovina:

They were reportedly held in unfurnished spaces without windows and kept for several hours or even overnight with insufficient food and water, before being expelled in larger groups. . . . The reports of being detained before pushbacks suggest the use of a detention centre in the proximity of the border, which aligns with reported indications that Dugi Dol, a container-based transit reception centre around 30 km into the Croatian territory from the border with BiH, intended for the temporary registration of asylum seekers for up to 72 hours, was increasingly being used for prolonged de facto detention.[109]

Croatian police began to use Dugi Dol as a migrant detention center in the second half of 2024, with children and adults held there for extended periods—in some cases between three and seven days. The Center for Peace Studies has reported:

The site lacks basic infrastructure, including running water, electricity, proper beds, adequate sanitation, and heating or cooling, rendering it unfit for human habitation, particularly during extreme weather conditions. . . . The facility, functioning as a de facto detention centre, is not officially registered and remains under the jurisdiction of the Karlovac Police Department, operating without transparency.

The Croatian ombudsman observed in 2025:

The material conditions of the accommodation at [Dugi Dol] remain inadequate, especially for families with children and vulnerable groups. People are housed in containers without mattresses or bedding, without guaranteed access to showers, hot water, and adequate sanitary facilities, while chemical toilets are located outside the living areas. Only dry food is provided, and clothing is supplied through donations . . . . Such conditions, particularly with regard to children and other vulnerable groups, may amount to inhuman or degrading treatment within the meaning of Article 3 of the ECHR.

Family Separation During Pushbacks

In some instances, Croatian police separated families during pushbacks. Patience F., from Ghana, said that when Croatian police apprehended her and her family:

We told them that we are a family, but they still took my husband away in one van and me and my daughters in another. . . . We were separated for two days from my husband. They pushed me and my daughters to Bosnia through the woods. No phone, no food, no water. We were walking all day. We were lost and scared for many hours. We didn’t know where my husband was. We all got very sick. One of my daughters collapsed and needed to go to the hospital in Bihać. They treated us like animals.

All we wanted was to go to camp in Zagreb. They don’t listen to us. Maybe we have some problem, maybe? someone is chasing us. But they don’t want to hear our reasons. They don’t care. They push us back.

Her husband, Stephen F., said, “The Croatian police they took my phone and released their dog on me. They pushed me through the bush back to Bosnia. I didn’t know where my daughters and wife were. I found them in the camp in Bihać.”

Inadequate Reception Conditions in Bosnia and Herzegovina

Families with children and unaccompanied children in Bosnia and Herzegovina are accommodated in the Lipa reception center, which has separate sections for each of these populations and a larger area allocated to men who are not travelling with their families. The Ministry of Internal Affairs was due to assume full responsibility for the day-to-day management of the Lipa center in 2026. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) had provided operational and technical support for the administration of the camp.

When Human Rights Watch visited Lipa in March 2026, the family section housed 21 children, 31 parents (18 men and 13 women), and 11 single women. The center also had 21 unaccompanied boys in the dedicated section for them and 273 adult men.

Lipa is relatively remote. There is no regular local bus service between Lipa and Bihać, the nearest city, some 25 kilometers away, and taxis are expensive—particularly for migrants, who often said they have to pay as much as €50 each way, far more than locals are charged. Many of the people we interviewed for this report described walking for hours along a busy highway to reach the shops, services, and recreational opportunities available in Bihać. Winters are often harsh, with snowfall sometimes reaching adults’ waists and increasing people’s sense of isolation.

The center has faced persistent water shortages and frequent power outages. Housing units, in a series of modules, are spartan and compact—adequate for short stays by adults but not designed for the needs of families, who are each usually accommodated in a single room regardless of the number, age range, and gender of children.

Health care professionals were only available at the center three days a week for an hour and a half on each of those days, according to the posted signs Human Rights Watch saw on the clinic door and the accounts of aid workers who were familiar with the center’s operations. Health services outside of those hours and emergency or specialized care required a transfer to Bihać, as do child vaccinations and other pediatric services.

In December 2025, Alimamy Alusine Jalloh, a computer engineer from Sierra Leone, died at the center several days after a violent pushback by Croatian police. He reportedly told center staff he was experiencing severe abdominal pain and dizziness and exhibited other symptoms of internal bleeding, but staff did not arrange a hospital transfer until the following day, which may have been a contributing factor in his death. When his sister travelled to Bihać to bury him, she requested medical documentation to determine the precise cause of his death. Authorities did not respond to her request.

As we saw during our March 2026 visit, the center made some effort to provide space for children to play, but even these areas offered little variation from the grey walls of the modules and the unshaded gravel courtyards.

There were no classes at the center and no plans to offer any classes there. Although the center director and staff told us that children can attend local schools nearby, that opportunity had several important caveats: only children of elementary school age had access to education, and the bus used to take them to and from class only seats six children.

Haliah M., 12, and her sister Roya, 14, whose cases are profiled at the beginning of this report, told us they and their 16- and 17-year-old brothers had no access to education because the center offered no options for children of secondary school age. Zahra N., from Iran, said that only her younger child was able to attend class, and then only when there was space on the bus. “Usually children who are 12 years of age and up don’t receive education,” an aid worker commented. Asked about children’s access to education, the Lipa center director did not directly acknowledge these limitations, saying only, “It is up to the parents whether they want to send their children to school.”

If a social worker cannot accompany the bus, if the bus is out of service, or if it is being used for another purpose, children do not go to school. In practice, these limitations can mean that children are more often out of school than not, we heard. In particular, “unaccompanied children in Lipa rarely have access to education outside of the camp because they need a social worker to accompany them,” said Tatjana Ristić, advocacy and campaigns specialist with Save the Children’s Northwest Balkans Country Office.

Until late 2025, unaccompanied children and families with children were housed at a facility close to the Bihać city center, offering them ready access to schools, health clinics, shops and other services, and parks and other places for children to play. Local government officials told Human Rights Watch the arrangement to use Borići as a family migrant center was intended from the outset to be temporary. When local officials told the families in Borići that they would instead be offered accommodations at Lipa, “a lot of families refused to go,” an aid worker told us.

As a consequence of these factors, “children and families don’t find it suitable in Lipa,” Ristić told us, adding, “They are frightened and lonely.”

The Ongoing Need for European Union Oversight

As supported by the numerous accounts of pushbacks documented in this report, the Croatian government, through inadequate oversight, ineffective investigations and a lack of meaningful accountability, and repeated official minimization if not outright denial of the existence of the practice, continues to demonstrate official tolerance of these persistent collective expulsions, often violently and accompanied by other serious human rights violations.

In response to our request for comment on the findings of this report, the Croatian Ministry of the Interior denied that its police engaged in pushbacks, stated that all migrants who arrive in Croatia have access to international protection procedures, and told us that police had received guidance and training on the implementation of the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum. The ministry’s reply appears in full in the annex to this report. Faced with persistent violations by Croatian police and the Croatian government’s failure to effectively prevent, investigate, and seek accountability for these violations, the European Union has in turn failed to prevent collective expulsion and ill-treatment by Croatian authorities.

To its credit, the Croatian government strengthened the authority of the Croatian Independent Monitoring Mechanism (IMM), a border monitoring mechanism established in 2021 with EU funding. For instance, the mechanism was able—in the final year of its mandate—to conduct unannounced visits to police stations and other places of detention and is now able to visit areas between border crossing stations, known as the “green border,” as recommended by Human Rights Watch and other groups. The mechanism’s advisory board observed in June 2026:

In response to past concerns expressed by the Advisory Board, the IMM has improved significantly its monitoring methodology, carrying out frequent announced and unannounced field visits, examining multiple sources of evidence and, together with the police, piloting a “letter of rights and complaints” procedure.

The Border Police Administration has also directed agents at border crossings not to turn away people who “approach entry border control to express an intention to seek international protection.”

Croatia’s Ministry of the Interior informed Human Rights Watch that 25 Croatian police officers have faced disciplinary proceedings between 2020 and 2025 “in connection with their treatment of migrants, of whom seven were given a disciplinary sanction.” In 2026, in addition, “one complaint was recorded regarding the conduct of police officers toward migrants, and the investigation into the complaint’s merits is ongoing.” It does not appear that any Croatian police officer has ever been prosecuted and convicted for abuses against migrants.

Nonetheless, the border monitoring mechanism’s final report, published in March 2026, does not clearly indicate what violations it found—or, in the words of its advisory board, “to what extent relevant national, European and international fundamental human rights standards and safeguards are respected.” The report does not draw on the findings of human rights and humanitarian groups and makes no reference to the reports of the Croatian ombuds office. It refers to the baseline requirement of compliance with legal norms as “best practices” and minimizes accounts of pushbacks and associated ill-treatment. In one case “baton strikes and other physical assaults, resulting in visible injuries to two persons” who were not resisting apprehension are represented as “detected irregularities in individual cases.”

The Croatian Ministry of the Interior announced the replacement of the IMM with a fundamental rights monitoring mechanism, a new requirement for all EU member states under the Screening Regulation and the Asylum Procedure Regulation. The Croatian ombuds office has warned that the new mechanism does not appear to have complete independence.

In September 2025, the Council of Europe’s Division on Migration and Refugees undertook a joint mission to Croatia to examine border monitoring and the treatment of unaccompanied children, releasing a superficial report of the mission’s findings the following month. .

European Union institutions have tools for direct oversight and enforcement of Croatia’s adherence to human rights norms, including the principle of nonrefoulement, the prohibition of collective expulsion, the best interests of the child, the right to asylum, and the prohibition of torture and other ill-treatment.

For instance, the European Rule of Law Mechanism allows an annual dialogue between the European Commission and member states, using the Commission’s Rule of Law report as a basis for these discussions. Recent Rule of Law reports have noted the challenges faced by the Croatian ombuds office with access to information on specific cases on the treatment of irregular migrants, but they have not examined the weaknesses of the border monitoring mechanism, nor have they addressed pushbacks more directly.

The European Commission can open infringement proceedings against an EU member state that fails to implement EU law.

The European Parliament has a broad oversight role, with the authority to establish a committee of inquiry to examine violations of EU law by member states.

Funding and other agreements between EU institutions (including the European Commission and EU agencies) and one or more EU member states, including EU funding for border enforcement, should be implemented in conformity with the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights and EU law. Compliance audits by the European Court of Auditors can examine whether these EU funds are spent in a manner consistent with EU laws and regulations.

Moreover, under the EU Conditionality Regulation, the European Commission may suspend EU funding for breaches of the principles of the rule of law “that are widespread or due to recurrent practices or omissions by public authorities.” Such breaches include “failing to prevent, correct or sanction arbitrary or unlawful decisions by public authorities, including by law-enforcement authorities.”

The European Union can and should make greater use of these tools to address ongoing reports of pushbacks by Croatian authorities.

Legal Standards

The prohibition on collective expulsions is a norm under international law and explicitly set out in article 4 of Protocol No. 4 to the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) and article 19(1) of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights (CFR), to which Croatia is a party. The prohibition is violated when states remove people “without examining their personal circumstances and, consequently, without enabling them to put forward their arguments against the measure taken by the relevant authority.” Pushbacks, which prevent people from reaching, entering, or remaining in a particular territory and usually afford summary or no screening for protection needs, meet this standard.

The prohibition of torture and other cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment or punishment is one of the core absolute prohibitions under international law, and permits no exceptions nor justifications. It is a peremptory norm of international law and enshrined in multiple treaties to which Croatia is a party, including the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, the ECHR, the CFR, and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR).

The accounts Human Rights Watch documented from victims demonstrate that these pushbacks to Bosnia and Herzegovina are not only an extralegal response to irregular migration but given the manner in which Croatian police conducted them, they often constitute cruel, gratuitous, vindictive, and humiliating treatment intended to harm and degrade those who are pushed back. Accordingly, Croatian police frequently violate the prohibition of torture and other ill-treatment when they carry out pushbacks.

The principle of nonrefoulement prohibits states from transferring anyone, directly or indirectly, to a place where they would have a well-founded fear of persecution or would face a risk of torture or other cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment. The non-refoulement principle applies to actions at the border such as rejection or non-admission. Accordingly, the UN Human Rights Committee has called on states to ensure the right to make asylum applications at border crossing points to “[f]ully respect the principle of non-refoulement.” The Committee against Torture has called on states to “[e]nsure access to the territory and sufficient and effective protection from refoulement at borders.” Similarly, the Committee on the Rights of the Child has called on states to guarantee children “access to the territory, regardless of the documentation they have or lack, and to be referred to authorities in charge of evaluating their needs in terms of protection of their rights, ensuring their procedural safeguards.”

The prohibition of refoulement is not limited to direct forcible returns; it applies to expulsions or returns effected “in any manner whatsoever,” meaning that it covers indirect measures. These include transferring a person to a state that does not effectively protect against onward transfer to harm—that is, indirect, chain, or secondary refoulement. The creation of circumstances that leave a person with no real alternative other than returning to a place of danger is also a form of refoulement.

Children as well as adults benefit from the prohibition on collective expulsion and the principle of nonrefoulement. In addition, they have the right to additional specific protections by virtue of their status as children, as provided by the ICCPR and the Convention on the Rights of the Child. These include broad protection against expulsion or return to harm, an obligation on the part of the state to assess the child’s best interests prior to expulsion, and the right of unaccompanied children to special protection and assistance.

The right to seek asylum is affirmed in article 14 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, reflected in the 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol, and guaranteed under the EU Charter. EU regulations and directives, including the Asylum Procedures Regulation and the Return Regulation, should be applied in a manner that is consistent with the EU Charter and with international human rights obligations.

Video shows protesters clashing with police outside Providence Saint Joseph Medical Center in Burbank on Monday night as what police say are immigration agents appear to take a man in a wheelchair into their custody.

The man was driven from the hospital to the downtown Los Angeles detention center.

The video from around 8 p.m. shows a line of Burbank police officers standing between protesters and the entrance to the hospital. Details about what led up to the confrontation were not immediately available.

Moments later, a group of what Burbank police say are immigration agents come out of the hospital, with one of them pushing a man in a wheelchair.

The Burbank officers are seen linking arms and blocking the protesters from the agents. At one point, there is pushing and shoving between officers and some of the protesters.

Then, an agent wearing a face mask is seen reaching for a man's camera before appearing to spray something into his face.

The video shows the immigration agents wheeling the man to a gray SUV, putting him inside and then driving away to the detention center.

Burbank police say they were called by the hospital because the protesters were blocking ambulance access to the property and that they did not make any arrests.

Some of the protesters said their goal was to disrupt the immigration agents.

"We've been trying to do our best to show up where ICE is and to counterprotest," a man who wished only to be identified as Toby told NBC Los Angeles. "And we always do it peacefully. But we can't handle this happening, not only in our state and in our cities anymore, but in this country."

NBCLA has reached out to the hospital and to ICE for a statement but has not received a response.

This is a developing story.

text:
The lack of transparency from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) regarding a policy that expands electronic monitoring of immigrants has reached the federal court in Charlotte.

At the center of the controversy is the “Helland Memorandum,” formally titled “Increasing Face-to-Face Appearances at Contractor Offices for Participants in the Alternatives to Detention Program.”

The lawsuit seeks to compel the agency to publish the memorandum in its entirety and comply with its disclosure obligations under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA).

“People shouldn’t have to sue the government to find out the rules they are expected to follow,” said Evan Benz, a lawyer for Amica Center for Immigrant Rights“This litigation really shouldn’t have been necessary,” he added.

The hearing was scheduled for November 18 at the Charles R. Jonas Federal Building, where the Charlotte Federal Court operates. Amica Center and the Carolina Migrant Network are pursuing the lawsuit, with legal representation that includes The Melo Law Firm, PLLC.

What does the memorandum impose?

According to the organizations, it instructs ICE agents to impose ankle monitors "whenever possible" and requires pregnant women under GPS surveillance to wear the devices on their wrists.

Mariam Ruiz, a community organizer with the Carolina Migrant Network, questioned whether these rules would be applied without making the document public.

“When government agencies create rules that affect people’s lives, those people have the right “No one should have to file requests for access to documents or go to court to find out what is expected of them,” he said.

ICE delivers incomplete version of memorandum

The organizations noted that ICE did not initially respond to their request for information. After the lawsuit was filed, ICE provided a redacted version.

“They agreed to publish the memo, but in a completely redacted version that renders it useless,” Benz argued. According to the lawyer, this disclosure violates both the letter and the spirit of the law.

The case raises the question of whether FOIA requires proactively publishing policies that affect the public and whether ICE can keep hidden portions of a document that, according to the plaintiffs, it has already disclosed in full in other proceedings in the Pennsylvania court.

The physical and psychological damage caused by monitors

Benz warned that the consequences go beyond access to documents. “They cause psychological harm, they cause physical harm,” she said about the monitors. She added that the in-person appointments and home visits can lead to lost work shifts and income.

As an example, Benz recounted the case of a Venezuelan asylum seeker he identified as José. According to the lawyer, José was released on bail after being detained at the Stewart Detention Center in Georgia, but ICE subsequently placed a monitor on him, even though the immigration judge had not ordered it.

“No justification was given,” he stated. The lawyer asserted that the device causes him physical discomfort and that the monitoring obligations interfere with his employment at a restaurant.

Benz stated that more than 50,000 people wear ankle monitors in the United States, and that ICE intends to extend their use to all participants in the Alternatives to Detention program, which totals more than 180,000.

You may be interested: Families without income and children living in fear: the aftermath of Charlotte's Web

A favorable ruling from the judge is expected.

Following the hearing, Benz expressed confidence in a favorable ruling, although he clarified that there were still documents to be filed. “We are optimistic after today’s hearing that the judge will rule in our favor,” he noted.

At the end of the hearing, which lasted about two hours, the judge told the prosecutor that she would have 10 days to present her argument as to why the memorandum should not be published in its entirety.

The prosecutor responded that she did not want to do so and suggested to the judge that the plaintiffs should present their arguments first.

“I don’t think it’s fair; they (ICE) don’t want to say why they don’t want to publish a four-word phrase,” he told Enlace Latino NC Stefania Arteaga, founder and co-director of Carolina Migrant Network.

The court gave the organizations 10 days to present their arguments, and after that, it will give ICE 10 days to present its own.

text:
A father and daughter detained by masked immigration officers on an airport jet bridge in Seattle, causing chaos in front of other passengers, were heading to a family baptism ceremony in California, their lawyer said Monday.

Other passengers boarding the Alaska Airlines flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Sunday used their cell phones to film the father and daughter being detained by the officers, who were wearing unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The recordings were widely viewed on social media.

The videos show the officers struggling with someone on the ground. The flight, bound for Los Angeles, was delayed.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers detained Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who it said had overstayed his visa "in violation of our nation’s laws".

During the confrontation, another passenger "hurled hot coffee on the officers," the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the US illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

The father and daughter were travelling to attend a baptism ceremony in California and are seeking asylum in the US, where they have lived since 2015, their lawyer, Olia Catala, told The Associated Press in a telephone interview Sunday. They have no criminal record, Catala said.

Mejia, in her mid-20s, had married a US citizen and filed paperwork for adjustment of her status, the attorney said. Mejia's husband was accompanying Mejia and her father when they were detained Sunday. Catala added. The husband was not detained, the attorney said.

"They’ve done everything correctly, and these are educated people," Catala said of the father and daughter. "She went to college, to university, she worked for a nonprofit. No criminal history [for] any of them. So it's just heartbreaking."

Both were being held at the Northwest ICE Processing Centre in Tacoma, Catala said.

She said Mejia was carrying a cup of coffee when the confrontation occurred.

"When somebody’s charging at you, you’re going to drop a cup of coffee," Catala said.

"It was just a lot of commotion, and honestly, if somebody is running at you or charging at you and they’re not wearing a uniform, you don’t know who they are," Catala said. "There was a lot of panic, chaos, not knowing what's going on."

Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people it says have overstayed visas.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns "directly with the appropriate authorities".

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would "engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred".

Washington Governor Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE's tactics were "deeply un-American" and called for the agency's abolition.

"The video is horrific and it is chilling," Ferguson said at a news conference Saturday with labour leaders and local elected officials.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — The National Immigration Project and the End SIJS Backlog Coalition condemn two U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) policies, issued November 20, that let immigration officials second-guess state juvenile court judges who have found a child was abused, abandoned, or neglected by a parent. The policies also allow USCIS to revoke protection young people have already won and to place them into deportation proceedings when they apply for a green card. Both took effect immediately and apply to every pending and future case under Special Immigrant Juvenile Status (SIJS), the protection Congress created in 1990 for these children, for whom a juvenile court has found it is not in their best interest to be returned to their home country. The organizations said the policies are clearly built to increase denials.

SIJS is available to young people under 21 whom a state juvenile court has found cannot safely reunify with one or both parents because of abuse, abandonment, neglect, or a similar basis under state law, and for whom returning to their home country is not in their best interest. Because of a visa backlog, young people approved for SIJS already wait years before they can apply for a green card.

Under the new policies (PA-2026-17 and PA-2026-18), USCIS will:

Stop deferring to the expertise of juvenile state courts, and let officers decide whether a young person went to court “primarily” for protection from a parent, using government databases as well as court records.

Give “additional scrutiny” to cases where one parent abandoned the child, though Congress made those children eligible in 2008.

Question traumatized youth about their petitions and add new screening and vetting, forcing them to discuss the abuse and neglect they suffered.

Reopen approved SIJS petitions and revoke them if officers decide the agency’s consent was “granted in error.”

Stop treating a young person’s SIJS eligibility as a point in their favor when deciding whether they deserve a green card.

Issue a Notice to Appear, the document that starts deportation proceedings, after a green card denial or a revocation.

Tens of thousands of vulnerable youth with pending SIJS petitions and green card applications are subject to the new policies.

“Behind every application is a young person who has had to confront painful childhood experiences and find the strength to rebuild their life despite circumstances they never chose,” said Eniley, a SIJS recipient and advocate who asked that their real name not be used. “These new USCIS policies add another layer of fear and uncertainty to a system that has already failed so many of us. We are not loopholes, security threats, or statistics. We are young people who have survived, advocated for ourselves, and fought for the stability we deserve. Our futures should not be held hostage by an immigration system that continues to move the finish line.”

These policies follow the administration's repeated attempts to end deferred action for SIJS youth, which has protected roughly 200,000 young people from deportation during that wait. A federal court blocked the first attempt in November 2025 in A.C.R. v. Noem, a case brought by the National Immigration Project and partners. USCIS ended the policy again in April 2026.

"Nelson Mandela said there can be no keener revelation of a society’s soul than the way in which it treats its children. By that measure, this administration has told us everything we need to know about it," said Rebecca Scholtz, Supervising Attorney at the National Immigration Project and a member of the steering committee of the End SIJS Backlog Coalition. "The law Congress wrote hasn't changed. USCIS changed the rules anyway, in the middle of young people’s cases, and told its officers to treat a child who survived neglect, abuse, and abandonment like a suspect. Singling out children Congress chose to shield, who lack the power to fight back, is cruelty by design. We will keep fighting to protect the rights of SIJS youth, alongside the young people these dangerous policies target."

The organizations are reviewing the policy and are evaluating every legal option. Young people with a pending or approved SIJS petition should talk with their attorney before taking any action.
