Alice Huang kept in contact with spy agency during affair: report

Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the Nvidia scandal, kept in contact with China’s top spy agency from the spring of 2025 until fall 2026, according to The New York Times. That time period overlaps with her relationship with Jensen Huang who was ousted as the chip company’s CEO and reinstated today.

Trump posts altered picture of Huang holding up a red bra

In a post on Truth Social, the president posted a doctored picture of a bloodied Huang holding up a red bra.

The picture is a takeoff of the famous Trump "fight, fight, fight" picture following the attempt on his life in Butler, Pennsylvania, during the 2024 campaign, where Trump pumped his first in the air after the shooting.

The version he posted shows Huang instead of Trump, with a bra in the hand he pumped in the air, and an Nvidia flag flying behind him instead of Old Glory.

White House turkeys to live large after pardon ceremony

Expected presidential pardon recipients Freedom and Feathers gobbled up attention at a press conference today, ahead of their scheduled appearance at the White House.

The beefy birds — Freedom is 42 pounds and Feather 40 pounds — were introduced at the Willard InterContinental hotel in Washington.

They are headed tomorrow to the White House South Lawn, “where President Donald Trump will hopefully grant them a presidential pardon,” National Turkey Federation Chair Christy Puffenbarger said.

People can vote for which of the two will receive the traditional ceremonial pardon on the White House’s website until midnight, but both will be spared, Puffenbarger said.

The two hail from West Virginia, where turkey farmer Scott Reitzel said they were raised to be accustomed to people and photographers.

After the ceremony, the turkeys will be taken to their new home at Texas A&M University’s Poultry Science Department, where they’ll live out their days in a “brand new climate controlled home with a front porch and outdoor access,” the school’s Audrey McElroy said.

Schumer says Congress must investigate Trump's role in bringing Huang back to Nvidia

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said the White House's involvement in Huang's reinstatement at Nvidia "underscores the need for Congress to act."

“Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he’s learned nothing from his resounding election defeat," Schumer said in a post on X.

The senator added that "Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain."

Democrats will become the majority in both houses of Congress in January.

Huang’s reinstatement 'changes nothing' for House panels set to interview him, committee spokesperson says

Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO “changes nothing” for the three House committees that are set to conduct a closed-door transcribed interview with Huang on Dec. 1, a spokesperson for the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence told NBC News.

“When Jensen was CEO, our three committees were demanding answers. When he was removed and no longer CEO, we were still pursing the facts. The fact that he was been reinstated as CEO, changes nothing. There are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers. Seems like the only thing that is consistent these days on this issue is our three Committee’s commitment to oversight,” the spokesperson said in a statement.

Huang is scheduled to appear before the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party for a transcribed interview Dec. 1. Nvidia's general counsel is also set to also appear Dec. 2 for transcribed interviews.

Last week, a spokesperson for the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence said there is a “good chance” that transcripts of the interviews will be released after they are conducted.

Trump says he spoke ‘directly and indirectly’ with Nvidia’s board about reinstating Huang

Trump said he spoke with Nvidia’s board about reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO in an interview on CNBC this morning, where he sought to provide assurances to address the concerns of lawmakers and others about national security.

“I’ve been speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it,” Trump said today. “And I felt more strongly as I saw what was happening with the company, because that was, to me, a very important part of our country.”

Read the full story here.

Lawmakers condemn Nvidia's decision to reinstate Huang

Lawmakers from both sides of the aisle criticized Huang's reinstatement and raised concerns over potential national security implications.

Retiring Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., said that Nvidia should have not brought Huang back and should have "ignored the Administration’s inexplicable desire to save Huang."

"Congress needs to get to the bottom of who approved high end computer chips sales to China," Bacon said in a post on X. "We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology. We need sunlight on who is responsible."

Similarly, outgoing Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, threw doubt on Nvidia saying in this morning's statement that the company was "confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk."

"No national security risk?" Cornyn asked in an X post. "Based on what?"

Across the aisle, Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., accused Trump of "selling out our national security to keep the stock market high." Similarly, Illinois' Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker said in a post to X that "this is the greed and lack of accountability that the country just rejected."

"There are serious national security concerns being raised about Jensen Huang that should not be papered over by this administration or the Nvidia board," he continued.

Jay Clayton will serve as acting national cyber director

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will serve as the acting national cyber director while Kirsten Davies, currently the Defense Department's chief information officer, awaits Senate confirmation to lead the office, a senior White House official and a U.S. official confirmed to NBC News.

The White House official added that the strong support Davies received convinced Trump to nominate her to lead the office permanently rather than keep her in an acting capacity.

Axios first reported Clayton would serve as acting cyber director.

Clayton said in a statement provided by the White House that Davies "has the experience and capabilities needed to help America navigate our increasingly complex and powerful digital infrastructure as our next National Cyber Director. I look forward to working with the ONCD team to ensure Kirsten has a seamless transition into the role upon her confirmation by the Senate.”

The senior White House official also said Davies will provide expertise to the office and assist Clayton while her nomination is pending, noting her leadership over the department’s information technology and cybersecurity strategy, budget and execution.

The previous cyber director, Sean Cairncross, is leaving the administration after tech outages that hit both the private and public sectors, a White House official confirmed last week.

Trump says Nvidia 'made the correct and proper decision' to reinstate Jensen Huang

Trump said in a Truth Social post that Nvidia "made the correct and proper decision" to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO.

"The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy," Trump wrote. "The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security."

Huang resigned after allegedly having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Last week, Trump traveled to China and met with Chinese President Xi Jinping, though the White House had said before the trip that they did not expect Trump to bring up Alice Huang, the alleged spy. Trump said at a Friday press conference, though, that he "did discuss that" with Xi.

Trump said in his post that the government does not have evidence that Huang "engaged in any unlawful conduct."

"On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure," Trump added.

Trump called for Huang to be reinstated over the weekend, saying in a Truth Social post that "it would be the best thing for the Company" and the country.

Trump hosts exclusive dinner for investors in his declining meme coin

Trump rewarded top investors in his declining meme coin with an exclusive dinner last night as Democrats focus future congressional probes on the president’s business dealings, including his crypto ventures.

The event came as the president’s meme coin, known as $TRUMP on crypto exchanges, has declined dramatically in worth since its launch just days before his second inauguration in January 2025. The coin’s value peaked at $74 per coin but now trades below $1.

Read the full story here.

Democrats win largest House majority since 1992

Democrat Chuck Hubbard has defeated GOP Rep. Virginia Foxx for a congressional seat in North Carolina, NBC News projects, adding to a Democratic wave that is projected to deliver the party at least 258 House seats.

It’s the largest House majority that any party has held this century, according to the Office of the House Historian, and four races are yet to be called. It’s also the largest Democratic majority since 1992, when the party also won 258 seats.

Read the full story here.

Democratic National Committee sets broad rules for the party’s 2028 presidential debates

The Democratic National Committee will hold 12 debates next year and in 2028 for candidates seeking the party’s presidential nomination, the party announced, as it sets rules of the road for what’s expected to be a crowded campaign for the White House.

The DNC's announcement lays out a process that hews closely to the rules under which Democrats ran in 2020, the last time the party had an open primary.

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed says he’s open to working with the Trump administration

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., said he’s open to working with Trump and Vice President JD Vance to bring down costs and improve healthcare for Americans, just weeks after the two Republicans and the Democrat traded verbal attacks during a tense campaign.

Asked whether he intended to meet with the president or vice president soon, El-Sayed told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that “plans are in the works.”

Trump to deliver remarks at the DOJ this afternoon

This afternoon, Trump will deliver remarks at the Justice Department. The White House said that the speech will be on “protecting American families,” but the administration has not yet shared further information. The president held a lengthy press conference Friday, and it’s not clear whether he will take further questions at the Justice Department event.

First lady Melania Trump, meanwhile, will welcome the new White House Christmas tree earlier in the day, the White House said.

The White House is traditionally decorated ahead of the holidays, and the first lady often has a prominent role in the decor.

Later, Melania Trump and second lady Usha Vance will participate in a Red Cross care package assembly alongside military spouses, the White House said. The president is not scheduled to attend the program.

text:
Twenty-one states and Pennsylvania's governor have sued the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development over a rule that would deny federal housing assistance to families if any household member lacks eligible citizenship or immigration status.

The states say the rule could split up families or evict U.S. citizens from public housing. States including California, New York, Arizona and Massachusetts joined the suit. HUD defends the rule, arguing illegal immigrants are taking advantage of the current eligibility requirements.

The rule takes effect on Dec. 14. It would require people to verify their citizenship or eligible immigration status to receive federal housing assistance.

“No child should lose their home over a parent's immigration status,” said California Attorney General Rob Bonta during a press conference. “This rule is cruel, and it’s unlawful."

For over three decades, Congress has authorized prorated federal housing assistance for mixed-status families, whose members have different citizenship or immigration statuses. These families receive less assistance if a household member is ineligible because of their immigration status. The new rule would ban mixed-status families from receiving any assistance.

“Picture a mom with two kids in public housing. All U.S. citizens. Their dad is not eligible. Under this rule, all four of them lose their home,” Bonta said.

One in five children in California is part of a mixed-status family, said Bonta, estimating that the rule will affect 7,000 households in his state. The new rule would also require public housing authorities and private landlords to report tenants who fail verification to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

“Congress never gave HUD the power to throw mixed-status families out of their homes or turn private landlords into immigration enforcement. But that’s exactly what this rule does,” Bonta said.

The new rule is the latest in a series of moves by President Donald Trump's administration targeting legal immigrants. Those moves include restricting healthcare, nutrition benefits and other subsidies while stripping legal protections from some immigrant groups to make more people eligible for deportation.

HUD Secretary Scott Turner first announced the proposed rule in January, but the department finalized it only last week.

“HUD’s final rule fully implements the 1980 Housing and Community Development Act and ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars. This rule guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing. This change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist," said Turner in an emailed statement on Monday.

Earlier this year, HUD conducted an audit with DHS and identified 20,000 mixed-status households receiving federally funded housing assistance nationwide. The department said illegal immigrants were using “loopholes” to access benefits while the department struggled to provide housing for all who need it.

text:
Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell is suing Immigration and Customs Enforcement for continuing to make civil immigration arrests inside state courthouses.

"Under the 10th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, Massachusetts retains sovereign authority over its judicial system and its administration of justice," said Campbell at a press conference on Monday.

On November 3, the PROTECT Act, a state law aimed at keeping ICE away from sensitive locations like courthouses, schools, daycares, and healthcare facilities without a judicial warrant, went into effect. Since that time, Campbell says ICE has made at least 38 civil arrests at state courthouses in violation of the state law. Campbell argues that ICE activity is interfering with the state's constitutional right to run its courts as it chooses.

"Survivors of domestic violence have been afraid to come to court to seek restraining orders against their abusers," said Campbell, listing the ways she argues ICE has disrupted the Commonwealth's court system.

In recent months, federal courts have ruled both for and against states seeking to clamp down on ICE. In June, a U.S. District Court judge in California ruled that ICE cannot conduct immigration enforcement in California courts. Last week, a U.S. District Court judge in Connecticut issued a preliminary injunction blocking certain sections of the state's law restricting ICE enforcement, including the ability of federal agents to wear masks.

With the conflicting rulings, Attorney Dina Haynes, the executive director of the Orville H. Schell, Jr. Center for International Human Rights at Yale Law School and a constitutional law expert, says she expects the case to head all the way to the Supreme Court.

"I haven't seen any sign that the federal government is unwilling to use its considerable resources to challenge every lawsuit that they lose," Haynes said.

Haynes told WBZ that Massachusetts has a valid argument against federal immigration officials and could expand its case to include the argument that the president himself overstepped his authority by issuing an executive order allowing ICE arrests in state courts even when state law prohibits them.

"Congress is the branch of government that writes the law on immigration," Haynes said.

An ICE spokesperson told WBZ that federal law supersedes state law and that, "The Supremacy Clause makes it clear that sanctuary politicians do not control federal law enforcement."

text:

EVERETT — Federal immigration agents detained a father and daughter from Mountlake Terrace as they were preparing to board a flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday morning.

The two people detained by the federal agents were Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza and Sofia Larrondo Hernandez Mejia, according to Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which shared a statement about the arrest on social media Saturday. They are both from Mountlake Terrace, their attorney, Olia Catala, told KING 5 and KUOW.

The two are currently being held in the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, according to an ICE database.

Videos of the Saturday morning arrests, shared on social media and by news outlets, show masked people in unmarked clothes taking a man and woman out of a jet bridge as passengers were preparing boarding a flight to Los Angeles. People can be heard screaming and crying, and at one point, a person is thrown to the floor.

The arrests drew strong condemnation from both civil rights advocates and elected officials.

In March, Gov. Bob Ferguson had signed a bill prohibiting law enforcement, including federal immigration agents, from wearing masks while conducting official business in Washington state. An ICE spokesperson previously said following an Everett immigration arrest that the agency would not abide by that law and that the officers wear masks “to protect themselves and their families from real-world threats including agitators.”

In a video posted to social media Sunday, Gov. Ferguson called to abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

“It is beyond changing a culture, okay? The culture of ICE is bankrupt,” Ferguson said. “It lacks morals, it lacks any decency, it is un-American.”

In a statement Saturday, the ACLU of Washington’s executive director, Michele Storms, condemned the arrests and wrote that “the Trump administration’s practice of conducting immigration enforcement with masked and unidentifiable agents has resulted in civil rights violations at an unprecedented scale.”

ICE wrote in its statement Saturday that both Mendoza and Hernandez Mejia had overstayed their visas. Catala told KUOW that Mendoza had applied for asylum status and Hernandez Mejia had applied for a Green Card, with both applications stuck in lengthy backlogs, according to KUOW. Both entered the country legally in 2015 on tourist visas, Catala told KUOW.

ICE also alleged that Hernandez Mejia “hurled hot coffee on the officers” and would be charged with assaulting a federal officer. Catala rejected that allegation in an interview with KUOW, saying that Hernandez Mejia was holding a cup of coffee when the agents suddenly charged at the family, KUOW reported.

Mendoza and Hernandez Mejia were traveling to Los Angeles on Saturday for a baptism ceremony, Catala told the Associated Press.

Rep. Suzan DelBene wrote in a statement Saturday that she was “outraged” by the incident and said that “ICE is out of control, creating unnecessary fear and instability in communities at home and across the country.” Rep. Rick Larsen wrote on Monday that “Congress will Congress will hold ICE accountable if the President will not.”

“ICE agents must follow the same laws, rules and standards that all local, state and federal law enforcement officers follow,” Larsen wrote.

In a statement, the city of Mountlake Terrace wrote that it is “deeply saddened to hear about an incident at SeaTac involving our residents.”

“We are known for being a welcoming city to all and are proud of our diverse community,” the city wrote. “We will continue to work to be a safe place to live and raise a family.”

Sam Doyle, a member of the Mountlake Terrace City Council who spoke out on social media after the arrests, said in an interview Monday that the way ICE agents approached the two Mountlake Terrace residents during the arrests was “horrific” and that ICE as an agency has “completely gone rogue.” She added that the recent increase in immigration enforcement activity has left some people in her community fearful.

“I don’t really think that ICE as an organization is fixable,” Doyle said Monday. “I really think we have to abolish it and then have a new look at immigration reform in this country.”

The Port of Seattle, which operates the Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, wrote in a statement Saturday that “we are outraged about this morning’s incident involving ICE and two passengers as travelers boarded AS 1306 to Los Angeles.”

The port wrote in the statement that immigration enforcement actions at the airport are conducted without the Port’s participation or knowledge, and that the port has continually asked federal immigration authorities to agree to protocols at the airport.

In a separate statement Monday, the Port of Seattle Commission wrote that it is preparing a comprehensive review of the incident and will call on federal leaders to end domestic ICE enforcement activities at SEA Airport.

“We will continue sharing what we know about the immigration enforcement event that took place on Saturday, but we also want to stress that the type of immigration enforcement happening at airports in America right now is new, disruptive, and needs to stop,” the commission wrote. “We are calling on our federal delegation to use their authority to stop ICE from making this kind of enforcement actions at U.S. airports.”

She fears someone facing serious criminal charges could ultimately be released from ICE custody without their criminal case ever being resolved, and says that violates the state’s right to see justice served.

text:
Massachusetts has filed a lawsuit against the federal government for making warrantless civil arrests at courthouses.

State Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell filed the suit Monday against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), claiming that agents have been violating the Massachusetts PROTECT Act.

The act came into force on November 3 to ensure citizens can access judicial services without fear of arrest; however, 38 people have been detained since then.

Read More on News

The suit alleges that ICE has been interfering with the state's ability to operate its judicial system, disrupting court proceedings, causing fear and undermining constitutional principles and public safety.

The suit states: "The defendants have continuously infringed on the Commonwealth’s sovereign rights by completely disregarding these restrictions when they enforce federal immigration law in Massachusetts.

"Defendants are violating Massachusetts law nearly every single day by conducting civil arrests in Massachusetts state courthouses.

"Public access to and safety in these courthouses are essential to the orderly administration of justice, which lies at the heart of the sovereign authority retained by the States."

In just two and a half weeks since the PROTECT Act’s courthouse protections took effect on November 3, ICE arrested at least 38 people in Massachusetts courthouses without judicial warrants, a press release from Mass.gov states.

ICE arrested more than 600 people at Massachusetts state courthouses in 2025 and more than 500 people during the first 10 months of 2026, it added.

The lawsuit specifically challenges a May 2025 ICE directive that allows arrests in state courts even when the state prohibits them.

This policy was ruled unlawful and vacated by a federal court in California in June 2026, but ICE is continuing to carry out such arrests, the lawsuit claims.

Newsweek has reached out to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement for comment on the suit.

What Is the PROTECT Act?

Under the Tenth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, the state retains sovereign authority over its court system and its administration of justice. Massachusetts exercised that authority when it enacted the PROTECT Act.

Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey signed the PROTECT Act into law on August 5, 2026.

The Act, dubbed by the state as having the strongest protections against ICE in the country, strengthens public safety by ensuring residents can access medical care, courts and schools without fear of arrest.

It prohibits most civil arrests, including immigration arrests, without a judicial warrant or court order in:

Public K-12 schools, charter schools, vo-tech and agricultural schools

Child care centers, family day cares or group care facilities that are licensed or funded by the Massachusetts Department of Early Education and Care.

Health care facilities (including nonpublic areas of hospitals, Community Health Centers, substance use disorder programs, and nursing homes)

State property (including nonpublic areas of buildings, land and other property controlled by the state)

Courthouses (beginning November 3, 2026)

The law also provides stronger protections for parents in case they are detained or deported.

Governor Healey lauded Monday's lawsuit and said in a statement: “The Trump Administration’s ICE arrests at Massachusetts courthouses are interfering with our justice system and undermining public safety.

"When people are afraid to go to court, victims are less likely to report crimes, survivors are less likely to seek protection, and our communities are less safe. That’s why I signed the PROTECT Act. We expect ICE and all federal agents to follow Massachusetts law."

Citizens Living in Fear

The lawsuit gave a number of examples of instances where people had been too afraid to go to the courts for fear of arrest.

One example was a woman who refused to report a rape, "fearing that ICE would arrest her if she went to a state courthouse to testify against the individual who raped her," the suit, viewed by Newsweek, stated.

Another example was given of a woman who had missed multiple court dates at which she could have testified against her partner, who had threatened her with a knife, because she feared ICE’s presence in the courthouse.

She had also stated that she was not willing to seek a restraining order against her abuser because she was afraid ICE would arrest her at a state courthouse, according to the suit.

It adds that some survivors of domestic violence have faced a stark choice: "stay with the partner who poses a physical threat or seek a restraining order at a courthouse where immigration officers could be waiting."

Lawyers for Civil Rights (LCR) Staff Attorney Brooke Simone said in a statement that Campbell's action sends a clear message that no agency, including ICE, is above the law.

"Access to justice cannot depend on immigration status, and everyone deserves to know that a courthouse is a safe place, as the law requires,” Simone said.

Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here.

text:
November 23, 2026 (SAINT PAUL) — Today, Attorney General Ellison announced that he and a coalition of attorneys general are suing to challenge a new U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) rule that would strip federal housing assistance from mixed-status families. Under the new rule, any household with at least one member who is not a U.S. citizen or eligible immigrant would be cut off from HUD assistance entirely, even though federal subsidies are already prorated to only include eligible individuals.

The rule would also require all U.S. citizens in federal housing programs to take on the burdensome task of proving their citizenship or risk eviction. In a lawsuit filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, Attorney General Ellison and the coalition argue that the rule illegally reverses nearly 30 years of federal policy allowing mixed-status families to stay together and violates the Administrative Procedure Act by exceeding HUD’s authority to enact this arbitrary new restriction.

“Minnesotans are sick and tired of Trump’s politics of cruelty, and that’s exactly what this new rule from HUD is,” said Attorney General Ellison. “This rule will illegally take housing support from low-income Minnesotans for no good reason. I will not sit back and allow that to happen, so I’m taking the Trump administration to court to protect the roofs over Minnesotans’ heads."

For nearly 30 years, federal housing programs have provided housing assistance to low-income families even if not every household member is eligible for assistance. Under this system, known as proration, HUD reduces the family’s subsidy so it covers only the eligible household members. Congress codified this protection in 1997, explicitly stating that families receiving prorated assistance “shall not” lose their benefits just because an ineligible family member lives with them. The new HUD rule eliminates this protection. Under the rule, a family can stay in HUD-assisted housing only if every household member is a U.S. citizen or an eligible immigrant. As a result, U.S. citizens and eligible immigrants who live with an ineligible relative will be forced to choose between maintaining their housing and keeping their family together.

HUD estimates that around 20,000 mixed-status families, totaling 78,100 people, will lose their housing assistance. This includes 55,000 people who are fully eligible for federal housing assistance, many of whom are children and seniors. The agency also acknowledges that the rule will lead to evictions and displacement, and that many of these families could become homeless.

The rule would also make it harder for millions of U.S. citizens to keep the housing they already qualify for. Under the new rule, every U.S. citizen would also need to provide their Social Security number and consent to have their citizenship status checked through the federal SAVE database. If SAVE cannot automatically confirm their citizenship, U.S. citizens would have to produce official documents to prove their status, such as an original or certified birth certificate, naturalization certificate, or passport. Nationwide, an estimated 3.8 million adult U.S. citizens lack a document proving their citizenship, and another 17.5 million face barriers to getting one.

The coalition asserts that the rule will increase homelessness and shift major costs onto state and local governments. By HUD’s own estimates, sheltering people displaced by the rule could cost governments between $20,000 and $50,000 per person each year. The rule would also shrink the supply of affordable housing more broadly. HUD acknowledges that losing rental assistance could leave many subsidized units vacant, reduce rental income for housing providers, and drive private landlords out of the Section 8 voucher program, making it even harder for eligible families to find a home.

Attorney General Ellison and the coalition argue that HUD’s new rule exceeds the agency’s authority and violates federal law, which expressly allows prorated assistance for mixed-status families and establishes different documentation requirements for U.S. citizens and eligible immigrants aged 62 and older. They argue that HUD also violated the Administrative Procedure Act by issuing an arbitrary and capricious rule. The coalition is asking the court to declare the rule unlawful, strike it down, and block HUD from implementing or enforcing it against the plaintiff states, their local governments, and their public housing authorities.

Joining Attorney General Ellison in filing this lawsuit, which is led by the attorneys general of New York, California, and Massachusetts, are the attorneys general of Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawai’i, Maine, Michigan, Oregon, Rhode Island, and Washington, and the governor of Pennsylvania.

text:
The Tahirih Justice Center warns that changes will deny immigrant survivors a meaningful opportunity to challenge life-altering decisions.

Falls Church, VA — The Tahirih Justice Center strongly opposes a new Department of Justice final rule, “Appellate Procedures for the Board of Immigration Appeals,” published on November 17, 2026. The innocuously titled final rule is scheduled to take effect on December 17 and will dramatically change how individuals are able to appeal their cases in immigration court.

For survivors seeking to challenge an immigration judge’s decision in federal court, appealing to the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) is generally a required step in the legal process. Yet the government has made that step increasingly difficult to access. In just two years, the filing fee for a standard BIA appeal has skyrocketed over ninefold, from $110 in 2024 to $1,060 as of October 1, 2026. Now, these new rules threaten to create even more barriers for survivors seeking a fair opportunity to have their cases heard.

The rule makes several key changes, but most significantly:

It requires the Board to summarily dismiss appeals within 15 days of the appeal’s filing, before the parties have had an opportunity to submit any briefs and before the underlying record and transcript have been prepared.

To avoid summary dismissal, a Board member would have to refer the case to the full Board for a vote and the full Board would have to vote on whether to consider that appeal – all within 10 days of the appeal’s filing.

It shortens the deadline to file appeals from 30 days to just 10 days (with a few categorical exceptions).

“An appeal is not just an administrative step in the process,” said Casey Carter Swegman, Director of Public Policy at the Tahirih Justice Center. “For survivors of domestic violence, human trafficking, and other forms of gender-based violence, this rule robs survivors of their right to due process. It removes the opportunity to submit briefs to the Board before dismissal and their opportunity to update or correct the record which can be the difference between safety and being returned to danger, either in this country or their home country.”

Allowing immigrant survivors to challenge life-altering immigration court decisions is critical because survivors often face significant barriers to obtaining legal representation, gathering evidence, and documenting the violence they have experienced. Trauma, language barriers, and fear of law enforcement can make navigating the legal system even more difficult. This rule compounds those challenges by shortening deadlines and allowing fewer opportunities for review of a case.

Earlier this year, a federal court blocked several of the rule’s most harmful provisions. At that time, Tahirih stated that the court’s ruling “protects one of the most basic principles of our legal system: the right to a meaningful appeal.” This new rule attempts to push forward with those previously blocked restrictions.

The Tahirih Justice Center calls for the protection of meaningful appellate review and due process for all immigrants. No one should be denied a fair opportunity to seek protection simply because the system prioritizes removals over justice.

About the Tahirih Justice Center

The Tahirih Justice Center is a national nonprofit organization that serves women, girls, and all immigrant survivors of domestic violence, sexual assault, and other forms of gender-based violence. By amplifying the experiences of survivors, Tahirih’s mission is to create a world in which all people share equal rights and live in safety and with dignity.

text:
BOSTON — Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell filed a federal lawsuit Monday against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement over its repeated violations of the courthouse arrest provisions of the PROTECT Act.

Provisions of the law prohibiting arrests in courthouses without a signed judicial warrant verified by a judge on site went into effect Nov. 3. Since then, ICE has arrested at least 38 people in Massachusetts courthouses without judicial warrants, according to Campbell.

“With our lawsuit, we hope to demonstrate that ICE’s policy violates federal law by interfering with Massachusetts’ ability to operate our courts and enforcing our state laws including the PROTECT Act,” she said.

The announcement came after ICE arrested a Haitian man at the Fall River Judicial Center Friday, the first such arrest at a Bristol County courthouse confirmed by The Light since the provisions went into effect. According to Massachusetts Trial Court, at least 10 people have been arrested by ICE at New Bedford District Court this year, though no arrests have been confirmed since Nov. 3.

The PROTECT Act became law after Gov. Maura Healey signed it at a ceremony in Chelsea on Aug. 5. The law prohibits civil immigration arrests at child care facilities, healthcare facilities, educational institutions, and it required the attorney general to establish guidelines for handling ICE activities at the institutions listed. It also requires employers to provide notice to workers within 48 hours of an I-9 audit and more.

Yet there have been questions about the enforceability of the law — the courthouse provisions in particular — with state guidance even advising court security to merely document such arrests. Court security personnel are expressly prohibited from aiding or interfering in a civil immigration arrest in state courthouses.

Among the legislators who expressed support for the lawsuit was Rep. Christopher Hendricks, who represents the 11th Bristol state House district on Beacon Hill.

“This action reiterates that the people of the Commonwealth will not tolerate a rogue federal agency that is blatantly and sadistically disregarding our state laws and U.S. Constitution,” Hendricks said in a news release. “The policy of sending under-trained, unfit agents to terrorize our Massachusetts communities was wholeheartedly rejected on November 3rd.

“This lawsuit sends a clear message: that we in the Commonwealth — led by AG Campbell — are only getting started when it comes to holding this fascist agency and its under-qualified employees accountable.”

ICE did not immediately return a request for comment.

“Time and time again, sanctuary politicians in Massachusetts have made the dumbfounding choice to prioritize dangerous criminal illegal aliens rather than their law-abiding American citizens,” acting ICE Boston Field Office Director Joseph Sher, who is named as a defendant in Campbell’s suit, said in an October news release. “While these politicians continue to waste valuable time, energy and resources passing embarrassingly performative legislation such as the Protect Act, [Enforcement and Removal Operations] Boston will continue to proudly protect Massachusetts communities from these dangerous criminals.”

Allegations

The civil suit, filed in U.S. District Court Massachusetts, alleges that ICE arrests at state courthouses have disrupted court proceedings and harmed those subject to criminal due process as well as victims who now fear arrest. It claims that the law falls well within the state’s right under the 10th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution to maintain sovereignty over its courts.

“The Commonwealth of Massachusetts has the sovereign right to both manage its judicial system and determine whether and how to deploy state resources,” the civil suit reads. ”Among other restrictions, the PROTECT Act bans civil arrests in courthouses without a judicial warrant. The Defendants have continuously infringed on the Commonwealth’s sovereign rights by completely disregarding these restrictions when they enforce federal immigration law in Massachusetts.”

The suit also claims the use of state courts to carry out such arrests amounts to confiscating state resources to carry out federal policy.

“They are commandeering state personnel and resources by using the infrastructure of state government to enforce federal immigration law,” the suit reads. “Specifically, they are relying on state-generated information, state infrastructure, state law enforcement, and state security systems to identify, locate, disarm, and contain federal targets.”

Constitutional question

The suit revolves around an ICE policy issued in May 2025 that overturned years of practice where such arrests were avoided and expanded those subject to civil immigration action at courthouses. It was struck down by a federal court in June 2026.

In 2018, Middlesex District Attorney Marian Ryan led a lawsuit against a similar policy — one that permitted targeted apprehensions at courthouses. That lawsuit resulted in a brief injunction before the First Circuit Court of Appeals overturned it, ruling that the plaintiffs had not demonstrated an existing statute that banned civil immigration arrests, a power presumed to belong to the federal government.

Ryan said that she was hopeful this suit would succeed where hers failed.

“[Trial Court policy] was not sufficient to defeat ICE’s purposes in going into the courthouse,” she said at the news conference. “It is our belief now that the structure put in place by the PROTECT Act is sufficient.”

Campbell added that she was confident her office’s legal reasoning would overcome criticism that the PROTECT Act goes against the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution. Nonetheless, she argued, holding the agency to account was an uphill battle.

“We have been a part of a lot of lawsuits across the country to hold ICE accountable,” Campbell said. “Sadly, it is not easy to do.”

In a separate lawsuit also filed Monday in U.S. District Court in Massachusetts, Campbell co-led a multistate coalition that is looking

to quash a U.S. Housing and Urban Development rule to remove government assistance from mixed-status families in which at least

one member is not a U.S. citizen or eligible immigrant. The lawsuit argues HUD “lacks authority to rewrite federal law to exclude

families this Administration disfavors from federal “affordable housing programs” and has violated the Administrative Procedure Act.

State House News Service contributed to this report.

STATE HOUSE, BOSTON, Nov. 23, 2026. .... Attorney General Andrea Campbell sued U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Monday and accused the agency's officers of continuing to make civil arrests at courthouses in violation of a state law that took effect earlier this month.

"We have over-communicated with ICE," she continued. "I have sent correspondence to them — not only laying out what the PROTECT Act requires, but also what compliance looks like — and pointing out to them that their officials are not adhering to the PROTECT Act and they're violating the PROTECT Act. And we have gotten no response."

"No, by no means," Vargas said, as he referenced similar laws in nearby states that led to a "full stop" in ICE arrests at courthouses.

The law also incorporates protections against federal immigration enforcement activity at public schools, childcare programs and healthcare facilities. Campbell asked the public to report any potential violations to her office.

"We are leaving the door open in terms of what next steps may be in terms of other locations," Campbell said.

description:

text:
Share:

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California, along with 21 other states and Washington D.C., filed a lawsuit on Monday challenging a Trump administration rule that would bar tens of thousands of low-income households from receiving federal housing assistance, including more than 7,000 in California.

Earlier this month the Trump administration finalized a rule to bar all households with “mixed” immigration status — meaning, those with some members who are citizens or legal residents and others who live in the country illegally — from receiving housing vouchers or living in public housing.

The new rule would terminate aid for all of these households on Dec.14. The states’ lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for Massachusetts argues that the Trump administration overstepped its authority in overriding a congressional statute and asked the federal court to freeze the new rule from going into effect.

Undocumented immigrants have been banned from receiving federal housing subsidies for decades. But starting during the Clinton administration, Congress has required the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development to provide assistance in proportion to the share of members who have legal status. A family with two undocumented parents and two citizen children, for example, would receive half the eligible aid.

“California won’t stand idly by while the Trump administration forces families to choose between staying together and keeping a roof over their heads,” said Attorney General Rob Bonta in a press conference announcing the suit.

In a written response, the HUD press office said the rule “ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars.”

“This rule guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing,” the statement, attributed to Secretary Scott Turner, continued. “This change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist.”

Since the Trump administration published the final version of the rule earlier this month, local public housing agencies have been racing to figure out how to comply while minimizing the eviction of residents and financial collateral damage for the agencies themselves. Some warn that many U.S. citizens and legal residents may struggle and ultimately fail to comply with the more stringent requirements to prove eligibility. They also warn that housing agencies will be squeezed financially as they evict lower-cost mixed status households and replace them with households entitled to full benefits.

Housing agencies and local governments across the country, including in Los Angeles, San Diego, San Francisco, Fresno, Santa Barbara and Santa Clara County, filed their own suit on Monday.

text:
18

WASHINGTON (OSV News) — President Donald Trump signaled potential areas of cooperation with a Democratic Congress during a Nov. 20 press conference, notably on immigration policy.

His comments came just a few days after key Catholic bishops said they would continue to encourage lawmakers in both parties to work toward humane immigration policies, during the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops’ fall plenary assembly in Baltimore on Nov. 17.

In the aftermath of Republicans losing control of both chambers of Congress in a Democratic landslide, Trump offered mixed signals about the degree to which he would be willing to work with the new Congress on the issue, at first suggesting his approach may have been “too tough” and that he was open to working with Democrats, before his administration indicated its deportation policy would continue. Trump also named Stephen Miller, seen as a main architect of his immigration policy, as his chief of staff.

In response to a question on the subject of immigration policy, Trump did not rule out working with Democrats.

Trump seems open to talks with Democrats on healthcare, immigration

“You know, what’s happened is, I’ve been called by a lot of Democrats, I will tell you, you’ll have to figure out who,” Trump said, adding, “They want to talk to me about healthcare and they want to talk to me about immigration.”

Trump said he was potentially interested in working with Democrats on immigration policy that would allow him to continue to deport “the worst of the worst” but suggested potential cooperation on avenues for “very hardworking people that came in.”

But Trump did not eschew his hardline immigration policy, also saying, “We are not going to let immigration destroy our country.”

Citing a recent phone call with Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, D-Texas, Trump said he may be able to work with Democrats on border security.

“It was a very productive call, and she wants to have a strong border, and we’ll be able, I think we’ll be able to work something out,” Trump said.

Previously, Hinojosa told The Texas Tribune, “He understands my commitment to keeping a secure border.”

Texas Gov-elect Hinojosa says she has reached out to president

“I reached out to him to make sure that he had a direct line to me, and it was a very positive conversation,” Hinojosa said. “He indicated his desire to help Texas, and any friend of Texas — anybody who wants to help Texas — is a friend of mine.”

In response to a question about how the bishops planned to navigate the new political environment in their advocacy for humane immigration policies, Archbishop Paul S. Coakley of Oklahoma City, president of the USCCB, told reporters at a Nov. 17 press conference, “Many of our concerns will remain the same.”

“We are concerned about treating migrants with respect and dignity. We’re concerned about the policies of mass deportation, to try to rein that in,” the archbishop said. “We’re concerned about conditions in detention centers and providing adequate pastoral and spiritual care in those settings. So those are some of the things that are kind of low-hanging fruit. We’ll just continue to try to advocate as we have been.”

Bishop Daniel E. Flores of Brownsville, Texas, USCCB vice president, pointed to the special pastoral message on immigration the conference approved at its previous fall plenary assembly, saying, “I think we continue to have the concerns that we raised.”

In Nov. 18 remarks to the assembly, Bishop Brendan J. Cahill of Joliet, Illinois, chair of the USCCB’s Committee on Migration, said a year after that message, “much of what we addressed at that time continues to be relevant today,” identifying family separation and the ability to provide pastoral care to those in detention centers as among the conference’s key concerns.

Catholic social teaching on immigration balances three interrelated principles: the right of persons to migrate; the right of a country to regulate its borders and control immigration; and a nation’s duty to regulate its borders with justice and mercy.

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has abducted multiple people from airports ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday, sparking outrage among onlookers and renewed calls for the agency to be abolished.

This past weekend, masked ICE agents arrested two people on an airport jet bridge in Seattle as passengers boarded a flight to Los Angeles. Video of the arrests, which has gone viral on social media, shows multiple ICE agents dragging a passenger before restraining her, handcuffing her, and pulling her off of the jet bridge. As the arrest is taking place, the woman desperately cries out that she and her father are in the U.S. on work permits. Other passengers scream in horror and attempt to intervene — demanding that the masked agents identify themselves and show warrants — only to be shoved by agents.

The two arrested were later identified as Sofia Larrondo Hernandez Mejia and her father, Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, who is a Mexican national. A lawyer representing them stated that they were on their way to a family baptism.

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson (D) described the footage as “horrific” and “chilling,” stating that ICE “is beyond reform” and echoing calls for the agency to be abolished.

“ICE is completely and totally out of control. Like many Americans, I’m outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities,” Ferguson said in a statement.

The November 21 incident sparked a protest at the Seattle airport on Sunday, with demonstrators calling for the abolition of ICE.

The abductions come following a separate incident on November 19, when ICE arrested a Princeton University PhD student in D.C.’s Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport as she was returning from presenting her research at a conference.

Eva Yi Xie, a third-year neuroscience student, came to the U.S. with her parents from China as a child in 2016 and has had a pending asylum application for a decade. According to her lawyer, Xie had a court date scheduled for January 2028, and a valid work permit.

ICE detained Xie in a holding center in Virginia before moving her to an immigrant jail elsewhere in the state. On Friday, a federal judge ordered ICE not to move Xie out of Virginia, and to respond to her lawyer’s petition for habeas corpus, which stated that ICE had no grounds to arrest Xie without a warrant.

In 2020, after being named a finalist in a prestigious high school research competition, Xie wrote that her parents “were compelled to flee to America to seek refuge after being politically persecuted.”

According to the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, at least five people, including Xie, have been detained by ICE at Virginia’s Dulles and Reagan National airports in recent weeks.

This summer, ICE expanded its arrests at airports, increasingly coordinating and sharing information with TSA and targeting travelers on domestic flights — not those with deportation orders as previously targeted, but often people with expired visas or pending asylum applications. Throughout the summer, ICE arrests at airports averaged 20 to 40 per day. At the time, immigrant rights groups had advised individuals without permanent status to reconsider taking domestic flights.

Last week, prior to the recent abductions, Democratic Senators Jacky Rosen (Nevada) and Alex Padilla (California) introduced a bill to limit ICE operations at airports. The legislation would prevent ICE agents from accessing passenger data without a warrant and require ICE to notify airlines and airports ahead of their arrests.

“ICE is out of control, and these are bare minimum standards for reining it in,” said Padilla.

text:
BASILE, LA - Today, four people filed a federal lawsuit for rape, sexual abuse, harassment, and forced labor while detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at a for-profit detention center run by the GEO Group, Inc. in Basile, Louisiana. Defendants include the GEO Group and two former GEO employees at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center (SLIPC): then-assistant warden Emmanuel Reyes and former detention officer David Courvelle.

The plaintiffs, Luis Renteria-Gonzalez, Mario Garcia-Valenzuela, Kenia Campos-Flores, and Jane Doe*, claim the for-profit group and its employees targeted primarily transgender and nonbinary immigrants at SLIPC. Among other abuses, the lawsuit cites instances of rape, groping, voyeurism, physical abuse, denial of medical care, and retaliatory solitary confinement.

The lawsuit states that Renteria-Gonzalez, Garcia-Valenzuela, Campos-Flores, and Doe were detained at SLIPC between 2023 and 2025 and repeatedly abused by Reyes and other GEO employees. Using his position of authority as assistant warden, Reyes coerced plaintiffs to perform hard physical labor, sex acts, or both, threatening them with death, deportation, further sexual abuse, physical harm, and harm to their families and loved ones. Plaintiffs were also denied basic necessities, life-sustaining medical care, and placed in solitary confinement in retaliation for filing complaints against these abuses.

“The treatment and the conditions that they had us living in, nobody should go through that,” said Renteria-Gonzalez. “It’s unbelievable that this happened under the care of the people who are supposed to protect us.”

Renteria-Gonzalez and Garcia-Valenzuela, who are transgender men, and Campos-Flores, who is nonbinary, were targeted by Reyes for an off-the-books “work program” of predominantly LGBTQ+ individuals. Assigned hard manual labor without proper protective equipment, they were forced to work through the night. At one point, while stripping floors, the harsh chemicals dissolved the fabric on Renteria-Gonzalez’s shoes and burned his feet. The lawsuit also details sexual harassment and abuse from Reyes and other SLIPC officers.

Doe was detained in November 2023. In the complaint, she stated that after she turned down Reyes’ offer to join his night “cleaning crew,” he began stalking and harassing her with aggressive, inappropriate sexual comments. Within months, he escalated his attacks, cornering Doe and forcibly groping her. From February to May 2024, Reyes regularly forced Doe to perform oral sex on him, threatening her life and her family if she refused.

The abuse didn't end with Reyes. In 2025, GEO detention officer David Courvelle sexually assaulted Garcia-Valenzuela three times and forced Renteria-Gonzalez and Garcia-Valenzuela to stand guard outside a closet while he raped a woman detained at SLIPC. Courvelle later pleaded guilty to sexual abuse of a ward and was sentenced in June to three years in federal prison.

The plaintiffs reported this abuse through Prison Rape Elimination Act (PREA) complaints, grievances, the Department of Homeland Security inspector general’s hotline, and interviews with ICE officials and the FBI. Reyes left SLIPC of his own accord in July 2024.

“Enough is enough,” said Garcia-Valenzuela. “This is America. We’re supposed to have a voice, to be able to speak out. I’m sharing my story so that other people can have the courage to speak up about what happens in these detention centers.”

The lawsuit, filed by the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, National Immigration Project, National Immigrant Justice Center, ACLU of Louisiana, and Southern Poverty Law Center under the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act (TVPRA) and Louisiana state law in the Western District of Louisiana, follows prior complaints in September 2025.

"Despite these failures long and thoroughly documented by detained people, non-governmental organizations, and ICE itself, GEO has continued to operate SLIPC without taking steps to meaningfully address mistreatment or otherwise improve conditions of detention,” said the representing organizations in a joint statement. “It was under these conditions of lax oversight that Defendants Reyes and Courvelle were allowed to wage abuse against plaintiffs."

*Jane Doe is proceeding under a pseudonym.

###

About Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center

The Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center is a nonpartisan, not-for-profit organization that works across the courtroom, the boardroom, and the classroom to build a more just and peaceful world. Inspired by the legacies of Senator Robert and Ethel Kennedy, we work with international and domestic partners to protect fundamental human rights. We pursue strategic litigation to hold governments accountable at home and around the world; foster a social good approach to business; and train the next generation of changemakers through our human rights education programs.

About National Immigration Project

The National Immigration Project is a membership organization of attorneys, advocates, and community members who believe that all people should be treated with dignity, live freely, and flourish. We litigate, advocate, educate, and build bridges across movements to ensure that those most impacted by the immigration and criminal systems are uplifted and supported. Learn more at nipnlg.org. Follow the National Immigration Project on Bluesky, Facebook, Instagram, and Threads at @NIPNLG.

About National Immigrant Justice Center

The National Immigrant Justice Center is a nongovernmental organization dedicated to ensuring human rights protections and access to justice for all immigrants, refugees, and asylum seekers through a unique combination of direct services, policy reform, impact litigation, and public education. Visit immigrantjustice.org.

About the ACLU of Louisiana

The ACLU of Louisiana leads the charge to protect the civil rights and liberties of Louisianians, especially those most marginalized and historically harmed. True to our founding during the Civil Rights Movement, we are fearless in the face of intimidation and fight tirelessly to protect and empower Louisiana’s Black, Brown, Immigrant, and LGBTQ+ communities. We are part of a nationwide network of affiliates working in courts, legislatures, and communities in all 50 states, Puerto Rico, and Washington, D.C.

About the Southern Poverty Law Center

The Southern Poverty Law Center is a catalyst for racial justice in the South and beyond, working in partnership with communities to dismantle white supremacy, strengthen intersectional movements and advance the human rights of all people. For more information, visit www.splcenter.org.

text:
THE US DEPARTMENT of Housing and Urban Development is facing yet another legal challenge to a rule that would require households receiving federal housing assistance to prove that every member has citizenship or eligible immigration status.

Days after a coalition of public tenant advocates and residents filed a federal class-action lawsuit on behalf of mixed-status families whose housing is endangered by the new rule, a coalition of 22 state attorneys general dropped their own suit Monday arguing that the change illegally reverses nearly 30 years of federal policy.

The rule “leaves families no real choice because they must either break apart, forcing ineligible members out of the home so that the rest of the family can keep its HUD assistance, or be driven out of assisted housing altogether, at grave risk of homelessness,” wrote the tenant and public housing group in its complaint. “Families forced out of assisted housing will be thrown into a housing market that is already desperately short of affordable units.”

Both suits argue that the “arbitrary and capricious” rule change exceeded the agency’s authority and violated federal law, including the Administrative Procedure Act.

The tenants also claim that the rule and requirement that residents produce substantial documentation violate the equal protection and due process guarantees of the Fifth Amendment to the US Constitution.

Since 1996, Congress has allowed families whose members have different legal immigration statuses to live in federally funded housing so long as the assistance was pro-rated so that only eligible household members received support.

“HUD’s final rule fully implements the 1980 Housing and Community Development Act and ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars,” HUD Secretary Scott Turner said in a statement Monday evening. “This rule guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing. This change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist.”

Turner said earlier this month that the rule change reflects that “the federal government is not good at providing housing,” and long-term subsidies are “not the way that it’s intended to be.

The attorneys general argue what HUD wants is irrelevant.

“Federal financial assistance is not a slush fund that executive agencies can redirect at will to the groups they favor,” they assert in the complaint. “HUD is charged with administering a statutory scheme in furtherance of Congress’s goals, which are clear: Congress seeks to ensure a decent home and suitable living environment for all American families, and Congress’s definition includes mixed- status families.”

Tenants and the attorneys general are asking a Massachusetts federal judge to declare the rule unlawful, strike it down, and block HUD from implementing or enforcing it against the states, their local governments, and their public housing authorities.

Around 20,000 mixed-status families, totaling 78,100 people, could lose their housing assistance under the new rule. The state prosecutors note that this estimate includes 55,000 people who are fully eligible for federal housing assistance, many of whom are children and seniors. In Massachusetts, about 910 households would likely be impacted.

One of the class-action plaintiffs is a Massachusetts mother of four. She has lived in the country for 15 years and is currently authorized to live and work in Massachusetts, but her immigration status is not among those deemed eligible. She lives in a Section 8 subsidized apartment with her four children, all of them 12 or younger and three of them US citizens.

“Under the mixed-status rule challenged in this case, the family would lose their housing subsidy entirely,” the suit asserts. Because her “citizen children cannot live independently from her, the family would face eviction and homelessness.”

The City of Boston announced on Monday that the city and the Boston Housing Authority were also suing HUD. More than 500 Boston families could have federal housing assistance stripped away, according to city officials.

“Almost every family we house at the Boston Housing Authority has previously suffered through a period of homelessness,” said Kenzie Bok, administrator of the Boston Housing Authority. “These are Boston kids, they are eligible for federal housing in their own right, and they deserve to stay safely in their homes.”

The lawsuit, also filed in the District Court of Massachusetts, is brought by public housing authorities including Boston, New York, San Francisco, and Chicago.

The rule, the cities argue, is “callous, ill-conceived, and illegal. It radically departs from statutory authority, congressional intent, and prior regulations, all of which permit mixed status families to remain in federally subsidized housing and access prorated assistance.”

Lawyers and advocates cautioned that although the new rule is set to take effect on December 14, that does not mean immediate withdrawal of benefits. Housing authorities would have about a month to begin sending out notifications to impacted families. Those families would then have until March 14 to verify the eligibility of every family member.

Zafiro Patiño, director of organizing for the Massachusetts Union of Public Housing Tenants, one of the groups in the class- action suit, urged families to be prepared but patient.

“We are basically saying to people, ‘Do not sign anything yet.’ The law still is the same, so do not panic,” she said. The group has already heard that some housing authorities are already sending out notices, which Patiño expects will spook many households.

The class-action group emphasized that a severe regulatory burden will land on tenants and housing authorities if the rule takes effect. “We expect that the housing authorities already are feeling terrorized with this because they have a lot of work,” said Patiño, “and now it’s going to be even more.”

HUD’s impact review estimates that sheltering people displaced by the rule could cost state and local governments between $20,000 and $50,000 per person each year.

About 8.8 million tenants across the country will be impacted, because all tenants would have to verify their status, said Annette Duke, a senior housing attorney at the Mass Law Reform Institute.

That burden, she noted, will fall disproportionately on people of color, women, children, and people with disabilities.

“The rule really seeks to divide the communities,” she said, “and what’s great is this lawsuit shows that people are standing together to fight this.”

title: ICE Cancels Deportation Flights for Afghan War Refugees But Continues to Jail Them
authors: Mike Ludwig, Jamila Osman, Thomas Kennedy
description:
Ahmad has been in the custody of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) since December 2024, when he claimed asylum at the U.S.-Mexico border.
Paktiawal fought alongside U.S. troops but died in March shortly after being arrested by ICE agents near his home in Texas.
Even the Taliban’s foreign ministry issued a statement expressing “serious concern” about the U.S. plan to deport Afghan refugees to Pakistan, which remains in a tense and protracted conflict with the Taliban government.
While the Afghan refugees remain in ICE custody, VanDiver said the canceled flights were a victory for AfghanEvac and activist veterans who have lobbied lawmakers to protect their wartime allies.
When Democrats take the majority in Congress next year, VanDiver said they must go further to reverse the policies that turned Afghan war allies and refugees into targets for mass deportation.
text:
Attorneys for an Afghan physician and refugee going by the pseudonym Ahmad say he worked as a doctor in support of United States and NATO forces during the U.S.-led war on Afghanistan. Facing persecution from the Taliban after the U.S. withdrawal in 2021, Ahmad fled to join thousands of other Afghan allies who assisted the war effort and were offered asylum in the U.S. under the Biden administration.

“Mr. Ahmad was an ally to the United States against the Taliban and helped his family members escape to refugee camps outside the country,” said Katie Blankenship, a managing operator of the legal aid group Sanctuary of the South, in a statement. “When he fled Afghanistan, he faced grave danger in his journey to the United States.”

Now Blankenship says Ahmad faces the cruelty of the U.S. immigration system. Ahmad has been in the custody of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) since December 2024, when he claimed asylum at the U.S.-Mexico border. Ahmad remains locked up inside the Adams County Correctional Center, a Mississippi prison run by CoreCivic that contracts with ICE, where Blankenship says he is becoming increasingly desperate to be released and receive treatment for pre-existing medical conditions, including a tumor in his neck.

“He’s so desperate to get out of Adams because his health is deteriorating so much,” Blankenship told Truthout in an interview. “I am worried for him physically, and I am worried for him mentally — he is deteriorating.”

Blankenship has reason to worry. Despite claims by ICE that immigration prisoners receive adequate health care, reports of medical neglect within ICE’s privately run jails and prison camps are widespread. A 2025 investigation by Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff uncovered dozens of credible reports of medical neglect, and detainees have staged hundreds of hunger strikes in protest of inhumane conditions at ICE facilities across the country amid President Trump’s mass deportation campaign.

At least 60 people have died in ICE custody since Trump took office, including Mohammad Nazeer Paktiawal, an Afghan special forces veteran and father of six children. Paktiawal fought alongside U.S. troops but died in March shortly after being arrested by ICE agents near his home in Texas. Family members said they pleaded with officers to give Paktiawal his asthma inhaler.

In a November 11 joint statement, Sanctuary of the South, the Council on American Islamic Relations-Legal Defense Fund, the Mississippi American Civil Liberties Union, and the Atlanta chapter of Asian Americans Advancing Justice said that Ahmad should be welcomed to the U.S. and celebrated for resisting the Taliban. Instead, his condition is worsening behind bars.

“This is normal procedure for ICE, to keep people locked up for as long as possible,” Blankenship said, adding that ICE’s private contractors are paid for each detainee under their watch. “The longer they are locked up the more money they get.”

Despite promises made by previous administrations to protect Afghans who helped the U.S. from Taliban retribution, the Trump administration dismantled the federal program for resettling Afghans who served as allies to the U.S. following the invasion of Afghanistan in 2002, in addition to revoking asylum protections known as Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Afghan refugees.

As a result, about 8,000 Afghans are at risk of deportation back to Taliban-controlled Afghanistan, which could amount to a death sentence, according to human rights advocates. Additionally, more than 1,000 Afghans have been stranded at a former U.S. Army base-turned-refugee camp in Qatar since the Trump administration suspended the resettlement process last year.

The As Sayliyah refugee camp in Doha was scheduled to shut down on September 30, leaving the Afghans stranded there with few options but to return to Afghanistan. About 150 of them are family of U.S. servicemembers. On September 29, a bipartisan group of lawmakers sent Secretary of State Marco Rubio a letter requesting emergency relief for the war refugees, and the State Department agreed to push back the deadline for closing the camp by nine months.

The uncertainty and ever-shifting statements by Trump administration officials are taking a severe psychological toll on the refugees, and that may be intentional, according to Shawn VanDiver, executive director of AfghanEvac, a group of veterans advocating for Afghan war allies.

“It’s always meant to incite fear; it’s always meant to scare the shit out of somebody, and they never give resolution,” VanDiver told Truthout. “So, people just live with that fear. And that is some shit that can cause some real mental health issues.”

The most recent scare came in the fevered days ahead of the midterm elections, when reports surfaced of a deportation flight scheduled to transfer Afghan refugees to Pakistan on November 3, which was also Election Day. Advocates feared the asylum seekers, including women and children, would be quickly handed over to the Taliban. The Trump administration has deported thousands of people to countries other than their own, which immigrant rights advocates say is illegal in cases where refugees are put in danger.

Even the Taliban’s foreign ministry issued a statement expressing “serious concern” about the U.S. plan to deport Afghan refugees to Pakistan, which remains in a tense and protracted conflict with the Taliban government. U.S. veterans and lawmakers sprang into action, with Rep. Scott Peters (D-California) spearheading another emergency letter from members of Congress to Rubio demanding the deportation flight be canceled.

“We are extremely concerned that sending vulnerable people who sought safety in the U.S. to Afghanistan or Iran will result in their persecution, torture, or even death,” the lawmakers wrote, arguing that deporting them would be a “violation of that promise and our moral obligations to the Afghan community who stood alongside our troops.”

The November 3 deportation flight never took off. The initial flight was canceled after a judge issued a federal injunction temporarily blocking the deportations to Pakistan, and VanDiver said that advocates for the refugees later learned from court filings that another deportation flight that was scheduled to remove Afghan refugees on November 16 was also canceled.

While the Afghan refugees remain in ICE custody, VanDiver said the canceled flights were a victory for AfghanEvac and activist veterans who have lobbied lawmakers to protect their wartime allies. VanDiver said there was no announcement about the cancellation from the Trump administration, which likely failed to properly plan for the deportations with the Pakistani government.

“This administration is unwilling to admit when they are wrong and is always looking to hide their fuckups,” VanDiver said.

Rep. Jason Crow, a veteran Army Ranger and Democrat from Colorado, introduced a petition on November 9 to force a vote on legislation that would restore TPS protections for Afghans. So far, 114 lawmakers have signed the petition, all of them Democrats.

When Democrats take the majority in Congress next year, VanDiver said they must go further to reverse the policies that turned Afghan war allies and refugees into targets for mass deportation. He encouraged lawmakers to look at “chief of mission” approvals under the Special Immigrant Visa program, which were withdrawn by the State Department in order to make Afghan war allies and their families ineligible for asylum and targets for deportation.

While many Afghan allies and their families remain in ICE custody or stranded at Camp As Sayliyah, VanDiver said the sweeping victory for Democrats in the midterm elections is reason for hope.

“We are really hoping to see oversight on Camp As Sayliyah, the ‘chief of mission’ revocations, and on these deportations and detentions,” VanDiver said.

Blankenship fears relief will come not fast enough for Ahmad, who is desperate to be released from the prison in Mississippi and receive medical treatment. Despite risking Taliban retribution to help the U.S. in wartime and making a harrowing escape from Afghanistan, Ahmad’s application for asylum was denied and he now faces a removal order.

In 2024, before Trump took office, immigration judges granted about 88 percent of asylum petitions from Afghans. Between October 2025 and September 2026, that rate had fallen to less than 55 percent. The overall asylum denial rate reached 94 percent in June 2026, up from 60 percent at the end of 2024. Under policies guided by White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, the Trump administration has transformed refugee assistance into a system of mass incarceration, family separation, trauma, displacement, and death.

Blankenship says Ahmad’s case went before an immigration judge in Louisiana who is notorious for denying the vast majority of asylum claims. He is now desperate and wishes to be deported in order to receive medical treatment — even to a third country if necessary. Ahmad is eligible for a visa in Italy on humanitarian grounds after previously passing through the country, but Blankenship said ICE is not responding to requests filed by his attorneys, including a petition for release on medical grounds.

“There are multiple avenues that he should be able to get out — habeas corpus, parole for medical reasons, a visa to Italy because we can get it done,” Blankenship said. “But they won’t hear any of it.”
