text:
Boston Mayor Michelle Wu sued the Trump administration, alleging that a new HUD rule would illegally cut off federal funding that helps to pay rent for mixed immigration status households, including “thousands of children.”

Wu filed the lawsuit in federal court Monday against the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development and its Secretary Scott Turner on behalf of the City of Boston and Boston Housing Authority, the city’s public housing arm.

In the lawsuit, Wu, BHA and a coalition of 17 major cities and public housing authorities across the country take aim at a new rule announced this month by HUD that, per Wu’s office, would largely prohibit households with mixed immigration statuses from receiving federal rental assistance.

“Under this cruel and illegal rule, hundreds of children and families in Boston could lose their housing,” Wu said in a statement. “Today, the city and Boston Housing Authority are joining cities nationwide to halt this unlawful plan and keep families together.”

Wu contends that families with mixed immigration statuses have been allowed to live together for decades in federally subsidized housing, receiving financial support only for family members with lawful immigration status.

The new HUD rule seeks to undo that practice — where the financial support provided by the feds is based on the amount of eligible legal family members — by cutting off rental support for the entire household, should it consist of people without legal immigration status.

“U.S. citizens or eligible immigrants who live with an ineligible spouse, parent, child, or other family member now face an untenable choice: either evict loved ones or forgo the protected assistance that they qualified for so their family can remain together. This is a Hobson’s choice for most families,” the lawsuit states.

Wu’s office said more than 500 Boston families, including nearly 900 children, would be impacted, should the court allow the new HUD rule to stand.

The new federal policy would also impose citizenship verification checks on people 62 and older for the first time, putting seniors at risk of losing their subsidized housing should they reside in the country unlawfully, per the lawsuit.

Turner, the HUD secretary, framed the new policy as being aimed at ensuring fairness by ensuring only American citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded public housing, as intended, in a Nov. 10 press release.

A HUD and DHS audit of all HUD-assisted households identified nearly 200,000 tenants with incomplete or unknown eligibility verification. HUD-funded housing serves only a quarter of eligible households in need, Turner’s office said.

“President Trump warned that the days of illegal aliens and ineligible noncitizens exploiting government-funded welfare programs would be over,” Turner said in a statement. “It’s unacceptable that America’s homeless veterans, disabled, elderly, and victims of domestic violence languish on waitlists while illegals and ineligibles scam our system.

“American taxpayers will no longer foot the bill. Promises made, promises kept.”

HUD did not respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit.

text:
GRAHAM, N.C. (AP) — As he ran for sheriff in North Carolina against a longtime incumbent who had joined forces with the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, Shannon Long found his campaign van was an obstacle with some voters.

The trust between law enforcement and Alamance County's growing Latino community was so fractured, Long said, that the vehicle emblazoned with "sheriff" made it a struggle to get some people to speak with him.

"They've been living in fear. They feel like they don't have a voice. They have been suppressed, oppressed; a lot of them are depressed. So they feel that they live in a community where they don't belong," Long, a pastor, business owner and former sheriff's deputy, told The Associated Press two weeks after defeating Republican Sheriff Terry Johnson in a campaign that some activists, voters and local officials say turned partly on questions about immigration enforcement and the treatment of Latino residents.

Johnson is one of a few sheriffs around the country who were ousted by challengers critical of their cooperation with President Donald Trump's push for mass deportations of people in the country illegally. While only a smattering, the results could spell trouble for other sheriffs who are seen as participants in Trump's crackdown and possibly hinder agreements that have become a cornerstone of the administration's efforts.

Johnson was among the first sheriffs to allow his deputies to enforce federal immigration laws under what's known as a 287(g) agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Long, who ran as an independent, promised to curtail cooperation with ICE, which continues to rely on the cooperative pacts to boost arrest numbers despite a one-time infusion of $75 billion from Congress and hiring about 12,000 officers.

The administration has more than 2,700 such pacts with state and local agencies, up from 135 when Trump began his second term. The agreements, predominantly in the South, have deputized over 29,000 local law officers and resulted in more than 6,600 arrests in July, about 15% of all ICE arrests, according to government data obtained by the Deportation Data Project that was analyzed by the advocacy group fwd.us.

The AP reviewed about 250 elections held this month for sheriffs whose offices had 287(g) agreements, identifying races in Indiana, Maryland, North Carolina, Wisconsin and elsewhere in which ICE pacts played a role in a candidate's defeat. Many sheriffs who ran this year were unopposed. But the ICE agreements could become a focus again in two years, when sheriffs from Florida, Texas and other states with large numbers of 287(g) agreements are up for election.

A new sheriff is coming to 'No Chance Alamance'

Alamance County is a longtime Republican stronghold of just under 200,000 residents that sits between Greensboro and the Research Triangle metropolitan area that includes Raleigh, Durham and Chapel Hill. It has become more politically competitive as its population has grown increasingly diverse — from 750 residents who identified as Hispanic in the 1990 census to nearly 25,000 in 2020. The sheriff's office currently participates in the 287(g) program, a spokesman confirmed, though last year it ended an agreement to house ICE detainees.

Johnson, who is white, was first elected in 2002 and has been a prominent and polarizing figure. He has insisted he welcomes lawful immigrants and denied persistent allegations — including in a Justice Department lawsuit over a decade ago that ended with a settlement — that his office racially profiled minority residents.

The county acquired the moniker "No Chance Alamance" because of a perceived sense of unjust policing and a lack of political representation among Black and Latino residents, school board member Seneca Rogers said.

Johnson initially said in a phone call that immigration policy could have contributed to his loss. But in a brief interview later, he said it likely didn't and laid blame with his long tenure and a national political environment that was brutal for Republicans, acutely so in North Carolina, where Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper flipped a U.S. Senate seat, winning by nearly 20 percentage points. He said he always followed the law and protected public safety.

Lawyer: Father and daughter detained by ICE at Seattle airport were traveling to family baptism

Activists and longtime residents said the Latino community — and to some extent, the Black community — feared engaging with the sheriff's office and described a sense that non-white residents were far likelier to be pulled over or detained after a traffic stop. Some people were afraid to call 911 or even go to work, said community organizer Leslie Arevalo.

Voter Renee Russell said the sheriff's cooperation with ICE gave a false impression of Alamance as unwelcoming. She was excited to see fresh leadership. Long will be the county's first Black sheriff, local media reported.

But Republican state Sen. Amy Galey, whose district includes the county, defended Johnson's record. She said he had worked to improve training opportunities and mental health services. Although Galey didn't think immigration played a big role in the race, she wondered if hard-line ICE tactics elsewhere could have contributed to simmering concerns about law enforcement more broadly.

Candidates who backed ICE cooperation lost elsewhere

The sheriff's office in Frederick County, Maryland, northwest of Washington, D.C., was another longtime participant in the 287(g) program. Since 2008, the county detained and turned over 1,884 people to ICE, Republican Sheriff Chuck Jenkins said. But that came to a halt this year when Democratic Gov. Wes Moore signed a law banning immigration enforcement pacts with the federal government.

Public sentiment also turned against Jenkins, who said the program made the community safer but acknowledged it likely cost him reelection. He was defeated by Democrat Karl Bickel, a retired U.S. Department of Justice employee who had lost four previous elections to Jenkins and pledged not to cooperate with ICE.

"In general, people are fed up with the sheriff's negativeness about immigrants," said retired social worker Carol Antoniewicz, who distributed emails, social media posts and campaign literature in support of Bickel.

In Wisconsin's Winnebago County, ICE's arrest and detention of a schoolteacher weeks before Election Day sparked backlash against anyone seemingly supportive of immigration officers, including a Republican vying to replace a retiring sheriff.

"Any kind of perceived alignment definitely is considered a liability at this point," said Molly Smiltneek, a local advocate and immigration lawyer who attended a vigil for the teacher.

Though the sheriff's department had nothing to do with the teacher's arrest, its 287(g) agreement became central to the campaign, boosting Democrat Jason Rippl, who promised to end it.

A newly elected sheriff seeks a better community partnership

Long, who formerly worked as a deputy in a neighboring North Carolina county, said he will uphold the law in his new role and hold offenders accountable. But he said he won't participate in the 287(g) program.

He has set up meetings with the Latino community in the hopes of building new relationships.

"I want them to see the sheriff's office in the community, creating a partnership, letting them know that they have a voice. … There's no need to operate in fear," he said.

Schuettler reported from Phoenix and Lieb from Jefferson City, Missouri. Associated Press journalist Allen G. Breed contributed from Graham.

Schuettler is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

text:
California, along with 21 other states and Washington D.C., filed a lawsuit on Monday challenging a Trump administration rule that would bar tens of thousands of low-income households from receiving federal housing assistance, including more than 7,000 in California.

Earlier this month the Trump administration finalized a rule to bar all households with “mixed” immigration status — meaning, those with some members who are citizens or legal residents and others who live in the country illegally — from receiving housing vouchers or living in public housing.

The new rule would terminate aid for all of these households on Dec.14. The states’ lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for Massachusetts argues that the Trump administration overstepped its authority in overriding a congressional statute and asked the federal court to freeze the new rule from going into effect.

Undocumented immigrants have been banned from receiving federal housing subsidies for decades. But starting during the Clinton administration, Congress has required the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development to provide assistance in proportion to the share of members who have legal status. A family with two undocumented parents and two citizen children, for example, would receive half the eligible aid.

“California won’t stand idly by while the Trump administration forces families to choose between staying together and keeping a roof over their heads,” said Attorney General Rob Bonta in a press conference announcing the suit.

In a written response, the HUD press office said the rule “ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars.”

“This rule guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing,” the statement, attributed to Secretary Scott Turner, continued. “This change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist.”

Since the Trump administration published the final version of the rule earlier this month, local public housing agencies have been racing to figure out how to comply while minimizing the eviction of residents and financial collateral damage for the agencies themselves. Some warn that many U.S. citizens and legal residents may struggle and ultimately fail to comply with the more stringent requirements to prove eligibility. They also warn that housing agencies will be squeezed financially as they evict lower-cost mixed status households and replace them with households entitled to full benefits.

"ICE's intentional violation of state law has created unnecessary fear, made it more difficult to operate our courts and hold defendants accountable," Campbell said. title: Arizona and Trump administration clash over immigrant in-state tuition law
authors: Frank Gluck, Howard Fischer, Capitol Media Services
description:
At issue is Proposition 308, a voter-approved 2022 measure granting resident tuition to local high school graduates regardless of immigration status.
Because Prop 308 doesn’t extend resident rates to all out-of-state American citizens, federal lawyers contend the law must be voided.
Assistant Attorney General Hayleigh Crawford argued that if federal law trumps the state measure, then the underlying 1996 federal statute the Justice Department cites is itself unconstitutional.
The Department of Justice claims that when Arizona voters approved the 2022 ballot measure, they effectively nullified the federal law.
No date has been set for a hearing on the bid to void the Arizona law.
text:
Key Points:

The Trump administration wants a federal judge to strike down a 2022 Arizona law allowing certain undocumented students to pay in-state tuition

Attorneys for the state argue that the federal government is overstepping its authority

More than 51% of Arizona residents voted in favor of the ballot measure authorizing the in-state tuition rate for “Dreamers”

PHOENIX — The Trump administration is asking a federal judge to reject arguments from Arizona state attorneys in support of a law allowing undocumented students to pay in-state tuition, arguing the state has no authority to override federal immigration policy.

In new court filings, Justice Department attorney Garrett Greene said Congress sets policy regarding tuition discounts for non-citizens and that states must comply.

At issue is Proposition 308, a voter-approved 2022 measure granting resident tuition to local high school graduates regardless of immigration status.

Federal prosecutors filed suit in August, pointing to a 1996 federal statute prohibiting states from granting resident tuition rates to undocumented immigrants unless the same benefit is offered to all U.S. citizens regardless of residence.

Because Prop 308 doesn’t extend resident rates to all out-of-state American citizens, federal lawyers contend the law must be voided.

Attorneys for the state presented fresh arguments Friday to U.S. District Court Judge Murray Snow, countering that the Justice Department’s position lacks both legal and logical foundation.

Assistant Attorney General Hayleigh Crawford argued that if federal law trumps the state measure, then the underlying 1996 federal statute the Justice Department cites is itself unconstitutional. She noted that the U.S. Constitution gives Congress “only certain enumerated powers.” Everything else, she added, is reserved for the states.

“Consequently, if no enumerated power authorizes Congress to pass a certain law, that law may not be enacted, even if it would not violate any of the express prohibitions in the Bill of Rights or elsewhere in the Constitution,” Crawford said.

The Department of Justice claims that when Arizona voters approved the 2022 ballot measure, they effectively nullified the federal law. And that, Greene said, represents “an injury to the United States.”

“A sovereign’s core interests include the power to create and enforce a legal code,” he told Snow in the federal government’s latest legal filing. “And a state that administers a program negating a federal statute within its borders nullifies that code.”

Greene said the 1996 law is clearly within the federal government’s power because it addresses immigration. “Congress’ power reaches the status and treatment of aliens, not just the entry and removal,” he said.

Greene also noted that the 1996 law specifically says it was designed “to remove the incentive for illegal immigration provided by the availability of public benefits.”

“A state that hands unlawfully present aliens the very benefit Congress withheld clearly interferes with immigration enforcement,” he told the judge. “Here, Congress itself expressly declared the state policy incompatible with federal law.”

Crawford counters that the 1996 law also had a stated purpose to “encourage self-sufficiency among immigrants, limit their dependence on public assistance, and prevent public benefits from serving as an incentive for illegal immigration.”

Prop 308, she argued, is designed to promote self-sufficiency by providing more affordable education to all Arizona residents, regardless of legal status.

“Indeed, it is hard to imagine a plausible explanation (for the federal case) given that Arizona’s law encourages self-sufficiency through education,” Crawford wrote.

And if nothing else, she said the federal government has not shown any obvious connection between Arizona offering lower college tuition rates and anyone’s decision to immigrate to the U.S. illegally.

“And regardless, Congress cannot define its own authority,” Crawford added.

More than 51% of Arizona voters approved Prop 308 in 2022.

The ballot measure followed a 2012 Obama administration decision to create the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program. It allows people who arrived in this country illegally as children before 2007 — colloquially called “Dreamers” — to remain and even work if they meet certain criteria.

As a result, the Maricopa Community College system and, later, the Arizona Board of Regents agreed to let DACA recipients pay in-state tuition.

But the Arizona Supreme Court ruled in 2018 that Proposition 300, a 2006 ballot measure that denies various public benefits to those not legally in the country, precludes that option — including any form of subsidized tuition. Prop 308 was crafted to create an exception.

Crawford argues that Congress, in enacting the 1996 law, acted illegally because it dictates to states “what a state legislature may and may not do.” And that, she told the judge, makes the federal law unenforceable — at least when it comes to trying to overturn the will of Arizona voters.

DACA still exists, and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services is accepting initial applications. But the agency isn’t acting on them, with the program’s legality tied up in federal court.

No date has been set for a hearing on the bid to void the Arizona law.

BASILE, La. (Acadiana News First) - Four people who were detained by ICE at a privately-owned prison in Basile have sued the company that owns it, alleging “a nightmare of rape” and other abuses during their time there.

The lawsuit was filed Monday in federal court by the National Immigration Project, the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, the Southern Poverty Law Center and the ACLU of Louisiana against the GEO Group, a former assistant warden and another former employee at the prison - who now is serving a federal prison sentence for sex crimes.

The alleged abuses outlined in the suit all took place at the GEO Group’s South Louisiana Immigration and Customs Enforcement Processing Center in Basile, described as the nation’s largest female immigrant detention facility.

We’ve reached out to GEO Group and will update this story with any response we receive.

The lawsuit, which you can read for yourself by scrolling down, alleges that the four people “endured a months-long nightmare of rape, sexual abuse, degrading harassment, and hard manual labor that targeted primarily transgender and non-binary detained people.”

“The primary perpetrator was Defendant Emmanuel Reyes, then an Assistant Warden at the facility. Using his position of authority, Defendant Reyes coerced Plaintiffs to perform physical and sexual labor with threats of death, deportation, further sexual abuse, physical harm, harm to their families and loved ones, and through denial of basic necessities, denial of life-sustaining medical care, and isolation in solitary confinement,” the suit alleges.

The other individual defendant, David Courvelle, is accused of sexually assaulting one of the plaintiffs multiple times, and of using two plantiffs to stand guard while he raped another person who was held there.

Courvelle pleaded guilty to a federal sex abuse charge and in June was sentenced to three years in prison.

The four plaintiffs make claims under the federal Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act and under Louisiana state law for unlawful sexual assault, infliction of emotional distress and negligence.

Two of the plaintiffs are identified as transgender men and one is identified as a non-binary person. Two are residents of Mexico and one is a native of El Salvador in federal custody in South Carolina. The fourth is only identified as “Jane Doe.”

The suit accuses Reyes of using detained people in a “forced labor scheme.” He would wake them up in the middle of the night and assign them to do heavy manual labor, or work with strong chemicals, the suit alleges, and if they didn’t he would threaten to withhold their medications, to harm their family members or put them in solitary, the suit alleges.

The suit also claims that Reyes would find the plaintiffs’ children using social media and make comments about them that led the plaintiffs to stop visitation from their family members.

The lawsuit claims that Reyes told them that he was “protected by the higher ups” and there was “nothing anyone could say or do to hurt or affect him.”

The suit details repeated sexual assault of the plaintiffs, including the allegation that Reyes forced Jane Doe to perform oral sex on him almost daily for four months.

Any attempts to file complaints, get medical attention for injuries or resist the labor or sexual abuse led to retaliation and more threats, the plaintiffs allege.

The suit asks for damages, punitive damages and restitution.

text:
Earlier today, the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals vacated a preliminary district court injunction of Virginia Code § 15.2-1726.1, which places limits on state and local officers in participating in federal civil immigration enforcement. Enacted in April 2026, the law was partially enjoined on August 31, 2026, by a federal district court, and thus briefly did not apply to existing 287(g) agreements. However, as of this morning, this law is no longer enjoined and is now fully in effect. The Legal Aid Justice Center supported this litigation by filing amicus briefs at both the federal district court and at the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals.

“This decision affirmed what we knew to be true—Virginia can and will protect its immigrant communities by refusing to entangle itself with ICE,” said Legal Aid Justice Center Senior Supervising Organizer John Cano.

This decision means that 287g contracts and IGSA contracts must adopt certain required conditions or be rendered void, effective immediately. “State and local officers should not be allowed to terrorize immigrants in Virginia under the guise of federal immigration enforcement,” explained Emily Lopynski, Senior Supervising Attorney at the Legal Aid Justice Center.

While there may be new developments in this case, today, we celebrate this huge win with all of those that pushed for this monumental law in Virginia. LAJC will continue to monitor the case and share updates as it proceeds back to the district court for further proceedings.

title: ICE airport arrests spark outrage during busy holiday travel week - Scripps News
description:
Asylum seekers sue Trump administration over ICE rearresting immigrants A broader shift at the gate The Seattle arrests are part of a broader shift in immigration enforcement at airports.
Immigration attorneys say ICE arrests at airports are becoming more common.
The information sharing has contributed to hundreds of immigration arrests at airports, including Doyle's client, Princeton Ph.D. student Eva Yi Xie.
"Masked ICE agents in plainclothes without badges charging through our work space upends these tenets of safety and security," she said.
In a statement to Scripps News, the Department of Homeland Security defended the arrests and cast it as a reversal of previous immigration enforcement policy.
text:
Immigration arrests at the nation's airports are drawing fierce backlash from state officials, immigration attorneys and airline workers, after federal agents detained travelers at the gate in two high-profile cases on opposite sides of the country.

The arrests, days apart during one of the busiest travel weeks of the year, are raising new questions about how U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is using airline passenger data to find and detain people before they fly.

At Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, a father and daughter were about to board an Alaska Airlines flight Saturday when masked federal agents detained them on a jet bridge, which led to hours-long flight delay. Bystander video of the chaotic encounter, shared widely on social media, captured a woman crying for help.

The pair, identified as Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza and his daughter, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, were were headed to a baptism, according to their lawyer. The two have lived in the U.S. since 2015, are seeking asylum and have no criminal record. ICE said both overstayed their visas. The agency also said Hernandez Mejia threw hot coffee at officers during the encounter and could face a charge of assaulting a federal officer.

The detentions set off immediate outrage. Washington Governor Bob Ferguson said at a news conference Sunday that he placed the blame of the encounter squarely on the agency.

"It's completely and totally out of control, which is why I think it needs to be abolished," Ferguson said.

The governor called on airlines to help keep ICE out of the airports, saying the agency is "deeply, deeply un-American," and “beyond reform.”

“It is time to abolish Donald Trump's ICE and replace it with something that is more sane," he added.

Asylum seekers sue Trump administration over ICE rearresting immigrants

A broader shift at the gate

The Seattle arrests are part of a broader shift in immigration enforcement at airports. Immigration attorneys say ICE arrests at airports are becoming more common.

Kerry Doyle, an immigration attorney and former DHS official under the Biden administration, told Scripps News immigrant travelers have become targets of President Trump’s mass deportation agenda.

“I've had some clients arrested right as they came through the screening and then many of the others arrested in between the screening and the gate or at the gate or on the jet way,” Doyle said.

"They're in the process. They filed applications the way they're supposed to. They're waiting for interviews. They've gotten their work authorization. They're following the system and this administration – ICE – is just being so aggressive and often violent with people.”

Doyle said these ICE operations at airports are "a big scare tactic” to “deport as many people as they can, force as many people out of the country as they can.”

"What ICE is doing is they see people flying as easy pickings," Doyle said. "And they are info sharing with TSA, they're running manifests and flagging anybody that has overstayed a visa."

Since May 2025, TSA and ICE have shared passenger information under an agreement revealed this past summer. The information sharing has contributed to hundreds of immigration arrests at airports, including Doyle's client, Princeton Ph.D. student Eva Yi Xie.

"I don't think they picked her out of a hat," Doyle said.

RELATED STORY | Mullin faces lawmakers on cyber threats, immigration enforcement at House hearing

'Heartbreaking message’

Four days before the Seattle arrests, agents detained Xie during what DHS called a “targeted immigration enforcement operation” at Reagan National Airport as she was heading home from a science conference. Her lawyer said the 24-year-old asylum seeker came to the U.S. from China as a child in 2016, has no criminal history and was arrested without a warrant.

A DHS spokesperson told Scripps News Xie overstayed a visa, noting "a pending application does not confer legal status in the United States.”

Her Ph.D. adviser, Princeton neuroscience professor Carlos Brody, said word of Xie’s arrest reached their lab in a “heartbreaking message” that was cut short.

"It said, 'I'm detained by ICE. Please help. I'm in DCA, that's Ronald Reagan National Airport.' And then it said, 'I'm being taken to,' and there it just stopped,” Brody said.

Brody said the lab had no idea where she was being taken until she was able to call his office. He described Xie as a dedicated researcher who, according to her attorney, asked about her ongoing experiments on a call from an ICE processing center.

“She is someone that really loves science, really loves trying to gain new knowledge, and she also loves sharing it,” Brody said. “I didn't know how many undergraduates, friends, colleagues she had helped, and so many have been contacting us now, and are distraught at losing this person that just helped them so much.”

Both Xie’s adviser and attorney said her detention is already being felt across Princeton's community and beyond.

"The outpouring of support for her has been unbelievable,” Doyle said, noting she’s been contacted by Xie’s high school, MIT, where she went for undergrad, and members of the Princeton community.

"She's a very gentle, kind, caring person who is a pillar of our community," Brody said. "She is one of us, and not only is she one of us, she's one of the best of us. And this shouldn't be happening to any of us."

Xie remains at the Caroline Detention Center in Virginia. A federal judge on Friday barred ICE from moving her out of the state while the court weighs whether her arrest was legal.

RELATED STORY | DHS: Nearly 4,200 arrested during 10-Day Texas immigration operation

Flight attendants warn of danger

The arrests have also alarmed airline workers. Sara Nelson, president of the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, which represents 55,000 flight attendants, said the enforcement actions threaten safety in the airport and in the air.

"Aviation connects the people of the world," Nelson said in a statement to Scripps News. "We bring people together — especially right now, as millions of people travel to visit loved ones and celebrate our American traditions and global holidays."

Nelson said transparency and trust are central to airport safety, and that masked agents disrupt it. "Masked ICE agents in plainclothes without badges charging through our work space upends these tenets of safety and security," she said. "It puts crew and the passengers we serve in physical danger, and creates a culture of fear in our workplaces."

She warned the disruptions can endanger flights. "When risk is present, flights are diverted, delayed, or never take off at all," Nelson said. "This kind of extreme, out-of-control disruption of our liberties makes all of us less safe." She called on "the entire traveling public" to join flight attendants in "demanding ICE out of our airports."

In a statement to Scripps News, the Department of Homeland Security defended the arrests and cast it as a reversal of previous immigration enforcement policy.

"DHS reversed the horrendous Biden-era policy that allowed aliens in our country illegally to jet around our country," the spokesperson said. "Under President Trump, DHS will no longer tolerate this. This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport."

3rd grade student taken into ICE custody

What travelers should know

The cases come amid growing issues for domestic travel, but particularly rising uncertainty for immigrant travelers. Advocates say for many immigrants, flying inside the U.S. has become a greater risk — even for people with legal status or pending applications.

Immigration groups say certain groups face higher risk, especially those with deportation orders, people who have lost legal protections like TPS and immigrants with pending asylum or green card applications.

Experts advise noncitizen immigrants heading into the holidays to know their status and talk to an immigration attorney before booking a flight.

text:
Donald Trump's administration appeared to have cut off a government contractor from running its "self-deportation" program after blowing through tens of millions of dollars as part of a contract worth nearly $1 billion.

But the Department of Homeland Security handed the company another $150 million this month, according to government procurement records.

Salus Worldwide Solutions — founded by a donor to ousted DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, whose handling of contracts at the agency came under bipartisan scrutiny leading to Trump firing her — was awarded a no-bid aviation contract last year despite no prior federal contracting experience .

The company was tapped to run the administration's Project Homecoming, which offered $1,000 and a flight out of the country to immigrants who sign an agreement to "self-deport."

In September, reportedly unimpressed with the company's performance, DHS under Noem's successor Markwayne Mullin awarded a separate contract — potentially worth more than $2 billion — to rival firm Response AI Solutions, The Daily Beast's PunchUp first reported.

Salus filed a challenge to that decision with the Government Accountability Office last month.

But on November 10, 11 days before its existing agreement was supposed to come to an end, DHS approved another $150 million for Salus, PunchUp first reported.

That new injection of cash brings the government's total commitment to the company to at least $898 million, according to federal spending records.

Salus was founded by William Walters III, a former State Department official and a political donor to the president and Noem. Walters donated $10,000 to the Noem-backing American Resolve super PAC in 2024.

Last year, the company received a contract worth up to $915 million to support the administration's self-deportation plan, intended to boost the numbers of immigrant removals as federal agencies pump enormous resources into deporting tens of thousands of people from the country.

Daedalus Aviation Corp. received a separate $464 million no-bid contract to buy 10 airplanes that were reportedly kept out of service or have been used to ferry around Trump administration officials instead.

Noem has also disputed reporting that her agency vastly overpaid one Walters' company for five airplanes at a substantial markup just hours before she left office.

In a furious social media post last month, Noem demanded that The New York Times "entirely" retract claims that the agency spent $108 million for a luxuriously appointed Boeing 737 that the company bought months earlier from a seller who asked for less than $90 million.

Noem also said that characterizing Walters a "donor" was "materially misleading" and "conveys a false implication of a direct financial relationship obviously intended to influence official action."

Democrats on the Senate Appropriations Committee, which is reviewing the agency's "wasteful use" of taxpayer dollars, said earlier this year that DHS appears to be "running an in-house private jet service."

Previous reporting has alleged that Salus had approached subcontracting firms with proposals to perform work for DHS only if it would then direct lucrative kickbacks to Noem's chief aide Corey Lewandowski or consulting firms connected to him.

The Trump administration has cited "emergency" conditions hundreds of times to rush through no-bid contracts, dozens of which are under congressional scrutiny and the subject of federal lawsuits.

The agency has failed to use its massive pile of taxpayer funding to "actually improve the lives of Americans by requiring basic compliance with the Fourth Amendment, acquiring and deploying body-worn cameras to every law enforcement officer in the field, mandating minimum officer identification, or properly training new hires," according to a group of Democratic senators demanding investigations.

Instead, "this administration has lit taxpayer dollars on fire by acquiring new and unnecessary planes to jet Trump officials around in extreme luxury that the vast majority of Americans will never experience," they said.

Last week, incoming House Oversight Chairman Robert Garcia demanded White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, Noem and Lewandowski preserve records ahead of Democratic investigations into DHS spending and alleged misconduct.

More than two-thirds of the more than 980,000 deportations in the first 18 months of the second Trump term involved immigrants initially intercepted at the U.S-Mexico border, but deportations resulting from arrests in the country's interior have accounted for a rising share of all removals, according to a recent analysis from the Migration Policy Institute.

But the overall impact of the government's "self-deportation" campaign has been difficult to measure independently under Homeland Security's reduced immigration enforcement reporting.

Last year, DHS declared that 1.6 million people self-deported, a figure that the Center for Migration Studies has called a "self-serving fantasy."

That figure would account for 15 percent of the estimated total population of unauthorized immigrants in the U.S., or about 200,000 people per month voluntarily leaving the country, according to the nonpartisan think tank.

text:
Los Angeles joined a growing national coalition of housing authorities and local government partners to challenge the Trump administration over a new federal housing rule that threatens mixed-status immigrant families, it was announced Monday.

Since 1995, mixed-status families have been authorized to live together in HUD-funded housing as long as federal subsidies covered only eligible household members.

However, HUD issued a new rule Nov. 11 that eliminates those protections. Under the new policy, families with both immigration-eligible and ineligible members will need to choose between separating their households or losing the housing assistance.

The new rule is scheduled to take effect Dec. 14.

The Housing Authority of the City of Los Angeles, the Los Angeles County Development Authority and the Los Angeles City Attorney joined a lawsuit that seeks judicial review of the rule and asks the court to block its implementation and enforcement.

HUD’s new rule eliminates a longstanding approach and establishes extensive new citizenship and immigration-status verification requirements for participants in public housing and Housing Choice Voucher programs, according to LA housing authorities.

The coalition’s lawsuit, filed under the Administrative Procedure Act, argues that HUD’s rule is unlawful because it exceeds the authority granted by Congress, fails to adequately consider the impacts on families, housing providers, local governments, and homelessness prevention efforts, and does not meaningfully consider less harmful alternatives.

Furthermore, the coalition of housing authorities from cities across the U.S, such as San Francisco, Boston, Chicago, Providence, New York, San Diego, Seattle, Santa Barbara and San Diego, and now Los Angeles, argues new verification, notice, documentation requirements will place a financial burden on them that will divert resources away from housing families and preserving affordable housing.

According to HACLA, approximately 1,700 mixed-status families, representing an estimated 7,500 Angelenos, could be impacted by the rule. Many of these households include U.S. citizen children who now face the threat of losing their homes because of the immigration status of a parent or another family member.

“As one of the nation’s largest public housing authorities, we are joining this legal challenge because housing stability strengthens families, communities, and local economies,” HACLA President and CEO Lourdes Castro Ramírez said in a statement.

“This rule threatens the housing stability of more than 1,800 households we serve, including more than 2,500 children, while extending far beyond mixed-status families to create significant new administrative burdens for housing authorities. We are concerned that it could undermine years of progress in reducing homelessness and keeping families safely housed. These issues deserve prompt and thorough judicial review,” Ramírez said.

In L.A. County, the LACDA serves just under 400 mixed-status households, with the rule impacting more than 1,500 individuals and more than 600 minors.

“We stand firm in our commitment to advocating for County residents and to preserving housing opportunities for the vulnerable households we serve,” LACDA Executive Director Emilio Salas said in a statement.

Salas explained the HUD rule creates an unnecessary hardship on families, by forcing family separation or homelessness, and displacing U.S.-born children.

“This rule also harms legally present immigrants who may not be eligible for assistance under the new framework. Ultimately, the harm caused by this new policy far outweighs any perceived benefit.,” Salas added.

Coalition members believe the rule replaces a longstanding framework that was already compliant with federal law and successfully balanced program integrity with family stability.

They argue that by eliminating the ability of mixed-status families to remain together while receiving prorated assistance, the rule increases the risk of family disruption, housing instability, displacement, and homelessness while imposing substantial implementation costs on public housing agencies and local governments.

“No family should have to choose between staying together and keeping a roof over their heads,” Los Angeles City Attorney Hydee Feldstein Soto said in a statement. “This rule threatens to uproot thousands of vulnerable families, including children who are U.S. citizens, and worsen an already devastating housing crisis.”

In a previous statement, HUD Secretary Scott Turner defended the new federal rule.

“President Trump warned that the days of illegal aliens and ineligible noncitizens exploiting government-funded welfare programs would be over,” Turner said in a statement the day before HUD finalized the new housing rule. “It’s unacceptable that America’s homeless veterans, disabled, elderly and victims of domestic violence languish on wait lists while illegals and ineligibles scam our system. American taxpayers will no longer foot the bill. Promises made, promises kept.”

Turner noted that a recent audit found nearly 200,000 tenants with incomplete or unverified eligibility status. HUD-funded housing serves only a quarter of eligible households in need, according to HUD.

Los Angeles previously opposed a nearly identical proposal in 2019 during the first Trump administration.

That year, HUD tried to revise the longstanding policy but eventually withdrew the proposal in 2021. In February 2026, HUD again, under Trump’s presidency, reintroduced the proposed rule change, which prompted an outpour of opposition. More than 11,000 public comments from individuals, advocacy groups and members of Congress urged against it.

U.S. Department of Homeland Security. The ruling follows a federal lawsuit filed in October 2026 by higher education organizations challenging ICE’s Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) restrictions.

The court’s order blocks two SEVP broadcast messages issued on Aug. 12 and Aug. 24, 2026, which attempted to limit CPT authorization solely to internships and practical training required for all students in a degree program—eliminating elective for-credit training opportunities that had been permitted since 1991.

Nationwide Stay

Enforcement or application of the Aug. 12 and Aug. 24, 2026, SEVP Broadcast Messages is suspended nationwide pending ongoing judicial review.

Elective CPT Restored

Designated School Officials (DSOs) at member institutions of the plaintiff associations—including the Association of American Universities, Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts and NAFSA—may resume authorizing CPT under the prior regulatory standard, which permits elective practical training taken for academic credit.

Protection Against Retroactive Enforcement

The government is barred from enforcing the restricted CPT standard against plaintiff institutions, their employees and their students, both prospectively and with respect to CPT approvals issued prior to the August 2026 broadcasts.

Background of the Ruling

In October 2026, higher education associations filed suit alleging that SEVP violated the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) by abruptly reversing a 35-year policy without explanation or consideration of institutional and student reliance interests.

The court found that the plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits because SEVP failed to acknowledge or justify its departure from decades of regulatory interpretation. The court also noted that the broadcasts caused irreparable harm by forcing universities to deny or rescind fall CPT authorizations and threatening schools and DSOs with loss of certification and legal liability.

title: AG Campbell sues feds over ICE courthouse arrests - CommonWealth Beacon

A provision restricting courthouse arrests took effect on November 3.
Last year, immigration agents arrested 614 people on Massachusetts courthouse grounds, according to the Trial Court.
Courthouse arrests “damage our entire justice system by chilling access to courts,” wrote Lawyers for Civil Rights in a letter last week calling for action from Campbell’s office.

text:
IT’S BEEN LESS than a month since a ban on warrantless civil arrests at Massachusetts courthouses took effect, and federal immigration agents have already detained 38 people on courthouse grounds.

Amid public complaints that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement was blatantly violating the state’s courthouse arrest law, Attorney General Andrea Campbell sued Monday to protect what she says is the state’s constitutional right to limit immigration actions on its property.

Arguing that an ICE directive to ignore state bans on courthouse arrests violates federal law and the Constitution, she wants a Boston federal judge to block the directive and declare that civil immigration arrests at state courts are prohibited unless state law permits them.

“These aggressive actions in Massachusetts state courthouses are no accident,” her office wrote in its complaint. Federal agents “are intentionally disregarding state law and the sovereign interests of Massachusetts in regulating what happens inside its courthouses.”

The PROTECT Act, signed into law on August 5, laid out an array of new rules for federal immigration agents. It immediately prohibited most civil arrests, including immigration arrests, without a judicial warrant or court order in “sensitive locations” including public K-12 schools, licensed child care centers, health care facilities, and state property.

A provision restricting courthouse arrests took effect on November 3.

Last year, immigration agents arrested 614 people on Massachusetts courthouse grounds, according to the Trial Court.

But just hours after the new court restrictions kicked in early this month, agents detained a man in a Chelsea courthouse. Four other people were also arrested that day, according to the Trial Court, and dozens more were detained over the next two weeks in courthouses in Chelsea, Framingham, Marlborough, Peabody, and Medford.

Courthouse arrests “damage our entire justice system by chilling access to courts,” wrote Lawyers for Civil Rights in a letter last week calling for action from Campbell’s office. “Faced with the risk of arrest and deportation, victims hesitate to report crimes, witnesses decline to testify, and families miss legal proceedings that decide their futures.”

ICE officials did not immediately respond to request for comment, but have previously said that detaining people at courthouses is a “common-sense” move, because people there are already correctly identified and screened for weapons.

In an October press release touting the arrest of a Dominican man, ICE lambasted the PROTECT Act.

“Time and time again, sanctuary politicians in Massachusetts have made the dumbfounding choice to prioritize dangerous criminal illegal aliens rather than their law-abiding American citizens,” said acting ICE Boston Field Office Director Joseph Sher.

The PROTECT Act created a right for people to sue ICE agents in state court alleging violations of their rights under the US Constitution. It also allowed the attorney general to sue if federal agents interfere with voting or arrest anyone in protected locations without a judicial warrant.

Campbell argues the Bay State arrests violate Massachusetts’s sovereign authority. She filed her lawsuit under the Administrative Procedures Act and is also arguing a violation of the 10th Amendment.

Immigration officers are making their arrests under a directive issued in May 2025 that said courthouse arrests “are often required when jurisdictions refuse to cooperate with ICE, including when such jurisdictions refuse to honor immigration detainers.”

The directive was vacated by a California federal judge in June, in a decision the administration has appealed.

The courthouse arrest suit drops Massachusetts into an ongoing legal quagmire about state and federal supremacy.

Federal courts in Connecticut, California, New York, and Pennsylvania have blocked state laws that required ICE agents to identify themselves and barred them from wearing masks while making arrests. The Connecticut law also allowed the state to investigate and prosecute federal immigration actions it believes involve excessive force.

The Supremacy Clause of the US Constitution prohibits states from “interfering with or controlling the operations of the Federal Government,” wrote US District Judge Vernon Oliver in his ruling on the Connecticut case, “and federal officers are immune from state prosecution when acting within the scope of their federal authority.”

Before Donald Trump’s first presidency, for years federal immigration agencies had restricted immigration activities around sensitive locations like schools, courts, and places of worship. After the Trump administration rolled back that guidance last year, Massachusetts lawmakers moved to enshrine those restrictions in state law.

Sen. Cindy Friedman, a Democrat who was one of the lead negotiators of the PROTECT Act, said Monday that lawmakers are confident they are “on really solid constitutional grounds” after deploying “an enormous amount of energy, resources and research” to craft it.

“Everything that we put in the PROTECT Act, we felt like we were walking right up to the constitutional line of what we were well within our rights as a state to do,” added Rep. Andy Vargas, another member of the bill-negotiating team and chair of the Legislature’s Black and Latino Legislative Caucus.

He contrasted the Massachusetts law with measures in other states that aimed to place new restrictions on how ICE agents do their jobs, including bans on wearing masks.

Asked if he had expected ICE to ignore the law, Vargas replied, “No, by no means.”

While the state is generally barred from interfering with immigration enforcement, a task reserved for the federal government, Campbell’s office said immigration agents are not acting within a purely federal capacity.

Rather, the office wrote, ICE is “commandeering state personnel and resources by using the infrastructure of state government to enforce federal immigration law. Specifically, they are relying on state-generated information, state infrastructure, state law enforcement, and state security systems to identify, locate, disarm, and contain federal targets.”

The relationship between ICE, courthouses, and law enforcement is already under active consideration at the state’s highest court.

Supreme Judicial Court justices are considering a bundle of cases revolving around the power of state courts to demand the return of criminal defendants who are whisked away by immigration enforcement during the trial.

Campbell referenced such disruptions on Monday.

“That individual could spend months in ICE custody, only to be released if ICE cannot establish a legal basis for deportation,” she said. “Meanwhile, the criminal charges remain unresolved. The defendant has not been held accountable to our justice system, or provided an opportunity to mount the defense, and the victim has been denied the opportunity for justice. How does that make anyone safer?”

Middlesex District Attorney Marian Ryan — who back in 2019, along with then-Suffolk District Attorney Rachael Rollins, unsuccessfully challenged ICE’s patrolling of courthouses for immigrants to detain — said this state suit was on much firmer footing.

While that suit aimed to protect the courts’ ability to create and enforce their own policies around how to handle immigration arrests at their courthouses, she said, this complaint is defending state law on state infrastructure.

In an interview, Ryan described ICE arrests during prosecutions as deeply disruptive. Not only does the state’s plan to prosecute get interrupted, she said, but defendants disappearing and sometimes reentering the country without notice makes it difficult for victims to make safety plans.

Under President Trump, Ryan said, “the communication has been nonexistent. I’ve been a prosecutor for a long time. We’ve always dealt with ICE. They’ve always brought people back and forth. We were able to figure that out. Now we just have no idea.”

The SJC heard arguments on three ICE cases in early October and is now weighing whether state courts are empowered to order defendants be returned to Massachusetts, whether they must try to secure their return, and whether prosecutors should have to inform the court if they are aware ICE may be eyeing a defendant for removal. It’s expected to rule early next year.

Campbell’s courthouse arrest suit introduces another legal dispute over state versus federal supremacy.

“This is really a new area of the law, because we haven’t faced a federal administration that’s tried to step into the states and take away their authority before,” said Carol Rose, the executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union of Massachusetts. “So all of this is cutting-edge law.”

text:
BOSTON — Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell filed a lawsuit against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Monday, challenging the agency’s policy of making civil immigration arrests inside state courthouses without judicial warrants.

The lawsuit contends that the practice violates the Massachusetts PROTECT Act, which took effect Nov. 3 and prohibits civil immigration arrests in state courthouses unless officers have a judicial warrant. Campbell’s office argues that ICE’s continued arrests interfere with the state’s ability to operate its courts, disrupt proceedings, and conflict with the Commonwealth’s authority over its judicial system under the Tenth Amendment.

Governor Maura Healey: “The Trump Administration’s ICE arrests at Massachusetts courthouses are interfering with our justice system and undermining public safety. When people are afraid to go to court, victims are less likely to report crimes, survivors are less likely to seek protection, and our communities are less safe. That’s why I signed the PROTECT Act. We expect ICE and all federal agents to follow Massachusetts law. I want to thank Attorney General Campbell for filing this lawsuit to hold the Trump Administration accountable, enforce Massachusetts law and protect the safety and rights of our residents.”

According to the complaint, ICE arrested more than 600 people at Massachusetts state courthouses in 2025 and more than 500 during the first 10 months of 2026. In the roughly two and a half weeks since the PROTECT Act’s courthouse provisions took effect, ICE has arrested at least 38 people in Massachusetts courthouses without judicial warrants, the attorney general’s office said.

The suit specifically targets a May 2025 ICE directive that permits courthouse arrests even in states that prohibit them. A federal court in California ruled that directive unlawful and vacated it in June 2026, yet ICE has continued the practice, according to the filing.

State Senator Michael J. Rodrigues (D-Westport): “The Legislature passed the PROTECT Act to safeguard civil rights and due process for all Massachusetts residents, and this lawsuit makes clear that we will not permit overzealous federal agents to disregard the Constitution. A strong component of the PROTECT Act was to empower the Attorney General to hold ICE agents accountable for their actions against individuals, and especially families, for their recent unlawful activity in Medford, and in my district in Fall River. I commend Attorney General Campbell for her actions, and I hope this lawsuit sends a clear message to ICE and their agents that the Commonwealth will continue to exercise its authority to operate its own judicial system.”

Campbell’s office alleges the arrests have practical consequences for the court system. The complaint describes cases in which survivors of domestic violence hesitated to seek restraining orders and one instance in which a woman declined to report a rape out of fear of being arrested by ICE if she had to appear in court. It also cites a Nov. 3 incident at a Medford courthouse in which ICE arrested a defendant scheduled for trial, preventing his appearance, and damaged security barriers that the state must now replace.

In a statement, Campbell said ICE’s actions make it more difficult to hold criminal defendants accountable and can leave cases unresolved if individuals are later released from immigration custody. “I, along with our district attorneys, share the goal of holding defendants accountable for crimes, yet ICE’s unlawful tactics to arrest someone for a civil immigration violation is not the same as holding them accountable for a crime,” she said.

The lawsuit asks the court to block ICE’s courthouse arrest policies and prevent the agency from conducting civil immigration arrests at Massachusetts courthouses unless allowed under state law.

The case is being handled by attorneys from the Attorney General’s Office of State Trial Counsel. It is the latest action by Campbell’s office related to federal immigration enforcement practices. Earlier this month, she joined other state attorneys general in a letter to congressional leaders urging greater oversight of ICE.

New York state Attorney General Letitia James joined 21 other attorneys general to announce a lawsuit against the Trump administration as a new U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development rule revokes assistance for families of “mixed immigration statuses.”

“Everyone deserves a safe place to call home. Denying a child that security because of who they live with is cruel and indefensible. With our country already in the throes of a housing crisis, it is outrageous that the federal government would push even more families out of their homes,” James said during a press conference Monday.

James filed the lawsuit against HUD and Secretary Scott Turner with attorneys general from California, Massachusetts, Arizona, Colorado, Washington, D.C., Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico and Oregon, as well as Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro.

James said that the rule would force families to choose between keeping their housing and staying together. She said Congress wrote that into law in 1997.

“For nearly 30 years, families with mixed immigration statuses have been able to receive housing assistance for eligible household members and that assistance is already reduced to exclude anyone who is ineligible; Congress expressly protected that arrangement. In fact, when Congress established this prorated housing assistance, it explicitly said mixed-status families could not lose their assistance simply because an ineligible family member lived with them and HUD has no authority to rewrite a law Congress wrote,” James said during the press conference.

The new rules would only allow a family to stay in HUD-assisted housing if every person is a U.S. citizen or eligible immigrant. They estimate that 20,000 mixed-status families will lose their housing assistance, which equals about 78,000 individuals.

“There are children who could lose their bedrooms, their schools, and the stability every child needs to thrive, but this rule reaches even further, it would require American citizens receiving federal housing assistance to undergo citizenship checks using a system with a documented record of errors and then produce additional documents if that system fails to recognize them,” James said.

In New York City, James said that approximately 2,540 mixed-status families would be displaced from federally subsidized housing. James and the other attorneys general are asking that the courts strike down the rule, and block HUD from implementing or enforcing it.

The rule is set to go into effect on Dec. 14 but was proposed in February.

“I can say that during the period of time where individuals were submitting comments, despite the thousands of comments that were filed with HUD, the rule remains unchanged,” James said. “We are confident again that this rule will be struck down by the courts because HUD does not have the power to erase a protection Congress wrote into federal law.”

text:
​​Two federal judges in Massachusetts have blocked Trump administration policies affecting international students, preserving longstanding rules on how long students can remain in the United States and their ability to participate in internships and other practical training.

On Nov. 16, a federal judge struck down a rule that would have replaced the longstanding Duration o-Status policy for international students and exchange visitors with fixed periods of admission.

Under the existing system, students generally can remain in the United States as long as they maintain their immigration status and make satisfactory progress in their studies. The administration's rule would have limited student visas to four years, regardless of the field of level of study, and required them to apply for extensions if they needed more time to complete their programs. It also would have placed new restrictions on changing academic programs or transferring schools.

The judge struck down the rule nationwide, although the administration could appeal.

A day later, another federal judge in Massachusetts blocked new restrictions on Curricular Practical Training (CPT)​, which allows international students to gain work experience related to their studies.

The administration's August guidance sought to limit CPT to training required for graduation, excluding elective internships and other experiences taken for academic credit. The judge found that the restrictions marked a significant departure from longstanding federal policy and temporarily halted their enforcement nationwide while the lawsuit proceeds.

ACE Raises Concerns About H-1B Visa Proposal

The rulings come amid broader changes to federal immigration policies affecting international students, faculty, and researchers.

On Nov. 13, ACE and 16 other higher education organizations urged the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw a proposed rule​ that would make it harder for colleges and universities to renew H-1B visas for faculty and other employees.

The proposal would require immigration officials to review previously approved cases from scratch, even when nothing has changed. In their comments, the associations warned that the change would add to an already substantial processing backlog and create more uncertainty for institutions seeking to retain international faculty and staff.

International Enrollment Continues to Decline

The legal developments follow the release of new data showing a decline in international student enrollment at U.S. colleges and universities.

The annual Open Doors report​ found that overall international student enrollment fell 3 percent during the 2025–26 academic year. The number of new international students dropped 18 percent, while graduate enrollment declined 13 percent. One bright spot was a 14 percent increase in participation in Optional Practical Training (OPT), which allows eligible international students to gain work experience related to their studies.

text:
A coalition of nearly two dozen plaintiffs including New York City sued the Trump administration Monday to stop a rule barring families with undocumented members from living in public housing or receiving certain rental vouchers from taking effect next month.

The lawsuit, which was filed in Massachusetts federal court, argues the rule from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development would harm the plaintiffs and thousands of mixed-status families composed of undocumented people and those with legal status or citizenship. Those suing include other cities, counties and public housing agencies.

“We will not stand by while families are put at risk,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement. “New York City is proud to join our peers across the country in fighting this cruel and unlawful rule.”

New York Attorney General Letitia James in the same court Monday filed a separate suit on behalf of more than 20 states also seeking to block the rule on similar grounds.

“This rule runs counter to our nation’s values and the very purpose of these housing programs,” she said in a statement, citing a national “housing crisis.”

HUD did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In recent weeks, HUD Secretary Scott Turner has said the rule would prevent “illegal aliens and ineligible noncitizens” from benefiting from government-funded programs.

That’s not how the programs have worked. Mixed-status families have for years been allowed to live in subsidized housing, though only eligible individuals in the household receive a rental subsidy that is prorated based on who is eligible rather than the full household size.

HUD’s new rule — which the Trump administration proposed in February and is set to take effect on Dec. 14 — would no longer allow that to happen.

If implemented, about 20,000 households across the country would be at risk of losing their homes if they live in public housing, receive Section 8 project-based rental assistance or participate in the Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher Program.

Those households consist of nearly 80,000 people, most of whom are eligible for HUD housing assistance, according to the lawsuits, which cite HUD figures.

The city’s Department of Housing Preservation and Development assists more than 350 mixed-status families made up of about 1,280 people, according to the city complaint. Even more mixed-status families live in NYCHA housing, though the authority did not respond to questions about how many.

‘Impossible Choice’

Monday’s lawsuits challenging the rule follow another lawsuit that a group of housing advocates filed Thursday, also in the U.S. District Court in Massachusetts. One of the plaintiffs in that suit is the Alfred E. Smith Houses Resident Association, which represents tenants of a NYCHA development in Lower Manhattan. There are 16 mixed-status families at risk of losing their homes in the Smith Houses, according to the suit.

Another plaintiff, named as Jane Doe #2, is a Honduran woman living in a project-based Section 8 apartment in New York City with her husband, who is a U.S. permanent resident, and their three daughters, all of whom are U.S. citizens. According to the lawsuit, Doe #2 is the primary caregiver for her children, including her middle daughter, who has autism. Doe #2’s husband is the family’s sole provider, as she is unable to work because of pain from an accident on a job.

The lawsuit states that if the rule takes effect, Doe #2 would have to leave the home — and because she takes care of her daughters, her family would lose their apartment or else be separated from her. But the family, who pays $1,830 a month for rent, would be hard-pressed to find anywhere else they can afford.

Lucy Newman, an attorney for the nonprofit Legal Aid Society who is working on the suit filed last week, said mixed-status families should not voluntarily move out of their homes before the rule kicks in. But she said it would force families to make an “impossible choice.”

“If implemented, this rule inhumanely compels mixed-status families to choose between staying together and losing critical rental assistance or separating to allow eligible members to maintain it,” Newman said. “If implemented, this rule will cause the mass displacement of thousands of mixed status families in New York City from their homes.”

The new lawsuit by New York City and the coalition of municipalities makes a similar argument. It highlights the city’s low housing vacancy rate and relatively high asking rents. Sheltering the families affected by the rule would cost the city about $156 to $277 per day per household, depending on the number of family members, according to the complaint.

The suit also argues the rules’ requirements for housing agencies would increase delays and burden them financially and administratively.

title: Attorney says father, daughter arrested on Sea-Tac jetway were following legal pathways
description:

DHS alleged that during Mendoza’s arrest, Hernandez Mejía "hurled hot coffee on the officers" and will face a federal felony charge for assaulting a federal officer.
The dispute over their legal status comes down to a gray area in federal immigration law.
In reality, they had lived in Washington for more than a decade and held federal work permits years before the tournament.
KUOW also confirmed that Hernandez Mejía lives in Mountlake Terrace, graduated from Western Washington University, and worked for a Seattle-area youth nonprofit.
text:
An immigration attorney representing the Mountlake Terrace father and daughter arrested by federal agents inside a crowded Seattle-Tacoma International Airport jetway over the weekend says both entered the U.S. legally more than a decade ago, hold valid work permits, and were traveling to California for a family baptism ceremony when they were detained.

Video recorded by passengers Saturday morning shows masked officers dressed in black clothing wrestling two travelers to the floor on the jet bridge for Alaska Airlines Flight 1306 to Los Angeles, as bystanders screamed and prompted the flight crew to walk off the plane before a nearly three-hour departure delay.

The Department of Homeland Security identified the detainees as Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza and Sofia Hernandez Mejía, describing both as Mexican nationals who overstayed visas. DHS alleged that during Mendoza’s arrest, Hernandez Mejía "hurled hot coffee on the officers" and will face a federal felony charge for assaulting a federal officer.

The dispute over their legal status comes down to a gray area in federal immigration law. Applying for asylum or a Green Card does not grant a new visa, meaning an applicant's original entry visa still expires. Even so, federal law grants people with pending cases "authorized stay," allowing them to live and work in the U.S. legally while waiting for a decision.

In an interview with KUOW on Sunday after visiting both clients at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, attorney Olia Catala said the pair entered the U.S. legally on tourist visas in 2015, when Hernandez Mejía was 14. Those temporary visas expired after six months.

Within a year of arriving, as required under federal asylum rules, Mendoza applied for asylum for himself and his daughter. Hernandez Mejía later graduated from college, worked for a nonprofit, and married a U.S. citizen, allowing her to apply separately for a Green Card. Both applications remain stuck in years-long backlogs at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

Under federal rules, asylum seekers can get work permits about six months after filing, while marriage-based green card applicants can apply right away. Both held valid work permits when they were arrested, Catala said. She added that immigration authorities are increasingly detaining people in that waiting period by pointing to their expired entry visas.

"Congress created these legal pathways. Sofia and her father were using them," Catala said. "If we tell immigrants to follow the law, we cannot punish them later for doing so."

That 11-year timeline also contradicts false claims that circulated widely on social media over the weekend alleging Mendoza and Hernandez Mejía came to Seattle on tourist visas for this summer's World Cup and never left. In reality, they had lived in Washington for more than a decade and held federal work permits years before the tournament. KUOW also confirmed that Hernandez Mejía lives in Mountlake Terrace, graduated from Western Washington University, and worked for a Seattle-area youth nonprofit.

Catala also rejected DHS's allegation that Hernandez Mejía intentionally threw hot coffee at officers, saying she was holding a cup of coffee when unmarked agents suddenly charged at the family.

"When somebody's charging at you, you're going to drop a cup of coffee," Catala said.

Catala argued that federal authorities are increasingly detaining immigrants with pending applications by citing the expiration of their initial entry visas. She said the tactic pressures detainees without legal representation into accepting voluntary departure rather than fighting their cases from custody.

Catala said the Sea-Tac incident drew widespread attention only because bystanders recorded it, adding that similar arrests happen regularly at the airport.

"It's just the story that got a lot of attention, but honestly, it's happening daily to so many people," Catala said. "There's so many people currently in detention centers that were apprehended the same way at Sea-Tac Airport."

She described both clients as "very distraught" in Tacoma, noting that while the two are housed separately, they briefly crossed paths in a hallway during her back-to-back legal visits on Sunday.

"Sofia can't stop crying. She's worried about her father –extremely worried about him," Catala said. "They did get to walk into each other, so they did see each other, but they couldn't hug."

Governor cites state law banning law enforcement masks

The arrests have also triggered scrutiny from state and airport leaders over how masked federal agents operated inside a secure terminal area.

At a news conference following the incident, Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson called ICE’s tactics "deeply un-American" and "beyond reform," urging airlines at the Seattle airport to push back against terminal enforcement actions. Ferguson said state officials are examining whether the agents violated Senate Bill 5855, a law he signed in March 2026 prohibiting local, state, and federal law enforcement officers from wearing opaque face coverings while on duty. The statute allows unlawfully detained individuals to sue for civil damages.

Meanwhile, institutional finger-pointing continued Sunday between Alaska Airlines and the Port of Seattle. In a follow-up statement to KUOW, Alaska said it did not participate in the arrest or share passenger manifests, stressing that the Port of Seattle, not the airline, issues security credentials for law enforcement to enter jet bridges. Port officials called the incident "outrageous," noting Port policy bars local police from aiding civil immigration arrests, and said they are reviewing with DHS whether agreed-upon airport protocols were breached.

What happens next

Catala said her legal team is weighing next steps for Mendoza and Hernandez Mejía, including seeking an immigration bond hearing or filing a federal habeas corpus petition challenging the constitutionality of their detention. She argued that many similar airport detentions are ultimately overturned in court.

"This is such a waste of taxpayer money,” Catala said. “These people are being targeted, they're being put into detention centers. At the end, their detention is found to be unconstitutional, and they are released from custody."

In U.S. District Court in Western Washington, federal prosecutors have not yet filed formal criminal complaint paperwork for the alleged assault charge DHS announced over the weekend, but could do so as early as this week.
