DES MOINES — In a press conference on Saturday, November 21, after masked agents dragged passengers off a jetway at SeaTac airport, Governor Bob Ferguson made the following statement:

"ICE is completely and totally out of control. And today we were confronted with yet more evidence of this.

"The video is horrific and it is chilling. Masked agents who do not identify themselves drag screaming individuals off a jetway that were about to do something very ordinary in our country: Board a flight. There is no justification for this brutality.

"I spoke a couple hours ago with representatives from Alaska Airlines. I made my view very clear to Alaska Airlines. They need to call on ICE to get out of our airports. I’ll be making that request of every other airline that operates at SeaTac airport as well.

"I also said to Alaska, I was speaking not just as a governor, but as someone who flies on Alaska Airlines as I did earlier this week. And that I felt confident that many, many individuals who are their customers feel the same way we all feel about this as well.

"Today is the latest example of the violence that ICE has inflicted on our communities as it works to further Donald Trump's cruel immigration agenda.

"We need a system of immigration enforcement and border security that is effective, ethical and humane and ICE is not it. It is beyond reform. It is time to abolish Donald Trump's ICE. It's time.

"It is beyond changing a culture. The culture of ICE is bankrupt. It lacks morals. It lacks any decency. It is un-American. It is deeply, deeply un-American and it must be abolished and replaced with something that is more sane.

"Washington state has been a leader in standing up to this president from his first weeks there. I was Attorney General — first state to take him on in court, first state to beat him in court, with the first Muslim travel ban. Nick Brown has continued that excellent work in the Office of the Attorney General, standing up over and over again and winning.

"Immigrants in our country make our country great. Our communities are stronger because of our immigrants.

"The chaos and violence of ICE must come to an end."

text:
Civil arrests made by ICE in Massachusetts state courthouses violate the state’s sovereign control of its courts and unconstitutionally conscript court calendars and security screenings for federal immigration enforcement, according to a new lawsuit.

The lawsuit filed by the state Monday targets a May 2025 memo from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement authorizing the arrests — which Massachusetts claims ICE is still carrying out despite a California federal judge striking down the practice in June.

Massachusetts also points to a recent state law requiring judicial warrants for civil arrests in courthouses. Through Nov. 20, ICE had made 38 civil arrests in Massachusetts courthouses without the required warrants from when the law took effect Nov. 3, according to the complaint in the US District Court for the District of Massachusetts.

“ICE’s intentional violation of state law has created unnecessary fear, made it more difficult to operate our courts and hold defendants accountable,” Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell said in a statement.

ICE’s disregard of the law and a state Trial Court policy implementing it interferes with the Massachusetts’ ability to operate its courts and residents’ access to them, the state said. It cited examples of domestic violence survivors afraid to seek restraining orders and a woman who declined to report a rape for fear that ICE would arrest her if she testified in court.

The lawsuit claims the alleged interference violates the state’s sovereign authority over its courts as protected by the Tenth Amendment. The complaint also claims the ICE memo violated the Administrative Procedure Act by dropping a previous policy of allowing courthouse arrests only where states permit them.

The US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, during Trump’s first term in office, vacated an injunction against ICE’s 2018 courthouse arrest policy because challengers — local district attorneys, public defenders, and a nonprofit — were unlikely to show that a common-law ban on the arrests was built into the Immigration and Nationality Act.

Massachusetts now argues the state statute changes that analysis because federal law doesn’t override a state’s power to restrict arrests in its own courthouses.

Representatives for ICE weren’t immediately available for comment.

text:
The El Paso City Council is officially calling for the closure of Camp East Montana, the largest immigrant detention facility in the United States.

During its work session Monday, Nov. 23, the City Council approved a resolution calling for the facility's closure, citing the horrid conditions there that have led to multiple deaths and numerous alleged human rights abuses since its opening in 2025.

The move comes after City Council directed city staff to draft the resolution in late October.

On its own, the City Council has no authority to close the detention facility, which sits on federally-owned land, but the resolution is set to be sent to El Paso's delegation to the Texas Legislature. It likewise calls on Congress to take action to close the facility.

The resolution cites a number of failures at the massive immigrant detention facility, including findings from Human Rights Watch and the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) that showed detainees at Camp East Montana "endured conditions amounting to enforced disappearance; cruel, degrading, and inhuman treatment; excessive use of force; life-threatening medical neglect; barriers to legal representation; and coercive removals to third countries …"

For city Rep. Chris Canales, voting to approve the resolution calling for Camp East Montana's closure was one of the easiest decisions he's made during his time on City Council.

"Camp East Montana must be closed and the people involved in the violations there must be held to account as well," he said

Canales calling the facility "vile" and "inhumane."

City Rep. Lily Limon cited reports from an observer to described scenes of children arriving at Camp East Montana shrouded in hoods as babies and toddlers cried out for their mothers.

"This is a shameful situation for our city," she said. "We should all be ashamed and revolted by this inhumanity."

During public comments, more than 20 people turned out to voice their support for closing Camp East Montana. The City Council's vote was met with a round of cheers and applause from those gathered at City Hall.

"El Paso is a beautiful community and the last thing we want to be known for … is to be the city the largest detention facility," Mayor Renard Johnson said as the meeting came to a close. "No community wants to be known as that."

"And there is hope," he added. "We will continue to do what we can."

text:
A coalition of 22 states and the District of Columbia are suing to block a new Trump administration rule barring families with mixed immigration statuses from receiving federal housing assistance.

The complaint, filed Monday in federal court in Massachusetts, argues tens of thousands will end up displaced, costing the state and local governments millions to shelter them.

The Trump administration finalized the policy change earlier this month requiring that all people in a family be citizens or have legal immigrant status in order to get rental assistance or housing vouchers.

The Department of Housing and Urban Development’s new rule could take away housing assistance for more than 78,000 people in mixed status families, according to the department’s impact analysis. Households that include family members who are living in the country without authorization have received pro-rated benefits that only cover eligible members for 30 years.

Trending

“Despite being the federal agency charged with administering programs to provide low-income housing and reduce homelessness, HUD now seeks to implement a policy that will have the opposite effect, causing the mass displacement of U.S. citizens and eligible noncitizens from their homes,” the complaint states.

Attorneys general from California, New York, Massachusetts, D.C., Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, Vermont, Washington and Wisconsin and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro filed the lawsuit.

The lawsuit says the states will face millions of dollars in compliance costs, plus will have to spend $20,000 to $50,000 per person per year to provide shelter for those displaced by the rule.

The rule is set to go into effect on Dec. 14, and the mixed-status families face a March deadline to provide proof of their eligible immigration status or choose whether to live apart from family members to keep the federal assistance.

HUD estimates that $167 million to $218 million in assistance going to mixed status households could go toward fully eligible households. That same amount would result in services for fewer families under the new rule, since mixed status families get pro-rated assistance.

“Illegal aliens and ineligibles were siphoning up to $218 million a year in taxpayer-funded housing assistance,” Housing Secretary Scott Turner wrote in an X post the day the final rule was published. “That ends now.”

text:
Within the past few weeks, Albuquerque and Santa Fe construction sites have seen an increase in Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity at home construction sites.

In early November, the New Mexico Home Builders Association received around 20 calls from developers reporting that ICE agents had visited sites in unmarked SUVs, sometimes arresting multiple workers at a time, according to Source NM.

In a statement to the Daily Lobo, Director of Somos Un Pueblo Unido Marcela Diaz wrote that the increase in reported ICE activity at construction sites in Albuquerque, Santa Fe and other parts of the state is “an attack on New Mexico’s working families.”

“Immigrant workers are building our communities, including critically needed workforce housing, and sustaining our local economies. They deserve protections, not persecution,” Diaz wrote. “It is critical that workers, employers, and community allies stay informed, organized, and mobilized to defend workers’ rights and demand that our state and local governments do everything in their power to protect immigrant families.”

Source NM reported that on Nov. 10, ICE agents showed up to Albuquerque’s San Jose neighborhood as workers were pouring concrete for driveways on two nearly complete, single-family Habitat for Humanity homes.

A video circulating on social media shows masked ICE agents entering an Albuquerque construction site for a Hakes Brothers house and escorting a man in handcuffs on Nov. 5.

The Daily Lobo contacted the Department of Homeland Security for comment, to which they responded by asking for the names of the detainees in question.

The Daily Lobo was unable to provide names to DHS, but provided dates and specific locations, including Albuquerque’s San Jose neighborhood and the Twilight Homes construction sites in Mesa Del Sol, an area that Source NM reported had also been visited by ICE agents. There is no publicly available list of recent detainees except for the Online Detainee Locator System, which requires a detainee’s “A-number” and country of birth, neither of which the Daily Lobo has access to.

In response, the following statement, attributed only to an anonymous DHS spokesperson, was sent to the Daily Lobo:

“When the media refuses to give names, it makes it impossible to provide details on specific cases or even verify any of this even happened or that the people even exist. If you can’t do your job, we can’t do ours.”

The spokesperson wrote that “ICE agents uphold our nation’s immigration laws in all 50 states, seven days a week, 24 hours a day, including in New Mexico,” preceding a list of descriptions and photos of a handful of individuals arrested by ICE in New Mexico from the agency’s “Worst of the Worst” list.

In response to a series of questions regarding ICE activity at the sites, Albuquerque Police Department Director of Communications Gilbert Gallegos wrote that “APD does not coordinate or assist ICE with immigration enforcement.”

Paloma Chapa is the news editor for the Daily Lobo. She can be reached at news@dailylobo.com or on X @paloma_chapa88

text:
Short Reads

|

74% of U.S. Latinos Say They’ve Seen or Heard About ICE Activity in Their Local Area

Nearly three-quarters of U.S. Latinos (74%) say they’ve seen or heard of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) conducting arrests or raids in their local area in the past six months, according to a Pew Research Center survey conducted in November 2026. That’s up from 59% in October 2025.

Asian, Black and White adults have also become more likely to say they’re aware of such activity. Still, Hispanic adults continue to be the most likely to say this.

This increase in awareness comes as President Donald Trump’s administration continues to arrest and deport large numbers of unauthorized immigrants across the United States. The vast majority of people detained by ICE are citizens of Hispanic-origin countries, including Mexico, El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse.

We also asked U.S. adults whether they’ve been stopped by authorities and questioned about their U.S. citizenship or immigration status in the past six months. Similar to last year, Hispanic adults (7%) are about as likely as Black (5%) and Asian adults (5%) to say they’ve been stopped in this way. White adults (1%) are the least likely to say this.

About this research

Pew Research Center surveyed U.S. adults to learn how they view the Trump administration’s efforts to arrest and deport immigrants who are living in the country illegally.

Why did we do this?

Pew Research Center does research to help the public, media and decision-makers understand important topics. This project builds on our long-standing research about immigration attitudes.

Learn more about Pew Research Center.

How did we do this?

We surveyed 10,247 U.S. adults who are part of the Center’s American Trends Panel (ATP). The survey was conducted Nov. 9-15, 2026 and has an overall margin of error of plus or minus 1.3 percentage points.

Here are the questions used for this analysis, the detailed responses and the survey methodology.

Terminology

Immigrants are U.S. residents born in foreign countries to parents who aren’t U.S. citizens. People who are U.S. born are those born in the United States or its territories or born in foreign countries to U.S. citizen parents.

Second generation refers to people who are U.S. born with at least one immigrant parent.

Third or higher generation refers to people who are U.S. born with both parents who are U.S. born.

References to White, Black and Asian adults are those who are not Hispanic and identify as only one race. Views of Asian adults are representative of English speakers only.

The terms Hispanic and Latino are used interchangeably. Hispanics and Latinos are of any race.

A separate Center survey this fall found that Americans’ views of ICE had grown more negative over the last year and that the public sees ICE less favorably than other federal agencies and departments. Majorities of Black, Hispanic and Asian adults in that survey expressed a negative opinion of ICE, compared with about half of White adults.

Does ICE activity make U.S. adults feel safer or less safe?

In the more recent survey, 51% of Hispanics say efforts by the Trump administration to deport immigrants living in the U.S. illegally are making them feel less safe in their local area. Relatively few (15%) say these efforts make them feel safer.

Another 31% say the deportation efforts don’t make a difference in how safe they feel. That share is down 9 percentage points from last year.

Hispanic adults are more likely than Asian (39%), Black (36%) and White adults (27%) to say these efforts make them feel less safe. But their views differ by partisanship and nativity.

A majority of Hispanic Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents say the deportation efforts make them feel less safe in their local area (67%). Hispanic Republicans and Republican leaners are more divided: 41% say the efforts make them feel safer, while 40% say they don’t make a difference.

Meanwhile, Hispanic immigrants are more likely than U.S.-born Hispanics to say Trump’s deportation efforts make them feel less safe (58% vs. 46%). And among U.S.-born Hispanics, second-generation Americans are more likely than third- or higher-generation Americans to say this (51% vs. 40%).

(Second generation refers to U.S.-born adults who have at least one immigrant parent. Third or higher generation refers to U.S.-born adults who have U.S.-born parents.) For additional views by demographic group, refer to the detailed tables.

What are the legal statuses of Latino adults in the U.S.?

In 2023, the vast majority of U.S. Latino adults (82%) had full legal status, according to Center estimates. That includes Latinos who are U.S.-born citizens (54%), immigrants with naturalized citizenship (15%) and lawful immigrants without citizenship (13%).

Additionally, 18% of U.S. Latino adults were unauthorized immigrants, a group that includes those without full legal status. That’s a higher share than among U.S. adults who are Asian (9%), Black (2%) and White (1%).

These tables show additional details about how U.S. adults in different groups answered our questions about ICE awareness and feelings of safety.

text:
WASHINGTON -- A Chinese neuroscience researcher at Princeton University is in the custody of immigration authorities after she was detained while trying to get on a flight back from Washington, marking another instance of federal enforcement at airports.

Eva Yi Xie, a third-year doctoral student at Princeton, was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on Thursday as she tried to fly back to New Jersey from a conference in the nation's capital, her university adviser Carlos Brody said in a social media post.

The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, says Xie overstayed her visa and did not have authorization to study in the United States.

“News of Eva’s detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community,” Rodney Priestley, dean of the university’s graduate school, said in a statement. "We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton.”

Two days after Xie was taken into custody in Washington, masked immigration officers detained a father and daughter on an airport jet bridge in Seattle. ICE has ramped up detentions at airports since the summer, especially targeting people it says have overstayed their visas.

Kerry Doyle, Xie’s lawyer, said she came to the U.S. at age 14 with her family from China and has had an asylum application pending for years. Doyle insisted that Xie has permission to live, work and study in the U.S. while her case is pending.

Doyle said Xie is being held in ICE's Caroline Detention Center in Virginia.

DHS said in a statement that Xie came to the United States on a temporary visa on March 16, 2016, but “chose to violate our nation’s laws by refusing to depart by the required date of September 15, 2016.”

The agency said she did not have valid permission to study in the U.S. and “a pending application does not confer legal status.”

“Xie will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending her removal proceedings," the DHS statement said.

On her professional website, Xie said her research at Princeton Neuroscience Institute “seeks to understand the neural basis of decision-making.” She said she graduated from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2024.

text:
President Donald Trump is facing a dramatically different political landscape as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress with their largest House majority since 1992, giving the opposition party sweeping new powers to challenge his legislative agenda and investigate his administration during the final two years of his presidency.

Democrats have secured at least 258 seats in the 435-member House of Representatives, gaining 44 seats in the November midterm elections and surpassing even their 2018 gains during Trump's first presidency.

The party reached the historic milestone Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated veteran Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina following a recount, securing a narrow victory in one of the election's closest races.

Hubbard led Foxx by just 330 votes out of approximately 287,000 cast, according to the North Carolina State Board of Elections. Foxx conceded after the recount, ending her long tenure in Congress.

The victory brought Democrats to their largest House delegation since the 1992 election, when the party also won 258 seats as Bill Clinton secured the presidency. The new majority also exceeds the 257 seats Democrats won in 2008, when Barack Obama was elected president, according to election results compiled by the Associated Press.

Four House contests remain unresolved, including races in Minnesota and Tennessee and two Louisiana elections heading to December runoffs. Republicans have secured at least 173 seats.

Democrats have also won control of the Senate, securing a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber and setting up divided government when the 120th Congress convenes on Jan. 3, 2027.

The results represent a major setback for Republicans, who entered the midterms controlling the White House and both chambers of Congress.

For Trump, the incoming Democratic majorities could make it significantly harder to advance major legislation without bipartisan support while exposing his administration to congressional investigations and oversight hearings.

Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who has been chosen by his party as its candidate for House speaker, will have a much wider majority than outgoing Republican Speaker Mike Johnson, whose narrow margins repeatedly complicated efforts to pass legislation.

Jeffries is positioned to become the first Black speaker in House history if elected when the new Congress convenes.

The Democrats' 258 seats would allow the party to lose dozens of members on individual House votes and still reach the 218 votes generally required for passage, provided sufficient lawmakers are present and voting.

That gives party leaders considerable room to manage disagreements between progressive and moderate Democrats, although legislation would still face Senate procedural requirements and Trump's presidential veto.

The incoming majority is preparing an ambitious legislative agenda centered on living costs, health care and government accountability.

Democrats plan to move quickly to reverse Republican Medicaid cuts, restore expired Affordable Care Act tax credits and address other policies they argue have increased financial pressure on American households.

Jeffries also identified food assistance, tariffs and the economic consequences of the Iran war among the issues Democrats intend to confront early in the new Congress.

The New York Democrat said the party would focus on affordability while remaining open to working with Trump on health care and immigration during an interview on CBS's Face the Nation.

Jeffries proposed exploring a lower Medicare eligibility age and expanded coverage for vision, hearing and dental care, while acknowledging that negotiations with the administration would be necessary.

The Democrat also warned that voters would expect meaningful results from Washington on health care, immigration and the cost of living over the next two years.

Trump has indicated that he is open to discussions with Democrats on health care, although he has made clear that he does not support simply adopting their proposals.

The two sides remain divided over Medicaid spending, tariffs and other central elements of the president's economic agenda.

Beyond legislation, Democrats are preparing to use their congressional majority to intensify scrutiny of the Trump administration.

House committee chairmanships will change hands, giving Democratic lawmakers greater control over investigative hearings, committee agendas and subpoenas.

The party has signaled plans to investigate alleged government corruption, potential conflicts of interest involving Trump and his family, and the administration's immigration enforcement policies.

Jeffries also said House Democrats intend to pursue legislation banning members of Congress from trading individual stocks, presenting the proposal as part of a broader government accountability agenda.

Questions about impeachment could become another source of confrontation between Congress and the White House.

Jeffries has declined to rule out future impeachment proceedings against Trump, but he has not announced plans to pursue them.

Asked directly about impeachment during his CBS interview, Jeffries said Democrats had not ruled out possible action and that investigations should be guided by evidence and constitutional requirements.

Even if the Democratic-controlled House voted to impeach Trump, removing him from office would require conviction by a two-thirds majority in the Senate, a threshold the party's incoming majority alone would not meet.

The administration has pushed back against the prospect of extensive investigations, setting the stage for potential disputes over congressional oversight and executive authority.

The size of the Democratic victory also creates pressure within the party over how to use its newly expanded power.

Progressive lawmakers have called for substantial policy changes and stronger accountability measures, while centrists have emphasized the importance of addressing household expenses and demonstrating results to voters.

Rep. Tom Suozzi of New York has argued that Democrats should devote most of their attention to affordability while maintaining a smaller but significant focus on investigations, the Associated Press reported.

CBS News exit polling found that voters who viewed the economy negatively or said their personal financial circumstances had deteriorated were more likely to support Democratic House candidates.

Democratic gains extended beyond traditional swing districts, including victories in areas where Republicans had previously enjoyed substantial advantages.

In North Carolina, Democrats won 11 of the state's 14 House seats despite redistricting efforts designed to improve Republican prospects, highlighting the scale of the party's gains.

The national shift also surpassed the 40-seat increase Democrats recorded in the 2018 midterms, when opposition to Trump's first administration helped return the party to House control.

Republicans are preparing to operate with one of their smallest House delegations in decades.

Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, selected to lead House Republicans in the next Congress, has pledged to oppose Democratic policies and work to restore the party's congressional majority.

Why it matters The rule would bar households with people lacking qualifying immigration status from receiving rental subsidies, and residents who do not provide documentation face eviction.
The players U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development The federal agency that oversees public housing and subsidized rental programs across the United States, and the defendant in the states' lawsuit over the immigration status rule.
Mid-December 2026: HUD rule goes into effect.
The case will test how far federal housing agencies may tighten eligibility rules that Congress has already set in law.

text:
Nearly two dozen state attorneys general, including California, New York, Arizona and Pennsylvania, filed a lawsuit Monday in federal court in Massachusetts to block a HUD rule requiring every resident of federally-subsidized housing to provide immigration status documents. The suit alleges HUD does not have the authority to change a Congressional statute.

Why it matters

The rule would bar households with people lacking qualifying immigration status from receiving rental subsidies, and residents who do not provide documentation face eviction. The states argue it could worsen affordable housing shortages nationwide, while a separate challenge from the nonprofit Public Counsel was filed the prior week.

HUD estimates roughly 20,000 mixed-status families, comprising 78,100 individuals, could be affected by the rule, with about 7,190 affected households in California based on 2019 data. HUD says the rule reallocates up to $218 million to eligible Americans on waitlists, though the court outcome on HUD's authority remains unresolved.

The players

U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development

The federal agency that oversees public housing and subsidized rental programs across the United States, and the defendant in the states' lawsuit over the immigration status rule.

Scott Turner

The U.S. Housing and Urban Development Secretary who defended the rule as ending the use of taxpayer dollars to house people without qualifying status.

The details

Under the final rule, every resident of federally-subsidized housing, including public housing and Section 8 voucher holders, must provide immigration status documents by March, with eviction for those who do not. HUD says the rule implements the 1980 Housing and Community Development Act and Secretary Scott Turner says it ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars.

Timeline

Monday, November 23, 2026: State attorneys general file lawsuit in Massachusetts federal court.

Mid-December 2026: HUD rule goes into effect.

March 2027: Deadline for residents to provide immigration documentation.

Related coverage

Immigration

Nov. 11

HUD Requires Citizenship Verification for Housing Aid

Immigration

Nov. 20

DHS Shortens Refugee Response Deadline to 10 Days

Employment

Nov. 7

HUD Reports Largest Drop in Homelessness

Legal Context

The rule is HUD's implementation of the 1980 Housing and Community Development Act, and the states contend the agency cannot expand that statute's eligibility limits by regulation. The case will test how far federal housing agencies may tighten eligibility rules that Congress has already set in law.

Residents of federally-subsidized housing, including public housing and Section 8 voucher holders, must provide immigration status documents by March or face eviction. Households that cannot meet the requirement would lose eligibility for rental subsidies once the rule takes effect in mid-December.

The takeaway

The outcome of the states' lawsuit will determine whether federal housing rules can add eligibility requirements beyond what Congress wrote into statute. Families in mixed-status households should watch the December effective date and the March documentation deadline closely.

text:
San Ramon officials are updating the city’s protocols for responding to federal immigration enforcement authorities to comply with a new state law taking effect Jan. 1.

The City Council is set to review the proposed changes at its Tuesday meeting.

Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Senate Bill 580 into law in September 2025. It is one in a series of laws enacted by Newsom aimed at checking the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration crackdown in California.

Under the law, all city and state agencies have until Jan. 1 to adopt policies for managing interactions with immigration authorities, following guidance from California Attorney General Rob Bonta or an equivalent authority.

That guidance is based on five principles, including that city resources should not be used to assist immigration enforcement, except as required by law, and that the city should limit the collection, retention and disclosure of information that could identify individuals for immigration enforcement.

The guidelines also state that where no legal obligation exists, the city should require a judicial warrant, judicial subpoena or court order before complying with requests from immigration officials.

Additionally, under the attorney general’s model, all immigration enforcement requests should go to designated staff or legal counsel trained to evaluate them, and the city should document every interaction with immigration authorities.

San Ramon already had some protocols for interactions with immigration officials under the California Values Act, which has barred local law enforcement agencies from using resources for immigration enforcement, with limited exceptions, since 2018.

In addition, the Immigrant Worker Protection Act prohibits employers, including the city, from voluntarily consenting to immigration agents entering nonpublic areas of a workplace or reviewing employee records without a judicial warrant or subpoena.

However, until SB 580, no state law required cities to adopt a single policy covering every department. The attorney general’s model materials also include guidance, audit criteria and training recommendations for databases, including those maintained by private vendors.

San Ramon is developing its policies amid increased U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity in Contra Costa County. The county Board of Supervisors last week adopted a non-cooperation policy with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Civil rights groups have alleged that ICE officials have used the A.F. Bray Courthouse parking lot to stage multiple arrests in November.

The San Ramon City Council meeting is set for 6:30 p.m. Tuesday (Nov. 24). The agenda is here.

In other business:

• The council will consider a resolution authorizing the city to adopt the San Ramon Fiber Optic Master Plan, which establishes a citywide framework for expanding and upgrading the city’s fiber optic communications infrastructure to support current and future technology needs. The plan was originally incorporated into the city’s 2018 Intelligent Transportation System Master Plan but has since been expanded to address the needs of multiple city departments and facilities.

• The council will consider a resolution authorizing the city to adopt updates to its Intelligent Transportation System Master Plan to establish a framework for upgrading and expanding the city’s traffic management and transportation technology infrastructure to address citywide fiber optic needs.

text:
Texas' incoming Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa, has indicated she supports ending the detention of immigrant children in the state.

Hinojosa told children's educator Rachel Accurso that detaining children "should not be happening."

The governor-elect previously stated she would use the state's licensing power to prevent private prisons from holding children.

While Hinojosa and President Donald Trump both want a secure border, they differ on methods, with Hinojosa favoring technology over a physical wall.

Texas' incoming Democratic governor is signaling that she is on board with ending the detention of immigrant children in the state as she prepares to take office in January.

Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa spoke with children's educator Rachel Accurso — better known as Ms. Rachel — on Nov. 19 in a clip posted to social media, saying, "it should not be happening."

"We should be able to come together to stop hurting kids in this country and in this state," Hinojosa said.

Accurso, who has publicly called for an end to Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s practice of detaining families at Texas’ Dilley Immigration Processing Center, captioned the clip of the two of them talking with "Dilley detention center needs to close!"

This is not the first time Accurso has spoken out against the South Texas ICE facility. In March, she drew national attention when she advocated for the release of 9-year-old Deiver Henao Jimenez who hoped to compete in a spelling bee.

In the conversation with the governor-elect, Accurso called the detention of children "a violation of human rights of kids" and praised Hinojosa for calling for an end to the controversial immigration practice.

Hinojosa previously told The New York Times in a Nov. 8 interview that she would use the state’s licensing power to stop private prison companies from holding children in detention facilities in Texas.

“Locking up little kids like that, even with their parents, that is child abuse,” she told The Times.

Dilley is run by the private prison operator CoreCivic under contract with ICE, according to CoreCivic's website.

What is Hinojosa's stance on immigration in Texas?

In an interview with The Texas Tribune, published Nov. 18, Hinojosa, a Democrat, said she had a positive conversation with President Donald Trump, saying she and Trump want the same thing for the border — a secure border.

However, they differ in how they would go about achieving that.

"There’s different ways we can secure our border in 2026, 2027 that involve technology and not just necessarily a physical barrier," she said.

Trump, who prefers a physical border wall to deter and prevent illegal immigration into the nation, won a Supreme Court ruling to this month to allowing his administration to resume building its border wall in West Texas, including in Big Bend National Park.

text:
A coalition of civil rights groups filed an amicus brief today in the U.S. Supreme Court urging it to reconsider the deportation of LGBTQ+ migrants to countries where they face risk of persecution due to their identity.

In the brief, attorneys with Lambda Legal and Immigration Equality allege that the United States is aware of the risks these migrants face upon deportation to anti-LGBTQ+ countries, and is not doing enough to ensure their safety.

“The government cannot, in good faith, accept diplomatic assurances that LGBTQ people will not be persecuted or tortured in countries that still criminalize, harm, and fail to protect LGBTQ people,” the brief reads.

Keep LGBTQ+ Voices Strong

Sustain fearless LGBTQ+ journalism.

Your tax-deductible donation protects original reporting, investigations, and The Advocate's 60-year archive.

Related: Trump asks Supreme Court to intervene ahead of trial so the Pentagon can fire transgender troops

Also involved in the brief were the Council for Global Equality (CGE); Oasis Legal Services; Outright International; the Organization for Refuge, Asylum & Migration (ORAM), and Rainbow Railroad.

Under President Donald Trump, immigration officials began to deport undocumented immigrants to third-party countries in 2025 — often to countries with records of human rights violations where they have no prior ties. Many of these migrants are never given the chance to appeal their deportations in court.

The U.S. has signed deals with at least 37 countries to accept migrants from other nations, according to the brief. At least 19 of those countries criminalize same-sex intimacy, and anti-LGBTQ+ societal violence is prevalent in at least 28 of them, the brief reads.

The attorneys are not asking the government to block deportations to any particular country, but urge the Supreme Court to require prior notification before third-country deportations — and a more thorough chance to appeal these deportations over concerns related to violence or persecution.

Related: Conservative Supreme Court justices curb California’s effort to shield transgender students from forced outing

“For LGBTQ people, that opportunity can be the difference between safety and the very harm the U.S. has already found they are likely to suffer,” the brief reads.

The filing highlights the “life-or-death consequences” that LGBTQ+ migrants face upon deportation to anti-LGBTQ+ countries, said co-author Jenny Pizer, senior director of strategic initiatives at Lambda Legal, in a written statement.

Third-country deportations immediately came under fire over ethical concerns, including how they would impact LGBTQ+ refugees and migrants. Yet the U.S. Supreme Court upheld the practice of third-country deportations in October.

“The administration knows full well that many of these countries criminalize LGBTQ+ people simply for existing, with some even imposing the death penalty, and many more subject them to pervasive societal violence with no access to police protection,” Pizer said.

Related: Supreme Court passes on case over outing trans students

Many LGBTQ+ refugees come to the United States seeking safety from anti-LGBTQ+ violence abroad. Since third-country deportations began, reports of LGBTQ+ migrants facing danger, violence, and anti-LGBTQ+ discrimination abroad have become increasingly common.

The Trump administration sent Andry Hernández Romero, a gay Venezuelan hairdresser, to an El Salvador megaprison in 2025 without trial. Upon release, Hernández Romero came forward to detail experiences of physical and sexual abuse. “It was an encounter with torture and death,” he told journalists in August 2025.

In 2025, the Trump administration deported a gay migrant from Guatemala, first sending him to Mexico — a country where he was previously kidnapped and raped. Also under Trump, immigration officials deported a Ghanaian man to Equatorial Guinea despite a judge’s order prohibiting his removal, Keifer Buckingham, managing director of the Council for Global Equality, said in a written statement issued Monday.

Related: Anti-LGBTQ+ hate group loses Supreme Court bid over right to misgender transgender people

Last year, immigration officials ordered a gay woman from Morocco to be sent to Cameroon, where same-sex intimacy is illegal. And in October, reports surfaced of a transgender woman originally from Cuba hiding in fear in her government-issued apartment in the Central African Republic.

“The [Trump] administration is actively deporting LGBTQI+ people who have a credible fear of persecution or torture to third countries where they have no ties or support, and face precarious, emergency conditions,” said Oliver Williams, U.S. policy and advocacy officer at Rainbow Railroad, in a written statement Monday. “The United States has a legal and moral duty not to send people to countries where they will face imminent danger.”

text:
More than 500 Boston households, including nearly 900 children, could lose federal housing assistance; new requirements set to take effect Dec. 15

Copyright © 2026 Boston Neighborhood News, Inc. This content may not be re-published or re-used without written permission.

The Mary Ellen McCormack public housing development in South Boston. Boston Planning Dept. image.

The City of Boston and Boston Housing Authority (BHA) have joined a national lawsuit challenging a new Trump administration rule that could strip federal housing assistance from more than 500 Boston families, including nearly 900 children, according to city officials.

The lawsuit, filed Monday in US District Court in Massachusetts, challenges a new Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) rule that would largely prohibit families with mixed immigration statuses from receiving federal housing assistance, even when some members of the household are US citizens or otherwise legally eligible for the benefits.

The rule, issued on Nov. 12, is scheduled to take effect Dec. 15, with tenants required to submit proof of citizenship or eligible immigration status by March 14, according to reporting by WBUR.

“Under this cruel and illegal rule, hundreds of children and families in Boston could lose their housing,” Wu said in a statement Monday. “Today, the City and the Boston Housing Authority are joining cities nationwide to halt this unlawful plan and keep families together.”

Nearly 1,000 households across Massachusetts could be affected by the change, according to estimates from the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a nonpartisan research organization cited by WBUR. Massachusetts has the fourth-highest number of potentially affected households in the country, behind California, New York, and Texas.

Since 1995, federal housing policy has allowed families with mixed immigration statuses to live together in subsidized housing. Under that arrangement, federal rental assistance is provided only for household members who qualify, while families pay a higher, prorated share of their rent to account for members who are ineligible.

The new HUD regulation would eliminate that longstanding arrangement, potentially forcing families to separate to maintain assistance for eligible members or leave federally subsidized housing altogether.

Kenzie Bok, administrator of the Boston Housing Authority, warned that the policy could reverse years of work to provide stable housing for families that previously experienced homelessness.

“Almost every family we house at the Boston Housing Authority has previously suffered through a period of homelessness,” Bok said. “It is wrong to suddenly change program rules and plunge hundreds of children into that nightmare a second time. These are Boston kids, they are eligible for federal housing in their own right, and they deserve to stay safely in their homes.”

The Trump administration has defended the policy as an effort to ensure that federal housing assistance is reserved for citizens and immigrants who meet eligibility requirements.

HUD Secretary Scott Turner cited lengthy waiting lists for subsidized housing as justification for the new verification requirements. In a statement, Turner argued that the federal government should prioritize eligible applicants, including homeless veterans, seniors, people with disabilities, and victims of domestic violence.

HUD also said an audit conducted with the Department of Homeland Security identified nearly 200,000 tenants nationwide whose eligibility verification was incomplete or unknown.

Housing advocates dispute the administration’s approach, arguing that the existing system already prevents ineligible household members from receiving federal subsidies while allowing families to remain together.

Zafiro Patiño, director of organizing for the Massachusetts Union of Public Housing Tenants, told WBUR that some residents may leave their homes voluntarily rather than submit sensitive immigration information to federal authorities.

“They are going to be separated, or they have to self-evict,” Patiño told WBUR. “That’s what we are hearing mainly — that people are going to be afraid of actually revealing these documents, and they are going to self-evict.”

The regulation could also create significant administrative challenges for housing authorities and tenants. More than 180,000 Massachusetts households receiving federal housing assistance would be subject to the new citizenship or immigration verification requirements, according to WBUR.

The rule would also impose new citizenship verification requirements on residents age 62 and older, potentially creating additional paperwork burdens for thousands of eligible seniors.

The Boston lawsuit is part of a broader legal challenge to the administration’s policy. The city and BHA have joined a coalition that includes New York City, Chicago, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Providence, San Diego, Seattle, and several California housing authorities.

The plaintiffs allege that HUD violated federal law by reversing decades of established housing policy without adequate justification and that the rule conflicts with congressional intent governing federal housing assistance.

Massachusetts has also joined 21 other states and the District of Columbia in a separate legal challenge. Another lawsuit has been filed by a coalition of housing advocacy and tenant organizations, including the Massachusetts Union of Public Housing Tenants, represented by legal organizations including Greater Boston Legal Services and the Massachusetts Law Reform Institute.

Wu urged residents who may be affected to seek guidance from local housing and legal aid organizations while the litigation proceeds. Families concerned about their housing status are encouraged to contact the Massachusetts Union of Public Housing Tenants at 617-825-9750 or Info@massunion.org.

The Boston Housing Authority is expected to provide additional information directly to residents about their due process and appeal rights.

Material from WBUR reporter Rachell Sanchez-Smith’s Nov. 16 report was used in this story. The Reporter and WBUR share content through a media partnership.

title: HUD Mixed-Status Rule Sued by 22 States Ahead of Dec. 14 Start - Immigration Analytics
description:
The HUD mixed-status rule now faces its biggest challenger yet: the states themselves.
Tenants argue about their own homes; states can argue about their budgets, their shelter systems and the housing authorities that must carry the rule out.
They ask the court to declare the rule unlawful, vacate it and bar HUD from enforcing it against the plaintiff states, their localities and their public housing authorities.

text:
The HUD mixed-status rule now faces its biggest challenger yet: the states themselves. New York Attorney General Letitia James and 21 other attorneys general, joined by Pennsylvania’s governor, sued the Department of Housing and Urban Development on Nov. 23 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, asking a judge to strike down the rule before it takes effect on Dec. 14. The rule would end prorated rent assistance for households in which one member lacks eligible immigration status, and it would require every assisted tenant, citizens included, to document their status.

Three weeks before the effective date, the rule faces suits from Los Angeles tenants, a proposed tenant class in Boston and now a coalition of states. The new plaintiffs matter. Tenants argue about their own homes; states can argue about their budgets, their shelter systems and the housing authorities that must carry the rule out.

Why state plaintiffs change the HUD mixed-status rule fight

The coalition includes Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, along with New York. According to the attorney general’s office, the states claim HUD exceeded its authority under Section 214 of the Housing and Community Development Act of 1980 and acted arbitrarily and capriciously under the Administrative Procedure Act. They ask the court to declare the rule unlawful, vacate it and bar HUD from enforcing it against the plaintiff states, their localities and their public housing authorities.

That request reflects Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court’s June 2025 decision limiting universal injunctions. An order confined to the plaintiff states would leave the rule in force elsewhere, so the outcome could split along state lines: families in Illinois protected, families in Texas not. Vacatur under the APA would set the rule aside for everyone, and how far that remedy reaches after CASA remains unsettled.

The states also bring a cost argument tenants cannot. Citing HUD’s analysis, the attorney general’s office says sheltering a displaced person costs $20,000 to $50,000 a year and that about 2,540 New York City families would be displaced. Costs that land on state and city systems are the kind of direct injury likely to support state standing.

What the statute says, and what HUD says it means

The final rule, published Nov. 12 at 91 FR 72978, requires verification of citizenship or eligible status for every applicant and recipient regardless of age, and turns prorated assistance into a temporary arrangement that lasts only until each household member’s status is verified. HUD estimates in the rule that $167 million to $218 million in assistance would shift to fully eligible households, with $17 million to $33 million in upfront costs. (See the earlier breakdown of the final rule.)

The legal fight turns on 42 U.S.C. 1436a. Congress has barred HUD assistance to ineligible noncitizens since 1980, but the same section tells HUD to prorate assistance for mixed families and, the states argue, says such families “shall not” lose benefits solely because an ineligible member lives with them. It also sets lighter documentation rules for citizens and for eligible immigrants 62 and older. HUD reads the statute as never requiring indefinite proration. Secretary Scott Turner said in response to the earlier Los Angeles suit, according to Newsweek, that the rule “guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing.” No HUD response to the states’ suit had been posted as of Monday.

Since Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo ended deference to agency readings of ambiguous statutes in 2024, the judge will decide what Section 214 requires without weighing HUD’s interpretation as controlling.

Who is affected. The attorney general’s office says HUD’s analysis shows about 20,000 mixed-status families, roughly 78,100 people, would lose assistance, and that about 55,000 of them are themselves eligible, most of them children. The Boston complaint, citing the same analysis, puts the total near 80,000. The states add that 3.8 million adult citizens lack proof of citizenship, a reminder that the verification mandate reaches every assisted household, not only immigrant ones.

Assistance does not stop on Dec. 14. Current mixed-status households would have 90 days to document eligibility, with extensions possible, as detailed in the coverage of the Boston class action. Notices and verification would begin on the effective date unless a court steps in.

What to watch

Dec. 14: the effective date; a stay under 5 U.S.C. 705 or an injunction must come first to stop verification.

Boston assignment: the states’ case may be treated as related to the tenants’ class action, Massachusetts Union of Public Housing Tenants v. Turner, No. 1:26-cv-15176.

Los Angeles: the tenants’ suit in the Central District of California could produce a competing ruling.

Around March 14, 2027: the documentation deadline for current mixed-status households if the rule stands.

The rule is one of several new status-based limits on federal programs, alongside the Feb. 1 Medicare eligibility cutoff. What sets housing apart is that, on the states’ reading of HUD’s figures, most people in the affected households are eligible themselves.

This article is for general information and is not legal advice.

Sources

New York Attorney General, press release on the multistate lawsuit (Nov. 23, 2026)

Multistate complaint, U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts (Nov. 23, 2026)

HUD, final rule, Housing and Community Development Act of 1980: Verification of Eligible Status, 91 FR 72978, FR Doc. 2026-23003 (Nov. 12, 2026)

42 U.S.C. 1436a, restriction on use of assisted housing by noncitizens

Newsweek, report on the Los Angeles lawsuit and HUD Secretary Scott Turner’s statement (Nov. 2026)

title: From courthouse arrests to 're-detentions,' ICE's tactics test legal limits - People's World
description:
Officials gave Alvarez his belongings, and he walked through the lobby and out into a public area — where, unbeknownst to him, ICE agents were waiting to detain him again.
According to agency data, the administration made more than 491,000 immigration arrests in the fiscal year that ended on Sept. 30, the most in ICE’s history.
Nevertheless, CBS Massachusetts reported that between Nov. 3-12, Massachusetts courthouses recorded 22 arrests by ICE.
DHS has said the Supremacy Clause of the Constitution, which sets federal law above state and local statutes, overrides Massachusetts restrictions on courthouse arrests.
Prolonged confinement is also drawing a court challenge at the border, where arrests have fallen to record lows.
text:
Late last month, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer told Ramon Quintero Alvarez he was being released from immigrant detention, even offering the father of two a celebratory fist-bump, Alvarez would later testify.

It had been eight months since he was first detained. Without the aid of a lawyer, he filed a habeas corpus petition and secured an order for his release from the Aurora ICE Processing Center in Colorado. Officials gave Alvarez his belongings, and he walked through the lobby and out into a public area — where, unbeknownst to him, ICE agents were waiting to detain him again.

Department of Justice officials argued in federal court that this brief moment of freedom satisfied U.S. District Court Judge Charlotte Sweeney’s ruling that Alvarez be released, at which point they could arrest him again. A week after the re-arrest, government lawyers told Sweeney that Alvarez was still in custody and that they wouldn’t file a brief defending the new detention. They asked her to close the case on the grounds that ICE had already carried out her original order to release him.

Sweeney declined that request, and on Wednesday, found multiple senior ICE and Trump administration officials in contempt of court, arguing that the practice of re-arresting people like Alvarez made a “mockery of court orders.” She declined to take further action after Denver’s acting-ICE chief testified that he had ordered an end to these “re-detention” efforts, which as of early November, had been used against at least 18 people in Colorado, including Alvarez.

Despite that promise to stop, DHS has defended the practice broadly, saying that a judge’s release order “does not immunize the alien from immigration enforcement for all time,” provided any new arrest complies with the ruling that ordered them released.

Officials in Minnesota, where these kinds of re-arrests have also occurred, have made no such pledge to stop. Judges there have split on whether the practice represents a violation of their release orders.

Re-arrests are one of the ways ICE has been testing the legal limits of who it can take into custody, where, and on what grounds, as it works to deliver on President Donald Trump’s promise of mass deportations. According to agency data, the administration made more than 491,000 immigration arrests in the fiscal year that ended on Sept. 30, the most in ICE’s history.

In Massachusetts, ICE has been making arrests at “sensitive locations” despite the state’s PROTECT Act. Signed into law in August, the act is intended to keep agents away from schools, daycares, healthcare facilities, and courthouses. Nevertheless, CBS Massachusetts reported that between Nov. 3-12, Massachusetts courthouses recorded 22 arrests by ICE.

DHS has said the Supremacy Clause of the Constitution, which sets federal law above state and local statutes, overrides Massachusetts restrictions on courthouse arrests. The text of the PROTECT Act, though, authorizes the state attorney general to seek a court order enforcing the restrictions, setting up a legal fight over how much authority the state has to govern access to its courts. A spokesperson for state Attorney General Andrea Campbell told WGBH that her office was “actively evaluating all available legal options to protect access to our courthouses and hold federal authorities accountable.”

In Virginia, a lawsuit filed Monday alleges that ICE agents have been arresting people without warrants or first establishing that they’re in the country unlawfully and likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained. Six residents and an immigrant rights group accused the agency of targeting people it perceives to be Latino in its drive to meet arrest quotas. Among the plaintiffs is an 18-year-old U.S. citizen who says agents shackled and detained her for hours after she came to retrieve a car following her fiance’s arrest.

The broader immigration crackdown has also reached longtime green-card holders returning from trips abroad. Authorities are detaining some over old offenses that previously hadn’t prevented them from renewing their immigration status or traveling, signaling a shift in the treatment of longtime legal residents who have already undergone government vetting, The Washington Post reported this week.

Take San Juanita Guerra, then 74, who earlier this year spent 22 days in detention after officials at a South Texas border crossing flagged a 1994 misdemeanor for carrying an unloaded pistol into an airport. At the time, she said she’d taken the gun from her teenage child who was struggling with suicidal thoughts and forgotten it was in her purse. After a fine and probation, the gun case was dismissed, and a notary public incorrectly advised her that she didn’t need to disclose it on future applications, she told The Post.

The Post reported that DHS did not respond to questions about how many green-card holders it has detained, and that the agency has said background reviews of noncitizens are essential for safeguarding the country.

ICE’s unprecedented arrest push has also filled rooms meant for brief stays. At the agency’s Miramar office in Florida, civil rights groups allege people have been held for 27 days or longer at a site intended for check-ins and processing. A complaint filed Tuesday alleges agents routinely pressure detainees to sign deportation papers, including one account that officers threatened to withhold access to medications unless people signed voluntary departure forms. Angel Cata, a supervisory detention and deportation officer with ICE, disputed the allegations in a sworn declaration.

Prolonged confinement is also drawing a court challenge at the border, where arrests have fallen to record lows. Legal advocates told a federal court last week that children were spending up to a month in cold, sunless Border Patrol facilities meant to hold them for no more than 72 hours, sometimes locked in a cell for 23 hours a day.

In both cases, immigrant rights groups are turning to courts and federal watchdogs for help.

They may soon have allies with subpoena power. Congressional Democrats are preparing to investigate the administration’s crackdown when they take the majority in January. On Wednesday, Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, told White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller in a letter to preserve records concerning arrest quotas, enforcement tactics and the treatment of detainees.

“Oversight Democrats have documented 1,165 instances of concerning uses of force, arrests or detentions, deportations, enforcement actions at sensitive locations, and acts of intimidation or retaliation by DHS personnel, and we want answers,” Garcia wrote.

title: Legal, LGBTQ+, and Immigration Organizations Urge U.S. Supreme Court to Block Unlawful ...
description:
The coalition includes Immigration Equality, Lambda Legal, Oasis Legal Services, the Council for Global Equality (CGE), Outright International, the Organization for Refuge, Asylum, and Migration (ORAM), and Rainbow Railroad.
Denying them the chance to object violates decades-long immigration policy and due process guarantees.
Some of those countries have sent refugees back to the very places a U.S. judge said they could not be sent.
The Supreme Court paused the district court’s early orders in June 2025, allowing these deportations to continue while the case proceeded.
The organizations supporting the amicus brief are committed to advocating for the rights and safety of LGBTQ+ refugees and will continue to monitor the case closely.
text:
“Outrageous and cruel.” Immigration Equality, Lambda Legal, the Council for Global Equality, Oasis Legal Services, Outright International, the Organization for Refuge, Asylum, and Migration, and Rainbow Railroad file a friend-of-the-court brief highlighting the absurdity and bad faith of the Trump administration’s treatment of LGBTQ+ refugees.

Para leer este artículo en español, haga clic aquí.

A coalition of leading LGBTQ+ immigration and rights advocacy, research, and support organizations filed today a friend-of-the-court brief in the U.S. Supreme Court highlighting the unlawfulness of the Trump administration’s practice of deporting LGBTQ+ refugees to third countries without legally adequate notice and the opportunity to object based on fears of persecution or torture in the country selected by the government.

The coalition includes Immigration Equality, Lambda Legal, Oasis Legal Services, the Council for Global Equality (CGE), Outright International, the Organization for Refuge, Asylum, and Migration (ORAM), and Rainbow Railroad. In its amicus curiae brief in Department of Homeland Security (DHS) v. D.V.D., the coalition shows that the administration is violating the rights of individuals already shielded by U.S. immigration judges from deportation back to their countries of origin due to credible fears of persecution or torture there. The administration is doing so by failing to provide fair notice and a reasonable opportunity to explain why deportation to a third country the government has chosen is too dangerous for them because of who they are.

The brief includes powerful examples of clients represented by these amici, which show vividly the particular vulnerability of LGBTQ+ refugees who, after fleeing severe abuse, have been granted protection by U.S. immigration judges from being returned to their countries of origin, but are being deported instead to other countries where they will face similar risks of violence, persecution, and even torture based on their LGBTQ+ identities. Because same-sex relationships and expressions of an LGBTQ+ identity are criminalized and/or systematically persecuted by governmental and non-governmental actors in many of the countries that the administration has chosen for its aggressive deportation efforts, the legally required opportunity to object to a particular destination country is essential for LGBTQ+ people who are subject to deportation.

Quotes From Friend-of-the-Court Organizations

Lambda Legal

“The Trump administration’s illegal policy of hastily deporting LGBTQ+ refugees to countries the government knows are extremely dangerous for them because of who they are – without giving them the legally required chance to object to that danger – is outrageous and cruel,” said Jenny Pizer, a co-author of the brief and Senior Director of Strategic Initiatives at Lambda Legal. “The administration knows full well that many of these countries criminalize LGBTQ+ people simply for existing, with some even imposing the death penalty, and many more subject them to pervasive societal violence with no access to police protection. Denying them the chance to object violates decades-long immigration policy and due process guarantees. The case examples provided in this brief show starkly that this administration’s unlawful practice creates life-or-death consequences for real people who already have been horribly traumatized.”

“In short, the Trump administration is deporting immigrant people, including LGBTQ+ refugees, who have already been granted protection by the U.S. government due to credible fear of persecution or torture in their home countries, to third countries they don’t know and might never have heard of, where they would face extreme danger. Many of them have sought refuge in the U.S. after escaping vicious abuse by their governments or communities due to their sexual orientation or gender identity. These deportations, without the required chance to object, plainly violate U.S. law and are unconscionable,” said Malcolm Dort, a co-author of the brief and Senior Counsel for Strategic Initiatives at Lambda Legal.

Immigration Equality

“A U.S. judge found that these refugees would likely be persecuted or tortured if sent home, and the administration responded by sending many of them somewhere else equally dangerous, without a warning and without a hearing,” said Bridget Crawford, a co-author of the brief and Director of Law and Policy at Immigration Equality. “The law is clear that the government may not deport people to countries where they face persecution or torture, and it must give them a fair opportunity to raise that fear first. These safeguards are being ignored. Notice and a meaningful chance to object are required by federal law, by our treaty obligations, and by the Constitution, and for LGBTQ refugees, they are the difference between safety and the threat of imprisonment, violence, or death. We are urging the Supreme Court to ensure that, when a U.S. judge says someone cannot be sent to persecution or torture, that protection means something.”

Oasis Legal Services

“Third-country deportations place LGBTQ+ migrants in grave danger. Oasis has worked with many LGBTQ+ migrants who fled harm in their home countries and tried to find safety in a third country like Mexico, only to suffer brutal persecution. Without a correct outcome in this case, LGBTQ+ immigrants will be sent to third countries where being LGBTQ+ is illegal or where their identities place a target on their backs. They will be sent without community support, without government protection, and at very high risk of being harmed. LGBTQ+ immigrants have the right to a real opportunity to show that they would be persecuted or tortured in another country before the government attempts to send them there,” said Celia Meredith, Staff Attorney at Oasis Legal Services.

Council for Global Equality

“Today, we are raising the voices of people like Michael, a Ghanaian man, who was persecuted and tortured due to his sexual orientation as a gay man,” noted Keifer Buckingham, Managing Director of the Council for Global Equality. “A U.S. judge granted him withholding of removal. But the Trump administration shackled him, put him on a plane without telling him where he was being sent, and flew him to Equatorial Guinea, a country where LGBTQI+ people face high levels of violence and torture. He was then forcibly deported back to Ghana. The Trump administration’s practice of third country removals – including the usage of opaque bilateral agreements with countries that routinely abuse human rights – is the very embodiment of what has been a hateful and inhumane immigration policy over the last two years. We hope the Supreme Court will see this policy for what it is: not only cruel, but illegal.”

Outright International

“LGBTIQ people from all over the world seek refuge in the U.S. when their lives are in danger because they expect to find safety, fairness, and dignity on U.S. shores. Yet the Trump administration, in flagrant violation of international law, is shipping them off to countries that its own human rights reporting has deemed unsafe for sexual and gender minorities. These inhumane policies must be reversed. No one should be deported to a country where they face the risk of arbitrary arrest, ill-treatment, and even death just for being who they are,” said Neela Ghoshal, senior director of law, policy, and research at Outright.

Rainbow Railroad

“The United States has a legal and moral duty not to send people to countries where they will face imminent danger. However, the administration is actively deporting LGBTQI+ people who have a credible fear of persecution or torture to third countries where they have no ties or support, and face precarious, emergency conditions that demand immediate protection,” said Oliver Williams, U.S. Policy & Advocacy Officer at Rainbow Railroad. “The United States must uphold the protection it has already granted and stop the practice of third-country removals.”

Organization for Refuge, Asylum & Migration (ORAM)

“LGBTQ+ people who seek protection in the United States place enormous trust in its laws and institutions. For those who have already been granted protection by an immigration judge, being sent to another potentially dangerous country without a meaningful opportunity to be heard is a profound betrayal of that trust,” said Steve Roth, Executive Director of ORAM – Organization for Refuge, Asylum & Migration. “It also undermines the credibility of the United States and its commitment to protecting people fleeing persecution.”

Stories of Impacted People

Thelma: Thelma, a bisexual woman, fled Ghana after her father threatened to kill her and an armed group attacked her and her girlfriend. After a U.S. immigration judge granted her protection from being returned to Ghana, she was shackled and flown to Cameroon, a country to which she has no connection. She remains in Cameroon with restrictions on her movement and has gone without adequate food or medical care, fearing for her safety and fearing she will be sent back to Ghana. (Amicus brief, p.14-15; 18; 26-28)

Thelma says inclusion in the amicus filing gives voice at the nation’s highest court to her experience: “Going through a third-country removal was one of the hardest experiences of my life, and for a long time, it felt like no one was listening. Knowing that my truth is now being offered to protect others from going through the same pain brings real meaning to what I endured. I am hoping with everything I have that this case achieves justice—not just for me, but for every person seeking safety and a chance to live freely.”

Additional Representative Stories in the Brief:

David, a bisexual man from Cameroon (p. 14)

Michael (a gay man), Samuel (a gay man) and Abina (a lesbian) from Ghana (p. 17-19; 26-28)

Alexandra and Maria, transgender women from Mexico (p. 20-21)

Farah, a gay woman from Morocco (p. 16)

Abdul, a gay man from Togo (p. 22)

What the Case is About

Federal immigration law bars the government from deporting anyone to a country where they are likely to be tortured, or persecuted because of who they are, including their sexual orientation or gender identity. That bar applies to any country, not just a person’s home country. When a U.S. immigration judge finds this risk in a refugee’s home country, the refugee is granted “withholding of removal,” a protection like asylum but weaker: it requires a higher standard of proof, yet offers no path to a green card or citizenship.

Withholding blocks return only to the home country, and prior administrations generally allowed those who received it to remain in the U.S. The Trump administration is instead deporting LGBTQ+ refugees with withholding, along with other noncitizens with final removal orders, to third countries never identified in their immigration proceedings, including to countries it knows are hostile to LGBTQ+ people. Some of those countries have sent refugees back to the very places a U.S. judge said they could not be sent.

The policy allows deportation with as little as six hours’ notice, or none at all if the receiving country has given a blanket “diplomatic assurance” that deportees will not be harmed. Under the Trump administration’s legally defective policy, refugees subject to removal from the U.S. can be deported with minimal or no notice at all to countries that have given “diplomatic assurances” that refugees it receives from the U.S. will not be harmed. In the LGBTQ+ context, such assurances are hollow and absurd. In many countries – with Cameroon, Ghana, South Sudan, Eswatini, Honduras, and El Salvador as just a few examples – criminal laws and brutal social conditions for LGBTQ+ people are well-established. Moreover, many of the countries to which the administration is sending LGBTQ+ people engage in “chain refoulement,” the practice of sending people received from the U.S. back to the countries from which they originally fled. According to Refugees International and Human Rights First, more than 25,000 people have been deported to at least 28 third countries in 2025 and 2026.

Lawsuit Background

Human Rights First, the National Immigration Litigation Alliance (NILA), and the Northwest Immigrant Rights Project (NWIRP) filed the case in March 2025 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, on behalf of a nationwide class. The Supreme Court paused the district court’s early orders in June 2025, allowing these deportations to continue while the case proceeded. In February 2026, the district court struck down the administration’s third-country removal policy, holding that people must receive meaningful notice and a meaningful opportunity to show they fear persecution or torture in a new country before being sent there. In September 2026, the First Circuit largely affirmed. The U.S. government then turned to the U.S. Supreme Court, which again paused the district court’s ruling, allowing third-country deportations to continue while it decides whether the policy violates federal immigration law, the Due Process Clause, and/or the Convention Against Torture. Amicus briefs are due today and oral argument is set for December 9, 2026.

The organizations supporting the amicus brief are committed to advocating for the rights and safety of LGBTQ+ refugees and will continue to monitor the case closely.
