### Statements of Support: Governor Maura Healey: “The Trump Administration’s ICE arrests at Massachusetts courthouses are interfering with our justice system and undermining public safety.
text:
Boston — Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell today filed a lawsuit against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) challenging its directive that instructs ICE agents to make civil arrests in state courthouses without judicial warrants, violating the Massachusetts PROTECT Act; interfering with the Commonwealth’s authority to operate its judicial system; disrupting court proceedings; causing fear, chaos, and confusion; and undermining constitutional principles and public safety.

“The Massachusetts PROTECT Act makes it illegal for ICE to conduct civil arrests in our courthouses without a judicial warrant. ICE’s intentional violation of state law has created unnecessary fear, made it more difficult to operate our courts and hold defendants accountable,” said AG Campbell. “ICE is misleading the public by suggesting that these arrests make us safer when, in fact, ICE's actions are preventing criminal cases from moving forward, denying a victim’s ability to obtain accountability, violating a defendant’s due process, and leaving open the possibility that someone facing serious criminal charges could ultimately be released from ICE custody without their criminal case ever being resolved. I, along with our district attorneys, share the goal of holding defendants accountable for crimes, yet ICE’s unlawful tactics to arrest someone for a civil immigration violation is not the same as holding them accountable for a crime.”

Today’s lawsuit claims that ICE’s policy allowing civil arrests in courthouses without a judicial warrant is unlawful, blatantly disregarding Massachusetts law, and interfering with the Commonwealth’s ability to operate its state courts. The PROTECT Act establishes clear restrictions on civil immigration arrests in its courthouses. A provision in Massachusetts’ PROTECT Act, which went into effect on November 3, explicitly prohibits civil immigration arrests in state court without judicial warrants. ICE has ignored this provision and continues to carry out arrests in Massachusetts state courts without a judicial warrant.

ICE arrested more than 600 people at Massachusetts state courthouses in 2025 and more than 500 people during the first 10 months of 2026. In just two and a half weeks since the PROTECT Act’s courthouse protections took effect, ICE has arrested at least 38 people in Massachusetts courthouses without judicial warrants.

The lawsuit specifically challenges a May 2025 ICE directive that allows arrests in state courts even when the state prohibits them. This policy was ruled unlawful and vacated by a federal court in California in June 2026, but ICE continues to carry out such arrests.

The lawsuit alleges that these arrests have had serious consequences for Massachusetts residents and their access to the court system. The lawsuit, for example, describes survivors of domestic violence who have been afraid to seek restraining orders against their abusers. In another case, a woman declined to report a rape because she feared being arrested by ICE if she had to testify in court.

ICE’s arrests are also disrupting ongoing court proceedings and causing physical property damage. On November 3, ICE arrested a defendant scheduled to appear for a criminal trial at a courthouse in Medford, preventing him from appearing in court. During enforcement activity at the same courthouse, ICE agents also damaged security barriers that must now be replaced at the state’s expense.

Under the Tenth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, the state retains sovereign authority over its court system and its administration of justice. Massachusetts exercised that authority when it enacted the PROTECT Act, establishing clear restrictions on civil immigration arrests in its courthouses. The lawsuit claims that by openly violating those legal restrictions and using state courts and resources to carry out federal immigration enforcement, ICE is unlawfully interfering with the Commonwealth’s sovereign authority.

By conducting these arrests, ICE is unlawfully using state courts and resources to carry out federal immigration enforcement. ICE agents use court schedules to identify and locate individuals, take advantage of security screenings conducted by state employees, and target individuals who have been compelled by the Commonwealth to appear in court. In doing so, ICE is using the Commonwealth’s judicial system, authority, and resources to advance federal immigration enforcement despite Massachusetts’ explicit decision, reflected in the PROTECT Act, to prohibit civil arrests in its courthouses.

With this lawsuit, AG Campbell is asking the court to block ICE’s unlawful courthouse arrest policies and prevent ICE from conducting immigration arrests at Massachusetts courthouses unless permitted by state law.

This matter is being handled by Chief of the AGO’s Office of State Trial Counsel (OSTC) Katherine Dirks, State Trial Counsel Andrew Batchelor, and Assistant Attorneys General Haily D’Ambrosio, Jak Kundl, and Alex Shura, all of OSTC.

This lawsuit is representative of AG Campbell’s broader effort to protect immigrant communities from unlawful, aggressive, and cruel immigration policies. Earlier this month, AG Campbell joined other attorneys general in sending a letter to Congressional leaders encouraging them to hold ICE accountable for immigration enforcement abuses.

###

Statements of Support:

Governor Maura Healey: “The Trump Administration’s ICE arrests at Massachusetts courthouses are interfering with our justice system and undermining public safety. When people are afraid to go to court, victims are less likely to report crimes, survivors are less likely to seek protection, and our communities are less safe. That’s why I signed the PROTECT Act. We expect ICE and all federal agents to follow Massachusetts law. I want to thank Attorney General Campbell for filing this lawsuit to hold the Trump Administration accountable, enforce Massachusetts law and protect the safety and rights of our residents.”

Senate President Karen E. Spilka (D-Ashland): “The Attorney General is taking an important step to uphold the rule of law and defend Massachusetts’ sovereignty. The Legislature overwhelmingly enacted the Protect Act this year to keep federal immigration officers out of our courthouses, schools, and hospitals. Unfortunately, ICE appears to be willfully ignoring the law as they continue to sow fear throughout our communities. I deeply appreciate Attorney General Campbell for standing up for civil order and the rights of our residents.”

House Speaker Ronald J. Mariano (D-Quincy): “When ICE arrests witnesses and defendants at courthouses, they threaten the Commonwealth’s ability to uphold its laws. That’s why the PROTECT Act prohibits ICE from carrying out warrantless arrests at courthouses in Massachusetts — a reflection of the Legislature’s commitment to doing all that we can to ensure that the Trump Administration cannot undermine the pursuit of justice. I’m grateful to Attorney General Campbell for taking action to hold ICE accountable, and to the Black and Latino Legislative Caucus for their continued leadership on this issue.”

Middlesex County District Attorney Marian Ryan: “ICE’s flagrant disregard of the PROTECT Act is a direct attack on public safety in Massachusetts. Through their actions, ICE is not only violating state law, but also undermining my, and every other District Attorney’s Office’s, ability to enforce our laws, protect the public safety and hold defendants accountable for their alleged criminal conduct. ICE should not be empowered to decide whether a victim has the opportunity to be heard or whether a defendant is afforded their legal right to a fair trial. Removing a defendant does not resolve the question of their culpability, put safety conditions in place or appropriately punish those who might be convicted of violating the criminal law of the Commonwealth. When ICE arrests defendants on courthouse property in the midst of a criminal case, the District Attorney’s Office loses all control over where they are going, whether they will be released on bail by an immigration court, whether conditions such as stay aways or surrender weapons are in place and whether a victim has any information needed to create a safety plan. ICE has created the mistaken impression that there are immediate removals and no possibility of reentry. They disregard a defendant’s ability to engage in a terror campaign against a victim from a different location. They do this while striking fear in victims and witnesses which may prevent them from seeking help from our courts. This lawsuit is a necessary step in both defending the safety of every person in this Commonwealth and in holding ICE accountable for their unlawful actions.”

Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden: “Our courthouses have always stood as centers of justice and havens of safety for crime victims and witnesses. Today, too many consider them places of fear for their own persecution. When victims and witnesses refuse to appear in court or their perpetrators are snatched away, accountability, justice and public safety all suffer. This is the true legacy of the Trump administration’s ICE policies. We’re here today in an effort to stop more offenders from going unprosecuted because of this chilling effect on victims, witnesses and our entire criminal legal system.”

State Senator Cindy F. Friedman (D-Arlington): “Every resident of Massachusetts deserves equal protection under both the United States Constitution and the Massachusetts Constitution, regardless of where they were born, their race, religion, or immigration status. Free and safe access to our courts is a cornerstone of our system of justice, and the PROTECT Act reflects the Commonwealth’s commitment to safeguarding that access for all who rely on our courts. ICE's continued practice of conducting civil immigration arrests in Massachusetts courthouses without judicial warrants directly undermines those protections, interferes with the administration of justice, and disregards duly enacted Massachusetts law. I support the actions of Attorney General Campbell and thank her for taking this important step to defend the Commonwealth’s authority, uphold the rule of law, and ensure that every person can access our courts without fear. When constitutional rights and the integrity of our justice system are threatened, Massachusetts has both the responsibility and the resolve to act.”

State Representative Andy Vargas (D-Haverhill), Chair of the Massachusetts Black and Latino Caucus: “Our courts exist to deliver justice. There is no justice when a victim is too afraid to walk into a courthouse, or when a defendant is whisked away before they can be held accountable in our courts. The PROTECT Act is clear: no civil arrests in our courthouses without a judicial warrant. We’re grateful to Attorney General Campbell for enforcing Massachusetts law and the Commonwealth’s right to run its own courts.”

State Senator Pavel Payano (D-Lawrence): “No one should have to fear being detained simply for walking into a school or courthouse. We passed the PROTECT Act to safeguard fundamental rights, and those protections mean nothing if they are not upheld. I stand with Attorney General Campbell in demanding accountability because the rule of law must apply to everyone, including those entrusted with enforcing it.”

State Representative Christopher Hendricks (D-New Bedford): “I am grateful for Attorney General Andrea Campbell for bringing this lawsuit against ICE. This action reiterates that the people of the Commonwealth will not tolerate a rogue federal agency that is blatantly and sadistically disregarding our state laws and U.S. Constitution. The policy of sending under-trained, unfit agents to terrorize our Massachusetts communities was wholeheartedly rejected on November 3rd. This lawsuit sends a clear message: that we in the Commonwealth - led by AG Campbell - are only getting started when it comes to holding this fascist agency and its under-qualified employees accountable.”

State Senator Lydia Edwards (D-Boston): “I am grateful to Attorney General Campbell for standing up for our residents, defending Massachusetts law, and making clear that no administration is above the law. The PROTECT Act is a constitutional law that balances public safety with due process. It requires federal agents to obtain a judicial warrant before pursuing an individual in our courthouses, ensuring transparency and protecting the rights of everyone who enters our court system. ICE’s refusal to follow the law and its deliberate disregard for local protections are intentional attempts to intimidate the people of this Commonwealth. We will not back down. In fact, we will remain even more steadfast. I hope our federal delegation sees the havoc ICE is creating in our court systems as yet another reason why this agency must be defunded.”

State Senator Michael J. Rodrigues (D-Westport): “The Legislature passed the PROTECT Act to safeguard civil rights and due process for all Massachusetts residents, and this lawsuit makes clear that we will not permit overzealous federal agents to disregard the Constitution. A strong component of the PROTECT Act was to empower the Attorney General to hold ICE agents accountable for their actions against individuals, and especially families, for their recent unlawful activity in Medford, and in my district in Fall River. I commend Attorney General Campbell for her actions, and I hope this lawsuit sends a clear message to ICE and their agents that the Commonwealth will continue to exercise its authority to operate its own judicial system.”

Boston Mayor Michelle Wu: “Even after voters overwhelmingly rejected President Trump’s policies of chaos and violence, we must continue to stand against ICE’s dangerous and unlawful conduct, including courthouse arrests. We thank AG Campbell and her team for defending our laws and protecting the safety of Bostonians and all Massachusetts residents.”

Chelsea City Manager Fidel Maltez: “The constant presence of immigration enforcement agents at the Chelsea District Court has traumatized our residents and created an atmosphere of fear that is deeply affecting our community. Residents are missing court appointments, avoiding our downtown, and are afraid to report crimes or seek help. Our courthouse should be a place where everyone feels safe, respected, and supported, regardless of immigration status. We are deeply grateful to Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell for taking this bold stand to protect our immigrant communities and hold federal agents accountable. Every Chelsea resident deserves to feel safe, welcome, and protected in our city.”

Lynn Mayor Jared Nicholson: “Lynn has felt the direct impact of the federal government’s harmful overreach in immigration enforcement. Their dangerous tactics have trampled due process and upended lives. We staunchly support Attorney General Campbell’s unyielding commitment to stand up for the civil rights of our residents.”

La Colaborativa President and CEO Gladys Vega: “It’s time for ICE to be held accountable for its illegal arrests in our courthouses that have created fear and uncertainty among our immigrant communities. I am grateful to Attorney General Campbell for filing this lawsuit and standing up against the federal government’s overreach in our justice system.”

Latinos Unidos en Massachusetts (LUMA) Founder and Executive Director Lucy Pineda: “Our team at Latinos Unidos en Massachusetts (LUMA) has witnessed ten ICE arrests in Massachusetts courthouses. We have spoken out about these injustices, and we condemn these actions. No one should have to choose between showing up for a court hearing and risking separation from their family. Everyone in Massachusetts deserves to walk into a courthouse without fear. We stand with Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell in the lawsuit she is bringing today against ICE, and we thank her for defending the protections of the PROTECT Act and for standing with community organizations like LUMA as we support families affected by these arrests. What we have witnessed in our courthouses is unacceptable. Our families deserve to be heard, to seek justice, and to return home safely.”

LUCE Immigrant Justice Network: “Every immigrant in Massachusetts deserves to access our courts and navigate legal proceedings without fear of being detained or separated from their family. We fought for the PROTECT Act to protect that right. Our families are discouraged and terrified to show up to court when they see others detained at required hearings. Since the courthouse protections took effect, LUCE has documented eyewitness accounts, verified reports of ICE detentions, and brought those reports to Attorney General Andrea Campbell’s office. This lawsuit is a step toward the accountability our communities have demanded. Protections are only meaningful when enforced. We stand with immigrant families and will keep organizing with our neighbors until everyone in Massachusetts can seek justice without fear. ICE out of our courts. ICE out of Massachusetts.”

Brazilian Worker Center Executive Director Lenita Reason: “Our communities have witnessed the fear and harm caused by immigration enforcement firsthand. This lawsuit is an important step toward accountability and ensuring that the rights, dignity, and safety of immigrant communities are protected.”

Massachusetts Immigrant and Refugee Advocacy (MIRA) Coalition Chief of Staff Sarang Sekhavat: “While Massachusetts has put in place safeguards for our immigrant communities, we continue to see violations of our laws at the hands of the Trump administration. Our courthouses should be places where people have access to justice, not places where our communities fear to go. MIRA remains fully committed to fighting for permanent protections, providing direct community resources, and ensuring our Commonwealth remains safe and welcoming for everyone.”

American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Massachusetts Executive Director Carol Rose: “The Commonwealth of Massachusetts has the right and the obligation to operate a state court system that ensures access to justice for everyone. ICE’s policy of making civil immigration arrests in state courthouses — in clear disregard of Massachusetts law and sovereign authority— undermines that fundamental principle and erodes public confidence in the legal system. The ACLU of Massachusetts is proud to stand with Attorney General Campbell as she defends the state’s authority over its courts and stands up for equitable access to the legal system.”

Greater Boston Legal Services (GBLS) Executive Director Jacquelynne J. Bowman: “Our clients come to court to stand up for their rights in so many different ways, whether it is to seek protection from abuse, fight for earned wages, or keep their family together. They should not have to fear being arrested by ICE simply for showing up. Massachusetts passed the PROTECT Act to ensure that everyone can access our courts and seek justice without fear. Now we need to make sure the law is enforced and that everyone can exercise their rights in court.”

Lawyers for Civil Rights (LCR) Staff Attorney Brooke Simone: “We thank Attorney General Campbell for filing today’s lawsuit to enforce the PROTECT Act. Her action sends a clear message that no agency, including ICE, is above the law. Access to justice cannot depend on immigration status, and everyone deserves to know that a courthouse is a safe place, as the law requires.”

Massachusetts Law Reform Institute (MLRI) Executive Director Georgia Katsoulomitis: “The PROTECT Act was passed to safeguard our courthouses as places where everyone who lives here can pursue justice. ICE is not above the law and we applaud Attorney General Campbell for taking action to hold ICE accountable and protect access to justice.”

Attorney General Bonta is committed to standing up for California’s immigrant communities and fighting for affordable housing.
Earlier this year, Attorney General Bonta co-led a coalition in filing a comment letter opposing HUD’s proposed rule change while it was still in its early stages.
In filing this lawsuit, California Attorney General Bonta, New York Attorney General Letitia James, and Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell are joined by the attorneys general of Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawai’i, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia, as well as the governor of Pennsylvania.
text:
OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today co-led a coalition of 21 attorneys general and the governor of Pennsylvania in filing a lawsuit challenging a final rule by the U.S Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) that prohibits mixed-status families from living in public housing and from receiving other federal housing assistance, including Housing Choice Vouchers (Section 8) and project-based rental assistance. Mixed-status families are households composed of at least one individual eligible to qualify for federal housing assistance and one or more individuals who are ineligible due to their immigration status. The rule would also impose new verification requirements that will subject U.S. citizens and elderly noncitizens to more burdensome verification and documentation processes that will potentially displace low-income citizens and elderly people from subsidized housing. In the lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, Attorney General Bonta and the coalition assert that the rule exceeds HUD’s statutory authority and is arbitrary and capricious in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

“With families already struggling to afford basic necessities, the last thing our economy needs is a rule that would exacerbate the already existing housing crisis, and force citizens and noncitizens alike out of their homes and communities,” said Attorney General Bonta. “This new Trump Administration rule would put tens of thousands of Californians at risk of eviction and saddle states with the financial burdens associated with the forced displacement of entire families, including those with U.S. citizen children. With today’s lawsuit, we are fighting to block these unlawful changes in court and once again standing up for all who rely on federal assistance to ensure they are not stripped of their homes. Families should not have to choose between remaining together and keeping a roof over their heads.”

For decades, HUD regulations under Section 214 of the Housing and Community Development Act have permitted mixed-status families to receive federal housing assistance that is reduced or prorated according to the number of ineligible people living in the household to intentionally allow U.S. citizens and eligible noncitizens to receive assistance if they are part of a mixed-status home.

Under HUD’s new final rule, these households would face eviction from subsidized housing if even one member of the household is ineligible because of their immigration status. Among other things, the final rule imposes new proof of eligibility requirements for U.S. citizens and elderly people receiving and applying for federal housing assistance. The final rule also requires public housing authorities and private landlords participating in HUD programs to notify participants and applicants of their obligation to immediately notify the U.S. Department of Homeland Security if they determine any member of a household is undocumented.

In California alone, this rule would impact over 7,000 mixed-status households, potentially displacing thousands of U.S. citizen children from their homes and imposing financial and administrative burdens on state and local agencies forced to fill in the gaps for families who will lose their homes as a result of the rule’s implementation.

In today’s lawsuit, Attorney General Bonta and the coalition argue that:

The rule exceeds HUD’s statutory authority in violation of the APA because it unlawfully interferes with Section 214. Various provisions of the rule violate the protections Congress expressly authorized in Section 214. For example, Section 214 provides for prorated housing assistance for mixed-status families, gives public housing authorities discretion as to whether to verify the immigration status of every person in a household, and exempts eligible noncitizens 62 years old or older from the statute’s additional documentation requirements.

The rule is arbitrary and capricious in violation of the APA. HUD failed to provide a justified explanation for the policy changes and relied on factors Congress did not intend it to consider. HUD also failed to adequately consider Congress’s purposes underlying Section 214, how the rule would harm the States and housing providers who relied on the prior longstanding policy, and reasonable policy alternatives.

Attorney General Bonta is committed to standing up for California’s immigrant communities and fighting for affordable housing. Earlier this year, Attorney General Bonta co-led a coalition in filing a comment letter opposing HUD’s proposed rule change while it was still in its early stages. In September, Attorney General Bonta also secured a win in a lawsuit challenging unlawful conditions the Trump Administration attempted to place on Fair Housing Assistance Program funding which would have limited state and local agencies’ ability to enforce their fair housing laws.

In filing this lawsuit, California Attorney General Bonta, New York Attorney General Letitia James, and Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell are joined by the attorneys general of Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawai’i, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia, as well as the governor of Pennsylvania.

text:
Dr. James J. Zogby ©

President

Arab American Institute

The results of this year’s elections made it clear that Arab Americans are making a difference as an organized and empowered community. The first two Arab Americans of Egyptian descent have just been elected to federal posts—one to the Senate, the other to Congress; two of Lebanese descent are newly elected to Congress; another Arab American of Lebanese descent has been elected as a State Treasurer; and a host of others from Palestinian, Lebanese, Sudanese, Somali, Syrian, and Yemeni backgrounds ran and won federal, state and local positions across the US.

These victories were supported by Arab Americans nationwide. They raised millions of dollars to support our candidates, worked to assist their campaigns, and voted in their cities in record numbers to make these historic wins possible. As important was the extent to which the Arab American voters demonstrated an impressive level of convergence on the issues that were at stake this year. Of course, the top concerns shared by most in the community were corruption and the economy. But between two-thirds and three-quarters of Arab Americans were motivated by the genocide in Gaza and the devastation of Lebanon, and the impact of the anti-Arab and anti-Muslim bigotry on display in various campaigns, as well as efforts to silence free speech and debate on America’s unconditional support for Israel.

Building an Arab American community has never been easy. From the beginning we faced a number of internal challenges that were a function of our incredible diversity. We shared a common heritage and a pride in our history and culture, but we came from many countries and different religious traditions. These differences have sometimes been compounded by the fact that there have been separate waves of immigrants from Arabic-speaking countries, with each having its own distinct characteristics.

Throughout our history there have been those who sought to divide us by emphasizing differences. This was especially intense during the Lebanese civil war or the period around the Arab Spring. And while those who aggravated these internal fissures may have found some temporary success, none have been able to permanently disrupt the ongoing effort to build a community. This has especially been the case for younger Arab Americans, who have displayed both passion and determination in their advocacy and their penchant for finding common ground.

As I’ve noted, this effort to find unity wasn’t always easy for those who had come to America fleeing wars and civil strife. But as Rev. Jesse Jackson cautioned us back in the 1980s: “Do not import the divisions of the Middle East. Instead, take what you’ve learned here in America, and export it to the Middle East.” This is what we did.

During the past five decades, when we created the National Association of Arab Americans, the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee, the network of Arab American social service centers in cities across the country, the Arab American Institute, or the Arab America Foundation, the logic was the same. We put aside differences and joined together to: advocate for our common concerns, combat defamation, discrimination, and hate crimes defamation, and to protect our civil rights and liberties. In the process, we worked to promote and protect our shared culture and heritage, provided needed support for new immigrants and guaranteed access to services, and we politically empowered our community to play our rightful role in American life.

One of the negative consequences of our growth and increased capacity was that, as we developed as a community, we were confronted by external challenges represented by those who didn’t want Arab Americans to gain recognition or support. In too many instances, they worked to exclude us from politics and devoted resources and their considerable influence to have us marginalized or to defame us in our efforts. Beginning in the 1980s, we were forced to deal with groups that worked to have Arab Americans excluded from foreign policy or human rights coalitions, fired from political campaigns, or have our contributions rejected by candidates who were pressured to return “Arab money” from Arab American donors. These exclusionary tactics began with ominous warnings of “petrodollar influence,” and later morphed into the danger of association with terrorism, and then finally into naked anti-Arab and anti-Muslim bigotry. We met these challenges by further organizing and empowering our constituency, demonstrating our capacity to win, and building alliances with other groups who shared our values and concerns.

While challenges remain, seeing Arab Americans win elections, and the leadership role we are now playing in: institutions combating hate crimes, advocating for changes in US foreign policy, fighting for immigration reform, and gaining recognition for the importance of Arab contributions to human history—it’s clear we are facing down and overcoming the internal and external obstacles we have been forced to confront.

text:
A father and daughter detained by masked immigration officers on an airport jet bridge in Seattle were travelling to attend a family baptism ceremony in California, their lawyer stated on Sunday.

Bystanders boarding the Alaska Airlines flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday captured mobile phone footage of the pair being restrained by officers wearing unmarked jackets and khaki trousers. The resulting videos were widely shared across social media platforms.

The video recordings show officials grappling with an individual on the floor, causing significant delays to the flight bound for Los Angeles.

In an official statement, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) confirmed that its officers apprehended Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, a Mexican national who had overstayed his visa "in violation of our nation’s laws."

ICE noted that during the confrontation, another passenger "hurled hot coffee on the officers." That individual, identified as Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was also determined to be residing in the US unlawfully from Mexico after overstaying her visa, and she could face charges for assaulting a federal officer.

According to defence lawyer Olia Catala the father and daughter have lived in the US since 2015 and are currently seeking asylum. She emphasised that neither possesses a criminal record.

Mejia, in her mid-20s, had married a U.S. citizen and filed paperwork for adjustment of her status, the attorney said. Mejia's husband was accompanying Mejia and her father when they were detained Saturday, Catala added. The husband was not detained, the attorney said.

“They’ve done everything correctly, and these are educated people," Catala said of the father and daughter. "She went to college, to university, she worked for a nonprofit. No criminal history (for) any of them. So it’s just heartbreaking.”

Both were being held at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Catala said.

She said Mejia was carrying a cup of coffee when the confrontation occurred.

“When somebody’s charging at you, you’re going to drop a cup of coffee," Catala said.

“It was just a lot of commotion, and honestly, if somebody is running at you or charging at you and they’re not wearing a uniform, you don’t know who they are," Catala said. "There was a lot of panic, chaos, not knowing what’s going on.”

Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people it says have overstayed visas.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns “directly with the appropriate authorities.”

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would “engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred.”

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE’s tactics were “deeply un-American” and called for the agency’s abolition.

“The video is horrific and it is chilling,” Ferguson said at a news conference Saturday with labor leaders and local elected officials.

title: Global Perspective: Five EU countries plan to set up deportation center in Rwanda
description:
Five members of the European Union are working on a deal with Rwanda to send rejected asylum seekers to the east African country.
Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands announced on Nov. 16, that they will soon begin negotiating the terms of such an agreement with Kigali.
Whether this plan for a deportation hub will even come to fruition is not clear, either.
Once a deal is made between Rwanda and the five European countries, human rights organizations will likely take it to court.
Only then will the future of European immigration reform be made clearer.
text:
Five members of the European Union are working on a deal with Rwanda to send rejected asylum seekers to the east African country. Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands announced on Nov. 16, that they will soon begin negotiating the terms of such an agreement with Kigali.

The current proposal is to send about 100 people at a time to the hub, specifically unmarried men who were not granted asylum but cannot return to their home countries.

The five European countries want to send a message to prospective migrants that they will be cracking down on undocumented immigration, and they hope it will aid in solving the issue of people being trafficked into Europe, according to U.S. News. If the countries deem the program a success, it can be expanded to more hubs.

Support for far-right parties has been growing across the continent. In September, the German far-right party, Alternative for Germany (AfD), won the parliamentary election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. Some governments have decided to tighten immigration laws in hopes of garnering support from the rightwing to stay in power.

These plans follow a decision made in early October by the Council of the EU that created a more standardized system for deporting people living in the EU who do not have the legal right to stay there. One provision of this agreement allows the formation of “return hubs” in non-EU countries as long as a deal is made with the non-EU country and the non-EU country “respects international human rights standards.”

Several human rights groups do not believe that Rwanda meets this criterion. Amnesty International reported that Kigali has supported the March 23 (M23) movement that has caused hundreds of thousands of people to flee their homes in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and has killed a large number of people. The organization has also reported that the Rwandan government suppresses workers’ rights and people’s right to protest.

As this program is still in the works, several crucial factors are not yet known, such as where deportees would be housed within Rwanda. Kigali says that deportees will be given the opportunity to stay and work in the country and will be aided in the integration process through programs such as language courses. What benefits Rwanda will receive from the deal is also yet to be determined.

Whether this plan for a deportation hub will even come to fruition is not clear, either. A similar agreement between the United Kingdom and Rwanda was struck down by the UK’s Supreme Court in 2023, and the Supreme Court demanded the policymakers to reform the deal due to Rwanda’s designation as an unsafe country for immigrants.

Once a deal is made between Rwanda and the five European countries, human rights organizations will likely take it to court. Only then will the future of European immigration reform be made clearer.

text:
Traffic stops have become an increasingly popular strategy for immigration enforcement during the second Trump administration, and a Banner review of court documents found that approach is playing out across Maryland.

Federal immigration agents have in some cases ordered or dragged passengers out of vehicles and arrested them without explanation, the documents show.

“We’re not talking about a traffic stop. We’re really talking about an ambush,” said Shana Khader, legal director of We Are CASA, an immigrant rights group in Maryland.

The way U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement uses traffic stops gained national attention this summer after agents fatally shot two men during stops in Texas and Maine over the course of six days in July. The agency suspended the use of vehicle stops after the killings, but President Donald Trump quickly reversed course, writing in a social media post, “we CANNOT give up one of I.C.E.’s most important and effective Crime Fighting tools, THE TRAFFIC STOP!”

To get a fuller picture of how ICE operates in Maryland, The Banner analyzed more than 500 habeas corpus petitions filed in federal court between November 2025 and August 2026. Habeas corpus is a foundational legal concept that allows anyone to challenge their detention in court, even if they are not citizens.

The Banner’s review of habeas petitions found repeated allegations of people being chased and surrounded by unmarked vehicles even though they hadn’t committed any traffic violations. The petitions said that officers sometimes yanked open car doors, struck windows, or forcibly pulled people out of their vehicles before asking for identification.

Habeas petitions offer only the detained person’s perspective of an immigration arrest, but they are filed under penalty of perjury. They also don’t cover every arrest in Maryland — only those in which the detained person was able to hire a lawyer — but they point toward trends. Among the 500 petitions:

More than one-third of those arrested were driving at the time.

Roughly one in four were driving to or from work.

More than a dozen were parents transporting their children to and from school.

In traffic stop cases where a country of origin was specified, all but one driver was from a Latin American country.

The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, didn’t answer questions from The Banner about its use of traffic stop arrests and reports of aggressive behavior in Maryland.

Immigration attorneys and law enforcement experts say aggressive traffic stops are dangerous for everyone involved and, if made without probable cause, may not hold up in court.

In one such case, a Glen Burnie man named Jose was driving with his wife and daughter on a muggy August morning when he noticed an SUV tailing his car.

He decided to turn off his route to see if the SUV followed. Suddenly, police lights started flashing and four vehicles swooped in to block the car, he told The Banner through a translator.

The Banner agreed not to use Jose’s full name because he feared retaliation for talking about his case.

An officer approached the car and told Jose he was a police officer doing a “routine stop.” But when the officer turned around, Jose saw “ICE” emblazoned across his back.

The officers ordered Jose out of the car and handcuffed him. Jose turned to his distraught daughter, sitting in the back seat.

“Don’t worry, my love,” he said. “These things will happen, and today it’s come for me.”

Jose spent three weeks in ICE detention before a judge found that his arrest was unlawful and ordered him released. Originally from El Salvador, Jose entered the U.S. without authorization in 2002 and had never been arrested, according to his habeas petition. People who entered the country illegally have rights, including protection against improper warrantless arrests and illegal detention.

Chief U.S. District Judge George L. Russell III wrote on Aug. 28 that the ICE officers who pulled Jose over did not meet the “probable cause” standard required to arrest him without a warrant and conducted an “unlawful warrantless arrest.”

Cases like Jose’s and hundreds of others detailed in court records are at the center of a federal class action lawsuit over warrantless arrests in Maryland. The lawsuit, brought in September by We Are CASA and four Maryland residents, alleges “a sweeping pattern of warrantless arrests targeting Brown and Black Marylanders” dating to January 2025.

Officers use “‘reasonable suspicion’ to investigate immigration status and probable cause to make arrests consistent with the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution,” an unnamed DHS spokesperson said in an email responding to questions about the lawsuit. “The Supreme Court has already vindicated us on these practices.”

The lawsuit includes firsthand accounts of ICE traffic stops.

David Aguirre, a 25-year-old Howard County man, was driving to work with his cousin in January when the car traveling ahead of them suddenly braked on the highway, he said. Another car then slammed into his rear bumper. A third car came alongside them, leaving him no choice but to stop on the road.

Officers jumped out of their cars and started yelling. When Aguirre and his cousin didn’t immediately respond, agents smashed the car windows, opened doors and dragged them out, according to his declaration. Aguirre said the agents did not tell them why they were stopped or why they were being arrested. Only after agents drove Aguirre behind a nearby school to put cuffs on his legs did they ask to see his driver’s license, he said.

Aguirre’s lawyers declined to disclose his immigration status, but court documents show his cousin is a U.S. citizen.

The agents then drove around with him in the car and looked for more people to arrest, searching license plates on a computer and pulling over only those who appeared to be Latino, Aguirre said in his declaration.

Jose said something similar: After the ICE agents arrested him in Glen Burnie, they drove around looking for other people to stop.

“Any person that looked Hispanic, they would stop and ask for papers,” Jose said.

A DHS spokesperson wrote in an email that “what makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is if they are illegally in the U.S. —NOT their skin color, race, or ethnicity.”

In another case from the CASA lawsuit, a 40-year-old construction worker from Silver Spring said he was driving his boss’s Toyota Tacoma to work when agents in three unmarked vehicles surrounded the truck, pulled him out by his arms, forced him to the ground and put a leg on his head.

Partially handcuffed and in pain, J.M.R., as he is described in court documents, attempted to stand up. According to his account in the lawsuit, agents tased him and drove him to a fire station because he needed medical attention, and eventually to a hospital to remove a taser barb still stuck in his chest.

These traffic stop tactics can quickly escalate, said Emily Gunston, a former deputy chief in the U.S. Department of Justice’s special litigation section, which conducted civil investigations of police departments. Drivers could think they’re being abducted or robbed, escalating a traffic stop.

Ramming and blocking cars can also be hazardous to both officers and bystanders, Gunston said, so most local police departments have policies on when officers can initiate these maneuvers and allow them only in response to serious crimes.

Eric Balliet, who served as the head of ICE’s Integrity Investigations Division and retired in August 2024, said that under certain circumstances, and often as a last resort, there’s a place for aggressive traffic maneuvers. But officers are supposed to take steps to mitigate public safety risks.

Balliet said some of what he’s seeing from ICE street enforcement is now “unrecognizable” compared with what he was taught and flouts general policing principles, like identifying oneself or asking a subject for identification.

“You have people wearing masks, driving unmarked vehicles, in a non-uniformed presence with aggressive tactics,” he said. “The recipe for disaster ... It goes through the roof.”

title: Recent Changes in Immigration and Fiscal Policy - Fullerton Observer
description:
As these developments unfold, the financial implications for undocumented workers and the associated enforcement costs remain a critical area of scrutiny, raising questions about who bears the burden of these sweeping policy changes.
What Undocumented Immigrants Pay Many people believe undocumented immigrants pay no taxes, but many do.
The Congressional Budget Office estimates that about half of undocumented immigrants pay federal, state or local taxes.
What Services Cost The fiscal impact of undocumented immigrants is complex and contested.
What Enforcement Costs Any account of costs also has to include what the government spends to find, detain and deport undocumented immigrants.
text:
In a shift in immigration policy, the 2025 budget reconciliation law, dubbed the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” has introduced stringent new restrictions on benefits for certain lawfully present immigrants, specifically targeting some refugees and asylees. While undocumented immigrants were already prohibited from accessing these programs, the new law intensifies existing barriers. Starting October 1, 2026, eligibility for Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) will become even stricter for lawfully present immigrants, and the federal matching rate for emergency-only Medicaid in states that have expanded Medicaid will be reduced.

Compounding concerns, in July 2025, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) took a controversial step by reinterpreting the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act (PRWORA). This reinterpretation expanded the list of “federal public benefits” to include 13 additional programs, such as Head Start, community health centers, and Title X family planning services. The move drew immediate backlash, leading over 20 states to file lawsuits against the HHS.

On September 21, 2026, a federal judge ruled against the HHS directive, citing the agency’s failure to adhere to the required notice-and-comment process. While this ruling temporarily halts the controversial changes, it leaves the door open for HHS to pursue a new rule that follows proper procedures. The administration has already proposed an alternative Head Start rule that includes immigration-status requirements, suggesting that the debate over access to vital services for vulnerable populations is far from over.

As these developments unfold, the financial implications for undocumented workers and the associated enforcement costs remain a critical area of scrutiny, raising questions about who bears the burden of these sweeping policy changes.

What Undocumented Immigrants Pay

Many people believe undocumented immigrants pay no taxes, but many do. They pay sales and excise taxes, and they pay property taxes either directly or through their rent. Many also pay income and payroll taxes, using Individual Taxpayer Identification Numbers (ITINs) or through paycheck withholding.

The Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP), a progressive think tank, estimates that undocumented immigrants paid about $96.7 billion in federal, state and local taxes in 2022. The federal government received $59.4 billion of that and state and local governments $37.3 billion. That works out to about $8,889 per undocumented person.

ITEP also reports that more than a third of those payments were payroll taxes for programs these workers cannot use: $25.7 billion for Social Security, $6.4 billion for Medicare and $1.8 billion for unemployment insurance in 2022. The Penn Wharton Budget Model at the University of Pennsylvania estimates that unauthorized workers paid about $24 billion in Social Security taxes in 2024, although they cannot collect benefits.

The Congressional Budget Office estimates that about half of undocumented immigrants pay federal, state or local taxes. Their payroll taxes help Social Security: the Social Security Administration estimated that unauthorized workers added a net $12 billion to the trust funds in 2010. Penn Wharton estimates that deporting these workers would raise Social Security deficits by $133 billion over 10 years and drain the trust fund about six months sooner.

According to Pew Research Center, a record 9.7 million unauthorized immigrants were in the U.S. labor force in 2023. They are concentrated in certain industries. They made up about 5% of all workers but 17% of agricultural workers and 13% of construction workers, and they were a large share of workers in crop production, private household work and landscaping (2014 figures).

What Services Cost

The fiscal impact of undocumented immigrants is complex and contested. Governments spend money on these workers and their families, mainly on K-12 education, emergency health care and law enforcement, and most of that cost falls on state and local taxpayers. The Congressional Budget Office has reported that most studies find the taxes paid by unauthorized immigrants do not cover the cost of the state and local services they use.

By nonpartisan estimates, undocumented immigrants are likely a net cost to state and local governments, mainly because of K-12 education, but no one has produced a reliable national dollar figure. At the federal level, the evidence leans toward a net gain or a small effect, because they pay payroll and other taxes while being barred from most federal benefits.

What Enforcement Costs

Any account of costs also has to include what the government spends to find, detain and deport undocumented immigrants. That spending has grown dramatically since 2025.

– Baseline: ICE’s total funding in fiscal year 2024 was about $9.9 billion, according to the Congressional Research Service. In fiscal year 2025, its annual appropriation for detention was about $3.8 billion, according to the Government Accountability Office (GAO).

– One Big Beautiful Bill Act (July 2025): The law gave ICE $45 billion for detention capacity through fiscal year 2029, plus about $29.9 billion for personnel, transportation and other deportation operations. Its total for immigration and border enforcement across all agencies is about $170 billion.

– Secure America Act (June 2026): This law added roughly $70 billion more, including $38.6 billion for ICE, $26 billion for Customs and Border Protection and $5 billion for other Homeland Security enforcement, available through fiscal year 2029.

Together, the two laws give ICE alone about $113 billion in new multi-year funding, on top of its regular annual budget. For comparison, ITEP’s estimate of ALL taxes paid by undocumented immigrants in one year is $96.7 billion, and Penn Wharton’s estimate of their yearly Social Security contributions is about $24 billion.

Cost per deportation: ICE puts the average cost to arrest, detain and remove one person at no less than $17,121. Penn Wharton reviewed outside studies that put the figure between $30,591 and $109,880, with an average of $70,236. The main reason estimates differ is how long people are held, because detention averaged about $152 per person per day as of September 2025. DHS reported about 527,000 deportations by late October 2025. At ICE’s own per-person figure, that is roughly $9 billion. At Penn Wharton’s average, it is closer to $37 billion.

These figures do not include the revenue that disappears when a taxpayer is deported. Penn Wharton estimates that permanently deporting the unauthorized population would cost an additional $900 billion over 10 years, even after counting the new 2025 funding.

What Litigation Costs

Lawsuits over deportation policy are another cost, but they are much harder to measure. No agency publishes a total.

– Legal fees paid out: When courts rule that the government acted unlawfully, taxpayers can end up paying the other side’s lawyers. Courthouse News identified 97 habeas corpus cases in 2026 where courts ordered the government to pay legal fees for immigrants it had illegally detained, totaling more than $1.1 million. Bloomberg Law reported in July 2026 that the government could owe millions more in fees as hundreds of lawsuits against administration policies reach final judgments.

– Government lawyers: The Justice Department’s Office of Immigration Litigation has seen its workload rise 63% while losing nearly 80 attorneys, according to internal documents reported by The Hill.

– Fines and collection suits: The government is also suing. DHS issued 65,101 civil fines totaling more than $36 billion between January 2025 and mid-March 2026, and the Justice Department had filed more than 50 lawsuits to collect them, according to Bloomberg Law. The fines face their own court challenges. How much of that $36 billion will actually be collected is unknown.

title: U.S. Citizen From Texas Deported to Mexico Before Feds Conceded His Legal Status
description:
Morales García said he was transferred through five different facilities before signing the deportation paperwork.
U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons wrote in the filing that Morales García "is a dual citizen of the United States and Mexico."
'No U.S. Citizen Should Face the Threat of Detention' His attorney did not let the admission pass quietly.
"No U.S. citizen — dual citizen or not — should face the threat of detention," Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch said, calling on the government to "underline it right there" in its own court document.

text:
An HVAC Worker on His Way to a Job

On April 3, 2026, Morales García was seated in a pickup truck alongside coworkers, heading toward an air-conditioning installation job, when a Texas Department of Public Safety trooper pulled the vehicle over near Fredericksburg for a window tint violation. Morales García, who does not speak English, said he repeatedly told authorities that he was born in Denver and had his birth certificate and Social Security card at his Austin home. He said he offered to provide the documents. The officer called immigration enforcement anyway.

Morales García had entered the United States in January 2025, crossing at El Paso with his birth certificate, and had spent the following months working in Austin. He was booked into the Gillespie County Jail within hours of the stop and transferred to U.S. Border Patrol custody. Morales García said he was transferred through five different facilities before signing the deportation paperwork.

Four Days, Five Facilities, and Removal at the Border

By April 7, he had been removed to Mexico through the Harlingen, Texas port of entry after spending five days in detention, according to federal court filings (though he initially recalled being flown out of the country in an early interview with The Texas Tribune). He later said he signed the removal paperwork not because he accepted the government's characterization of his status, but because he feared an indefinite detention and wanted to reach his wife and newborn daughter, who live in Mexico. He was removed from the country where he was born.

Family Blocked, Signature Allegedly Coerced

The lawsuit Morales García's attorneys filed in May 2026 against ICE, the Texas Department of Public Safety, and the Gillespie County Sheriff's Office describes more than a clerical failure. His legal team alleges that agents pressured him into signing a statement in which he acknowledged entering the country without authorization — a claim he has never accepted. His family sought to establish his citizenship while he was detained, but his relatives were unable to secure his release before he was deported.

His legal team refused to let the case rest. Working across two countries, his attorneys assembled certified hospital records, sworn witness affidavits, and his official Colorado birth certificate, then placed them before the federal court. The effort produced results: on August 30, 2026, the DOJ reached an agreement with his counsel allowing him to re-enter the United States while his lawsuit moved forward. His attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, drove to Laredo to meet him at the border.

The Government Reverses Seven Months of Denial

For months, the Department of Homeland Security had maintained that Morales García had entered the country illegally, pointing to Mexican records that listed a Mexican birthplace and to statements agents attributed to him during detention processing — statements his lawyers say were the product of coercion. The November 20 motion marks the collapse of that position. U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons wrote in the filing that Morales García "is a dual citizen of the United States and Mexico."

'No U.S. Citizen Should Face the Threat of Detention'

His attorney did not let the admission pass quietly. "No U.S. citizen — dual citizen or not — should face the threat of detention," Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch said, calling on the government to "underline it right there" in its own court document.

The admission, however, came as part of the government's motion to dismiss the lawsuit. Federal attorneys argue that the government is immune from the claims involving immigration enforcement, while Morales García's legal team maintains that he was pressured into signing the removal documents.

The Morales García case sits inside a larger reckoning. A ProPublica investigation documented more than 170 U.S. citizens detained by immigration agents during the first nine months of President Trump's second term, with accounts of physical abuse, prolonged custody, and documentation dismissed outright. ProPublica's investigation documented more than 170 U.S. citizens detained by immigration agents during the first nine months of President Donald Trump's second term but did not identify anyone who had been deported. Morales García's case is now an acknowledged example of a U.S. citizen being deported under the current administration.

What the Judge Must Now Decide

Judge Pitman has not yet ruled on the government's motion to dismiss. If the immunity argument succeeds, Morales García would leave court without any legal remedy for an ordeal that covered nearly eight months, spanned two countries, and forced him away from the Austin life he had been building. He is seeking an unspecified amount in damages.

His attorneys have framed the case as a constitutional test with broad implications: whether U.S. citizens can be detained and deported through immigration enforcement procedures without a meaningful opportunity to establish their citizenship and challenge their removal.

title: El Paso High Student, Family Released from ICE Detention but Still Face Deportation
description:
The statement indicates that the family remains subject to immigration enforcement despite being allowed to return to El Paso.
The family’s immigration attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, said that they were legally processing their immigration status when they were detained.
El Paso High Students Rallied for Classmate Michell’s detention drew attention from classmates and teachers at El Paso High School, where she is a senior, a member of the Tigerettes dance team and a cosmetology student at the El Paso Independent School District’s Center for Career and Technology Education.
On November 17th, students and community members gathered at El Paso High School to demand her release.

text:
EL PASO, Tx., November 23, 2026: An El Paso High School senior and her family have returned home after nearly a month in federal immigration detention, but their legal battle remains unresolved as U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials say the family could still be deported.

Michell Germán, 17, her 11-year-old sister Paola and their parents, Pablo Jose Guerrero-Pimentel and Dolores Emilia Zarraga-Colina, arrived at the El Paso International Airport on Friday evening, after being released from the Dilley Immigration Processing Center in South Texas.

The family, originally from Venezuela, had been detained since October 22, when ICE agents arrested the parents and their daughters during an enforcement operation in El Paso. Their release followed public demonstrations, congressional appeals and a letter signed by 57 current and incoming Texas House Democrats demanding that federal officials explain why the two children remained detained beyond 20-days that a federal court settlement governing the detention of migrant minors advices as a limit for minors.

On Saturday, ICE confirmed the family’s release to KVIA-TV but said the four had been placed under its Alternatives to Detention program pending removal from the United States.

“They have been released from ICE custody on Alternatives to Detention until ICE removes them from the United States,” the agency said in a statement reported by KVIA.

The statement indicates that the family remains subject to immigration enforcement despite being allowed to return to El Paso.

ICE and Attorney Dispute Family’s Immigration Status

ICE maintains that the family entered the United States illegally on August 12, 2022, and was subsequently released into the country during the Biden administration. In its statement, ICE said the parents acknowledged that they lacked documents authorizing them to remain permanently in the United States.

The family’s immigration attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, said that they were legally processing their immigration status when they were detained. According to Lincoln-Goldfinch, the family presented themselves to Border Patrol in August 2022, were paroled into the United States and have been pursuing asylum through immigration court. She has said the parents hold work permits, have no criminal records and were complying with the immigration process when they were detained.

Immigration parole and employment authorization do not necessarily confer permanent legal status. An individual may be authorized to work while pursuing an immigration claim without having received permission to remain permanently in the country. The family therefore faces continued uncertainty over the outcome of its immigration case.

ICE has not publicly explained why it decided to release the family after nearly a month in detention.

Texas Lawmakers Demanded Release

State Representative Vince Perez, (D-77), announced on Friday that 57 Texas House Democrats, 44 sitting members and 13 members-elect, had signed a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Acting ICE Director David Venturella seeking the family’s release.

The letter questioned why Michell and Paola remained detained after November 11th, 20 days since their arrest. The lawmakers cited the federal Flores settlement, which establishes standards for the detention and treatment of immigrant children.

Although the settlement requires the government to release children without unnecessary delay, the application of a 20-day detention benchmark has been the subject of federal litigation.

The lawmakers had asked ICE to provide a written explanation by December 1 if the family remained detained, including the results of individual reviews of the sisters’ cases and whether either child had been determined to present a flight risk or danger to the community.

“Nothing in the public record says either girl is a flight risk or a danger,” the letter stated.

The lawmakers also requested medical care for Paola and her mother, confidential attorney access and assurances that the family would remain together. The release occurred the same day the state lawmakers released their letter.

El Paso High Students Rallied for Classmate

Michell’s detention drew attention from classmates and teachers at El Paso High School, where she is a senior, a member of the Tigerettes dance team and a cosmetology student at the El Paso Independent School District’s Center for Career and Technology Education. She also works part time and volunteers with older adults, according to Perez’s office.

In September, Michell was named Lady-in-Waiting during the school’s homecoming activities. Her classmates carried her photograph onto the football field during Senior Night on November 6 because she remained in detention.

On November 17th, students and community members gathered at El Paso High School to demand her release. The rally included representatives of the Border Network for Human Rights, Perez, Lincoln-Goldfinch and former U.S. Representative Beto O’Rourke. The students said Michell’s absence had affected the school community and prevented her from participating in senior-year activities and dance preparations.

The family’s attorney also raised concerns about conditions at Dilley, reporting that Paola had lost weight because she was having difficulty eating the food provided at the facility. She alleged that the girls’ mother was not receiving adequate medical treatment.

Congress Member Intervened

The Texas lawmakers’ letter follows a separate November 17th appeal led by U.S. Rep. Veronica Escobar and signed by other Democratic members of Congress and members-elect. The congressional letter described the family’s pending asylum case and urged immigration officials to permit them to continue their proceedings from El Paso. U.S. Representative Joaquin Castro also advocated for the family.

Following their release, Escobar welcomed the news and said families should not have to endure detention while separated from their communities.

The congressional appeals also raised broader concerns about the detention of children at Dilley, a facility that reopened in 2025 as the Trump administration expanded immigration enforcement and family detention. The facility is operated by private prison contractor CoreCivic.

Pending Detention Legislation

Although the family’s release resolved the immediate detention dispute, Perez is pursuing legislation addressing the operation and oversight of civil immigration detention facilities in Texas. He has filed three bills for the legislative session beginning January 12, 2027.

House Bill 736 would establish civil liability for detention facility operators in cases involving injuries, deaths and failures to maintain or disclose custody records.

House Bill 738 would direct the Texas Health and Human Services Commission to establish minimum standards for civil detention facilities.

House Bill 818 would prohibit state agencies and local governments from entering, renewing or expanding agreements involving civil immigration detention.

Immigration Proceedings to Continue

The family’s release allows Michell and Paola to return to school and resume their lives in El Paso, but it does not resolve their immigration status. According to ICE, the family remains under its Alternatives to Detention program, which allows certain individuals to live outside detention facilities while remaining subject to immigration supervision and enforcement.

The program can involve reporting requirements or electronic monitoring, depending on the conditions imposed in an individual case. ICE has not publicly detailed the specific supervision requirements placed on the family. The family’s attorney has said they are pursuing asylum, a form of protection available to people who meet federal requirements concerning persecution in their home countries. The outcome of their immigration case will determine whether the family can remain in the United States.

Cover photograph: Michelle Germán, center, her mother on the right, and sister, Paola at the El Paso High School Homecoming Court presentation in September via Rep. Joaquin Castro, Twitter, November 4, 2026.

title: A Pathway Towards the Rohingya's Legal Inclusion - Just Security
authors: Preeti Chemiti, Mark Jessup, David S. Rubenstein, Kateryna Rashevska, Amichai Cohen, Yuval Shany, Michael Schmitt
description:
On Nov. 19, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) delivered a landmark decision finding Myanmar responsible for committing genocide against the Rohingya.
But for the Rohingya community members at the heart of the case, a core question remains: what does this decision mean for their future?
