text:
On Nov. 19, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) delivered a landmark decision finding Myanmar responsible for committing genocide against the Rohingya. Nearly a decade after the Myanmar military’s campaign drove hundreds of thousands of Rohingya from their homes, the United Nations’ principal judicial organ has formally recognized these atrocities as genocide. For a community that has spent generations seeking recognition and accountability, the Court’s final, unappealable judgment marks the culmination of seven years of litigation.

Five thousand miles away, in Bangladesh’s crowded refugee camps, news of the judgment was met with cheers. But for the Rohingya community members at the heart of the case, a core question remains: what does this decision mean for their future? The judgment establishes Myanmar’s responsibility under international law, but realizing the remedies it orders will require years of legal and political work. Understanding the judgment itself presents immediate challenges. Issued in English and French, the decision will reach many Rohingya through broadcasters, social media networks, and a handful of English-speaking community members who can translate for others. Neither the public statement issued by The Gambia’s president nor its legal counsel has identified a plan for making the judgment accessible to Rohingya communities in their own languages, and it is unclear what dissemination frameworks may be under development. Each handoff risks distorting the Court’s findings or leaving the Rohingya without access to those findings altogether.

This is the first judgment in which the ICJ has found a state responsible for committing genocide. Now is the time to invest in the Rohingya community’s own capacity and vision for the decision’s implementation. Justice is an intergenerational undertaking that is ultimately driven by those affected. Such efforts require not only making the Court’s findings accessible, but also seriously investing in Rohingya-led advocacy, community organizing, and platforms for survivors to articulate their own priorities and be brought into the processes for implementing them. Without it, the ICJ’s decision will fall short of achieving the full meaning of justice.

Lost in Translation

The barriers to understanding the Court’s decisions are not new in this case. When the Court issued its provisional measures order in January 2020 and ordered Myanmar to prevent acts of genocide, it generated considerable hope among Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh. In Kutupalong, crowds gathered around televisions to watch live coverage. Others followed on their phones. Roughly 740,000 had fled the Myanmar military’s genocidal operations in 2017, and the world’s highest court had just declared emergency orders to protect those who remained. A community leader described the ruling as “some sort of justice.” Another predicted that the Rohingya could go home by the end of the year.

It is now 2026. More than 1.6 million Rohingya remain displaced from Myanmar – more than twice the approximately 630,000 that remain in the country.

That contrast between the Court’s announcements and the realities of ongoing displacement raises fundamental questions about how legal developments are understood by the communities they concern. I saw this firsthand while teaching Rohingya refugees in Kutupalong, which is now the world’s largest refugee camp. I taught daily university classes to Rohingya women from 2023 to 2024, and while my students regularly discussed their personal experiences with violence and displacement, not once did ICJ proceedings become a subject of classroom discussion. Just as importantly, even if my students had asked me about the ICJ case, I had no accessible curriculum materials in Burmese or Rohingya at the time through which to introduce the decision or explain its legal significance (some have since been issued in Burmese). I was teaching in a refugee camp that had expanded dramatically as a direct consequence of the events before the Court, yet in a classroom of English-speaking university students, the proceedings remained distant.

This week’s judgment must not be similarly difficult to access. This time, the international community’s responsibility extends beyond making the Court’s findings accessible. It must also equip Rohingya communities with the knowledge and resources to shape what comes next.

Narrowing the Distance

Effectively conveying the Court’s judgment confronts several obstacles. The first is simply getting the decision to communities thousands of miles away. Its dissemination depends on a chain of intermediaries, from international news organizations to informal community networks. For Rohingya communities in Bangladesh, that process may begin with information reported in English, relayed through Burmese, and eventually brought to Rohingya speakers through in-person conversations.

This challenge is not just one of literal translation. It also lies in translating the decision’s legal meaning into accessible concepts for those not trained in the law. Because Rohingya is predominantly an oral language, written translations are unlikely to reach enough community members. The technical language of a lengthy judicial opinion can also be difficult to navigate, even for those with legal training. Concepts such as provisional measures, state responsibility, reparations, and guarantees of non-repetition do not necessarily have straightforward equivalents in everyday conversation. Thus, communicating what the Court has decided requires more than rendering the ruling’s language into Rohingya; it requires explaining the legal significance of its findings in terms that people can understand, discuss, and act upon in the years to come.

Some will also face an additional barrier: the restrictive information landscape through which the judgment must travel. Myanmar ranks 166th out of 180 countries in Reporters Without Borders’ 2026 press freedom index, and for Rohingya still inside Myanmar, news access is particularly precarious. Rakhine State has experienced severe restrictions on communications as well as media and Internet shutdowns, making independent reporting extraordinarily difficult.

Even where information does circulate, its reliability is questionable at best given how rife misinformation and hate speech are within the country and on Burmese social media platforms. Overcoming this complex information environment will require coordinated efforts from the outset.

Shaping Justice for the Future

Getting reliable information to the Rohingya is only the beginning. Treating the decision as the culmination of accountability risks obscuring the difficult legal and political work that remains.

For Rohingya who have waited for years or decades to return home, the Court’s order for safe and dignified return may understandably morph into an assumption that the Court has granted them immediate relief. But a judicial finding of responsibility cannot force Myanmar’s compliance. Myanmar’s military authorities have repeatedly resisted international demands for accountability, and the Arakan Army now controls much of the Rohingya’s homeland in Rakhine State. The United Nations Security Council, which may enforce the Court’s decision, has also largely abdicated its responsibility on Myanmar.

An order recognizing the right to return does not make that return safe or possible. Because legal victories must be paired with political change, it is imperative that the Rohingya play a central role in influencing what accountability looks like and how it is pursued.

From Understanding to Designing: Centering Rohingya Voices

Although Rohingya survivors have testified and advocates have contributed to sustained accountability campaigns, they were not parties before the Court. Their experiences entered the courtroom through the arguments presented by others.

The judgment creates an opportunity to begin addressing that imbalance. In the weeks to come, the Rohingya community will need time to absorb the findings, ask questions, and consider what the decision means for their futures. This process should not depend exclusively on explanations prepared by international lawyers or organizations. Rohingya leaders and community organizations should have the resources to examine the judgment, identify its implications for their own priorities, and participate in shaping the political and legal efforts that follow.

And then the hard work begins. History tells us that justice is only sustained when it is shaped by affected communities. In South Africa and Argentina, imperfect but significant efforts to confront past atrocities hinged on years of public engagement and community participation. Neither experience offers a simple blueprint, but both exemplify how lasting justice must be locally driven and well-resourced to have any chance of a meaningful impact.

The Court’s decision should be viewed through this lens – as the beginning of a commitment that must endure for years, indeed decades, and be shaped by Rohingya communities themselves. That requires more than a series of translated summaries or community information sessions. It requires sustained investment in Rohingya-led organizations, legal education, documentation initiatives, and platforms through which survivors can articulate their priorities. These investments should build on, rather than duplicate, the work of existing organizations. Rohingya organizations like the Arakan Rohingya National Organization (ARNO) have already developed networks for publicizing atrocities and engaging international organizations like universities. Whether the immediate concern is safe return, guaranteed citizenship, property restitution, or accountability for continuing abuses, Rohingya communities must be able to shape the demands made in their name.

A Pathway for Investing in Justice

In reserving questions concerning the nature, form, and amount of reparations for a “subsequent phase of proceedings,” the Court emphasized that their determination must be consistent with the interests of the Rohingya. Thursday’s decision is a legal landmark, but it also lays bare the pathway for the sorts of key investments needed to bring the Rohingya into their own processes for justice.

First, The Gambia, the intervening states, United Nations agencies, and humanitarian organizations should support developing accessible explanations of the judgment in partnership with Rohingya-led groups. The Court cannot be expected to manage individual expectations for every community affected by its decisions, but others can. The International Criminal Court’s outreach program, which explains the Court’s scope and limitations in local languages, offers a useful institutional example. Although the ICJ operates under a different mandate, a modest first step is to immediately prepare a plain-language summary of its judgment and coordinate audio translations into Rohingya and Burmese. To ensure widespread dissemination, the actors named above should provide resources to Rohingya-led groups to develop accessible explanations, organize community discussions, and address questions about the judgment’s implications.

Materials must also be honest about what the judgment can accomplish. The Court has ordered Myanmar to provide reparations, including compensation and measures facilitating the safe, voluntary, and dignified return of displaced Rohingya. Yet the amount and modalities of compensation remain to be determined, and the Court declined to order Myanmar to grant full and equal citizenship to all Rohingya. Communicating these distinctions is not an exercise in tempering the Rohingya community’s hopes. It is about granting the Rohingya the ability to shape their pathway to justice.

With such understanding, the decision can be a starting point for long-term engagement. Sustained investment means equipping Rohingya-led organizations with the resources and expertise to lead these conversations themselves. It also means investing in educational materials and curricula that allow future generations of Rohingya to understand their history and the legal processes shaping their futures. Rohingya representatives should determine which questions need answering and how information is shared, rather than simply receiving explanations prepared elsewhere.

The Court’s 2020 provisional measures order generated enormous questions. Now, the Court has answered, but the distance between the Peace Palace and Kutupalong cannot be bridged by a judicial declaration alone. The international community should not wait until Myanmar’s two-year reporting deadline expires to invest in the Rohingya’s capacity to engage with the next phase of proceedings. Community organizing and survivor-led documentation must begin now so that Rohingya priorities can inform ongoing and future deliberations over reparations. The Rohingya should not simply be the people in whose name justice is pursued. They must have the means to shape what justice delivers.

text:

On election day, voters sent Democrats into office, up and down the ballot, in typically blue strongholds and in places where it had been hard to imagine Republicans losing power. As citizens cast their votes, many were reckoning with the most visible harms caused by this administration’s immigration policies, including mass raids and unprecedented violence — and the damage this inflicts on children.

In the coming months, these candidates — both at the national level and in local communities — will have to confront the consequences of ICE’s unrestrained, violent tactics. For local leaders, that should include recognizing and supporting the people who have been doing the vital work of sustaining immigrant families all along. One place to start is in public schools.

In the U.S., all students have the legal right to attend school, regardless of their or their parents’ immigration status. As a result, schools have long been vital — although imperfect — spaces for welcoming immigrant families as they lay down roots.

But it isn’t the law that makes schools welcoming. It is the everyday work of educators. Teachers have shown extraordinary dedication as their students suffer under Trump’s aggressive deportation regime. But there are others — secretaries, family liaisons, and other support staff — who also care for immigrant families, even though their invaluable labor is often hidden from the public eye.

In research for my book, Holding On to Home: Immigrant Women and the Promise of Sanctuary, I witnessed how these employees, many of whom were immigrants themselves, were essential to families as they adjusted to a new nation. They connected parents to food pantries, provided guidance about managing exploitative landlords and reiterated legal rights. They arranged transportation, enrolled children in afterschool programs and decoded English learner education.

And they listened: to stories of the difficult journeys families made to get to the U.S. safely, to their fears of deportation, to worries about kin in their countries of origin.

Yet the poor working conditions for these employees speaks to the societal value we place on women’s labor, especially when that labor entails immigrant women caring for other immigrant women.

In the small East Coast city I studied, for instance, family liaisons — school-based positions intended to bridge home and school — were capped at 19 hours, just below the threshold for benefits. The women who filled these jobs worked without district-issued cell phones or computers. They squeezed into closets or begged to borrow offices so they didn’t have to hold sensitive conversations in the middle of the hallway. They never worked just 19 hours a week.

A few years later, the city converted the family liaisons positions to full-time roles, a major win. But a liaison with seven years of experience made just $43,000 – 40% less than a teacher with similar experience, and barely enough to live in a city where the average salary hovered around $125,000 and housing costs are among the highest in the nation.

City council and school committee members have the power to fund these positions — or not. While the fates of long-term city employees may seem mundane in comparison to the existential threat of unrestrained immigration enforcement, their practices transform schools into places that protect and incorporate immigrant families.

Democrats are heading into power. They will need to address how this presidential administration’s decision to slash funds for the most basic necessities put enormous pressure on local governments to make cuts. One long-time district family liaison I know has already been laid off. For nearly three decades, she conducted home visits for immigrant mothers with new babies, weaving the families into a web of resources. To her close colleagues, she was an essential source of information and best practices. But her work wasn’t deemed valuable to the decisionmakers.

The labor of women like this liaison defies easy categorization. It is rarely public, unfolding instead in crowded living rooms, on front porches, in corners of school hallways. All of this makes it harder to recognize how this work safeguards the critical role schools play for immigrant families — and for our society as a whole.

In this election, voters chose politicians who vocally oppose Trump’s destructive immigration agenda. Now the new leaders at every level of government need to act. It might not be the most obvious place to start, but providing adequate funding for family liaisons and similar positions in schools and communities is a concrete, actionable way to ensure immigrant families have what they need to thrive. These women’s labor strengthens schools, preserves the fabric of society and makes real the promise of American education.

text:
A video circulating on social media appears to show federal immigration enforcement activity in Oakland on Sunday, prompting sharp criticism from Mayor Barbara Lee.

ICE activity in Oakland

What the video shows:

According to Lee, onlookers spotted six federal vehicles in the area of 87th Avenue and E Street and began taking pictures of the apparent U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity.

Lee accused federal agents of escalating the situation by deploying smoke bombs and chemical spray while pushing people away from the scene. The video was posted by @StopICEnet.

"ICE is not wanted in Oakland, the Oakland Police Department does not cooperate with ICE, and I am profoundly grateful to our residents for standing together to protect our neighbors," the mayor said in a statement.

The Alameda County Immigration Legal and Education Partnership, which is a rapid-response network of immigrant advocates, reviewed video footage and is in contact with the families of people who made contact with ICE to ensure they are connected with legal support, the mayor's office said.

ACILEP said at least one person was reportedly arrested by ICE. Another person was reportedly arrested on Saturday in Dublin, the nonprofit said.

"We are witnessing a disturbing and unacceptable surge in aggressive ICE operations," said Lee on social media. "Federal agents have no business terrorizing our neighborhoods or bringing violence into spaces where Oakland families live and work."

The mayor also stated that the city has been in contact with the families of two people who were arrested by federal agents during the encounter.

ICE statement

KTVU has reached out to ICE for a statement regarding the incident, but the agency has not yet responded.

In a prior statement, however, about respecting ICE-free zones and arrests at the Santa Rita Jail, the Department of Homeland Security said "ICE enforces the law 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, in all 50 states, including in California. No sanctuary politicians are going to stop that."
